home.what_youll_learn: The completed course will produce a small GPT implementation, a reproducible pretraining run with held-out loss and text samples, and two adaptations: a text classifier and an instruction-following model. A final report will compare the stages and state the limits of a small local run. The goal is to understand the pipeline, not to match a production LLM.
home.description:
::: {.callout-note}
This is a published course plan. The chapter pages describe intended lessons and labs; no completed instructional work is recorded yet.
:::

This course follows the core progression of Sebastian Raschka's [LLMs-from-scratch repository](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch). It is for Python programmers who want to examine each stage of a decoder-only language model in PyTorch: preparing text, computing causal attention, assembling GPT, training it, and adapting it to downstream tasks.

**Design rule:** Keep one traceable model and data lineage, so each new capability can be explained by a specific change to the inputs, architecture, objective, or evaluation.
home.hardware_access:
**Tools:** A Python and PyTorch environment, local storage for text and checkpoints, and a way to run notebooks. The source [setup guide](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/tree/main/setup) is a dependency reference. The default path is a small local experiment. A GPU, downloaded pretrained weights, and external model-based scoring are optional extensions.

The repository supplies reference code and supplementary experiments. These notebooks will develop their own explanations, checks, and comparisons. The [overview](00-overview.html) defines the shared artifact and evaluation plan.
home.knowledge: **Knowledge:** Comfortable Python, tensor shapes, gradients, and a basic neural-network training loop. PyTorch experience helps; the source repository offers an [introductory appendix](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/tree/main/appendix-A).

home.what_youll_learn: Complete a compact experiment report comparing a pretrained baseline with inference-time scaling, self-refinement, reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, and a distilled student. The report will record the model and prompt setup, task set, scoring method, compute used, quality, and latency. It should distinguish a working educational reproduction from claims about frontier-scale training.
home.description:
This course follows the main progression in [Sebastian Raschka's reasoning-from-scratch repository](https://github.com/rasbt/reasoning-from-scratch). It starts with a pretrained Qwen3 model and adds reasoning methods in stages: first by spending more computation at inference time, then by training with verifiable rewards, and finally by distilling the resulting behavior into a smaller model.

The notebooks will explain the mechanism behind each method and test its effect under a stated evaluation and compute budget. The course does not build or pretrain the base language model itself; that is a separate subject covered by the companion [LLMs-from-scratch repository](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch).

**Design rule:** Treat improved reasoning as an empirical claim: define correctness, measure quality and cost, and keep the evaluation fixed when comparing methods.

## Source and scope

The implementation sequence is adapted from [the official code repository](https://github.com/rasbt/reasoning-from-scratch), whose main chapters cover pretrained generation, evaluation, inference-time scaling, self-refinement, reinforcement learning, GRPO improvements, and distillation. This course will explain and compare those ideas in Watchtower notebooks; it will not reproduce the book's full code or imply that a small educational run matches frontier-scale systems.
home.hardware_access:
**Tools.** A Python environment with PyTorch and access to the model weights and example data used in the source repository. A CPU is enough to explore generation, evaluation, and smaller inference experiments. A GPU is recommended for reproducing the longer self-refinement and reinforcement-learning runs; results depend on the selected model, hardware, and settings.

The default path uses a compact model and small evaluation slices to make the mechanics inspectable. Scale up only after the prompt, scoring, and resource contract are working. The source repository includes optional optimized inference, larger-model, batching, and chat-interface material; those are extensions, not prerequisites for the core path.
home.knowledge: **Knowledge.** Python, basic PyTorch, neural-network training concepts, and familiarity with prompts and text generation. The course will introduce reinforcement-learning vocabulary as it is needed.

home.what_youll_learn: By the end, you will have a reproducible detector report and a local Jev-like decision model built by adapting a small pretrained LLM. Use PyTorch for the decision head and training loop, Hugging Face Transformers for the pretrained backbone and tokenizer, and PEFT for LoRA when useful. Train across text-classification tasks, expose Choice, Noul, and Score operations, and measure transfer to a task excluded from fine-tuning. The capstone develops a simple candidate scorer into an attention-based decision head. Unsloth's open implementation provides a concrete architecture reference and an optional performance comparison.
home.description:
This course builds an end-to-end **text classification system** using AI-written-text detection as its main case study. It follows the [ai-detector-from-scratch repository](https://github.com/rasbt/ai-detector-from-scratch) from data construction through evaluation and local inference, and adds a historical path from bag-of-words models to neural sequence classifiers, transformers, and general-purpose decision APIs.

**Design rule:** treat every score as evidence about a model on a defined data distribution, not as proof about an individual text or a promise of generalization to new tasks.

## Learning path

Begin with the classification problem, dataset audit, grouped splits, and TF–IDF baseline. The neural chapters connect model families to the decision-head derivation and supervised LLM adaptation. Evaluation and delivery cover calibration, resource use, and inference contracts before the final project combines them. The chapter table on this page follows the course outline.
home.hardware_access:
**Tooling.** Use the detector repository's documented Python environment, `uv`, Git, and a notebook environment. The neural project adds PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers; PEFT supplies LoRA adapters. Pin their versions in the project environment. Start with the lightweight logistic-regression path on a CPU. Adapting a pretrained LLM is most practical on a GPU; a tiny randomly initialized model can check tensor shapes and training logic on a CPU. Recreating the full detector corpus can require external model APIs or a local Ollama service.

For a quick local detector run, use the repository's published dataset and logistic-regression model artifact. Read each stage README before running it and record the artifact version. The detector's standard path can fine-tune selected transformer models using the published dataset. The capstone uses public task datasets to adapt a small pretrained decoder and train a decision head with an explicit PyTorch loop. A head-only warm-up checks the pipeline before LoRA or full fine-tuning updates the backbone. It requires no hosted Jev account. Full reproduction of the detector corpus starts with licensed human text and generates AI and AI-assisted text; that path uses substantially more compute and may make external API calls.
home.knowledge:
### Starting with the baseline

Basic Python, arrays/data frames, train/validation/test splits, and binary classification are assumed. Familiarity with precision, recall, calibration, and logistic regression helps; Chapters 01 and 07 establish the key terms. Start with the TF–IDF/logistic-regression path to learn the data and evaluation workflow.

### Preparing to train an LLM decision model

Be comfortable reading PyTorch tensor shapes, batching examples, defining an `nn.Module`, and running a training loop with automatic differentiation and an optimizer. Basic vectors, dot products, and matrix multiplication help explain how the model produces scores. Connect logits, softmax probabilities, and cross-entropy loss, and understand how tokenization, padding, and pooling turn variable-length texts into model inputs and representations.

For the attention-based head, prepare with **span pooling**, which combines token representations belonging to a question or option; **cross-attention**, which lets question or option representations retrieve input evidence; and self-attention, residual connections, and layer normalization. The [attention chapter](../llms-from-scratch/03-attention.html) and [LoRA chapter](../llms-from-scratch/08-lora.html) in Build LLMs from Scratch provide companion reading. Chapter 06 connects these concepts to the decision-model objective; Chapter 07 covers held-out calibration.

### What the implementation uses

The [worked fine-tuning chapter](06-finetuning.html) displays the complete PyTorch candidate scorer, joint attention head, loss, and optimizer loop, with equations and executed checks. The companion `projects/text-decisions` package supplies a runnable trainer for Qwen and ModernBERT, head warm-up, full fine-tuning or LoRA, and saved-model inference. Unsloth and AnyJev provide optional architecture and performance comparisons; their source code is not required reading.
home.references: **Reading sources.** The [detector repository](https://github.com/rasbt/ai-detector-from-scratch) supplies the running case study. [Language Models for Text Classification: From Bag-of-Words to Jev](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/classifier-history-and-jev) motivates the architecture history and simple candidate scorer. [Unsloth's decision-model guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/train-your-own-decision-model-with-unsloth) provides an LLM adaptation and joint-head reference; [AnyJev](https://github.com/nokia-applied-research/AnyJev) supplies a label-token readout comparison. Jev's proprietary internals remain outside the evidence available here. The course model is an independent educational implementation.

home.what_youll_learn:
You will be able to write an architecture brief, scope a change before implementation, enforce a dependency rule, test whether a guardrail detects a violation, and record the evidence for a review. The worked example provides a complete Python CLI with `add`, `checkin`, `list`, and versioned JSON `export`, backed by interchangeable memory and SQLite repositories.

This is a case study with practice tasks. The downloadable Habit Tracker project is the final implementation, so the journals describe earlier stages rather than a sequence of incomplete starter checkouts. The example demonstrates the mechanisms on a small codebase; it does not establish time savings or success at large scale.
home.description:
AI coding agents can produce code faster than its owner can build a mental model of it. This course follows the Habit Tracker (`habit-tracker`) project from pure domain logic to persistence, use cases, a command-line interface, and a deliberately injected architecture violation. The build journals show the plans, mistakes, review findings, and corrections that made each change inspectable.

**Design rule:** The human owns the architecture, and the important rules have executable checks.

## How to read the course

Start with the process overview, then follow the ordered course path. Each numbered chapter retains one build journal and adds a practice task. Read the historical plan before inspecting the final code, and use the review and lessons to compare intention with evidence. Historical test counts describe the original build stages.

## Run the worked example

[Download the Habit Tracker project](source/ai-assisted-project.zip) and open the included `ai-assisted/toy-project/` directory. In the Watchtower checkout, use this equivalent path from the repository root:

```sh
cd projects/ai-assisted/toy-project
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t . -v
python3 tools/audit.py
python3 -m habits --help
```

The CLI stores its database in `habits.sqlite3` in the working directory. Set `HABITS_DB` to a scratch database when experimenting, so each exercise can use independent data. The code, tests, and original journals live together under `projects/ai-assisted/`.

## Before you change the example

Read the [Habit Tracker architecture brief](source/toy-project/ARCHITECTURE.md), the [Habit Tracker agent rules](source/toy-project/AGENTS.md), and the [journal template](source/toy-project/journal/README.md). Perform practice changes in your own copy, write a new scoped journal entry, and keep deliberate violations in a separate scratch copy. The original project includes product decisions that are still open, including future-dated check-ins.

The [original whitepaper](source/WHITEPAPER.md) explains the process. The [original Git timeline](source/git-history.txt) preserves the build's commit identities and file statistics; those commits belong to the source repository, rather than Watchtower's Git history.
home.hardware_access: **Tools.** Python 3.9 or later, a terminal, and a text editor. The Habit Tracker project and its `unittest` suite use only the standard library. An AI coding agent is optional for trying the workflow; reading and running the case study requires no model API, paid service, or GPU.
home.knowledge: **Knowledge.** Basic Python functions, classes, exceptions, imports, and tests. Familiarity with Git diffs helps when reviewing the record. No machine-learning knowledge is required.

home.what_youll_learn: Implement a bounded tool-calling loop; score complete agent runs; compare lexical, dense, hybrid, and reranked retrieval; assemble permission-filtered evidence; validate structured answers and citations; compare prompt versions and iterative retrieval on fixed cases; report correctness, abstention, latency, tokens, and cost separately.
home.description:
Teach the application mechanisms around a pretrained language model: retrieval, tool execution, context selection, structured responses, and evaluation. Build small components whose contribution can be measured against a simple baseline. Model architecture, pretraining, and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning belong to the existing companion courses.

## The running project

A small document assistant over synthetic support notes and technical documents. Each chapter supplies a bounded fixture and can be implemented independently. An optional cumulative implementation combines ingestion, search, generation, and read-only tools behind explicit interfaces. Keep deterministic offline checks separate from live model experiments. Service deployment is developed in Deploy and Operate AI Systems.

## Practice and assessment

Every lab records its reproducing command, fixture and model versions, baseline, measured result, and one limitation. The final report separates retrieval misses, unsupported claims, wrong answers, unnecessary abstentions, permission leaks, and resource use. Compare changes on frozen development/test cases; reserve stronger statistical claims for results with suitable repeated runs and uncertainty estimates. Improvements, regressions, and inconclusive comparisons are all valid findings.
home.knowledge: Python programmers familiar with functions, classes, JSON, tests, and basic model inference. The AI-assisted development course supplies architecture and review habits; Build LLMs from Scratch supplies tokenizer and generation intuition. Neither completed pretraining nor a GPU is required. Early labs use local fixtures and recorded model responses; a small open model or hosted API is an optional measured extension.
home.references: Adapted from the reviewed 100-weeks-of-ai Foundations guides 8–9, 12–16, 20, 25, 27, 30–31 and AI Applications guides 1, 3, 14–15, 20–22. Source mappings are retained in chapter internal notes. Verify maintained library APIs and pin their versions when authoring executable lessons. Companion reading: Build LLMs from Scratch, Build Text Classifiers from Scratch, and AI-Assisted Development: A Process That Scales.

planned:
  chapters:
  - content: '## What the learner will build


      Teach the application mechanisms around a pretrained language model: retrieval,
      tool execution, context selection, structured responses, and evaluation. Build
      small components whose contribution can be measured against a simple baseline.
      Model architecture, pretraining, and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning belong
      to the existing companion courses.


      A small document assistant over synthetic support notes and technical documents.
      Each chapter supplies a bounded fixture and can be implemented independently.
      An optional cumulative implementation combines ingestion, search, generation,
      and read-only tools behind explicit interfaces. Keep deterministic offline checks
      separate from live model experiments. Service deployment is developed in Deploy
      and Operate AI Systems.


      The course consists of independently reproducible labs. Concepts accumulate,
      but another chapter''s source tree is not a hidden prerequisite. A supplied
      fixture or a small implementation can stand in for an earlier component. Combining
      the results into one portfolio is optional. Each lab''s command contract, interfaces
      and tests specify work to be implemented; this saved brief does not claim that
      code or benchmark results already exist.


      ## Prerequisites and execution paths


      Python programmers familiar with functions, classes, JSON, tests, and basic
      model inference. The AI-assisted development course supplies architecture and
      review habits; Build LLMs from Scratch supplies tokenizer and generation intuition.
      Neither completed pretraining nor a GPU is required. Early labs use local fixtures
      and recorded model responses; a small open model or hosted API is an optional
      measured extension.


      A small deterministic fixture is the first path for examining control flow and
      checking a boundary. A substantive measurement uses the actual component being
      studied: a model for model behavior, a database for locking and persistence,
      an inference server for scheduling, or a real provisioned environment for deployment.
      Reports state the path used. Recorded responses cannot establish the quality
      or resource behavior of a model that was never run. Costs in source examples
      are planning assumptions; record actual versions, hardware, usage and spending
      before making a comparison.


      ## Follow one question through the assistant


      A user asks which replacement part fits a support ticket. The request identifies
      the caller and a case ID. A lexical retriever first finds exact part numbers;
      an embedding retriever supplies paraphrased candidates. Candidate IDs refer
      to immutable document revisions and chunk offsets. Fusion combines rankings,
      and an optional reranker scores query/candidate pairs. Only authorized evidence
      is placed in the model request. The generated answer contains individual claims,
      cited source IDs and an abstention indicator. A tool request goes through an
      ordinary dispatcher before an observation enters the next turn.


      The same request can fail at different boundaries. A relevant document may be
      absent from candidates, its supporting passage may be lost during chunking or
      context fitting, the generator may invent a claim despite having evidence, or
      a citation may identify a real passage that does not support the claim. Those
      cases require separate labels. A schema-valid answer can still be false. A completed
      tool trajectory can still fail the task checker.


      ## Interfaces and versioned fixtures


      Use a Document record with ID, revision, text, source and access metadata; a
      Chunk with document revision, offsets and stable identity; and a QueryCase with
      expected facts, supporting sources, allowed evidence and answerability. Retrieval
      returns scores and IDs rather than losing provenance in a plain concatenated
      string. A RunRecord retains the exact model request, settings, response, tool
      calls/results, selected context, terminal reason and measured usage. Define
      each type before its implementation so fixture adapters and substantive model
      adapters obey the same observable contract.


      The fixture includes exact-name, paraphrase, single-source, multi-source, ambiguous,
      unsupported and restricted-document questions. Keep human evidence labels independent
      of the retriever and judge. Freeze development and held-out cases before selecting
      a configuration. When a model judge disagrees with deterministic checks, retain
      the disputed case and judge input rather than reducing disagreement to a single
      average score.


      ## The mechanisms developed across the course


      The tool loop exposes action parsing and independent completion checks. The
      harness adds exact budget boundaries, complete-exchange context selection, progress
      checks and transport cleanup. Search labs implement BM25 statistics, exact vector
      comparison and an approximate index before studying fusion and pairwise reranking.
      Ingestion preserves structure and revisions as documents change. The answer
      labs assemble permitted evidence, implement token-level grammar constraints,
      and verify each cited claim. Prompt experiments distinguish paired fixture comparisons
      from assigned live experiments and make repeated peeking visible. Iterative
      retrieval adds a bounded next-evidence action whose extra calls must be justified
      by the report.


      These are application mechanisms around a pretrained model. Pretraining, model
      architecture and reinforcement-learning training stay in the existing from-scratch
      courses. A maintained SDK can supply transport; it does not replace the retrieval,
      controller, grammar or evaluation mechanism when that mechanism is the lesson.


      ## What a credible comparison records


      For retrieval, separate relevant-candidate recall from final ranking. For generation,
      separate factual correctness, supported claims, schema validity and abstention.
      For actions, separate proposed calls, executed calls, terminal reasons and task
      success. For every path retain elapsed time, tokens, model/configuration identity
      and estimated or measured cost with its units. Compare the same case set and
      resource allowance, inspect regressions, and report uncertainty when stochastic
      comparisons justify a general quality claim.'
    lab_and_evidence: '### Walkthroughs to prepare


      Trace a successful request, an unsupported question, a forbidden cross-organization
      request, and a dependency failure. For each, record the initial fixture state,
      actual inputs to each component, intended boundary decision, final response,
      and any lasting effect. A failure report needs the same identity and version
      fields as a successful run.


      ### Baselines and artifact contracts


      Every lab records its reproducing command, fixture and model versions, baseline,
      measured result, and one limitation. The final report separates retrieval misses,
      unsupported claims, wrong answers, unnecessary abstentions, permission leaks,
      and resource use. Compare changes on frozen development/test cases; reserve
      stronger statistical claims for results with suitable repeated runs and uncertainty
      estimates. Improvements, regressions, and inconclusive comparisons are all valid
      findings.


      Before comparing a change, define the task set, independent expected results,
      allowed resource budget and simplest relevant baseline. Keep raw case-level
      records so the report can be recalculated. Declare which parts are fixture-based,
      which use a model, and which use actual services or provisioned resources. A
      useful artifact includes a lockfile, fixture version/hash, proposed reproduction
      command, configuration, measured units, result, observed failure and limitation.
      A negative or inconclusive comparison remains a valid completed learning artifact.


      ### Initial design exercise


      Draw the components and annotate the data passed across each boundary. Define
      one versioned fixture schema and one output record using the interfaces above.
      Write independent checks for one happy case and one failure before implementing
      the controller. Show how a result from a standalone lab can be consumed by the
      optional shared project without depending on private mutable state. Establish
      a small time and resource allowance for the first build; keep optional cloud
      or model runs separately budgeted.


      The overview deliverable is a diagram, interface/data inventory, fixture schema,
      baseline/report specification and resource plan. No benchmark value should be
      filled in until that workload has actually run. The following chapters implement
      these components and explain the results; the overview supplies their shared
      vocabulary and limits.'
    summary: Map the assistant's interfaces, offline and live execution paths, baselines,
      and separate failure measures.
    chapter_id: course/llm-applications/00-overview
    section: main
  - content: '## Make an action visible before adding a framework


      A user asks, “What is twelve times forty-seven, plus the shipping fee in note
      3?” The proposed lab has two read-only tools: a restricted calculator and a
      lookup over six synthetic support notes. A model response requests a calculation,
      the application executes it, and the next response requests the note. A final
      response combines the observations. The central artifact is the complete transcript,
      including malformed requests and failures, so the route to an answer can be
      inspected rather than inferred from the final text.


      This chapter implements that cycle with ordinary Python. An **agent** here is
      a program that lets model outputs select subsequent actions. The model produces
      proposals; the Python dispatcher performs actual work. **ReAct**, reasoning
      and acting, names an interleaving of action selection and observations. No hidden
      reasoning transcript is required. If a model offers a short action explanation,
      it can be retained as ordinary output, but correctness is established from tool
      requests, results, and the task checker.


      The prerequisites are functions, dataclasses, JSON, exceptions, and tests. Familiarity
      with system, user, assistant, and tool messages helps; none of the model-training
      courses has to be completed first. A deterministic scripted model makes the
      first runs inspectable without credentials. A substantive model-generated run
      can then use a pinned local or hosted model adapter. The scripts show controller
      behavior; their success rates do not estimate a language model''s ability to
      choose actions.


      ## Walk through one transcript


      Start with a plain-text action protocol that exposes the parser seam. The system
      instruction describes two terminal shapes: an action with an allowlisted tool
      name and validated arguments, or a final answer. For example, `Action: calculator({"expression":"12*47"})`
      proposes work and `Final Answer: 570` proposes completion. The exact grammar
      belongs in the task fixture and parser tests. JSON arguments keep quoting rules
      explicit while leaving the surrounding action syntax to the learner''s parser.


      The application appends the raw assistant response, parses exactly one accepted
      outcome, validates the selected tool, and appends a typed observation. A successful
      calculator observation contains the result and request identifier. An error
      observation identifies malformed arguments or an unavailable tool without presenting
      fabricated data. The next model call receives the updated conversation. A final-answer
      proposal ends action generation, after which an independent task checker determines
      whether the requested computation and required lookup were satisfied.


      A mixed response containing both an action and a final answer needs a documented
      policy. Rejecting ambiguous outputs is a reasonable default; silently selecting
      whichever marker appears last can execute an unintended request. Trailing commentary,
      embedded markers in strings, escaped quotes, empty arguments, and oversized
      payloads belong in parser cases. Strictness is useful only when errors become
      visible observations rather than unexplained crashes. A bounded corrective turn
      tells the model what failed and preserves the original malformed output for
      diagnosis.


      ## The interfaces the learner will implement


      The proposed lesson-local package is `tool_loop`, with `types.py`, `protocol.py`,
      `tools.py`, `model.py`, `controller.py`, `checker.py`, and `cli.py`. A `TaskCase`
      stores an ID, prompt, expected fields, checking policy, and optional required
      tools. A `Transcript` owns ordered messages. `ModelAdapter.complete(messages,
      tool_specs, settings)` returns raw output, parsed-provider metadata, usage counts
      when available, and a request ID. It does not execute tools.


      `parse_step(text)` returns one of `Action`, `FinalAnswer`, or `ParseError`.
      `Action` carries a name, JSON arguments, and call ID. `ToolSpec` carries a name,
      description, and argument schema. `ToolResult` carries `ok`, result data or
      an error code, and the matching call ID. `run(task, model, tools, max_steps)`
      returns a final proposal, terminal reason, task-checker result, and the full
      trace. These signatures are design targets; the files and commands are to be
      created in the lab, not existing Watchtower APIs.


      A native tool-calling adapter is a later comparison behind the same model interface.
      It translates provider tool-call fields into the shared `Action` type. It must
      still validate arguments locally, preserve call IDs, and handle parallel calls
      according to an explicit policy. This lab executes one call per turn; accepting
      a provider''s entire batch accidentally would change the step and cost accounting.


      ## Implement the tools without executing model text


      The calculator parses an expression into a restricted syntax tree, allowing
      numeric literals and a bounded set of arithmetic operators. Reject names, attribute
      access, function calls, and arbitrary imports. Bound input length, numeric magnitude,
      nesting, and exponent size: even arithmetic-only input can consume unreasonable
      resources. Division by zero produces a typed error observation. Passing the
      expression to `eval`, a shell, or an unrestricted interpreter defeats the tool
      contract.


      The note tool reads an in-memory dictionary keyed by a small integer ID. It
      returns the note ID, project code, fee, and text. Missing IDs are explicit failures.
      The model cannot provide a filesystem path, URL, or executable expression as
      a lookup argument. Tool dispatch occurs through an allowlisted dictionary, rather
      than dynamic imports or arbitrary attribute lookup. Both tools can raise internal
      exceptions during implementation, but the adapter converts expected failures
      into bounded observations and records unexpected exceptions as controlled terminal
      failures.


      Descriptions affect whether a model chooses a tool; schemas constrain whether
      its request is accepted. Neither description nor valid JSON establishes authorization.
      This chapter''s synthetic read-only inputs avoid a real permissions system.
      The enterprise companion course adds identity and per-resource checks without
      changing the distinction between a proposal and an executed operation.


      ## Bound the primitive loop


      Even this first controller has a maximum number of model turns and a maximum
      observation size. A final answer ends generation; exhausting the allowance returns
      `step_budget` and the partial trace. Count attempted actions separately from
      successfully executed calls. A rejected unknown-tool proposal consumes a model
      turn but does not count as tool execution. A successful tool request that returns
      no relevant fact may still be an executed call and an unsuccessful task.


      The transcript is the controller''s memory. It includes the initial instructions,
      user task, raw proposals, results, and corrections. Keeping a complete trace
      is different from sending an ever-growing trace to the model; the next chapter
      introduces working-context selection. Persist request settings, adapter/model
      identity, fixture hash, and observed usage alongside messages. Temperature zero
      can reduce some variation, but provider behavior and local numerical execution
      need not be perfectly deterministic. Replayable scripted tests and measured
      live repeatability answer different questions.


      ## Build sequence and handoff


      Begin by writing task cases and expected checkers, then implement and test the
      parser without calling a model. Implement calculator and note lookup with hostile
      and malformed inputs. Add a scripted adapter that returns success, parse-error
      recovery, unknown-tool, and wrong-final-answer sequences. Wire the controller
      only after these components work separately. Finally add the model adapter and
      an evaluation command that compares direct answering with action-based answering
      on the same cases.


      The next chapter receives the canonical action and observation types, trace
      schema, and independent checkers. Its budgets and context policy wrap this small
      loop. A learner taking the harness chapter independently can use supplied equivalent
      fixtures instead of importing this implementation. A large framework, memory
      database, browser tool, and multi-agent delegation are optional later studies;
      none is needed to understand this action-observation mechanism.'
    lab_and_evidence: '## Construct cases before scoring the controller


      Prepare 15–20 versioned tasks across calculator-only, note-only, combined lookup/calculation,
      and no-tool questions. Include numeric formatting variants and answers whose
      wording can vary while the required fields stay fixed. Write exact numeric checks
      for arithmetic and parsed-field comparisons for notes; use substring matching
      only where the task definition justifies it. A correct final number obtained
      without a required lookup is distinguishable from a fully satisfied task. Keep
      those two verdicts visible.


      The offline scripts include a clean calculation, malformed arguments followed
      by correction, unknown tool, missing note, tool exception, endless repeated
      action, and a plausible wrong final answer. Label each expected terminal reason
      and task outcome before running the controller. The fixture generator creates
      messages, not labels derived from the implementation. Keep transcript rendering
      free of credentials and real customer data.


      ## Proposed reproduction commands


      The learner will create a lesson-local environment and implement the following
      command contract. These commands specify the intended artifact; no `tool_loop`
      package is supplied by this plan.


      ```bash

      uv sync

      uv run pytest tests -q

      uv run python -m tool_loop.cli run --case calc-note-01 --model scripted --out
      artifacts/example.json

      uv run python -m tool_loop.cli evaluate --cases fixtures/tasks.jsonl --model
      scripted --out artifacts/offline.jsonl

      uv run python -m tool_loop.cli report --runs artifacts/offline.jsonl --out artifacts/offline-report.md

      ```


      An opt-in model experiment adds `--model local` or `--model hosted` and writes
      a separate artifact directory. Record the pinned model/client versions, prompt
      hash, sampling settings, token allowances, and actual request metadata. For
      hosted calls, read secrets through the workspace vault or local runtime configuration
      without writing them into fixtures. Set a small spending ceiling before the
      run and stop when the next bounded request cannot fit the remaining allowance.


      ## Compare what changes and explain failures


      Run direct-answer and tool-loop configurations on the same frozen task set with
      the same model and response settings. Report success counts, mean steps for
      successful tasks, failure terminal reasons, parse-error counts, attempted/executed
      tool calls, latency, and input/output tokens. Report no-tool cases separately
      to expose unnecessary work. A native-tool-calling extension may add a third
      configuration, allowing a comparison of parser failures while preserving the
      task and dispatcher.


      Inspect every failure transcript. Attribute the first relevant failure to protocol
      parsing, tool selection, arguments, tool execution, missing evidence, answer
      synthesis, or checking policy. A parser error is not automatically a model-reasoning
      failure, and a final-answer marker is not a success label. Retain partial and
      failed runs in denominators. Do not publish a table of invented target scores
      or claim that action selection must improve every question.


      Tests pin ambiguous outputs, quotes and escapes, unknown names, hostile arithmetic,
      numeric limits, missing notes, correction bounds, exact step boundaries, and
      wrong final answers. The final artifact contains the cases and checkers, a lockfile,
      raw sanitized transcripts, per-case results, a comparison table, and an explanation
      of one failure and one limitation.


      All parser/tool/controller tests run on a laptop CPU at zero API cost. A small
      local model needs enough memory for its pinned weights and context; a hosted
      model needs no GPU but incurs measured usage. If resources permit only replay,
      complete the mechanism report and label model-selection conclusions as unmeasured.
      Optional extensions include native calls or a second safe tool, with the same
      checker and budget rather than an expanded task domain.'
    summary: Follow model-proposed actions through validated tool calls to a checked
      final answer.
    chapter_id: course/llm-applications/01-tool-calling
    section: tool-use
  - content: '## Turn a tool loop into a program that stops predictably


      The proposed task asks an assistant to read notes 1, 3, and 6 and return their
      project codes. A scripted model requests each note once and finishes. A second
      script repeatedly requests note 3; a third requests distinct notes until its
      allowance is exhausted. Run the same scripts through a minimally bounded loop
      and through a controller with explicit limits. The difference becomes visible
      in terminal reasons, executed calls, token counts, and the retained trace.


      An **agent harness** is the ordinary application code surrounding a model: budgets,
      working-context selection, tool adapters, timeouts, progress checks, and cleanup.
      The model may propose another action after the useful work is complete, but
      the harness decides whether a call may begin. The task checker decides whether
      the final answer is acceptable. Separating these responsibilities makes a stalled
      task and a correct answer with excessive work distinguishable.


      The prerequisite is the action-observation cycle, plus dataclasses, enums, asynchronous
      context managers, and tests. The execution/cancellation chapter of Production
      AI Systems provides a bridge when asynchronous cleanup is unfamiliar. The harness
      lab supplies its own six-note corpus and scripted adapters, so completing another
      chapter''s code is not a dependency. The core runs locally without a model API.
      A live adapter is a separate bounded comparison.


      ## Define budgets as separate accounts


      Keep independent limits for model turns, cumulative input/output tokens, executed
      tool calls, working-context tokens, elapsed time, and consecutive no-progress
      actions. A single `max_steps` parameter cannot express all of these. Four model
      turns may include no tool requests; four tools can return very large observations;
      a short-looking request can carry a large tool schema. The trace must show which
      account caused a stop.


      Before a model call, fit the serialized request and reserve its maximum response
      allowance. Count system text, tool schemas, role/message framing where the selected
      counter supports it, and the conversation actually sent. Before a tool call,
      check its call allowance and remaining time. A limit of four calls permits four
      accepted calls and prevents a fifth. Rejected requests are attempted actions;
      executing a failing tool still consumes a tool call. Boundary equality and these
      accounting distinctions belong in tests.


      Use `done`, `step_budget`, `token_budget`, `tool_budget`, `context_unfit`, `loop`,
      `stalled`, `timeout`, `model_error`, and `tool_error` as explicit terminal outcomes.
      A task can terminate cleanly without succeeding. Stop reasons should be data
      fields, not inferred later from log text. If a provider returns usage greater
      than a local estimate, update actual cumulative accounting and preserve the
      discrepancy; do not retroactively erase that request to make the budget table
      look exact.


      ## Keep working context within the model window


      The complete saved trace and the next model request have different purposes.
      The saved trace preserves history for evaluation. The working request contains
      the material the model can currently use. Let $T$ be its counted size, $R$ the
      reserved response allowance, and $C$ the configured context window. Require
      $T+R\le C$ before calling the model. Pin the original task and system instructions.
      Preserve the newest complete assistant/tool exchange, including every result
      for its corresponding call.


      Drop the oldest complete unpinned exchanges until the request fits. A result
      detached from its call can become misleading evidence or an invalid provider
      message sequence. If pinned material plus the required recent exchange cannot
      fit, terminate with `context_unfit`. Repeatedly trying to compact the same unfit
      material wastes calls without changing the constraint. Bound a tool observation
      before adding it to working context and record that selection in the full trace.


      Summarization is an optional comparison, because a model-written summary adds
      cost and may lose the exact fact needed for the answer. The deterministic drop
      policy makes the first implementation inspectable. If a summary is added, record
      its request, source exchanges, tokens, and omissions. It must not turn tool-provided
      instructions into privileged system instructions. Test context counting with
      actual serialized messages rather than only concatenated visible strings.


      ## Detect repeated calls and task-specific stalls


      Canonicalize an action as the tool name and recursively sorted JSON arguments.
      Exact repetition of `read_note({"note_id":3})` can be detected even when key
      order changes. A changed search query may be useful refinement, so tool-name
      repetition alone is not a loop rule. For this note task, progress means obtaining
      a required note ID for the first time. Consecutive calls that add no required
      ID can trigger `stalled` without pretending that a general text-difference measure
      understands every task.


      A repeated result is sometimes legitimate, such as retrying after a transient
      unavailable tool. Define an allowed retry bound separately and expose it in
      the rubric. Compare an exact-loop rule with the task''s progress rule on cases
      containing changed arguments and duplicate evidence. These checks terminate
      pathological fixtures; they do not prove that every longer model trajectory
      is unproductive. Reflection, planning prompts, and delegation remain optional
      extensions after the controller''s limits are established.


      ## Connect one read-only tool through maintained MCP


      **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** supplies a common interface for discovering
      and calling tools. Use a pinned maintained Python SDK for a server exposing
      `read_note(note_id)` and for a client adapter. Implement application behavior,
      not protocol framing or JSON-RPC transport. Most tests use an in-process connection;
      one local standard-input/output transport test exercises subprocess startup
      and shutdown.


      At connection time, discover the tool, retain its schema/version metadata, and
      translate the selected specification into the model adapter''s format. At each
      invocation, reject unknown names, validate arguments, check the local allowlist
      and harness budgets, invoke with a timeout, inspect protocol error indicators,
      and normalize a bounded result. Tool discovery advertises capability; it does
      not grant the current caller permission. The synthetic note store is read-only,
      and the enterprise course later provides resource authorization.


      Protocol messages use stdout; diagnostics use stderr. Pass only required environment
      variables into the subprocess. Closing an asynchronous client context must stop
      the server and reap the process, including when a tool hangs or the task is
      cancelled. A timeout is effective only if it also controls the work being awaited
      or reports remaining work accurately. Cancellation does not automatically stop
      arbitrary blocking Python or an external service; the adapter''s behavior has
      to be tested.


      ## Proposed module boundaries and build sequence


      The learner creates `agent_harness/types.py`, `budget.py`, `context.py`, `progress.py`,
      `model.py`, `mcp_adapter.py`, `controller.py`, and `cli.py`, plus a tiny `note_server`
      and fixtures. `Limits` carries independent allowances and response reserve.
      `fit_context(messages, limits, counter)` returns selected messages and a selection
      record. `ToolAdapter.discover()` and `call(name, arguments, timeout)` abstract
      the SDK. `run(task, model, adapter, limits)` returns a trace, terminal reason,
      usage, and checker result.


      First define scripts, expected note mappings, and the trace schema. Implement
      exact budgets with a fake tool adapter, then exchange-aware context selection.
      Add loop/stall rules against canonical actions and the independent note checker.
      Only then connect the SDK server, exercising the same task through both fake
      and protocol adapters. Finally compare bare and bounded controllers and interpret
      the terminal traces. These modules and commands are proposed lab targets; no
      package or server has already been created.


      The downstream evaluation chapter receives serialized actions, observations,
      limits, actual usage, and stop reasons. It can also use independent recorded
      runs. A full memory service, remote MCP deployment, handwritten protocol, and
      multi-agent scheduler would expand this chapter''s purpose and remain elective
      work.'
    lab_and_evidence: '## Cases that expose the controller''s boundaries


      Create the three initial note scripts and add oversized pinned input, oversized
      observation, tool timeout, model exception, malformed tool arguments, and cancellation
      during a call. For every budget, test the exact permitted count and the first
      disallowed request. Assert that no new tool starts after its allowance is exhausted.
      Record attempts and executions separately, including error returns. A fake clock
      and deterministic token counter can isolate the controller; use the selected
      model tokenizer for the model experiment.


      For context tests, confirm no change when the request already fits, exchange-preserving
      removal when it exceeds the allowance, and an explicit stop when pinned material
      cannot fit. Test a multi-message assistant/tool exchange even if the chapter''s
      ordinary model proposes one call at a time. The trace keeps the complete removed
      content while the request snapshot reveals what the model actually saw.


      ## Proposed command contract


      The learner implements these commands in a lesson-local package:


      ```bash

      uv sync

      uv run pytest tests -q

      uv run python -m agent_harness.cli compare --fixtures fixtures --out artifacts/comparison.jsonl

      uv run python -m agent_harness.cli mcp-smoke --transport stdio --out artifacts/mcp-smoke.json

      uv run python -m agent_harness.cli report --input artifacts/comparison.jsonl
      --out artifacts/report.md

      ```


      The smoke command checks discovered schema, one valid call, one invalid argument,
      a controlled failure, bounded observation, timeout behavior, and child-process
      cleanup. Record the resolved SDK/client/server versions and lockfile. During
      authoring, verify SDK API usage against its official documentation for the pinned
      version; this plan deliberately does not promise a version-sensitive client
      snippet.


      ## Compare bare and harnessed runs


      Use the same scripts and tools for both controllers. The bare comparison still
      has a large emergency ceiling so the experiment cannot run forever. Tabulate
      expected outcome, observed terminal reason, task-checker result, model turns,
      attempted/executed calls, estimated/actual tokens, discarded exchanges, elapsed
      time, and transport. Include partial runs and explain when an earlier stop prevents
      wasted work but also removes evidence required for a correct answer.


      The report contains an interface diagram, limit definitions, complete sanitized
      traces, selected working requests, protocol smoke evidence, and one limitation
      per control. Examples include a lexical loop detector missing a semantically
      repeated query, a progress checker tied to the note task, and an approximate
      token counter differing from provider usage. The core conclusion concerns reproducible
      controller behavior on known fixtures; reliability of model action selection
      requires separately collected model runs.


      All scripted and SDK-local work is CPU-only and has no API charge. A live model
      comparison uses a small case set and an explicit request/token or spending ceiling,
      retaining raw usage and failure traces. No Docker or remote service is required.
      Optional depth includes a measured summary policy, a local model run, or one
      bounded delegated worker. Choose one extension and preserve the same controller
      accounting so its additional cost and task effect remain visible.'

  - content: "Evaluate supplied recorded trajectories for task completion, required\
      \ tools, repeated calls, budget adherence, and errors. Construct human labels\
      \ independently of the scorer. Compare deterministic rules with a model judge\
      \ and inspect disagreements, abstentions, and judge cost. Explain label leakage,\
      \ task selection, and why one aggregate success score can hide an unsafe or\
      \ wasteful trajectory.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment\
      \ to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab\
      \ artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results already\
      \ exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nBuild a small\
      \ evaluator for recorded agent runs. Score whether an agent used the required\n\
      tools, stayed within its limits, avoided repeated calls, and produced the expected\
      \ answer.\nThen compare those deterministic rules with a model-based judge on\
      \ the same labeled runs\nand inspect every disagreement.\n\nThe lesson supplies\
      \ a precise fixture specification for 30 serialized trajectories, so\nyou evaluate\
      \ fixed records rather than rebuilding agents from other weeks. The artifact\n\
      is a scorer-comparison report with accuracy, precision, recall, abstentions,\
      \ cost, and a\ngallery explaining where each scorer disagreed with the handwritten\
      \ labels.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n- The action–tool-result loop from\
      \ Guide 8 and the stop/budget\n  concepts from Guide 9, or equivalent understanding.\n\
      - Basic binary-classification metrics: true/false positives, precision, recall,\
      \ and\n  confusion matrices.\n- Python dataclasses, JSON Lines (JSONL), tests,\
      \ and simple plotting.\n\nMulti-agent delegation and implementing Model Context\
      \ Protocol from scratch are not\nprerequisites. No earlier agent implementation,\
      \ portfolio project, or saved API trace is\nrequired. The core rule scorer and\
      \ report run locally at $0. One hosted chat model is\nneeded only for the judge\
      \ comparison; a checked-in judge-response fixture keeps default\ntests offline.\n\
      \nUse Python 3.13 and pytest in a lesson-local environment. Pin the plotting\
      \ and optional\nmodel-client dependencies. The paths and commands below describe\
      \ files you will create.\n\n## Begin with a fixed run format\n\nA **trajectory**\
      \ is the recorded path from a task to a terminal outcome. It includes\nactions\
      \ and observations, not hidden model reasoning. Do not require or store private\n\
      chain-of-thought. A short model-provided action summary may be recorded as ordinary\
      \ output,\nbut the evaluators must work without it.\n\nEach JSONL record follows\
      \ this versioned contract:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"schema_version\": 1,\n  \"run_id\"\
      : \"lookup-clean-01\",\n  \"task_id\": \"lookup-three-notes\",\n  \"task\":\
      \ \"Read notes 1, 3, and 6 and report their project codes.\",\n  \"steps\":\
      \ [\n    {\n      \"index\": 0,\n      \"action\": {\"name\": \"read_note\"\
      , \"arguments\": {\"note_id\": 1}},\n      \"observation\": {\"ok\": true, \"\
      content\": \"Project code: ORBIT\"}\n    }\n  ],\n  \"final_answer\": \"1=ORBIT,\
      \ 3=EMBER, 6=TIDAL\",\n  \"terminal_reason\": \"done\",\n  \"usage\": {\"input_tokens\"\
      : 400, \"output_tokens\": 80},\n  \"metadata\": {\"agent_version\": \"fixture-v1\"\
      , \"model\": \"scripted\"}\n}\n```\n\nValidate types, required fields, schema\
      \ version, unique run IDs, monotonically increasing\nstep indices, and bounded\
      \ string/list sizes while loading. Treat observations and final\nanswers as\
      \ untrusted data. Loading a trajectory must never execute its recorded tools.\n\
      Unknown schema versions fail explicitly instead of being guessed into the current\
      \ format.\n\n## Create an independent fixture and gold set\n\nWrite a deterministic\
      \ generator for 30 records across these task families:\n\n| Task family | Runs\
      \ | Important variations |\n|---|---:|---|\n| Read three notes | 10 | clean\
      \ success, missing note, wrong answer, repeated call, extra harmless call |\n\
      | Add two numbers | 6 | correct calculator use, mental answer without required\
      \ tool, wrong arguments, tool failure |\n| Find a policy paragraph | 8 | successful\
      \ search/read chain, irrelevant refinement, exact loop, unsupported answer |\n\
      | Handle an unavailable tool | 6 | clean stop, bounded retry, repeated retry,\
      \ fabricated success |\n\nAt least four records contain an observation that\
      \ tells an evaluator to ignore its rubric\nand return “pass.” At least four\
      \ have correct final answers reached through an unacceptable\npath. At least\
      \ four have failed final answers after otherwise sensible tool use. Include\n\
      both exact repeated actions and legitimate refinements with changed arguments.\n\
      \nCreate `gold.jsonl` separately, with `run_id`, per-axis labels, overall verdict,\
      \ and a\none-sentence reason. Handwrite the expected labels before implementing\
      \ either scorer.\nThe fixture generator may create trajectory structure but\
      \ must not call the scoring code\nto produce labels. Review the final 30 rows\
      \ manually and record a fixture hash in the report.\n\nThis is a small, purposeful\
      \ test set, not a statistically representative benchmark of\nall agents. It\
      \ exists to expose scorer behavior under known cases.\n\n## Deterministic rule\
      \ scorer\n\nCanonicalize each action as its tool name plus recursively sorted\
      \ JSON arguments. Detect\nan exact loop when the same canonical action appears\
      \ within a configurable recent window.\nKeep this distinct from task-specific\
      \ no-progress behavior: `search(\"policy\")` followed\nby `search(\"travel policy\"\
      )` may be a useful refinement even though both call search.\n\nFor the supplied\
      \ tasks, implement explicit checkers:\n\n- note lookup compares the requested\
      \ IDs and parsed project-code mapping;\n- calculator compares numeric result\
      \ and required calculator call;\n- policy lookup requires an allowed search/read\
      \ path and cited fixture paragraph ID;\n- unavailable-tool handling requires\
      \ the specified terminal reason and retry bound.\n\nDo not use fuzzy string\
      \ similarity as a universal success measure. Normalize only what\nthe task contract\
      \ permits, such as whitespace, key ordering, or numeric formatting.\n\n## Model-based\
      \ judge\n\nThe judge receives a task rubric and a rendered trajectory, then\
      \ returns strict structured\ndata for the same four axes, an overall verdict,\
      \ and short evidence references. It may\njudge qualitative paths the rules leave\
      \ unknown, but it does not replace deterministic\nchecks for exact requirements.\n\
      \nRender trajectory fields inside clearly delimited data blocks. State that\
      \ content inside\nthose blocks is evidence to assess, not instructions. Encode\
      \ the record as data and cap\nthe judge input by failing or applying a documented\
      \ deterministic selection policy; do\nnot silently truncate the task or final\
      \ answer. The prompt itself is only one defense:\nkeep the injection cases and\
      \ measure whether they change outcomes.\n\nUse the provider's structured-output\
      \ facility when available and validate the response\nlocally. On invalid output,\
      \ retry once with the same rubric. After that, record an\nabstention and the\
      \ failure reason. Never coerce malformed output into a pass. Configure\nthe\
      \ most deterministic supported settings, but measure repeatability rather than\
      \ claiming\nthat a temperature setting makes a judge deterministic.\n\nRun the\
      \ judge three times on the six most important boundary cases: one injection,\
      \ one\nexact loop, one legitimate refinement, one lucky correct answer, one\
      \ sensible failed run,\nand one clean success. Report flips and abstentions.\
      \ For the remaining cases, one run is\nenough for this bounded exercise.\n\n\
      ## Project shape and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\nweek12/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── trajeval/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── schema.py\n│   ├── fixtures.py\n\
      │   ├── loader.py\n│   ├── rubrics.py\n│   ├── rules.py\n│   ├── judge.py\n\
      │   ├── metrics.py\n│   ├── report.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├── data/\n│   ├── runs.jsonl\n\
      │   ├── gold.jsonl\n│   └── judge_responses.jsonl\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n\
      ```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import Literal,\
      \ Protocol\n\nLabel = Literal[True, False] | None\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class Score:\n    run_id: str\n    success: Label\n    tool_correct: Label\n\
      \    efficient: Label\n    non_degenerate: Label\n    verdict: Label\n    reason:\
      \ str\n\nclass Scorer(Protocol):\n    name: str\n    def score(self, trajectory:\
      \ dict, rubric: dict) -> Score: ...\n\ndef load_trajectories(path: str, max_steps:\
      \ int = 100) -> list[dict]: ...\ndef canonical_action(action: dict) -> str:\
      \ ...\ndef score_rules(trajectory: dict, rubric: dict) -> Score: ...\ndef compare_with_gold(scores:\
      \ list[Score], gold: dict[str, Score]) -> dict: ...\n```\n\nAlign records by\
      \ `run_id`, reject duplicates, and account for missing/extra IDs. Metrics\n\
      must not compare two arrays merely because they happen to have the same order."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Keep evaluation axes separate\n\nScore four axes before\
      \ producing an overall verdict:\n\n- **task success:** the expected result or\
      \ terminal state is present;\n- **tool correctness:** required tools and acceptable\
      \ arguments were used, and forbidden\n  or fabricated operations were absent;\n\
      - **efficiency:** the trajectory stayed within the task's stated step/tool budget;\n\
      - **non-degeneracy:** it avoided defined loops and repeated no-progress actions.\n\
      \nStore `true`, `false`, or `null` per axis. `null` means the scorer abstained\
      \ or the axis\ndoes not apply; it is not silently converted to false. Define\
      \ the overall rule verdict\nin a task rubric, such as all applicable hard axes\
      \ being true. Report per-axis results\neven when an overall pass/fail is convenient\
      \ for regression gating.\n\nThe task rubric is versioned data containing expected\
      \ answer fields, required/allowed\ntools, argument constraints, and maximum\
      \ steps. A generic scorer cannot infer all valid\npaths from a task prompt alone.\
      \ The evaluator should be strict about properties the rubric\nactually states\
      \ and abstain from unsupported judgments.\n\n## Metrics and disagreement analysis\n\
      \nTreat non-abstaining overall verdicts as predictions against handwritten gold.\
      \ Report\nthe confusion counts and\n\n$$\n\\operatorname{precision}=\\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\\\
      qquad\n\\operatorname{recall}=\\frac{TP}{TP+FN}.\n$$\n\nWhen a denominator is\
      \ zero, report the metric as undefined rather than zero. Also report\naccuracy,\
      \ coverage (fraction receiving a non-null verdict), and abstention count. A\
      \ scorer\ncan appear accurate by grading only easy cases, so accuracy without\
      \ coverage is incomplete.\n\nFor rule-versus-judge agreement, report the 2×2\
      \ table and raw agreement on records where\nboth produced a verdict. Cohen's\
      \ kappa is optional for only 30 designed cases; if included,\nshow its formula\
      \ and warn that its value is unstable on a small, deliberately balanced set.\n\
      The disagreement gallery is more useful here than a single coefficient.\n\n\
      For every scorer disagreement, display the gold label, both verdicts/reasons,\
      \ and the\nminimal trajectory fields needed to inspect the case. Classify the\
      \ cause after review:\nliteral rule, missing rubric, judge error, injection\
      \ sensitivity, invalid judge response,\nor ambiguous gold label. If review exposes\
      \ a mistaken label, correct it transparently,\nregenerate the fixture hash,\
      \ and rerun both scorers.\n\n## Build sequence — 18 hours\n\n1. **Schema, rubrics,\
      \ and fixtures, 4 hours.** Define versioned records, generate the 30\n   trajectories,\
      \ hand-label them, and test loader rejection and bounds.\n2. **Rule scorer,\
      \ 4 hours.** Implement task-specific checks, action canonicalization,\n   loop\
      \ detection, abstention, and per-axis output. Test every designed variation.\n\
      3. **Metrics and offline report, 3 hours.** Compare rules with gold, calculate\
      \ coverage\n   and confusion counts, and render the initial disagreement cases.\n\
      4. **Judge scorer, 4 hours.** Add bounded rendering, structured parsing, retry/abstention,\n\
      \   recorded-response tests, and the six-case repeatability run.\n5. **Comparison\
      \ and interpretation, 3 hours.** Score all cases, inspect disagreements,\n \
      \  record actual latency/token/cost data, and write limitations.\n\n## Commands,\
      \ tests, and artifact\n\nImplement and run these commands from the lesson directory:\n\
      \n```bash\nuv sync\nuv run python -m trajeval.cli make-fixtures --out data\n\
      uv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m trajeval.cli score --scorer rules --runs\
      \ data/runs.jsonl --out artifacts/rules.jsonl\nuv run python -m trajeval.cli\
      \ score --scorer recorded-judge --runs data/runs.jsonl --out artifacts/judge-offline.jsonl\n\
      uv run python -m trajeval.cli compare --gold data/gold.jsonl --scores artifacts/rules.jsonl\
      \ artifacts/judge-offline.jsonl --out artifacts/report.md\n```\n\nThe recorded\
      \ judge responses exercise parsing and reporting without presenting them as\n\
      fresh model judgments. An opt-in `--scorer live-judge` command requires a local\
      \ environment\nvariable, records model/version and raw validated responses,\
      \ and refuses to overwrite the\noffline fixture. Keep secrets and sensitive\
      \ tool arguments out of all trajectory files.\n\nTests cover schema versions,\
      \ duplicate IDs, size bounds, each task checker, exact loops,\nlegitimate refinements,\
      \ missing rubrics, null axes, zero-denominator metrics, invalid judge\noutput,\
      \ abstention, injection fixtures, and report alignment. Default tests make no\
      \ network\ncalls and never execute a trajectory action.\n\nThe final report\
      \ contains dataset composition and hash, each scorer's per-axis and overall\n\
      metrics, coverage, confusion tables, judge repeatability, measured cost/latency,\
      \ every\ndisagreement, and at least one limitation. With 30 designed examples,\
      \ counts are often\nclearer than percentages alone. A higher score on this fixture\
      \ does not establish that a\nscorer is generally better.\n\n## Hardware, cost,\
      \ and optional depth\n\nCPU-only offline work costs $0 and requires no Docker.\
      \ Cap the optional live judge run at\n$3 and record actual usage. A hosted key\
      \ is not required to complete the rule scorer,\nrecorded-judge tests, or report\
      \ pipeline.\n\nPairwise comparison, routing only ambiguous cases to a judge,\
      \ and evaluating traces from\na real agent are optional extensions. Multi-agent-specific\
      \ metrics and MCP protocol tests\nbelong in those systems' own evaluations;\
      \ this lesson's stable trajectory contract can\naccept their future records\
      \ without requiring them now.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain\
      \ the pinned environment, fixture and configuration identities, case-level outcomes,\
      \ reproduction command and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism\
      \ checks from actual model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements.\
      \ Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are\
      \ planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set\
      \ a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate\
      \ from the baseline report."

  - content: "Start with a query containing an exact product code and inspect why\
      \ simple substring lookup fails. Build token normalization, an inverted index,\
      \ document and term statistics, and BM25 ranking. Define relevant-document labels\
      \ independently of ranking code. Explain recall at k, reciprocal rank, and the\
      \ effect of candidate cutoffs without assuming a lexical retriever is always\
      \ weaker than embeddings.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and\
      \ experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed\
      \ lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results\
      \ already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## Overview\n\nSparse lexical retrieval\
      \ is the baseline every fancier retrieval method is\nmeasured against, and it\
      \ is cheap enough that there's no excuse not to know it\ncold. This chapter\
      \ builds an inverted index and BM25 ranking with no retrieval\nlibraries, evaluated\
      \ on a small document set with known relevant answers.\nRecall@k and mean reciprocal\
      \ rank against the labeled set establish exactly how\nstrong this floor already\
      \ is. The result is the baseline every later retrieval\ntechnique in this arc\
      \ has to beat to justify its added complexity.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- **Tokenization\
      \ intuition** (Week 3, conceptually): you already know that turning\n  text\
      \ into discrete units is a lossy design choice. Here you build a *retrieval*\n\
      \  tokenizer — lowercase, split, optionally stem/stop — which is simpler than\
      \ BPE but\n  makes the same point: what you index determines what you can find.\n\
      - **Python fundamentals**: dictionaries, sets, `collections.Counter`/`defaultdict`,\n\
      \  and comfort writing a small class with clear method boundaries. No ML framework,\n\
      \  no PyTorch, no GPU.\n- **A little information theory / probability**, informally:\
      \ you should be\n  comfortable reading a log, a ratio, and the phrase \"how\
      \ surprising is this term.\"\n  The BM25 IDF term is derived below, so nothing\
      \ is assumed as a black box.\n- **No prior exposure needed** to inverted indexes,\
      \ TF-IDF, BM25, or IR evaluation\n  metrics — that is the point of this chapter,\
      \ and the arc.\n\n## What you're building\n\nA self-contained, dependency-light\
      \ lexical search engine plus an evaluation\nharness that scores it against a\
      \ labeled corpus. The whole thing is pure Python\nstandard library — the only\
      \ third-party packages you may reach for are `pytest`\n(tests) and, optionally,\
      \ `matplotlib` (to draw the parameter-sweep curve). **No\n`rank_bm25`, no `whoosh`,\
      \ no `sklearn`, no `elasticsearch`.** Reaching for those\ndefeats the week.\n\
      \nThree layers, built bottom-up:\n\n1. **Text → terms.** A deterministic analyzer\
      \ that normalizes and tokenizes text\n   the same way at index time and query\
      \ time.\n2. **Terms → index.** An inverted index mapping each term to the documents\
      \ that\n   contain it and the per-document frequency, plus the corpus statistics\
      \ BM25\n   needs (document lengths, average length, document frequency per term).\n\
      3. **Query → ranking.** A scorer that, given a query, produces the top-$k$\n\
      \   documents by BM25 score, and an evaluator that turns rankings into Recall@k\n\
      \   and MRR against relevance judgments.\n\n### Suggested file structure\n\n\
      ```\nweek13-bm25/\n├── README.md\n├── pyproject.toml            # or requirements.txt;\
      \ stdlib + pytest (+ matplotlib)\n├── .env.example              # only if you\
      \ add any config; no secrets this chapter\n├── data/\n│   ├── corpus.jsonl \
      \         # {\"doc_id\": \"...\", \"text\": \"...\"}\n│   ├── queries.jsonl\
      \         # {\"query_id\": \"...\", \"text\": \"...\"}\n│   └── qrels.tsv  \
      \           # query_id  doc_id  relevance(0/1)\n├── bm25/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n\
      │   ├── analyzer.py           # normalize + tokenize (index & query use the\
      \ SAME one)\n│   ├── index.py              # InvertedIndex: postings + corpus\
      \ statistics\n│   ├── scorer.py             # BM25 scoring over the index\n\
      │   └── evaluate.py           # Recall@k, MRR, parameter sweep\n├── scripts/\n\
      │   ├── build_index.py        # data/ -> in-memory (or pickled) index\n│   ├──\
      \ search.py             # CLI: query string -> ranked doc_ids\n│   └── run_eval.py\
      \           # produces the benchmark table + sweep\n└── tests/\n    ├── test_analyzer.py\n\
      \    ├── test_index.py\n    └── test_scorer.py\n```\n\n## The theory you need\n\
      \n### From term counts to TF-IDF\n\nLexical retrieval scores a document $d$\
      \ against a query $q$ by summing a\nper-term contribution over the query terms\
      \ $t \\in q$:\n\n$$\\text{score}(q, d) = \\sum_{t \\in q} w(t, d).$$\n\nThe\
      \ whole game is choosing $w$. Three intuitions constrain it:\n\n1. **Term frequency\
      \ (TF).** A document that mentions the query term more is more\n   likely about\
      \ it — but with *diminishing returns*. The 10th occurrence of\n   \"retrieval\"\
      \ tells you far less than the 1st.\n2. **Inverse document frequency (IDF).**\
      \ A term that appears in almost every\n   document (e.g. \"the\") is nearly\
      \ useless for discrimination; a rare term is\n   highly informative. Weight\
      \ terms by how *surprising* they are corpus-wide.\n3. **Length normalization.**\
      \ A long document accumulates term matches just by\n   being long. Without correction,\
      \ verbose documents win unfairly.\n\nClassic TF-IDF multiplies a (often log-dampened)\
      \ term frequency by an IDF factor.\nIt captures intuitions 1 and 2 but handles\
      \ saturation and length only crudely.\nBM25 is the principled fix.\n\n### BM25,\
      \ term by term\n\nFor a query $q$ and document $d$, BM25 scores:\n\n$$\\text{BM25}(q,\
      \ d) = \\sum_{t \\in q} \\text{IDF}(t)\\cdot\n\\frac{f(t, d)\\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(t,\
      \ d) + k_1\\left(1 - b + b\\,\\dfrac{|d|}{\\text{avgdl}}\\right)},$$\n\nwhere\n\
      \n- $f(t, d)$ is the raw frequency of term $t$ in document $d$;\n- $|d|$ is\
      \ the document length in tokens and $\\text{avgdl}$ the average document\n \
      \ length over the corpus;\n- $k_1 \\ge 0$ controls **term-frequency saturation**\
      \ — how quickly extra\n  occurrences stop helping (typical range $1.2\\text{–}2.0$);\
      \ as $k_1 \\to \\infty$\n  the term becomes linear in $f$, and at $k_1 = 0$\
      \ TF is ignored entirely;\n- $b \\in [0, 1]$ controls **length normalization**\
      \ — $b = 0$ disables it, $b = 1$\n  fully normalizes by relative length (typical\
      \ default $0.75$).\n\nThe IDF term is the Robertson–Sparck-Jones form:\n\n$$\\\
      text{IDF}(t) = \\ln\\!\\left(\\frac{N - n_t + 0.5}{n_t + 0.5} + 1\\right),$$\n\
      \nwhere $N$ is the number of documents and $n_t$ the number of documents\ncontaining\
      \ $t$. The $+1$ inside the log keeps the IDF non-negative even for very\ncommon\
      \ terms (the older form could go negative). Derive this once and you will\n\
      recognize it in every search system afterward.\n\nTwo properties worth internalizing\
      \ before you code:\n\n- The saturation term is a **rational function of $f$**\
      \ that asymptotes at\n  $\\text{IDF}(t)\\cdot(k_1 + 1)$. Sketch it for a couple\
      \ of $k_1$ values —\n  seeing the curve flatten explains why BM25 beats raw\

      ,|d|/\\text{avgdl}$ factor in the\n  denominator; a document exactly at average\
      \ length is unaffected regardless of\n  $b$. This is a good invariant to assert\
      \ in a test.\n\n### The inverted index\n\nYou never score every document against\
      \ every query term by scanning the corpus.\nThe **inverted index** maps each\
      \ term to a *postings list* — the documents that\ncontain it and the frequency\
