  - content: "Embed the same documents and queries with a pinned small model, or use\
      \ deterministic fixture vectors for offline checks. Implement exact cosine search\
      \ before studying a small HNSW or IVF mechanism. Use a maintained index for\
      \ the realistic path and separate algorithm understanding from production implementation.\
      \ Explain embedding normalization, dimensions, distance choice, and the loss\
      \ of neighbors caused by approximation.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation\
      \ and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are\
      \ proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured\
      \ results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected\
      \ components in the optional course project.\n\n## Overview\n\nEvery vector\
      \ database runs an approximate nearest-neighbor algorithm under the\nhood, and\
      \ building one removes the mystery from all of them. This chapter you\nimplement\
      \ HNSW (or IVF) by hand over a dense embedding index and compare recall\nand\
      \ latency against brute-force cosine search across a sweep of index-size and\n\
      search-parameter settings (`ef` or `nprobe`). The resulting recall-versus-latency\n\
      curves make the approximate-nearest-neighbor tradeoff explicit at every setting\
      \ in\nthe sweep, and compressing the vectors themselves — int8/binary quantization\
      \ and\nMatryoshka truncation to a shorter prefix — adds a second recall-versus-memory\n\
      axis measured on the same index. This is the same tradeoff every vector database\n\
      product page is quietly making a default choice about on your behalf.\n\n##\
      \ Prerequisites\n\n- **Embeddings as vectors.** You should be comfortable that\
      \ a text (or image)\n  embedding is a fixed-length dense vector, and that semantic\
      \ similarity is\n  measured by an inner product or cosine — i.e. nearby vectors\
      \ mean similar\n  meaning. You do not need to have trained an embedding model.\n\
      - **Retrieval evaluation.** The `recall@k` and MRR notions from the sparse-retrieval\n\
      \  week of this arc carry over directly. Here, though, \"relevant\" is defined\
      \ by the\n  exact brute-force top-k rather than a human label — you are measuring\
      \ how well the\n  approximation reproduces the *exact* answer, not how good\
      \ the embeddings are.\n- **Complexity intuition.** You should be able to reason\
      \ informally about\n  $O(n)$ vs. sublinear search and why a linear scan over\
      \ millions of vectors is the\n  thing we are trying to avoid.\n- **Python numerics.**\
      \ Comfort with NumPy vectorized operations (broadcasting,\n  `argsort`, `argpartition`,\
      \ dtype control) is assumed; the whole week lives in\n  NumPy with no ANN library.\n\
      \n## What you are building\n\nA small, self-contained ANN library plus a benchmark\
      \ harness. Concretely:\n\n1. A **brute-force exact index** — the ground-truth\
      \ oracle every measurement is\n   scored against.\n2. **One ANN index** — choose\
      \ either **HNSW** (a navigable small-world graph) or\n   **IVF** (inverted file\
      \ / coarse quantization). Pick one and do it well; the\n   \"or\" in the title\
      \ is a real choice, not a request for both.\n3. A **vector compression layer**\
      \ — int8 scalar quantization, 1-bit binary\n   quantization, and Matryoshka\
      \ prefix truncation — that plugs underneath the index\n   so you can measure\
      \ a second, memory-oriented tradeoff on the *same* index.\n4. A **benchmark\
      \ harness** that sweeps parameters and emits the recall/latency/memory\n   tables\
      \ and plots that constitute this chapter's checkable artifact.\n\nYou do **not**\
      \ need to train embeddings. Embed a small corpus once with any free\nlocal model\
      \ (e.g. a `sentence-transformers` MiniLM, ~384-dim) or even a cached\n`.npy`\
      \ of precomputed vectors, and treat that matrix as your fixed dataset.\n\n###\
      \ File structure\n\n```\nweek14-ann-search/\n├── README.md\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── .env.example              # only if you fetch embeddings from an API; prefer\
      \ local\n├── src/\n│   └── annsearch/\n│       ├── __init__.py\n│       ├──\
      \ dataset.py        # load/embed corpus -> (N, d) float32 matrix + queries\n\
      │       ├── distance.py       # cosine / L2 / dot; normalization helpers\n│\
      \       ├── exact.py          # brute-force oracle (ground-truth top-k)\n│ \
      \      ├── hnsw.py           # OR ivf.py — the one ANN index you chose\n│  \
      \     ├── quantize.py       # int8 / binary / Matryoshka codecs\n│       ├──\
      \ metrics.py        # recall@k, MRR, latency timing, memory accounting\n│  \
      \     └── protocols.py      # the shared VectorIndex interface\n├── scripts/\n\
      │   ├── build_dataset.py      # embed once, cache to data/*.npy\n│   └── run_benchmark.py\
      \      # sweep params -> results/*.csv + plots\n├── tests/\n│   ├── test_exact.py\n\
      │   ├── test_index_recall.py  # ANN recall must clear a floor at high ef/nprobe\n\
      │   └── test_quantize.py      # round-trip + monotonic recall/memory checks\n\
      ├── data/                     # gitignored embeddings cache\n└── results/  \
      \                # gitignored CSVs + figures\n```\n\nKeep `data/` and `results/`\
      \ out of git; commit the code and this README, not the\nartifacts.\n\n## Core\
      \ concepts\n\n### The problem, stated precisely\n\nGiven a dataset of $N$ vectors\
      \ $\\{x_i\\}_{i=1}^N \\subset \\mathbb{R}^d$ and a query\n$q \\in \\mathbb{R}^d$,\
      \ exact k-NN returns\n\n$$\\text{top-}k(q) = \\text*{arg\\,min}_{S:\\,|S|=k}\
      \ \\sum_{i \\in S} \\text{dist}(q, x_i).$$\n\nFor cosine similarity, if you\
      \ **L2-normalize every vector once** at load time, then\n\n$$\\cos(q, x) = \\\
      frac{q \\cdot x}{\\lVert q\\rVert\\,\\lVert x\\rVert} = \\hat q \\cdot \\hat\
      \ x,$$\n\nso cosine ranking reduces to a plain dot product and \"nearest\" (largest\
      \ cosine) and\n\"smallest L2 distance\" agree. Normalizing up front is the single\
      \ most useful\nsimplification this chapter — do it in `dataset.py` and let the\
      \ rest of the code assume\nunit vectors.\n\nBrute force computes all $N$ dot\
      \ products in $O(Nd)$ per query. ANN buys sublinear\n*expected* query time by\
      \ only ever looking at a small, cleverly chosen subset of the\n$N$ vectors —\
      \ at the cost of sometimes missing a true neighbor. **Recall is the\nprice you\
      \ pay for speed**, and quantifying that exchange rate is the entire point.\n\
      \n### Recall, defined against the oracle\n\nLet $A_k(q)$ be the set the ANN\
      \ index returns and $G_k(q)$ the exact top-k from the\noracle. Recall@k for\
      \ a query is\n\n$$\\text{recall@}k(q) = \\frac{|A_k(q) \\cap G_k(q)|}{k},$$\n\
      \naveraged over the query set. Note this is *approximation* recall, not\nretrieval-quality\
      \ recall: a perfect ANN index scores 1.0 even if the embeddings are\nbad, because\
      \ the oracle is computed from the same embeddings.\n\n### Path A — HNSW (a navigable\
      \ small-world graph)\n\nHNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph. Each node\
      \ exists on layer 0 and,\nprobabilistically, on some number of higher layers;\
      \ higher layers are sparse and act\nas an express skip-list over the space.\
      \ Search enters at the top layer's entry\npoint, greedily hops toward the query,\
      \ then descends a layer and repeats, doing a\nbest-first beam search on layer\
      \ 0.\n\nKey ideas to internalize:\n\n- **Layer assignment.** A node's maximum\
      \ layer is drawn as\n  $\\ell = \\lfloor -\\ln(U)\\cdot m_L \\rfloor$ with $U\
      \ \\sim \\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and\n  $m_L = 1/\\ln M$. This geometric decay\
      \ makes the expected graph height $O(\\log N)$.\n- **Neighbor selection.** On\
      \ insertion you connect a new node to up to $M$ neighbors\n  per layer, chosen\
      \ from a candidate pool of size `ef_construction` using a\n  heuristic that\
      \ keeps the graph *navigable* (diverse directions) rather than merely\n  keeping\
      \ the $M$ closest — the diversity heuristic is what prevents clustered dead\n\
      \  ends.\n- **Search.** A single knob, `ef` (search beam width), trades recall\
      \ for latency:\n  larger `ef` explores more of the graph. Expected search cost\
      \ is roughly\n  $O(\\text{ef}\\cdot \\log N \\cdot d)$.\n\n### Path B — IVF\
      \ (inverted file / coarse quantization)\n\nIVF partitions the space into `nlist`\
      \ Voronoi cells by running k-means over a sample\nof the data; each cell has\
      \ a centroid and an inverted list of the vectors assigned\nto it. At query time\
      \ you find the `nprobe` closest centroids and scan only those\ncells' lists.\n\
      \nKey ideas to internalize:\n\n- **Training.** k-means over (a sample of) the\
      \ dataset yields `nlist` centroids;\n  assignment is one $\\arg\\min$ over centroids\
      \ per vector.\n- **The single knob.** `nprobe` (how many cells to scan) trades\
      \ recall for latency,\n  exactly analogous to HNSW's `ef`. With `nprobe = nlist`\
      \ you degrade to brute force.\n- **Cost.** Query cost is roughly $O(\\text{nlist}\\\
      cdot d)$ to rank centroids plus\n  $O(\\tfrac{\\text{nprobe}}{\\text{nlist}}\
      \ N d)$ to scan the probed lists — the second\n  term is the payoff: you touch\
      \ a `nprobe/nlist` fraction of the data.\n\nA common heuristic is $\\text{nlist}\
      \ \\approx \\sqrt{N}$; treat that as a starting\npoint in your sweep, not a\
      \ law.\n\n### Vector compression (the second axis)\n\nIndependent of *which*\
      \ vectors you visit, you can shrink *how big each vector is*:\n\n- **int8 scalar\
      \ quantization.** Map each float32 component into 256 buckets via a\n  per-dimension\
      \ (or global) scale and zero-point:\n  $q = \\text{round}(x/s) + z$. Storage\
      \ drops 4× (32→8 bits). Distances are\n  computed in int8/int32 with a scale\
      \ correction. Expect a small recall dip.\n- **Binary (1-bit) quantization.**\
      \ Keep only the sign of each component;\n  similarity becomes Hamming distance\
      \ (a `popcount` on XORed bit-vectors),\n  ~32× smaller and extremely fast, with\
      \ a larger recall dip — often used as a fast\n  *first-stage* filter before\
      \ an exact re-rank.\n- **Matryoshka truncation.** If the embedding model is\
      \ Matryoshka-trained (or you\n  just accept the degradation), keep only the\
      \ first $d' < d$ dimensions. Storage and\n  compute scale as $d'/d$. Recall\
      \ degrades gracefully with $d'$.\n\nEach codec is a pair of functions — encode\
      \ the dataset, and score a query against\nthe encoded store — so it can slot\
      \ under the exact index *and* the ANN index without\nchanging either.\n\n##\
      \ Stub interfaces\n\nA single protocol lets the harness treat every index the\
      \ same way.\n\n```python\n# src/annsearch/protocols.py\nfrom typing import Protocol,\
      \ runtime_checkable\nimport numpy as np\n\n@runtime_checkable\nclass VectorIndex(Protocol):\n\
      \    \"\"\"Any index the benchmark can score: build once, query many.\"\"\"\n\
      \n    def build(self, vectors: np.ndarray) -> None:\n        \"\"\"Index an\

      \ TODO\n\n    def query(self, q: np.ndarray, k: int) -> np.ndarray:\n      \
      \  \"\"\"Return indices of the approximate top-k for a single (d,) query.\"\"\
      \"\n        ...\n\n    @property\n    def memory_bytes(self) -> int:\n     \
      \   \"\"\"Bytes held by the index payload (vectors + structure).\"\"\"\n   \
      \     ...\n```\n\n```python\n# src/annsearch/exact.py\nimport numpy as np\n\n\
      class ExactIndex:\n    \"\"\"Brute-force cosine/dot oracle. This defines ground\

      \ / ivf.py)\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\nimport numpy as np\n\n\

    lab_and_evidence: "## How to build it (milestones)\n\n1. **Dataset + oracle.**\
      \ Embed (or load) a small corpus — start at $N \\approx 10\\text{k}$,\n   $d\

      \ invariant: as the knob → its max, ANN recall → the exact oracle.\n3. **The\

      \   record recall@k and per-query latency, and write tidy long-format CSV to\n\

      \ knee sits.\n\nScope guard: one ANN algorithm, three codecs, one small dataset.\
      \ Resist adding PQ,\nOPQ, GPU kernels, or a second graph type — those are stretch\
      \ goals, not the week.\n\n## Checkable artifact — Benchmarks\n\nThe deliverable\
      \ that demonstrates the abstract's claims is a benchmark report with\ntwo axes,\
      \ all scored against the brute-force oracle on the same embeddings.\n\n**Axis\
      \ 1 — recall vs. latency (the ANN tradeoff).**\n\n- Sweep the single search\
      \ knob (`ef` for HNSW, `nprobe` for IVF) across ~6–8 values\n  from \"cheap/low-recall\"\
      \ to \"expensive/near-exact.\"\n- Repeat for ~3 dataset sizes $N$ (e.g. 1k /\
      \ 10k / 50k) to show how the curve shifts\n  as the index grows.\n- **Expected\

  - content: "Inspect queries where lexical and dense ranking disagree. Combine candidates\
      \ through reciprocal rank fusion and apply a small cross-encoder or recorded\
      \ reranker. Separate candidate recall from final ranking quality. Hold the corpus,\
      \ queries, and labels fixed while changing one stage, and account for the latency\
      \ added by reranking.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment\
      \ to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab\
      \ artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results already\
      \ exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## Overview\n\nSparse and dense retrieval\
      \ fail on different queries, and combining them — then\nreranking — is the actual\
      \ production pattern, not either technique alone. This\nweek fuses a BM25 sparse\
      \ retriever and an ANN dense retriever via reciprocal rank\nfusion, then reranks\
      \ the merged candidate list with a cross-encoder. Recall@k and\nnDCG are measured\
      \ for BM25-only, ANN-only, hybrid, and hybrid-plus-rerank on the\nsame query\
      \ set, isolating each stage's individual contribution. The results show\nprecisely\
      \ why hybrid retrieval beats either method alone, and what a reranker\nbuys\
      \ on top of fusion by itself.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- **Sparse retrieval (Week\
      \ 13, conceptually):** you understand an inverted index\n  and BM25 scoring\
      \ — term frequency saturation, IDF weighting, length\n  normalization — and\
      \ can produce a ranked list of `(doc_id, score)` for a query.\n  You re-expose\
      \ that here behind a `Retriever` interface; you do not import last\n  week's\
      \ code.\n- **Dense/ANN retrieval (Week 14, conceptually):** you understand embedding\
      \ a\n  query and documents into a shared vector space and retrieving by approximate\n\
      \  nearest neighbor (cosine/inner product). You wrap it behind the same interface.\n\
      - **Ranking metrics:** comfort with the idea of graded relevance and rank-aware\n\
      \  evaluation. We define Recall@k and nDCG@k below from scratch — no prior formula\n\
      \  memorization assumed.\n- **Python tooling:** virtualenv/uv, `numpy`, and\
      \ running a small local model via\n  `sentence-transformers` (or an equivalent\
      \ cross-encoder). No GPU, no cloud\n  account.\n\n## The problem: complementary\
      \ failure modes\n\nBM25 matches on **lexical overlap**. It is unbeatable when\
      \ the query and the\nanswer share rare exact tokens (identifiers, error codes,\
      \ proper nouns) and\nblind when they do not: a query for *\"car\"* will not\
      \ rank a document that only\never says *\"automobile\"*. Dense retrieval matches\
      \ on **semantic proximity** in\nembedding space. It bridges the *car/automobile*\
      \ gap but drifts on exact-token\nqueries, happily returning a topically-adjacent\
      \ doc while missing the one that\nliterally contains the requested error string.\n\
      \nThe key empirical fact this chapter is built on: **the two retrievers fail\
      \ on\ndifferent queries.** Their per-query error sets overlap far less than\
      \ either's\noverall miss rate would suggest, which is exactly the condition\
      \ under which\ncombining rankings helps. Fusion exploits *disagreement*; if\
      \ the two retrievers\nwere redundant, fusing them would gain nothing.\n\nReranking\
      \ is a second, orthogonal lever. Both retrievers score a query against a\ndocument\
      \ **independently** — the query is embedded (or tokenized) once, the\ndocument\
      \ once, and a cheap similarity combines them. That independence is what\nmakes\
      \ retrieval scale to millions of documents, but it throws away cross-token\n\
      interaction. A **cross-encoder** reranker feeds the query and one candidate\n\
      document *together* through a transformer, so every query token can attend to\n\
      every document token. It is far too expensive to run over the whole corpus,\
      \ but\nperfect for rescoring a short fused candidate list. So the pipeline is\
      \ a funnel:\ncheap recall-oriented retrieval widens the net, expensive precision-oriented\n\
      reranking sharpens the top.\n\n## Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)\n\nWe fuse by\
      \ **rank**, not by raw score. BM25 scores and cosine similarities live\non different,\
      \ non-comparable scales; normalizing them (min-max, z-score) is\nfragile and\
      \ query-dependent. RRF sidesteps this by using only each document's\n*position*\
      \ in each retriever's ranked list.\n\nFor a document $d$, given a set of retrievers\
      \ $R$ where $r(d)$ is the (1-based)\nrank of $d$ in retriever $r$'s list, the\
      \ fused score is\n\n$$\n\\text{RRF}(d) = \\sum_{r \\in R} \\frac{1}{k + r(d)}\n\
      $$\n\nwith $k$ a smoothing constant (Cormack et al. use $k = 60$; treat it as\
      \ a\ntunable). A document absent from a retriever's list contributes $0$ from\
      \ that\nretriever (equivalently, $r(d) = \\infty$). Properties worth internalizing\
      \ before\nyou implement it:\n\n- **Scale-free:** only ranks enter, so BM25 vs.\
      \ cosine scale mismatch is\n  irrelevant.\n- **Top-heavy but forgiving:** the\
      \ $\\tfrac{1}{k+r}$ curve rewards high ranks yet\n  the $k$ offset keeps rank\
      \ 1 from dominating rank 2 outright, so a document\n  ranked *decently by both*\
      \ retrievers can beat one ranked *first by only one*.\n  That is precisely the\
      \ hybrid win you want.\n- **Larger $k$ → flatter weighting** (ranks matter less,\
      \ presence matters more);\n  smaller $k$ → sharper preference for top ranks.\
      \ Your ablation should sweep it.\n\nYou will also want a **weighted** variant,\
      \ $\\sum_r \\tfrac{w_r}{k + r(d)}$, to ask\nwhether tilting toward the stronger\
      \ single retriever helps — but start unweighted.\n\n## Cross-encoder reranking\n\
      \nGiven the fused top-$N$ candidates, score each `(query, document)` pair with\
      \ a\ncross-encoder that returns a single relevance logit, then sort descending\
      \ and\nkeep the top-$k$. Formally, for candidate set $C$,\n\n$$\n\\text{score}(q,\
      \ d) = f_\\theta(q, d), \\qquad d \\in C,\n$$\n\nwhere $f_\\theta$ is the cross-encoder.\
      \ Unlike the bi-encoder retrievers,\n$f_\\theta$ cannot be precomputed per document\
      \ — it must see the query. Cost is\n$O(N)$ forward passes per query, which is\
      \ why $N$ (the fusion depth handed to the\nreranker) is a first-class knob:\
      \ too small and the reranker can't fix retrieval\nmisses; too large and latency\
      \ balloons. A small, CPU-friendly model such as a\nMiniLM cross-encoder (`cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`\
      \ or similar) is the\nright default.\n\n## What you're building\n\nA small retrieval\
      \ library plus an evaluation driver, structured so each stage is\nswappable\
      \ and independently measurable.\n\n```\nweek15-hybrid-rerank/\n├── README.md\n\
      ├── pyproject.toml\n├── .env.example              # only if you optionally cache/download\
      \ a model dir\n├── data/\n│   ├── corpus.jsonl          # {\"doc_id\": ...,\
      \ \"text\": ...}\n│   └── qrels.jsonl           # {\"query_id\": ..., \"query\"\
      : ..., \"relevant\": [doc_id, ...]}\n├── src/\n│   └── hybrid/\n│       ├──\
      \ __init__.py\n│       ├── types.py          # Doc, Query, ScoredDoc, Qrels\
      \ dataclasses/protocols\n│       ├── retrievers.py     # Retriever protocol,\
      \ BM25Retriever, DenseRetriever\n│       ├── fusion.py         # reciprocal_rank_fusion(...)\n\
      │       ├── rerank.py         # CrossEncoderReranker\n│       ├── pipeline.py\
      \       # composes retrieve → fuse → rerank\n│       └── metrics.py        #\
      \ recall_at_k, ndcg_at_k\n├── scripts/\n│   ├── build_index.py        # embed\
      \ corpus + build sparse/dense indexes\n│   └── evaluate.py           # runs\
      \ the 4 configs, prints the results table\n└── tests/\n    └── test_metrics.py\
      \       # tiny hand-checked fixtures for the metrics\n```\n\nYou will need a\
      \ **small labeled dataset**: a corpus of a few hundred to a few\nthousand short\
      \ documents and a query set with known relevant `doc_id`s. A slice\nof BEIR\
      \ (e.g. SciFact or NFCorpus), a subset of the MS MARCO dev set, or a\nhand-labeled\
      \ set over your own docs all work. Keep it small enough to run the\nwhole eval\
      \ on CPU in a couple of minutes.\n\n### Stub interfaces\n\nSignatures and shells\
      \ only — the bodies are yours.\n\n```python\n# types.py\nfrom dataclasses import\
      \ dataclass\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass ScoredDoc:\n    doc_id: str\n\
      \    score: float\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Query:\n    query_id: str\n\
      \    text: str\n    relevant: frozenset[str]   # gold doc_ids for this query\n\
      ```\n\n```python\n# retrievers.py\nfrom typing import Protocol\nfrom .types\
      \ import ScoredDoc\n\nclass Retriever(Protocol):\n    def retrieve(self, query:\
      \ str, k: int) -> list[ScoredDoc]:\n        \"\"\"Return the top-k docs ranked\
      \ best-first. Scores are retriever-local\n        and NOT comparable across\
      \ retrievers — fusion must use ranks, not these.\"\"\"\n        ...\n\nclass\
      \ BM25Retriever:\n    \"\"\"Sparse lexical retriever over an inverted index\
      \ (Week 13, re-derived).\"\"\"\n    def __init__(self, corpus: list[tuple[str,\
      \ str]]) -> None:\n        # TODO: build inverted index, doc lengths, IDF table\n\
      \        ...\n    def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int) -> list[ScoredDoc]:\n\
      \        ...  # TODO: BM25 score, sort desc, truncate to k\n\nclass DenseRetriever:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Dense ANN retriever over an embedding index (Week 14, re-derived).\"\
      \"\"\n    def __init__(self, corpus: list[tuple[str, str]], model_name: str)\
      \ -> None:\n        # TODO: embed corpus, build ANN (or brute-force) index\n\
      \        ...\n    def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int) -> list[ScoredDoc]:\n\
      \        ...  # TODO: embed query, ANN search, return top-k\n```\n\n```python\n\
      # fusion.py\nfrom .types import ScoredDoc\n\ndef reciprocal_rank_fusion(\n \
      \   ranked_lists: list[list[ScoredDoc]],\n    k: int = 60,\n    weights: list[float]\
      \ | None = None,\n) -> list[ScoredDoc]:\n    \"\"\"Fuse multiple ranked lists\
      \ by RRF: score(d) = sum_r w_r / (k + rank_r(d)).\n    Uses only ranks. Missing\
      \ docs contribute 0. Returns one merged best-first list\n    whose .score is\
      \ the RRF score.\"\"\"\n    ...  # TODO\n```\n\n```python\n# rerank.py\nfrom\
      \ .types import ScoredDoc\n\nclass CrossEncoderReranker:\n    def __init__(self,\
      \ model_name: str) -> None:\n        # TODO: load a small CPU cross-encoder\n\
      \        ...\n    def rerank(self, query: str, candidates: list[ScoredDoc],\n\
      \               corpus_text: dict[str, str], top_k: int) -> list[ScoredDoc]:\n\
      \        \"\"\"Score each (query, doc_text) pair jointly, sort desc, keep top_k.\n\
      \        .score becomes the cross-encoder logit.\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO\n\
      ```\n\n```python\n# metrics.py\ndef recall_at_k(retrieved: list[str], relevant:\
      \ set[str], k: int) -> float:\n    ...  # TODO: |retrieved[:k] ∩ relevant| /\
      \ |relevant|\n\ndef ndcg_at_k(retrieved: list[str], relevant: set[str], k: int)\
      \ -> float:\n    ...  # TODO: DCG@k / IDCG@k with binary gains\n```\n\n```python\n\
      # pipeline.py\nfrom .types import ScoredDoc\nfrom .retrievers import Retriever\n\
      from .rerank import CrossEncoderReranker\n\ndef hybrid_search(\n    query: str,\n\
      \    retrievers: list[Retriever],\n    fuse_depth: int,          # how many\
      \ to pull from each retriever before fusion\n    reranker: CrossEncoderReranker\
      \ | None,\n    corpus_text: dict[str, str],\n    final_k: int,\n) -> list[ScoredDoc]:\n\
      \    \"\"\"retrieve from each → RRF fuse → (optional) rerank top fuse_depth\
      \ → top final_k.\"\"\"\n    ...  # TODO\n```\n\n## The core idea: retrieve then\
      \ rerank — Candidate Generation vs. Re-ranking Split\n\nRecommendation at scale\
      \ is a *funnel*. A catalog of $N$ items is too large to score\neach one carefully,\
      \ so production systems split the work in two:\n\n1. **Candidate generation\
      \ (retrieval).** A cheap model narrows $N$ items down to a\n   small candidate\
      \ set of size $k \\ll N$ (say $k = 50$). It must be fast and have\n   high *recall*\
      \ — the right items need to survive this stage — but it does not need\n   to\
      \ get the fine-grained order right.\n2. **Re-ranking.** An expensive, high-quality\
      \ model scores only those $k$ candidates\n   and produces the final short ordered\
      \ list of size $m$ (say $m = 5$). It optimizes\n   *precision at the top* and,\
      \ in our case, also writes a short natural-language\n   explanation per pick.\n\
      \nThe whole point of the split is asymmetric cost. Let $c_\\text{gen}$ be the\
      \ per-item\ncost of candidate generation and $c_\\text{rank}$ the per-item cost\
      \ of re-ranking.\nThe two-stage pipeline costs roughly\n\n$$\nC_\\text{split}(N)\
      \ \\;=\\; \\underbrace{c_\\text{gen} \\cdot N}_{\\text{cheap, over all items}}\
      \ \\;+\\; \\underbrace{c_\\text{rank} \\cdot k}_{\\text{expensive, over }k\\\
      text{ only}},\n$$\n\nand with an ANN index the retrieval term is sublinear in\
      \ practice ($\\approx c_\\text{gen}\\cdot\\log N$ per query after a one-time\
      \ index build), so the expensive term is *constant in $N$*. Contrast that with\
      \ asking the LLM to recommend directly from the whole catalog:\n\n$$\nC_\\text{direct}(N)\
      \ \\;=\\; c_\\text{rank} \\cdot N,\n$$\n\nwhich grows linearly with the catalog\
      \ and, well before it gets expensive, hits a\nhard wall: the catalog stops fitting\
      \ in the context window at all.\n\n### Why the direct baseline breaks (not just\
      \ gets pricey)\n\nThere are three distinct failure modes, and your benchmark\
      \ should be able to\nattribute the collapse to them:\n\n- **Context overflow.**\
      \ At some $N$ the serialized catalog exceeds the model's\n  context window and\
      \ the request is impossible without truncation — and truncation\n  silently\
      \ deletes candidates.\n- **Lost-in-the-middle.** Even below the limit, LLMs\
      \ attend unevenly across a long\n  context; relevant items buried in the middle\
      \ of a huge list get systematically\n  under-ranked. Accuracy degrades *before*\
      \ you hit the token ceiling.\n- **Cost and latency blowup.** $C_\\text{direct}(N)$\
      \ is linear and paid *on every\n  query*, while the split pays the big cost\
      \ once at index-build time.\n\nThe crossover catalog size $N^\\*$ — where the\
      \ split's accuracy pulls decisively\nahead of direct prompting (or where direct\
      \ becomes infeasible) — is the number this\nweek exists to measure.\n\n### The\
      \ two-tower retriever\n\nCandidate generation uses a **two-tower** (dual-encoder)\
      \ model: one tower embeds the\n*query* (a user profile, a \"more like this\"\
      \ seed item, or a free-text request), a\nseparate tower embeds each *item*,\
      \ and relevance is the similarity of the two\nembeddings — typically cosine\
      \ or dot product:\n\n$$\ns(u, i) \\;=\\; \\frac{f_u(u) \\cdot f_i(i)}{\\lVert\
      \ f_u(u)\\rVert \\, \\lVert f_i(i)\\rVert}.\n$$\n\nThe critical property is\
      \ that $f_i$ is **query-independent**: every item embedding is\ncomputed *once*,\
      \ offline, and stored in an ANN index. At query time you embed only\nthe query\
      \ and do an approximate nearest-neighbor search. That is what makes the\nretrieval\
      \ term sublinear and what the direct baseline cannot do — the LLM must\nre-read\
      \ every item on every request.\n\nYou do not need to *train* the two towers\
      \ this chapter. Use a hosted or local\nsentence-embedding model as both towers\
      \ (a shared encoder is a valid degenerate\ntwo-tower), embedding a text rendering\
      \ of each item. The mechanism under test is the\n*architectural split*, not\
      \ embedding training (that is Week 13's subject)."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Evaluation metrics\n\nDefine both metrics yourself; do not\
      \ pull them from a library — computing them by\nhand is half the point of the\
      \ eval.\n\n**Recall@k** — did we retrieve the relevant documents at all, within\
      \ the top $k$?\nFor a query $q$ with relevant set $\\text{Rel}(q)$ and retrieved\
      \ top-$k$ set\n$\\text{Ret}_k(q)$:\n\n$$\n\\text{Recall@}k = \\frac{|\\text{Ret}_k(q)\
      \ \\cap \\text{Rel}(q)|}{|\\text{Rel}(q)|}\n$$\n\naveraged over queries. This\
      \ is a recall-oriented, order-insensitive check — the\nright lens for the retrieval\
      \ stages.\n\n**nDCG@k** — did we rank the relevant documents *high*? With graded\
      \ relevance\n$rel_i$ at rank $i$ (binary relevance is fine to start; $rel_i\
      \ \\in \\{0,1\\}$):\n\n$$\n\\text{DCG@}k = \\sum_{i=1}^{k} \\frac{2^{rel_i}\
      \ - 1}{\\log_2(i + 1)},\n\\qquad\n\\text{nDCG@}k = \\frac{\\text{DCG@}k}{\\\
      text{IDCG@}k}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\text{IDCG@}k$ is the DCG of the ideal ordering\
      \ (all relevant docs sorted\nto the top). nDCG is order-sensitive and thus the\
      \ metric that *rewards\nreranking* — a stage can leave Recall@k unchanged while\
      \ moving relevant docs\nupward, which only nDCG will see. Report both so the\
      \ two effects separate cleanly.\n\n## Build path\n\n1. **Data + metrics first.**\
      \ Load the corpus and qrels into `types`, implement\n   `recall_at_k` and `ndcg_at_k`,\
      \ and lock them down with `tests/test_metrics.py`\n   on tiny fixtures you can\
      \ verify by hand (e.g. one relevant doc at rank 3 →\n   known nDCG). Metrics\
      \ you don't trust will silently invalidate every later\n   number.\n2. **Two\
      \ retrievers behind one interface.** Re-derive BM25 and a dense retriever\n\
      \   (brute-force cosine is a fine stand-in for the ANN index this chapter —\
      \ the ANN\n   *tradeoff* was Week 14's subject; here the retriever just needs\
      \ to return a\n   ranked list). Confirm each runs standalone and its Recall@k\
      \ is sane.\n3. **RRF fusion.** Implement `reciprocal_rank_fusion` and eyeball\
      \ a couple of\n   queries: a fused doc that both retrievers ranked mid-list\
      \ should surface above\n   a doc only one retriever ranked first.\n4. **Cross-encoder\
      \ rerank.** Add the reranker over the fused top-$N$. Watch\n   latency as a\
      \ function of $N$.\n5. **Evaluation driver.** `scripts/evaluate.py` runs all\
      \ four configurations over\n   the query set and prints the results table.\n\
      \n## Evaluation (the checkable artifact)\n\nThe deliverable that proves the\
      \ abstract's claims is a single **results table**\ncomparing four configurations\
      \ on the *same* query set and the *same* metrics:\n\n| Configuration      |\
      \ Recall@10 | nDCG@10 |\n| ------------------ | --------: | ------: |\n| BM25-only\
      \          |         … |       … |\n| ANN-only           |         … |     \
      \  … |\n| Hybrid (RRF)       |         … |       … |\n| Hybrid + rerank    |\
      \         … |       … |\n\n**Methodology.** Fix `final_k` (e.g. 10) and `fuse_depth`\
      \ (e.g. pull 100 from\neach retriever). For each query, produce the top-$k$\
      \ `doc_id` list under each\nconfiguration, compute Recall@k and nDCG@k against\
      \ the gold `relevant` set, and\naverage over all queries. Hold every variable\
      \ constant across rows except the\nretrieval strategy — same corpus, same queries,\
      \ same $k$ — so each row isolates\nexactly one stage's contribution.\n\n**Expected\
      \ shape of the result** (this is the pattern to reproduce and explain,\nnot\
      \ a guarantee of exact numbers):\n\n- **Hybrid ≥ max(BM25, ANN)** on Recall@k\
      \ — fusion recovers documents that only\n  one retriever found, so the union-like\
      \ effect raises recall above either alone.\n  If it doesn't, your two retrievers\
      \ are too redundant (or one is broken).\n- **Reranking lifts nDCG@k more than\
      \ Recall@k.** The reranker reorders an\n  already-retrieved candidate list,\
      \ so it mostly moves relevant docs *up* (nDCG)\n  rather than pulling in new\
      \ ones (recall). Seeing Recall@k roughly flat while\n  nDCG@k jumps is the signature\
      \ of a reranker doing its job.\n\n**Interpretation to write up.** State the\
      \ RRF $k$ and `fuse_depth` you used,\nwhich stage bought the most, and — from\
      \ a couple of concrete queries — *why*:\nshow a query BM25 nailed that ANN missed,\
      \ one where the reverse held, and one the\nreranker rescued by promoting a relevant\
      \ doc the fusion buried.\n\n### Ablations (recommended)\n\nSmall sweeps that\
      \ turn the table into an argument:\n\n- **RRF depth / $k$:** vary `fuse_depth`\
      \ (10, 50, 100, 200) and the RRF constant\n  $k$; plot nDCG@10 vs. each. Bigger\
      \ `fuse_depth` gives the reranker more to work\n  with but costs more forward\
      \ passes.\n- **Weighted fusion:** does tilting RRF toward the stronger single\
      \ retriever beat\n  equal weights, or does equal weighting win by staying robust\
      \ across queries?\n- **Reranker depth:** rerank top-10 vs. top-50 vs. top-100\
      \ of the fused list and\n  plot nDCG@10 vs. rerank latency — the precision/latency\
      \ knee.\n\n## Running and testing\n\n- `python scripts/build_index.py` — embed\
      \ the corpus and build the sparse/dense\n  indexes once, cached to disk so evaluation\
      \ runs don't re-embed.\n- `python scripts/evaluate.py --k 10 --fuse-depth 100\
      \ --rrf-k 60` — prints the\n  four-row results table and any ablation you enable.\n\
      - `pytest` — the metric fixtures must pass before any headline number is\n \
      \ trustworthy. Add a fusion unit test (a two-list case whose RRF order you worked\n\
      \  out by hand) and a pipeline smoke test on a 3-document toy corpus.\n\n##\
      \ Security & hygiene\n\n- The cross-encoder and embedding models are downloaded\
      \ from a model hub — pin\n  exact model names/revisions and treat downloaded\
      \ weights as untrusted third-\n  party code; load them in your normal environment,\
      \ not as root.\n- No secrets are required for the local path. If you add an\
      \ optional hosted\n  embedding/reranker backend, read the key from the environment,\
      \ commit a\n  `.env.example` (never a real `.env`), and keep model caches and\
      \ `data/` out of\n  version control if the corpus isn't yours to redistribute.\n\
      - Treat query text as untrusted input: it flows into the tokenizer and model,\
      \ so\n  don't `eval`/format it into shell or code paths anywhere in the driver.\n\
      \n## Hardware, cost & subscriptions\n\n- **CPU-only.** Both retrievers and the\
      \ cross-encoder run on a laptop. The\n  reranker is a small local model performing\
      \ inference over a short candidate\n  list — no training, no GPU.\n- **\\$0.**\
      \ Local embedding, retrieval, and reranking models only. No hosted API\n  call,\
      \ no rented GPU, and no Docker required for this chapter.\n- **Storage/time:**\
      \ a few hundred MB for the small cross-encoder + embedding\n  models; the full\
      \ four-config evaluation over a few-thousand-doc corpus runs in\n  minutes on\
      \ CPU.\n\n## Build path — Candidate Generation vs. Re-ranking Split\n\nWork\
      \ outside-in: get a fair comparison harness running on a tiny catalog before\
      \ you\nscale anything.\n\n1. **Data + ground truth.** Load the catalog and interactions.\
      \ From the interactions,\n   construct queries with held-out `relevant_ids`\
      \ (e.g. leave-one-out per user, or a\n   temporal split). Freeze this — every\
      \ run uses the same queries so the sweep is\n   apples-to-apples.\n2. **Item\
      \ rendering.** Implement `Item.to_text` once and use it *everywhere*. If the\n\
      \   split and direct paths see different item text, your benchmark measures\
      \ prompt\n   wording, not architecture.\n3. **Embeddings + index.** Embed all\
      \ items once, build the ANN index. Add a\n   correctness check: for small $N$,\
      \ ANN top-k should match brute-force top-k.\n4. **Candidate generation.** Implement\
      \ `generate_candidates`. Before touching the\n   LLM, measure **retrieval recall@k**\
      \ alone — if the right item isn't in the\n   candidate set, no reranker can\
      \ recover it. This is the split's accuracy ceiling.\n5. **Reranker.** One structured\
      \ LLM call over the $k$ candidates returning ordered $m$\n   plus reasons. Validate\
      \ that every returned id is one you actually sent.\n6. **Direct baseline.**\
      \ Serialize a catalog slice into the prompt and ask for a ranked\n   list. Detect\
      \ and record context overflow explicitly rather than silently truncating.\n\
      7. **Sweep + report.** Wrap both in the `Recommender` protocol and run the size\
      \ sweep.\n\n### Choosing $k$ and $m$\n\n$k$ (candidate-set size) is the split's\
      \ main knob: too small and recall@k caps your\naccuracy; too large and the rerank\
      \ prompt bloats toward the direct baseline's cost.\nSweeping $k$ at a fixed\
      \ $N$ (a mini-ablation) is a worthwhile stretch — it shows the\nsplit degrades\
      \ *gracefully* into the baseline as $k \\to N$, which is a satisfying\nsanity\
      \ check that both paths are implemented consistently.\n\n## Benchmark: finding\
      \ the crossover $N^\\*$ — Candidate Generation vs. Re-ranking Split\n\nThe deliverable\
      \ is a benchmark that holds the query set, item text, embedding model,\nLLM,\
      \ and metric definitions constant, and varies **only** the catalog size $N$\
      \ and\nwhich recommender runs.\n\n**Methodology.**\n\n- Fix a query set $Q$\
      \ with ground-truth `relevant_ids`.\n- Choose a size grid, e.g. $N \\in \\{100,\
      \ 300, 1000, 3000, 10000, \\dots\\}$, geometric\n  so the crossover is visible\
      \ on a log axis. For each $N$, sample a sub-catalog that\n  **always contains\
      \ each query's relevant items** (otherwise accuracy is unmeasurable)\n  plus\
      \ $N-|\\text{relevant}|$ distractors, using a fixed seed.\n- For each $N$, run\
      \ **both** recommenders over all of $Q$ and record, per query:\n  accuracy (recall@$k$\
      \ for the candidate stage; NDCG@$m$ and hit-rate for the final\n  list), token\
      \ cost in dollars, and latency. Aggregate to means with error bars.\n- Mark\
      \ the $N$ at which `direct` first becomes **infeasible** (catalog no longer\
      \ fits\n  the context window) distinctly from where it becomes merely *worse*.\n\
      \n**Expected shape of the result.** Two families of curves over $N$:\n\n| $N$\
      \ (catalog size) | split NDCG@m | direct NDCG@m | split \\$/query | direct \\\
      $/query | direct feasible? |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| 100 \
      \ | ~high | ~high (ties)   | low | low  | yes |\n| 1000 | ~high (flat)  | starting\
      \ to sag | low (flat) | rising | yes |\n| 10000| ~high (flat)  | degraded /\
      \ n.a. | low (flat) | high | overflow |\n\nPlotted, you should see: **split\
      \ accuracy roughly flat in $N$** (it only ever reranks\n$k$ items), **direct\
      \ accuracy flat then falling** as lost-in-the-middle bites, and\n**cost diverging**\
      \ — split near-constant per query, direct climbing linearly until it\nhits the\
      \ context wall. The crossover $N^\\*$ is where the accuracy curves cross (or\n\
      where direct goes infeasible). Report $N^\\*$ as a single headline number with\
      \ its\ncurves; that number *is* the week's claim, and it must be visible in\
      \ your own output,\nnot asserted.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\n\
      Retain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration identities, case-level\
      \ outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline\
      \ mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements.\
      \ Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are\
      \ planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set\
      \ a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate\
      \ from the baseline report."

  - content: "Compare fixed-size chunks with headings, paragraphs, and table-aware\
      \ boundaries on supplied text documents. Preserve source IDs, revisions, offsets,\
      \ and access metadata. Add incremental upserts and deletions using content identity.\
      \ Develop a Postgres/pgvector path after the SQL bridge and compare authorized\
      \ filtered search with exact results. Keep multimodal parsing and broad connector\
      \ integration outside this chapter's core.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an\
      \ implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts\
      \ and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable\
      \ code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each\
      \ lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\n## Overview\n\
      \nIsolating chunking as the only variable in a RAG pipeline shows it dominates\n\
      accuracy more than model choice does — but only when everything else is held\n\
      fixed. This chapter builds a document Q&A pipeline where chunking uses detected\n\
      PDF layout structure (bounding boxes, reconstructed tables) instead of raw text\n\
      extraction, evaluated on a set of table-heavy PDFs. Retrieval accuracy is\n\
      measured for layout-aware chunking against naive text-chunking with the\nretriever\
      \ and model held constant. Chunking strategy turns out to be one of the\nhighest-leverage,\
      \ and cheapest to test, changes available in a RAG system.\n\n## Why this chapter\
      \ exists\n\nMost RAG post-mortems blame the model. The retriever returned garbage,\
      \ the\nanswer was wrong, so the reflex is to reach for a bigger generator or\
      \ a\nfancier embedding model. But retrieval quality is bounded by what's *in\
      \ the\nindex*, and what's in the index is decided by chunking — the step almost\n\
      nobody instruments. A `PdfReader.extract_text()` call on a table-heavy PDF\n\
      produces a stream of numbers with their column headers three lines away and\n\
      their row labels lost entirely. No embedding model recovers meaning that was\n\
      destroyed before it ever saw the text.\n\nThe controlled claim this chapter\
      \ defends is narrow and falsifiable: **hold the\nretriever, the embedding model,\
      \ the generator, the prompt, and the query set\nconstant; change only how documents\
      \ are split into chunks; and the accuracy\ndelta is large.** If you can't see\
      \ that delta in your own numbers, either your\nchunking variants aren't actually\
      \ different or your eval set isn't\ntable-heavy enough — both are bugs to fix,\
      \ not results to report.\n\nThe engineering discipline here — isolate one variable,\
      \ hold everything else\nfixed, measure the delta — is the spine of this entire\
      \ course. Week 3 is where\nyou build the harness that makes such a comparison\
      \ honest.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- You should already be comfortable embedding\
      \ text, building a small vector\n  index, and calling a hosted LLM — this chapter\
      \ goes one layer beneath all three,\n  into the text they consume.\n- Pairs\
      \ directly with **Foundations Week 16 (RAG with an eval suite)**: same\n  pipeline\
      \ shape (chunk → embed → retrieve → generate → score), but there the\n  eval\
      \ was the deliverable; here the eval is the *instrument* and chunking is\n \
      \ the single variable under test. Reuse the mental model, not the code.\n- Conceptual\
      \ familiarity with cosine similarity and top-$k$ nearest-neighbour\n  retrieval.\
      \ No ANN library internals required — a brute-force search over a\n  few thousand\
      \ vectors is fine at this scale.\n\n## Core concepts\n\n### The chunking → retrieval\
      \ → answer chain\n\nA RAG pipeline is a chain of lossy transforms:\n\n$$\n\\\
      text{PDF} \\xrightarrow{\\text{parse}} \\text{text} \\xrightarrow{\\text{chunk}}\
      \ \\{c_i\\} \\xrightarrow{\\text{embed}} \\{v_i\\} \\xrightarrow{\\text{retrieve}}\
      \ \\{c_j\\}_{j \\in \\text{top-}k} \\xrightarrow{\\text{generate}} \\text{answer}\n\
      $$\n\nThe week's thesis is that the **parse → chunk** stages, not the embed/retrieve/\n\
      generate stages, are where table-heavy documents lose the most information.\
      \ Once\na cell's value is separated from its row and column labels, the downstream\n\
      embedding is faithful to text that no longer means anything.\n\n### What \"\
      layout-aware\" actually buys you\n\nRaw text extraction reads a PDF's content\
      \ stream in roughly draw order and\nconcatenates it. For prose this is close\
      \ to correct. For a table it is a\ndisaster: a two-column financial statement\
      \ can interleave as\n`Revenue 2023 2022 412 388 COGS 210 195...`, and a chunker\
      \ splitting on a fixed\ntoken window will slice a row's label away from its\
      \ numbers.\n\nLayout-aware parsing instead recovers **structure** before chunking:\n\
      \n- **Bounding boxes** — every text span carries an $(x_0, y_0, x_1, y_1)$\n\
      \  rectangle. Reading order, columns, and table grids are reconstructed from\n\
      \  geometry, not draw order.\n- **Block classification** — spans are grouped\
      \ into paragraphs, headings,\n  and table regions.\n- **Table reconstruction**\
      \ — a detected table region is turned back into a\n  grid of cells with row/column\
      \ indices, so a cell can be serialized *with*\n  its headers attached.\n\nThe\
      \ chunking rule then becomes structural: **never split a table across a chunk\n\
      boundary, and serialize each table row (or the whole small table) as a\nself-contained\
      \ unit carrying its column headers.** A prose paragraph is chunked\nby size\
      \ as usual; a table is chunked by its own structure.\n\n### A worked contrast\n\
      \nConsider a 3-column table row. Naive extraction might yield the chunk:\n\n\
      ```\n...prior year. 412 388 9 Gross margin improved on...\n```\n\nThe numbers\
      \ `412 388 9` are unmoored — no reader, human or model, can say what\nthey measure.\
      \ Layout-aware serialization of the same row yields:\n\n```\n| Metric   | 2023\
      \ | 2022 | YoY % |\n| Revenue  | 412  | 388  |  9    |\n```\n\nor, row-linearized:\n\
      \n```\nRevenue: 2023=412, 2022=388, YoY %=9\n```\n\nThe second form embeds into\
      \ a vector that actually sits near a query like\n*\"what was revenue growth\
      \ year over year?\"*. That proximity is the entire\nmechanism — and it's created\
      \ at chunk time, not retrieval time.\n\n### Table serialization strategies\n\
      \nYou will implement at least two serialization formats and can treat the choice\n\
      as a secondary variable if you have time:\n\n- **Markdown grid** — preserves\
      \ 2-D structure; good for the generator to read,\n  more tokens per chunk.\n\
      - **Row-linearized** — one `header=value` string per row; each row becomes its\n\
      \  own retrievable chunk, which raises recall for row-specific questions.\n\n\
      The row-linearized form usually wins for retrieval because it puts every\n`header=value`\
      \ pair the query might match into an independently indexable unit.\n\n## What\
      \ you're building\n\nA self-contained document-Q&A repo with a pluggable **chunker**\
      \ interface, two\nconcrete chunkers (naive and layout-aware), and a benchmark\
      \ harness that swaps\n*only* the chunker while freezing everything else.\n\n\
      ```\nweek03-layout-aware-chunking/\n├── README.md\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── .env.example\
      \                 # LLM/embedding keys — never commit .env\n├── data/\n│   ├──\
      \ pdfs/                    # table-heavy source PDFs\n│   └── qa.jsonl     \
      \            # {question, answer, source_pdf, gold_chunk_id?}\n├── src/\n│ \
      \  ├── parsing/\n│   │   ├── layout.py            # PDF → LayoutDocument (boxes,\
      \ blocks, tables)\n│   │   └── tables.py            # table region → reconstructed\
      \ grid\n│   ├── chunking/\n│   │   ├── base.py              # Chunk, Chunker\
      \ protocol\n│   │   ├── naive.py             # NaiveTextChunker (baseline)\n\
      │   │   └── layout_aware.py      # LayoutAwareChunker (the mechanism)\n│   ├──\
      \ index/\n│   │   ├── embedder.py          # text → vector (local or hosted)\n\
      │   │   └── store.py             # in-memory vector store + top-k search\n│\
      \   ├── rag/\n│   │   ├── retrieve.py          # query → top-k chunks\n│   │\
      \   └── generate.py          # (query, chunks) → answer (frozen prompt)\n│ \
      \  └── config.py                # frozen pipeline config (seed, k, models)\n\
      ├── bench/\n│   ├── run.py                   # runs both conditions, writes\
      \ results\n│   ├── metrics.py               # recall@k, answer correctness\n\
      │   └── report.py                # table + delta summary\n└── tests/\n    ├──\
      \ test_tables.py\n    ├── test_chunking.py\n    └── test_metrics.py\n```\n\n\
      ### Key stub interfaces\n\nEverything the pipeline shares flows through a small\
      \ `Chunk` type and a\n`Chunker` protocol, so swapping chunkers is a one-line\
      \ change and nothing else\nin the pipeline can drift between conditions.\n\n\
      ```python\n# src/chunking/base.py\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\n\
      from typing import Protocol\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Chunk:\n    id:\
      \ str\n    text: str                      # what gets embedded AND shown to\
      \ the generator\n    source_pdf: str\n    page: int\n    kind: str         \
      \             # \"prose\" | \"table_row\" | \"table\"\n    meta: dict = field(default_factory=dict)\n\
      \nclass Chunker(Protocol):\n    name: str                      # appears verbatim\
      \ in the results table\n    def chunk(self, doc: \"LayoutDocument\") -> list[Chunk]:\n\
      \        \"\"\"Split one parsed document into retrievable chunks.\"\"\"\n  \
      \      ...\n```\n\nThe layout parser produces a structured document that *both*\
      \ chunkers consume —\nthe naive chunker simply ignores the structure and reads\
      \ `doc.raw_text`, which\nkeeps the comparison honest (same source bytes, same\
      \ parse entry point).\n\n```python\n# src/parsing/layout.py\nfrom dataclasses\
      \ import dataclass\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Box:\n    x0: float; y0:\
      \ float; x1: float; y1: float\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Span:\n    text:\
      \ str\n    box: Box\n\n@dataclass\nclass Table:\n    box: Box\n    rows: list[list[str]]\
      \          # rows[0] is assumed header unless meta says otherwise\n    page:\
      \ int\n\n@dataclass\nclass LayoutDocument:\n    source_pdf: str\n    spans:\
      \ list[Span]              # geometry-ordered text spans\n    tables: list[Table]\
      \            # reconstructed grids\n    raw_text: str                  # naive\
      \ extract_text() output, for the baseline\n\ndef parse_pdf(path: str) -> LayoutDocument:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Parse a PDF into spans + reconstructed tables + a raw_text fallback.\n\
      \n    Use a layout-capable parser (pdfplumber / PyMuPDF) for spans and boxes.\n\
      \    Detect table regions, then hand each to tables.reconstruct_grid.\n    \"\
      \"\"\n    ...  # TODO: extract spans with boxes; detect + reconstruct tables;\
      \ fill raw_text\n```\n\n```python\n# src/parsing/tables.py\ndef reconstruct_grid(spans:\
      \ list[\"Span\"], region: \"Box\") -> list[list[str]]:\n    \"\"\"Turn the spans\
      \ inside a table region into a dense grid of cell strings.\n\n    Cluster span\
      \ x-centres into columns and y-centres into rows, then place\n    each span\
      \ in its (row, col) cell. Missing cells become \"\".\n    \"\"\"\n    ...  #\
      \ TODO: 1-D cluster on x for columns, on y for rows; assign spans to cells\n\
      ```\n\nThe two chunkers are where the whole week lives. Bodies are intentionally\
      \ left\nfor you — the naive one is a few lines, the layout-aware one is the\
      \ assignment.\n\n```python\n# src/chunking/naive.py\nfrom .base import Chunk,\
      \ Chunker\n\nclass NaiveTextChunker:\n    name = \"naive_text\"\n    def __init__(self,\
      \ max_tokens: int = 256, overlap: int = 32):\n        ...\n    def chunk(self,\
      \ doc) -> list[Chunk]:\n        # Baseline: split doc.raw_text on a fixed token\
      \ window with overlap.\n        # Deliberately structure-blind — tables get\
      \ sliced mid-row.\n        ...  # TODO\n```\n\n```python\n# src/chunking/layout_aware.py\n\
      from .base import Chunk, Chunker\n\nclass LayoutAwareChunker:\n    name = \"\
      layout_aware\"\n    def __init__(self, max_tokens: int = 256, table_format:\
      \ str = \"row\"):\n        # table_format: \"row\" (linearized rows) | \"grid\"\
      \ (markdown table)\n        ...\n    def chunk(self, doc) -> list[Chunk]:\n\
      \        # 1. Chunk prose blocks by size, never crossing a table boundary.\n\
      \        # 2. For each table, serialize per table_format, attaching headers.\n\
      \        # 3. Emit table rows/tables as their own Chunks (kind=\"table_row\"\
      /\"table\").\n        ...  # TODO — this is the mechanism under test\n```\n\n\
      Retrieval and generation are shared, frozen infrastructure. Freeze the prompt,\n\
      the seed, `k`, and the models in `config.py` so the *only* thing that changes\n\
      between runs is which `Chunker` you pass in.\n\n```python\n# src/rag/generate.py\n\
      PROMPT_TEMPLATE = \"\"\"Answer strictly from the context. If unknown, say so.\n\
      Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}\nAnswer:\"\"\"\n\ndef answer(question:\
      \ str, chunks: list[\"Chunk\"], *, model: str) -> str:\n    \"\"\"Frozen generation\
      \ step. Identical across both chunking conditions.\"\"\"\n    ...  # TODO: format\
      \ PROMPT_TEMPLATE, call the hosted LLM, return text\n```\n\n## The one idea:\
      \ vector search is a database problem — Production Vector Search with pgvector\n\
      \nFoundations treated the index as the whole system — a graph in memory, queried\
      \ in\nisolation. Production inverts that. The embedding is one column on a row\
      \ that also\ncarries `tenant_id`, `created_at`, `language`, `is_published`,\
      \ and the source text.\nReal queries are never \"nearest neighbors of $q$\"\
      ; they are \"nearest neighbors of\n$q$ **among rows this user is allowed to\
      \ see, in English, published this quarter**.\"\nThe moment a `WHERE` clause\
      \ enters, the ANN index and the relational filter fight\nover who runs first,\
      \ and getting that order wrong doesn't crash — it silently\nreturns confident,\
      \ wrong answers. That failure mode, not recall on an unfiltered\nbenchmark,\
      \ is what separates a demo from a production vector store.\n\npgvector is the\
      \ cleanest place to learn this because it makes the seam visible. The\nvector\
      \ is just a column type; the index is just an index; the filter is just SQL.\n\
      Nothing is hidden behind a managed API, so every tradeoff a hosted vector database\n\
      makes for you is one you make explicitly here.\n\n### Distance operators and\
      \ what your metric must match\n\npgvector exposes distances as operators, and\
      \ the operator you index on must match\nthe metric your embedding model was\
      \ trained for:\n\n| Operator | Distance | Use when |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n\
      | `<->` | L2 (Euclidean) | model trained on Euclidean geometry |\n| `<#>` |\
      \ negative inner product | raw dot-product models |\n| `<=>` | cosine distance\
      \ | most sentence/text embeddings |\n\nMost modern text embeddings are cosine-normalized,\
      \ so you'll almost certainly use\n`<=>`. The subtlety: an HNSW or IVFFlat index\
      \ is built *for one operator class*.\nQuery with a different operator and Postgres\
      \ silently ignores the index and does a\nbrute-force scan — fast to write, catastrophic\
      \ at scale, and invisible until you\nread the `EXPLAIN` plan. Normalizing to\
      \ unit vectors makes cosine and inner product\nrank-equivalent; decide your\
      \ convention once and enforce it at insert time.\n\nFor unit-norm vectors $u,\
      \ v$, cosine similarity is $\\cos(u,v)=u\\cdot v$ and pgvector's\ncosine *distance*\
      \ is $1-\\cos(u,v)$, so ordering by `<=>` ascending returns most-similar\nfirst.\
      \ Keep that identity in mind when you sanity-check results against your own\n\
      brute-force NumPy computation.\n\n### The two indexes, and their opposite tradeoffs\n\
      \npgvector ships two approximate indexes. They are not interchangeable; they\
      \ sit at\nopposite ends of a build-cost/query-cost tradeoff.\n\n**IVFFlat**\
      \ partitions vectors into `lists` clusters (via k-means) and, at query\ntime,\
      \ scans only the `probes` nearest clusters. Fast to build, smaller, but recall\n\
      depends on data being present *before* you build the index — it must see the\
      \ vectors\nto cluster them. A useful rule of thumb pgvector's own docs give:\n\
      \n$$\\texttt{lists} \\approx \\frac{N}{1000}\\ \\text{for}\\ N \\le 10^6, \\\
      qquad \\texttt{lists} \\approx \\sqrt{N}\\ \\text{for}\\ N > 10^6$$\n\nand at\
      \ query time set `probes` in roughly the $\\sqrt{\\texttt{lists}}$ range, trading\n\
      recall for latency. Too few lists → giant clusters → slow. Too many → each cluster\n\
      tiny → you must probe many to find neighbors.\n\n**HNSW** builds a multi-layer\
      \ navigable small-world graph. Slower and more memory to\nbuild, but higher\
      \ recall at a given latency and — crucially — it can be built on an\nempty table\
      \ and stays good as you insert. Two build knobs, `m` (edges per node) and\n\
      `ef_construction` (candidate list size while building), and one query knob,\n\
      `ef_search` (candidate list size while querying). Larger `ef_search` → higher\
      \ recall,\nhigher latency, a monotone dial you'll sweep in the benchmark.\n\n\
      The headline you're going to verify with your own numbers: **IVFFlat wins build\
      \ time\nand memory; HNSW wins recall-at-latency and tolerates a growing table.**\
      \ Which matters\ndepends on whether your workload is write-heavy or read-heavy\
      \ — exactly the decision\na managed vector DB makes silently on your behalf.\n\
      \n### The pre-filter vs post-filter trap\n\nThis is the week's sharp edge. You\
      \ want the nearest neighbors *that also satisfy* a\n`WHERE` clause. There are\
      \ two ways it can happen, and they are not equivalent:\n\n- **Post-filter:**\
      \ the ANN index returns its top-$k$ by distance, *then* the filter\n  drops\
      \ rows that don't match. If your filter is selective — say 1% of rows match\
      \ —\n  the index's top-$k$ may contain **zero** matching rows, and you return\
      \ a short,\n  or empty, or wrong result set. The true neighbors were never fetched.\n\
      - **Pre-filter:** the filter restricts the candidate set *first*, and the vector\n\
      \  search runs within it. Correct, but the ANN index may not be usable over\
      \ an\n  arbitrary filtered subset, so Postgres can fall back to an exact scan\
      \ of the\n  filtered rows — fast if the filter is very selective, slow if it\
      \ isn't.\n\npgvector's actual behavior is subtler than \"pick one\": with an\
      \ approximate index and\na `WHERE` clause, it applies the filter and keeps scanning\
      \ the index until it has\nenough matching candidates, governed by `ef_search`\
      \ (HNSW) or `probes` (IVFFlat). If\nthose are too small relative to the filter's\
      \ selectivity, recall collapses — you get\n*approximate results over an approximately-filtered\
      \ set*. The mitigations you'll\nmeasure:\n\n- raise `ef_search`/`probes` so\
      \ more candidates survive the filter;\n- add a **partial index** or a **B-tree\
      \ index on the filter column** so a selective\n  filter can pre-restrict cheaply;\n\
      - for very selective filters, accept an exact scan (drop the ANN index for that\
      \ path)\n  because scanning 1% of rows exactly can beat an approximate index\
      \ that keeps missing.\n\nDefine filter **selectivity** as $s = \\frac{|\\{\\\
      text{rows matching WHERE}\\}|}{N}$. The\nbenchmark's whole job on this axis\
      \ is to plot recall against $s$ and show where each\nstrategy breaks. There\
      \ is no single right answer — there's a crossover, and you find\nit empirically."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build path\n\n1. **Corpus + gold set.** Collect 8–15 table-heavy\

      \ with the naive chunker. This is your\n   control condition.\n4. **Layout-aware\

      \ the *same* query set through both\n   chunkers, holding embedder/store/retriever/generator/prompt/seed\

      \ + interpret.** Produce the results table and read it: where does\n   layout-aware\
      \ win, where doesn't it, and is any win an artifact of chunk\n   count rather\
      \ than chunk *quality*?\n\n## Benchmark: chunking as the only variable\n\nThis\
      \ is the checkable artifact. Its credibility rests entirely on what you hold\n\

      \ acc | chunks | tok/query |\n| ------------ | -------- | -------- | --------\
      \ | ---------- | ------ | --------- |\n| naive_text   |    –     |    –    \
      \ |    –     |     –      |   –    |     –     |\n| layout_aware |    –    \
      \ |    –     |    –     |     –      |   –    |     –     |\n\nThe predicted\
      \ pattern: layout-aware shows a clear recall@k lift (concentrated on\nthe table-cell\

      \nRun everything with `uv run pytest`. Keep the pipeline deterministic\n(temperature\

      \ Everything runs from a single Python\n  environment.\n\n## Build path — Production\
      \ Vector Search with pgvector\n\nWork in milestones; each one produces something\

      \ — the checkable artifact — Production Vector Search with pgvector\n\nThe week's\
      \ abstract claims a \"production vector-store operating profile grounded in\n\
      your own numbers.\" The benchmark is what grounds it. Hold the corpus, embedding\n\
      model, query set, and $k$ constant; vary only one axis at a time.\n\n**Fixed:**\
      \ one corpus (10k–100k rows is plenty on CPU), one embedding model, one\nquery\

      - **Build/query knobs:** IVFFlat `lists` and `probes`; HNSW `m`, `ef_construction`,\n\
      \  and `ef_search`.\n- **Filter selectivity** $s \\in \\{1.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01\\\
      }$, each under post-filter,\n  pre-filter, and exact.\n- **Freshness:** recall\
