  - content: "Assemble generation context only from authorized retrieved chunks. Define\
      \ evidence sufficiency, grounded answers, citations, and abstention. Use two\
      \ synthetic users asking the same question to expose forbidden-context leakage.\
      \ Build query-level labels for supporting evidence and expected facts. Score\
      \ retrieval, generation, abstention, and access independently, using recorded\
      \ model responses for deterministic mechanism checks.\n\nThe lesson below specifies\
      \ an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts\
      \ and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable\
      \ code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each\
      \ lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\n## What\
      \ you will build\n\nBuild a small retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline\
      \ and an evaluation suite that\nshows where each failed answer went wrong. The\
      \ report separates missing evidence, claims\nunsupported by the retrieved text,\
      \ irrelevant answers, and permission leaks. You will run\nthe same question\
      \ as two users and observe that each receives only the documents they may\n\
      read.\n\nThe permission exercise uses supplied users, groups, documents, and\
      \ access lists. You do\nnot need to build login or reproduce Guide 35. The main\
      \ artifact is a per-case report plus\nan aggregate table that measures retrieval,\
      \ generation, abstention, and access control\nwithout hiding them in one score.\n\
      \n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n- The retrieval metrics and judge-comparison\
      \ ideas from Guide 12.\n- Sparse, dense, and hybrid retrieval concepts from\
      \ Guides 13–15.\n  Reimplement only the small interfaces this lesson needs;\
      \ no earlier repository is\n  required.\n- Python dataclasses, JSON Lines (JSONL),\
      \ and tests.\n\nAuthentication and document permissions are introduced through\
      \ a fixed fixture. Completing\nGuide 35 is optional. This lesson does not teach\
      \ login flows,\ndatabase row policies, or synchronization with an external identity\
      \ provider. Its narrower\nquestion is whether inaccessible text can enter retrieval\
      \ or generation.\n\nUse a CPU-friendly embedding model or deterministic fixture\
      \ embeddings. Keep generation\nand model-based judging behind interfaces with\
      \ recorded responses so the default tests run\noffline. The paths and commands\
      \ below describe files you will create.\n\n## Start with one question and two\
      \ users\n\nThe corpus contains two notes about the same project:\n\n- `public/orbit-overview`\
      \ says that Project Orbit launches in October and is readable by\n  everyone.\n\
      - `finance/orbit-budget` contains the canary phrase `COBALT-LANTERN-731` and\
      \ is readable\n  only by members of the `finance` group.\n\nBoth documents are\
      \ relevant to “What should I know about Project Orbit?” Run that question\n\
      as `alex`, who belongs to `engineering`, and as `bea`, who belongs to `finance`.\
      \ Alex's\ntrace may contain the overview but must contain no budget chunk, budget\
      \ identifier, canary,\nor citation. Bea may receive both documents.\n\nThis\
      \ example establishes the order of work:\n\n```text\nauthenticated subject +\
      \ groups\n            |\n            v\ndocument metadata -> apply permission\
      \ predicate -> rank readable chunks -> top k\n                             \
      \                                       |\n                                \
      \                                    v\n                                   \
      \                       generation context\n```\n\nA **subject** is the stable\
      \ identifier for the signed-in user. A **group** is a named set\nof subjects,\
      \ such as `finance`. An **access-control list** records which subjects or groups\n\
      may read a document. In this fixture, the caller identity is trusted input supplied\
      \ by the\ntest harness; the query text cannot choose or alter it.\n\nFiltering\
      \ after selecting the global top $k$ is incorrect. It can return too few results\n\
      even when useful authorized documents exist below the cutoff. Fetching forbidden\
      \ chunks\nand removing their citations only at the interface is also incorrect\
      \ because their text\nhas already reached the generation step.\n\n## Make every\
      \ pipeline seam visible\n\nFor a query $q$, identity $u$, and permission snapshot\
      \ $p$, the pipeline is\n\n$$\nC_k(q,u,p)=\\operatorname{TopK}_k\\left(\\left\\\
      {c:\\operatorname{can\\_read}(u,c,p)\\right\\},q\\right).\n$$\n\nThe generator\
      \ receives exactly $C_k$, not an unfiltered candidate set. Record a trace with\n\
      the identity reference, permission-snapshot version, candidate identifiers,\
      \ authorized\nretrieval results, assembled context, citations, answer, and terminal\
      \ reason. Do not copy\ntokens or group membership into logs when stable synthetic\
      \ identifiers are enough.\n\nKeep these failure categories separate:\n\n- **permission\
      \ leak:** a forbidden identifier, text fragment, canary, or citation appears\n\
      \  after the permission boundary;\n- **retrieval miss:** authorized supporting\
      \ evidence existed but was absent from top $k$;\n- **unsupported generation:**\
      \ the evidence was retrieved but an answer claim is not\n  supported by it;\n\
      - **irrelevant answer:** the answer is grounded in retrieved text but does not\
      \ address the\n  question;\n- **incorrect abstention:** authorized evidence\
      \ was available, but the pipeline claimed it\n  could not answer;\n- **correct\
      \ abstention:** no authorized evidence supported an answer and the pipeline\
      \ said\n  so.\n\nEvaluate permission leakage first. A fluent answer cannot compensate\
      \ for exposing a\nforbidden document.\n\n## Build the supplied fixture\n\nCreate\
      \ a deterministic corpus of 18 short documents across public, engineering, finance,\n\
      and human-resources collections. Give each document a stable identifier, revision,\
      \ source\ntext, and access list. Include unique synthetic canaries in every\
      \ restricted document so\naccidental context leakage is easy to detect.\n\n\
      Create 36 evaluation cases:\n\n| Case family | Cases | What it exposes |\n|---|---:|---|\n\
      | Public single-hop | 8 | ordinary retrieval and grounded answers |\n| Authorized\
      \ restricted | 8 | access granted through subject or group membership |\n| Same\
      \ query, different users | 8 | result changes caused only by identity |\n| No\
      \ authorized evidence | 6 | correct abstention and forbidden fallback |\n| Multi-document\
      \ answer | 4 | recall when several authorized chunks are required |\n| Out of\
      \ corpus | 2 | abstention unrelated to permissions |\n\nAt least four restricted\
      \ cases place a highly relevant forbidden document above an\nauthorized result\
      \ in the unfiltered ranking. At least four contain a forbidden canary that\n\
      also appears in an injected recorded model response. These are deliberate failing\
      \ inputs,\nnot examples the pipeline is expected to pass before you implement\
      \ the boundary.\n\nEach case stores `case_id`, `subject_id`, `group_ids`, `question`,\
      \ authorized gold document\nIDs, forbidden document IDs, expected answer facts,\
      \ and whether abstention is expected.\nWrite these labels directly from the\
      \ fixture definition. Do not derive gold permissions\nthrough the production\
      \ filter being tested.\n\n## Project shape and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\n\
      week16/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── rag_eval/\n│   ├── schema.py\n│   ├── fixtures.py\n\
      │   ├── permissions.py\n│   ├── retrieve.py\n│   ├── pipeline.py\n│   ├── judges.py\n\
      │   ├── metrics.py\n│   ├── report.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├── data/\n│   ├── documents.jsonl\n\
      │   ├── cases.jsonl\n│   └── recorded_responses.jsonl\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n\
      ```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import Protocol\n\
      \n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Principal:\n    subject_id: str\n    group_ids:\
      \ frozenset[str]\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Document:\n    document_id:\
      \ str\n    revision: int\n    text: str\n    public: bool\n    allowed_subjects:\
      \ frozenset[str]\n    allowed_groups: frozenset[str]\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class RetrievedChunk:\n    chunk_id: str\n    document_id: str\n    text: str\n\
      \    score: float\n    rank: int\n\nclass Generator(Protocol):\n    def answer(self,\
      \ question: str, context: list[RetrievedChunk]) -> dict: ...\n\ndef can_read(principal:\
      \ Principal, document: Document) -> bool: ...\n\ndef retrieve_authorized(\n\
      \    query: str,\n    principal: Principal,\n    documents: list[Document],\n\
      \    *,\n    k: int,\n) -> list[RetrievedChunk]: ...\n\ndef run_case(case: dict,\
      \ documents: list[Document], generator: Generator) -> dict: ...\n```\n\nThe\
      \ retriever may use the hybrid ranking method from Guide 15 or a supplied deterministic\n\
      score table. Permission checks must be ordinary application code with direct\
      \ unit tests.\nThe interface accepts a `Principal`; it never accepts a role\
      \ or group name copied from the\nquestion.\n\nFor this in-memory fixture, filter\
      \ readable documents before ranking. Production databases\nand vector indexes\
      \ may need row-level predicates, separate indexes, or filtered search,\nbut\
      \ those mechanisms are outside this lesson. State clearly that this implementation\n\
      demonstrates the invariant rather than production isolation.\n\n## Measure retrieval\
      \ for the current user\n\nLet $R_u$ be the gold relevant documents that user\
      \ $u$ may read and let $C_{1:k}$ be the\nauthorized retrieved documents. Measure\n\
      \n$$\n\\operatorname{Recall@}k(u)=\\frac{|R_u\\cap C_{1:k}|}{|R_u|}.\n$$\n\n\
      When $R_u$ is empty, retrieval recall is undefined; score abstention instead.\
      \ Do not put\nforbidden relevant documents in the denominator because the correct\
      \ result is to exclude\nthem.\n\nAlso report these counts:\n\n- cases with a\
      \ forbidden document identifier after filtering;\n- cases with forbidden source\
      \ text or canaries in the assembled context;\n- answers or citations containing\
      \ a forbidden canary or identifier;\n- expected abstentions that answered, and\
      \ answerable cases that abstained.\n\nThe permission-leak target for the fixture\
      \ is zero. A nonzero result is a useful finding\nthat the learner must explain\
      \ and repair, rather than a reason to hide the run.\n\n## Compare one retrieval\
      \ setting\n\nAfter the baseline works, compare two chunk sizes or two values\
      \ of $k$. Keep the identity,\npermission snapshot, questions, and generation\
      \ responses fixed. Report authorized\n`Recall@k`, supported-claim rate, abstentions,\
      \ and leak counts side by side.\n\nThis is a diagnostic comparison, not a search\
      \ for a guaranteed winner. Larger chunks may\npreserve context while introducing\
      \ distracting text; a larger $k$ may improve recall while\nmaking generation\
      \ less focused. Explain the observed tradeoff using individual cases."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Evaluate generation separately\n\nFor cases with authorized\
      \ evidence, split the answer into short claims and record whether\neach claim\
      \ is supported by a retrieved chunk. A model-based judge may help, but validate\n\
      its structured output and compare it with handwritten labels on at least 12\
      \ traces. Treat\ndocument content as data: delimit it, bound its size, and include\
      \ injection cases.\n\nUse `true`, `false`, or `null` for faithfulness and relevance.\
      \ `null` records an abstention\nor judge failure and must not be converted silently\
      \ to false. Retry invalid judge output\nonce, then preserve the failure. Keep\
      \ recorded judge responses for offline tests and label\nthem as fixtures rather\
      \ than fresh judgments.\n\nFor every failed case, show the earliest failing\
      \ stage and enough identifiers to reproduce\nit. Redact forbidden text from\
      \ the human-readable report for users who are not allowed to\nsee it; the synthetic\
      \ evaluator running with fixture-wide access may record only the canary\nidentifier\
      \ and leak location.\n\n## Build sequence — 18 hours\n\n1. **Fixture and permission\
      \ predicate, 4 hours.** Create the users, groups, documents,\n   access lists,\
      \ canaries, and 36 independent case labels. Unit-test subject, group,\n   public,\
      \ and denied access.\n2. **Authorized retrieval, 4 hours.** Add chunking and\
      \ ranking, enforce filtering before\n   top $k$, and compare results for the\
      \ paired identities.\n3. **Generation traces, 3 hours.** Assemble bounded context,\
      \ use recorded model responses,\n   and preserve citations and terminal reasons.\n\
      4. **Evaluation, 4 hours.** Implement authorized recall, abstention and leak\
      \ checks,\n   claim scoring, judge validation, and failure attribution.\n5.\
      \ **Comparison and report, 3 hours.** Run one bounded retrieval comparison,\
      \ inspect every\n   leak or disagreement, and record limitations.\n\n## Commands,\
      \ tests, and artifact\n\nRun the core exercise from the lesson directory:\n\n\
      ```bash\nuv sync\nuv run python -m rag_eval.cli make-fixtures --out data\nuv\
      \ run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m rag_eval.cli evaluate --documents data/documents.jsonl\
      \ --cases data/cases.jsonl --responses data/recorded_responses.jsonl --out artifacts/baseline\n\
      uv run python -m rag_eval.cli compare --baseline artifacts/baseline --chunk-size\
      \ 256 --out artifacts/comparison.md\n```\n\nTests cover direct-user access,\
      \ group access, public access, denied access, a user in\nseveral groups, filtering\
      \ before top $k$, empty authorized results, paired identities,\ncanaries in\
      \ candidates/context/answers/citations, missing document revisions, undefined\n\
      recall, invalid judge output, and report alignment by case ID. Default commands\
      \ make no\nnetwork calls.\n\nThe report contains the fixture hash and permission-snapshot\
      \ version, per-case failure\nstage, aggregate retrieval and generation measures,\
      \ abstention counts, all four leak\ncounts, the paired-identity comparison,\
      \ the retrieval-setting comparison, and at least\none limitation. Keep counts\
      \ beside percentages because 36 designed cases do not represent\nall RAG workloads.\n\
      \n## Hardware, cost, and optional depth\n\nThe offline exercise runs on a CPU\
      \ and costs $0. An optional live generation and judge run\nmay use a hosted\
      \ model with a $5 cap; record the provider, model version, requests, tokens,\n\
      latency, and actual cost. Docker is not required.\n\nDatabase row-level security,\
      \ an external identity provider, changing group membership,\npermission synchronization,\
      \ and deletion from a live index are optional studies here.\nThey receive focused\
      \ treatment in Guides 35 and Enterprise 3. This lesson establishes the\nevaluation\
      \ cases those systems should later be able to pass.\n\n### Report the actual\
      \ execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration\
      \ identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation.\
      \ Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server\
      \ or cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."

  - content: "Define a typed answer schema containing claims, supporting source IDs,\
      \ and abstention information. Compare free-form parsing, post-generation schema\
      \ validation, and maintained constrained-decoding support. Explain that valid\
      \ JSON is independent of semantic correctness. Verify individual claims against\
      \ the exact cited passages and use deterministic or labeled entailment checks\
      \ with documented limits.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and\
      \ experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed\
      \ lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results\
      \ already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## Scope of the experiment\n\nThe core\
      \ implementation is the by-hand incremental grammar acceptor and token mask.\
      \ A library adapter is a comparison after that mechanism works. A prefix that\
      \ remains extendable is different from a completed schema-valid object, and\
      \ both differ from a correct claim. Early token-limit termination can leave\
      \ an incomplete object. Use a local inference adapter exposing per-step logits\
      \ for the substantive decoding experiment; canned vectors test masking mechanics\
      \ only. Citation verification uses local synthetic sources in the core; any\
      \ open-web adapter is optional.\n\n## Overview\n\n\"Ask nicely for JSON\" is\
      \ a prompting trick with a real, measurable failure rate;\nmasking invalid tokens\
      \ at the moment they would be sampled turns the same\nrequest into an enforced\
      \ grammar-prefix constraint. This chapter implements token-level constrained\
      \ decoding\nby hand — masking logits at each step so only tokens valid under\
      \ a JSON schema\nor small grammar can be sampled — applied to a support-ticket\
      \ classifier.\nSchema-validity rate and latency overhead are measured for constrained\
      \ decoding\nagainst plain prompted JSON on the identical classifier and prompt.\
      \ The result\nputs a concrete price tag on the guarantee: the resource cost\
      \ and limitations of enforcing structure during decoding. A token budget can\
      \ still interrupt completion, and structure does not establish answer correctness.\n\
      \n## Prerequisites\n\n- **Autoregressive decoding concepts:** you should already\n\
      \  know that an LLM produces a logit vector over its vocabulary at every step,\n\
      \  that sampling (greedy / temperature / top-p) turns those logits into one\
      \ token,\n  and that generation is autoregressive — this chapter intervenes\
      \ *between* the\n  logits and the sample.\n- Comfort reading and writing a small\
      \ **finite-state machine / recursive-descent\n  parser**. The grammar side of\
      \ this chapter is classic parsing, not ML.\n- Familiarity with a local inference\
      \ stack that exposes per-step logits — Hugging\n  Face `transformers` `LogitsProcessor`,\
      \ `llama.cpp` logit callbacks, or\n  equivalent. Hosted chat APIs that only\
      \ return finished text are *not* enough on\n  their own (see Hardware).\n- You\
      \ do **not** need any other week in this course; Week 1 is self-contained.\n\
      \n## The idea in one paragraph\n\nA hosted \"return JSON\" request is unconstrained\
      \ generation with a hopeful prompt:\nthe model *can* still emit a stray token\
      \ — a prose preamble, a trailing comma, an\nunquoted key, a truncated object\
      \ — and when it does, your `json.loads` throws and\nyour pipeline is down. Constrained\
      \ decoding removes the possibility rather than\nreducing its probability. At\
      \ each step you compute, from the text generated so\nfar, the set of tokens\
      \ that could legally continue a valid document, and you\nforbid every other\
      \ token *before* sampling. Sampling then draws only from legal\ncontinuations,\
      \ so every emitted prefix follows the declared grammar; a completed output is\
      \ structurally valid if the acceptor reaches an accepting state. That prefix\
      \ property holds\nfor greedy, temperature, or top-p sampling alike, because\
      \ it is applied to the\ndistribution, not the draw.\n\n## Concepts and theory\n\
      \n### Decoding as a masked distribution\n\nLet $V$ be the vocabulary and $\\\
      textbf{\\textsf{z}}_t \\in \\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ the logits the model\nemits at\
      \ step $t$ given the prefix $y_{<t}$. Ordinary sampling draws\n\n$$ y_t \\sim\
      \ \\text{softmax}(\\textbf{\\textsf{z}}_t). $$\n\nConstrained decoding introduces,\
      \ at each step, an **allowed set**\n$A_t \\subseteq V$ of tokens that keep the\
      \ output on a path to a valid document.\nDefine a mask $\\textbf{\\textsf{m}}_t\
      \ \\in \\{0, -\\infty\\}^{|V|}$ with\n\n$$ \\textbf{\\textsf{m}}_t[v] = \\begin{cases}\
      \ 0 & v \\in A_t \\\\ -\\infty & v \\notin A_t \\end{cases} $$\n\nand sample\
      \ from the masked distribution\n\n$$ y_t \\sim \\text{softmax}(\\textbf{\\textsf{z}}_t\
      \ + \\textbf{\\textsf{m}}_t). $$\n\nBecause $e^{-\\infty} = 0$, every forbidden\
      \ token gets probability exactly zero;\nthe surviving mass is renormalized over\
      \ $A_t$ only. The model's *relative*\npreferences among legal tokens are preserved\
      \ — you are pruning the support of the\ndistribution, not reshaping it. Two\
      \ consequences worth internalizing:\n\n- If $A_t = \\varnothing$ you have hit\
      \ a **dead state** — the grammar admits no\n  token here. A correct acceptor\
      \ and supported tokenizer mapping should keep a valid continuation available,\
      \ including legal end-of-sequence at completion; if it does, your automaton\
      \ (or its alignment to the\n  tokenizer) is wrong. Treat an empty allowed set\
      \ as a hard invariant violation,\n  not a runtime edge case to paper over.\n\
      - The mask changes *which* token is sampled but not the forward pass, so the\n\
      \  per-step compute overhead is the cost of computing $A_t$, not of running\
      \ the\n  model again (analyzed under Benchmarks).\n\n### The grammar side: an\
      \ incremental acceptor\n\nThe clean way to think about the constraint is a language\
      \ $L$ (all valid JSON\ndocuments matching your schema) recognized by an **acceptor**\
      \ that can be driven\none symbol at a time and, at any point, reports which\
      \ next symbols keep the\nstring extendable into a member of $L$. For a JSON\
      \ *schema* fixed at build time\n(known keys, known enum of ticket categories,\
      \ a bounded integer for priority)\nthe acceptor is small and largely a regular/finite-state\
      \ object; general\nrecursive JSON needs a stack (a pushdown acceptor). Either\
      \ way the interface you\nneed from it is tiny:\n\n- feed one accepted symbol,\
      \ advancing internal state;\n- ask for the set of symbols allowed next;\n- ask\
      \ whether the current state is an accepting (complete-document) state.\n\nDesign\
      \ the acceptor over **bytes or characters first**, independent of any model.\n\
      It is far easier to test a character-level JSON acceptor in isolation than to\n\
      debug it tangled up with a tokenizer.\n\n### The hard part: tokenization mismatch\n\
      \nHere is the subtlety that makes this a real week rather than a `regex` exercise.\n\
      Your acceptor speaks **characters**; the model samples **subword tokens**. A\n\
      single token like `\":\"` or `\", \"` or `\"true\"` spans several grammar characters\
      \ at\nonce, and different tokens can share character prefixes. So \"which tokens\
      \ are\nallowed next\" is not a lookup — it is the question:\n\n> for each token\
      \ $v \\in V$, does appending its *string* to the current output\n> keep the\
      \ document on a path the acceptor still accepts?\n\nNaively that is a full acceptor\
      \ replay over every token in a 30k–150k vocabulary\nat every step — correct\
      \ but slow. The engineering is in making it cheap:\n\n- Precompute, from the\
      \ acceptor's current state, the set of allowed *characters*,\n  then admit a\
      \ token only if its string is consumable from that state (a token\n  may legally\
      \ cross into a new grammar state mid-token, so you must simulate the\n  acceptor\
      \ through the whole token string, not just check its first character).\n- Exploit\
      \ structure: build a **trie / byte-prefix index** over the vocabulary so\n \
      \ you can prune whole subtrees of tokens the moment a character is rejected,\n\
      \  turning a $|V|$ scan into something closer to proportional to the number\
      \ of\n  *viable* tokens.\n- Cache per-state allowed-token sets: many decoding\
      \ steps revisit the same\n  acceptor state (e.g. \"inside a string value\"),\
      \ so the expensive set is computed\n  once per state, not once per step.\n\n\
      Two classic traps to name up front:\n\n- **Partial tokens / token healing.**\
      \ The last token of the prompt may already be\n  a partial grammar symbol; the\
      \ acceptor must be seeded with the exact bytes\n  emitted so far, not with a\
      \ re-tokenization of the decoded string, or you will\n  silently allow an illegal\
      \ continuation.\n- **End-of-sequence.** The model's EOS token is only legal\
      \ when the acceptor is in\n  an accepting state. Allowing EOS early yields a\
      \ truncated-but-\"valid-looking\"\n  object; forbidding it in an accepting state\
      \ can loop forever. EOS is just\n  another token the acceptor must gate.\n\n\
      ### Why this beats prompting\n\nPrompting lowers the probability of malformed\
      \ output; it cannot make it zero,\nbecause nothing in the sampling loop is aware\
      \ of the schema. The failure rate is\nalso *model- and input-dependent* — it\
      \ spikes on long outputs, unusual field\nvalues, and smaller models — which\
      \ is exactly when you least want to find out.\nConstrained decoding converts\
      \ a probabilistic property (\"usually parses\") into a\nstructural one (\"a\
      \ completed accepting output parses under the supported grammar\"), and the\
      \ week's benchmark is what lets you state\nthe size of that gap in your own\
      \ numbers instead of asserting it.\n\n## What you are building\n\nA small library\
      \ plus a runnable classifier and a benchmark harness:\n\n```\ngrammar-constrained-decoding/\n\
      ├── README.md\n├── pyproject.toml                # or requirements.txt\n├──\
      \ .env.example                  # API/model config keys — never commit .env\n\
      ├── src/\n│   └── gcd/\n│       ├── __init__.py\n│       ├── acceptor.py   \
      \        # character-level JSON/schema acceptor (FSA/pushdown)\n│       ├──\
      \ schema.py             # ticket schema → acceptor construction\n│       ├──\
      \ vocab_index.py        # trie/byte-prefix index over the tokenizer vocab\n\
      │       ├── mask.py               # acceptor state → allowed-token mask over\
      \ V\n│       ├── processor.py          # LogitsProcessor wiring mask into the\
      \ decode loop\n│       ├── classifier.py         # the support-ticket classifier\
      \ (constrained + baseline)\n│       └── decode.py             # thin generate()\
      \ wrapper for both modes\n├── data/\n│   └── tickets.jsonl             # eval\
      \ inputs + gold labels (you assemble this)\n├── bench/\n│   ├── run.py     \
      \               # runs both modes, writes metrics\n│   └── report.py       \
      \          # aggregates into the results table/plot\n└── tests/\n    ├── test_acceptor.py\
      \          # acceptor accepts/rejects known strings\n    ├── test_mask.py  \
      \            # allowed set never empty on valid prefixes\n    └── test_end_to_end.py\
      \        # 100% schema validity under constraint\n```\n\n### The ticket classifier\
      \ task\n\nKeep the *task* deliberately simple so the *mechanism* is the only\
      \ interesting\npart. The classifier reads a support ticket and must emit exactly:\n\
      \n```json\n{\n  \"category\": \"billing | technical | account | other\",\n \
      \ \"priority\": 1,\n  \"needs_human\": false\n}\n```\n\n`category` is a fixed\
      \ enum, `priority` is a bounded integer (say $1$–$5$),\n`needs_human` is a boolean.\
      \ That schema is small enough to encode as a mostly\nfinite-state acceptor,\
      \ yet rich enough that unconstrained prompting *will*\noccasionally produce\
      \ an out-of-enum category, a stringified boolean, extra keys,\nor prose around\
      \ the JSON — which is precisely the failure you are going to\nmeasure and then\
      \ eliminate.\n\n### Key stub interfaces\n\nSignatures and shells only — you\
      \ implement the bodies.\n\n```python\n# acceptor.py\nfrom typing import Protocol\n\
      \nclass Acceptor(Protocol):\n    \"\"\"Character-level acceptor for the target\
      \ language.\n\n    Driven one character at a time; reports which characters\
      \ may come next\n    and whether the string so far is a complete, valid document.\n\
      \    \"\"\"\n\n    def allowed_chars(self) -> set[str]:\n        \"\"\"Characters\
      \ that keep the current string extendable into L.\"\"\"\n        ...\n\n   \
      \ def step(self, ch: str) -> \"Acceptor\":\n        \"\"\"Advance by one accepted\
      \ character (return new/updated state).\"\"\"\n        ...\n\n    def is_accepting(self)\
      \ -> bool:\n        \"\"\"True iff the string consumed so far is a complete\
      \ valid document.\"\"\"\n        ...\n\n\n# schema.py\ndef acceptor_for_ticket_schema()\
      \ -> Acceptor:\n    \"\"\"Build the acceptor for the fixed support-ticket JSON\
      \ schema.\n\n    Encode: object braces, the three known keys in some allowed\
      \ order,\n    the category enum, the bounded-integer priority, the boolean,\
      \ and\n    the surrounding structural tokens (quotes, colons, commas).\n   \
      \ \"\"\"\n    # TODO: construct states for each structural position + value\
      \ domains\n    ...\n\n\n# vocab_index.py\nclass VocabIndex:\n    \"\"\"Byte/char-prefix\
      \ index over the tokenizer vocabulary for fast masking.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self,\
      \ tokenizer) -> None:\n        # TODO: build a trie of token strings -> token\
      \ ids\n        ...\n\n    def tokens_consumable_from(self, acceptor: Acceptor)\
      \ -> list[int]:\n        \"\"\"Token ids whose full string is accepted starting\
      \ at this state.\n\n        Must simulate the acceptor through the entire token\
      \ string, since a\n        single token can cross grammar states.\n        \"\
      \"\"\n        ...\n\n\n# mask.py\nimport torch\n\ndef build_mask(acceptor: Acceptor,\
      \ index: VocabIndex, vocab_size: int,\n               eos_token_id: int) ->\
      \ torch.Tensor:\n    \"\"\"Return an additive logit mask (0 for allowed, -inf\
      \ otherwise).\n\n    EOS is allowed iff acceptor.is_accepting(). Assert the\
      \ allowed set is\n    non-empty (empty => bug in the acceptor or the alignment).\n\
      \    \"\"\"\n    # TODO: allowed = index.tokens_consumable_from(acceptor); gate\
      \ EOS; assert non-empty\n    ...\n\n\n# processor.py\nfrom transformers import\
      \ LogitsProcessor\n\nclass GrammarLogitsProcessor(LogitsProcessor):\n    \"\"\
      \"Applies build_mask() at every decode step and advances the acceptor.\n\n \
      \   Must reconstruct/track exactly the bytes emitted so far (token healing),\n\
      \    not a re-tokenization of the decoded text.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def __call__(self,\
      \ input_ids, scores):\n        # TODO: advance acceptor by newly generated token's\
      \ string;\n        #       add build_mask(...) to scores; return scores\n  \
      \      ...\n\n\n# classifier.py\ndef classify(ticket_text: str, *, constrained:\
      \ bool) -> dict:\n    \"\"\"Classify one ticket. constrained=True installs GrammarLogitsProcessor;\n\
      \    constrained=False is the plain prompted-JSON baseline on the SAME model.\n\
      \    \"\"\"\n    # TODO: build prompt; generate; parse; the ONLY difference\
      \ between modes\n    #       is whether the processor is attached\n    ...\n\
      ```\n\nThe single most important design rule: **the constrained and baseline\
      \ paths must\ndiffer only in whether the mask is applied.** Same model, same\
      \ prompt, same\nsampling parameters, same parser. If anything else differs,\
      \ your benchmark is\nmeasuring that other thing.\n\n## The core distinction\
      \ this week is about — Claim-Level Citation Verification\n\nMost \"cited\" agent\
      \ answers are checked for the wrong thing. A sentence like\n\n> The library\
      \ was founded in 1911 [3].\n\npasses a *presence* check the moment a marker\
      \ `[3]` appears and resolves to a real\nsource. Presence says nothing about\
      \ whether source 3 actually *supports* the\nsentence. The failure modes that\
      \ survive a presence check are exactly the dangerous\nones:\n\n- **Unsupported\
      \ claim** — the cited source is real and relevant but never states the\n  fact\
      \ (the model hallucinated a plausible detail and stapled a citation to it).\n\
      - **Misattribution** — the fact is true and *some* source supports it, but not\
      \ the\n  one cited.\n- **Overreach** — the source supports a weaker version\
      \ (\"around 1910\") than the claim\n  asserts (\"exactly 1911\").\n- **Contradiction**\
      \ — the source actually says the opposite, and the citation is\n  window dressing.\n\
      \nVerification is the property that rules these out: for each atomic claim $c$\
      \ and its\ncited source passage $s$, we require that $s$ **entails** $c$. This\
      \ is a textual\nentailment / natural-language-inference (NLI) relation, the\
      \ same three-way judgment\nNLI models are trained on:\n\n$$\n\\text{label}(s,\
      \ c) \\in \\{\\,\\textsf{entailed},\\ \\textsf{neutral},\\ \\textsf{contradicted}\\\
      ,\\}\n$$\n\nA claim is *faithful* only when its source entails it. Everything\
      \ else — neutral or\ncontradicted — is an unsupported claim regardless of how\
      \ clean the citation looks.\n\n### Why \"claim-level\" and not \"answer-level\"\
      \n\nGrading a whole answer as faithful/unfaithful is too coarse: a five-sentence\
      \ answer\nwith one fabricated number is neither fully faithful nor fully wrong,\
      \ and an\nanswer-level label can't tell you *which* sentence to fix. Decomposing\
      \ into atomic\nclaims turns a fuzzy judgment into a set of independent, checkable\
      \ propositions.\nDefine the **faithfulness rate** of an answer as\n\n$$\n\\\
      text{faithfulness} = \\frac{\\#\\{\\text{claims with } \\textsf{entailed} \\\
      text{ source}\\}}{\\#\\{\\text{total claims}\\}}\n$$\n\nand the **hallucination\
      \ (unsupported-claim) rate** as its complement,\n$1 - \\text{faithfulness}$.\
      \ The whole week is an exercise in driving that second\nnumber down with a verification-and-repair\
      \ pass and *measuring* that it moved.\n\n### Atomic claims, precisely\n\nAn\
      \ *atomic claim* is a single, independently verifiable proposition. \"The library\n\
      opened in 1911 and holds two million books\" is two claims, not one — the year\
      \ could\nbe right while the count is wrong, and a per-claim label needs to separate\
      \ them.\nDecomposition quality bounds the whole system: if you leave compound\
      \ sentences\nwhole, a partially-wrong sentence gets one label and you lose resolution.\
      \ You do not\nneed perfect linguistics — a decent LLM prompt that splits on\
      \ conjunctions and\nresolves pronouns to their referents is enough — but treat\
      \ decomposition as a real\nstep with its own failure modes, not an afterthought.\n\
      \n## Building the eval set — Claim-Level Citation Verification\n\nYou need queries\
      \ whose answers contain claims you can *ground-truth*. Two practical\nroutes,\
      \ mixable:\n\n- **Seeded-fact queries.** Pick facts from a stable, fetchable\
      \ source (e.g. a\n  reference page you cache), write a query that should surface\
      \ them, and label the\n  expected atomic claims as supported. Then deliberately\
      \ craft near-miss variants\n  (wrong year, swapped attribute) so the verifier\
      \ has contradicted/neutral cases to\n  catch, not only easy positives.\n- **Trap\
      \ sources.** Include at least a few pages where the relevant fact is\n  *absent*\
      \ or *contradicted*, so an answer that hallucinates a citation to them is\n\
      \  catchable. This is what separates verification from presence-checking.\n\n\
      Aim for ~30–60 queries — enough for a rate to mean something, small enough to\
      \ run on\na few dollars. Store each query with its gold claims and their expected\
      \ labels:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"query\": \"When did the example launch?\", \"gold_claims\"\
      : [{\"text\": \"It launched in 2024.\", \"label\": \"entailed\", \"source_id\"\
      : \"s3\"}]}\n```"
    lab_and_evidence: "## What you're building — Claim-Level Citation Verification\n\
      \nA local document assistant produces a cited answer, and a verification pass\
      \ checks its individual claims. The core search and fetch adapter reads versioned\
      \ synthetic passages; an open-web adapter is an optional extension. The verifier\
      \ decomposes the answer into atomic claims, retrieves the passage each claim\
      \ points at, checks whether it supports the claim, and repairs or flags failures.\
      \ Compare the same cases with the pass on and off.\n\n```\nweek15-citation-verification/\n\
      ├── README.md\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── .env.example            # keys only;\
      \ never commit a real .env\n├── src/\n│   └── citeverify/\n│       ├── __init__.py\n\
      │       ├── agent.py         # local retrieval + synthesis loop (produces a\
      \ cited draft)\n│       ├── browse.py        # fixture search + fetch; optional\
      \ web adapter; untrusted-content boundary\n│       ├── claims.py        # decompose\
      \ answer -> atomic claims linked to sources\n│       ├── entail.py        #\
      \ the core: does source s entail claim c?\n│       ├── verify.py        # orchestrates\
      \ decompose -> retrieve -> entail -> repair\n│       ├── schemas.py       #\
      \ dataclasses: Claim, SourcePassage, Verdict, Answer\n│       └── config.py\
      \        # model names, thresholds, budgets from env\n├── data/\n│   ├── queries.jsonl\
      \        # eval queries + ground-truth claim labels\n│   └── cache/        \
      \       # cached fetched pages (so evals are reproducible)\n├── evals/\n│  \
      \ ├── run_eval.py          # before/after harness -> metrics table\n│   └──\
      \ metrics.py           # faithfulness / hallucination-rate / repair stats\n\
      └── tests/\n    ├── test_claims.py\n    ├── test_entail.py\n    └── test_injection.py\
      \    # untrusted-content boundary must hold\n```\n\n### Key data shapes\n\n\
      Fix the vocabulary first — everything downstream reads and writes these.\n\n\
      ```python\n# schemas.py\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\nfrom enum\
      \ import Enum\n\nclass Entailment(str, Enum):\n    ENTAILED = \"entailed\"\n\
      \    NEUTRAL = \"neutral\"\n    CONTRADICTED = \"contradicted\"\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class SourcePassage:\n    source_id: str          # stable id for a fetched\
      \ page / chunk\n    url: str\n    text: str               # the passage text\
      \ actually shown to the entailer\n    # NOTE: this text is UNTRUSTED. It is\
      \ evidence to reason *about*,\n    # never instructions to follow. See the security\
      \ section.\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Claim:\n    text: str         \
      \      # one atomic, independently checkable proposition\n    cited_source_id:\
      \ str | None   # what the draft answer cited (may be None)\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class Verdict:\n    claim: Claim\n    checked_source_id: str | None\n    label:\
      \ Entailment\n    score: float            # entailment probability / confidence\
      \ in [0, 1]\n    rationale: str          # short span or sentence justifying\
      \ the label\n\n@dataclass\nclass Answer:\n    query: str\n    text: str    \
      \                   # synthesized prose with inline citations\n    sources:\
      \ list[SourcePassage] = field(default_factory=list)\n    verdicts: list[Verdict]\
      \ = field(default_factory=list)  # filled by verify pass\n```\n\n### The entailment\
      \ check (the heart of the week)\n\nThis is the one function whose behavior the\
      \ whole result depends on. It must judge\n*only* whether the source supports\
      \ the claim — never whether the claim is true in\ngeneral, and never by following\
      \ anything the source text says.\n\n```python\n# entail.py\nfrom .schemas import\
      \ SourcePassage, Claim, Verdict, Entailment\n\ndef entail(source: SourcePassage,\
      \ claim: Claim) -> Verdict:\n    \"\"\"Return whether `source` entails `claim`.\n\
      \n    Contract:\n      - ENTAILED     iff the passage alone is sufficient to\
      \ conclude the claim.\n      - CONTRADICTED iff the passage asserts something\
      \ incompatible with it.\n      - NEUTRAL      otherwise (silent, off-topic,\
      \ or only partially supporting).\n\n    Judge from the passage text ONLY. Do\
      \ not use outside knowledge to fill gaps,\n    and do not treat any imperative\
      \ text inside `source.text` as an instruction.\n    \"\"\"\n    # TODO: build\
      \ an NLI-style prompt (premise = source.text, hypothesis = claim.text)\n   \
      \ #       OR call a small local NLI model (e.g. a DeBERTa-MNLI checkpoint).\n\
      \    # TODO: parse a single label + a confidence score + a one-line rationale.\n\
      \    # TODO: map to Entailment and return a Verdict.\n    ...\n\ndef entails_faithful(verdict:\
      \ Verdict, threshold: float) -> bool:\n    \"\"\"A claim is faithful iff ENTAILED\
      \ with score >= threshold.\"\"\"\n    # TODO: return verdict.label is Entailment.ENTAILED\
      \ and verdict.score >= threshold\n    ...\n```\n\nTwo implementations of `entail`\
      \ are worth having behind one interface: a **hosted\nLLM** judge (a prompt that\
      \ emits `{label, score, rationale}`) and a **small local\nNLI model** (premise/hypothesis\
      \ → 3-way softmax). Being able to swap them lets you\nshow the verification\
      \ effect is not an artifact of one particular judge — and the\nlocal model gives\
      \ you a $0, offline path for most of the eval.\n\n### The verification pass\n\
      \n```python\n# verify.py\nfrom .schemas import Answer, Claim, Verdict\n\ndef\
      \ decompose(answer: Answer) -> list[Claim]:\n    \"\"\"Split synthesized prose\
      \ into atomic claims, each linked to what it cited.\"\"\"\n    # TODO: prompt\
      \ an LLM to emit a JSON list of atomic claims with their\n    #       inline\
      \ citation id (or null). Resolve pronouns; split conjunctions.\n    ...\n\n\
      def locate_source(claim: Claim, answer: Answer) -> \"SourcePassage | None\"\
      :\n    \"\"\"Pick the passage to check this claim against.\n\n    Not necessarily\
      \ the cited one: for misattribution detection, also search the\n    full fetched\
      \ corpus so a claim cited to source 3 but actually supported only\n    by source\
      \ 5 is caught.\n    \"\"\"\n    # TODO: retrieve top-k passages for claim.text\
      \ over answer.sources;\n    #       prefer the cited source, fall back to best-matching\
      \ passage.\n    ...\n\ndef verify(answer: Answer, threshold: float) -> Answer:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Attach a Verdict to every atomic claim in the answer.\"\"\"\n   \
      \ # TODO: for each claim -> locate_source -> entail -> collect Verdict\n   \
      \ # TODO: return answer with answer.verdicts populated\n    ...\n\ndef repair(answer:\
      \ Answer, threshold: float) -> Answer:\n    \"\"\"Rewrite or drop claims whose\
      \ source does not entail them.\n\n    Strategy options (pick and document one):\n\
      \      - drop unsupported sentences,\n      - re-cite to a source that *does*\
      \ entail (if locate_source found one),\n      - hedge the claim down to what\
      \ the source actually supports,\n      - or fetch more and retry the browse\
      \ loop for that claim.\n    \"\"\"\n    # TODO: apply the chosen repair to non-faithful\
      \ claims, re-verify, return.\n    ...\n```\n\nKeep `verify` (measurement) and\
      \ `repair` (intervention) separate. The eval needs a\nclean \"verification off\"\
      \ arm — the raw synthesized answer — and a \"verification on\"\narm — the repaired\
      \ answer — and blurring them together makes the before/after\nnumber meaningless.\n\
      \n### The browsing agent (the vehicle, kept deliberately thin)\n\n```python\n\
      # agent.py\nfrom .schemas import Answer\n\ndef research(query: str, *, max_fetches:\
      \ int, budget_usd: float) -> Answer:\n    \"\"\"Search, fetch a few pages, synthesize\
      \ a cited answer. No verification here.\"\"\"\n    # TODO: tool loop: search(query)\
      \ -> pick urls -> fetch(url) -> accumulate passages\n    # TODO: stop on max_fetches\
      \ or budget; synthesize prose that cites source_ids\n    # TODO: return an Answer\
      \ with sources populated and verdicts empty\n    ...\n```\n\nResist making the\
      \ agent clever. A search tool, a fetch tool that returns cleaned\ntext, a fetch\
      \ budget, and a synthesis prompt that must cite by `source_id` is the\nentire\
      \ agent. The intellectual weight of the week lives in `entail` and `verify`,\n\
      not in browsing.\n\n## Build path\n\nWork outside-in so each layer is testable\
      \ before the next depends on it.\n\n1. **Acceptor, in isolation.** Implement\
      \ and unit-test the character-level\n   acceptor against hand-written valid\
      \ and invalid ticket JSON strings. No model\n   involved yet. This is the piece\
      \ most likely to hide bugs, so it earns the most\n   tests.\n2. **Vocab index.**\
      \ Load a small local model's tokenizer, build the prefix trie,\n   and confirm\
      \ `tokens_consumable_from` on a trivial acceptor (e.g. \"any digit\")\n   returns\
      \ exactly the digit-leading tokens it should. Verify multi-character\n   tokens\
      \ are simulated through, not prefix-checked.\n3. **Mask + processor.** Wire\
      \ the acceptor and index into a `LogitsProcessor`.\n   Run greedy generation\
      \ on a couple of tickets and confirm the output is valid\n   JSON matching the\
      \ schema every single time — including the token-healing and\n   EOS-gating\
      \ cases.\n4. **Baseline path.** Add the unconstrained prompted-JSON mode on\
      \ the same model\n   and prompt. Confirm it *sometimes* fails to parse (if it\
      \ never does on your\n   inputs, your inputs are too easy — add longer/messier\
      \ tickets).\n5. **Benchmark harness.** Assemble the ticket set, run both modes,\
      \ and record the\n   metrics below.\n\n## Benchmarks\n\nThe checkable artifact.\
      \ It must demonstrate the abstract's claim — a guarantee\nwith a measurable\
      \ price — from your own output, not from this README.\n\n**Dataset.** Assemble\
      \ $N$ support tickets (aim for a few hundred; a mix of short,\nlong, and adversarial\
      \ phrasings that tempt the model off-schema) in\n`data/tickets.jsonl`. Gold\
      \ `category` labels let you *also* report accuracy, but\nthe primary metrics\
      \ here are about *validity*, which needs no labels.\n\n**Conditions.** Two,\
      \ differing only in the mask:\n\n| Condition | Schema constraint |\n| --- |\
      \ --- |\n| `prompted` | Prompt asks for JSON; no logit masking (baseline) |\n\
      | `constrained` | Same prompt + grammar logit mask |\n\n**Primary metrics.**\n\
      \n- **Schema-validity rate** — fraction of outputs that (a) `json.loads` cleanly\
      \ and\n  (b) satisfy the schema (known keys, enum member, in-range integer,\
      \ boolean).\n  Expected shape: `constrained` is $1.0$ by construction; `prompted`\
      \ is\n  meaningfully below $1.0$, with the gap widening on the harder tickets.\
      \ If\n  `constrained` is not exactly $1.0$, your acceptor has a hole — fix it\
      \ before\n  reporting anything else.\n- **Latency overhead** — per-token wall-clock\
      \ (or added milliseconds per token)\n  for `constrained` vs `prompted` on the\
      \ same hardware. Report median and a tail\n  percentile. Expected shape: a *bounded*\
      \ per-step overhead from computing the\n  mask, ideally near-constant after\
      \ caching; a naive per-token full-vocab replay\n  will show a large, obviously-improvable\
      \ overhead — measuring that first, then\n  the indexed version, makes a nice\
      \ before/after.\n\n**Secondary (optional).** Classification accuracy against\
      \ gold labels (does the\nconstraint change *what* the model decides, not just\
      \ its shape?); a breakdown of\n`prompted` failure modes (prose preamble, trailing\
      \ comma, out-of-enum, extra key,\ntruncation) — the catalog of exactly what\
      \ the mask is preventing.\n\n**Result to produce.** A small table of `{condition\
      \ → validity rate, median\nlatency, p95 latency}`, plus the failure-mode breakdown\
      \ for the baseline. State\nthe week's conclusion as a number: *\"Constraining\
      \ decoding took schema validity\nfrom X% to 100% at a cost of Y ms/token.\"\
      * That sentence is the deliverable.\n\n`bench/report.py` should emit that table\
      \ (Markdown or CSV) so the claim is\nreproducible from `bench/run.py` output.\n\
      \n## How to run and test\n\n```bash\n# setup\nuv venv && uv pip install -e .\
      \          # or python -m venv + pip\n# Supply runtime configuration; retrieve\
      \ secrets through wt vault.\n\n# unit tests — acceptor and mask invariants first\n\
      pytest tests/test_acceptor.py tests/test_mask.py -q\n\n# end-to-end: constrained\
      \ output must be 100% schema-valid\npytest tests/test_end_to_end.py -q\n\n#\
      \ benchmark both conditions and print the results table\npython bench/run.py\
      \ --data data/tickets.jsonl --out bench/out.json\npython bench/report.py bench/out.json\n\
      ```\n\nThe end-to-end test is your guarantee's regression net: assert that **every**\n\
      constrained output over the eval set parses and validates. If that test can\
      \ ever\nfail, the \"guarantee\" is only a strong suggestion.\n\n## Security\
      \ notes\n\n- **Never commit secrets.** Keep model/API config in `.env`, ship\
      \ only\n  `.env.example`, and keep `.env` in `.gitignore`.\n- **Treat model\
      \ output as untrusted** even when it is schema-valid: a valid enum\n  value\
      \ is not authorization to act. This chapter only *parses* the output, but\n\
      \  carry the habit forward — validate at the boundary, never `eval`/`exec` model\n\
      \  text.\n- The constraint guarantees *shape*, not *truth*: a well-formed\n\
      \  `{\"category\": \"billing\", ...}` can still be the wrong category. Keep\
      \ the\n  accuracy metric distinct from the validity metric so you never mistake\
      \ one for\n  the other.\n\n## Hardware, cost & subscriptions\n\n- **Compute:**\
      \ CPU-only is sufficient. Because real per-step logit masking needs\n  direct\
      \ access to the logits, prefer a **small local model** (e.g. a few-hundred-\n\
      \  million to a couple-billion-parameter instruct model via `transformers` or\n\
      \  `llama.cpp`) so you can attach a `LogitsProcessor`; a small model is *more*\n\
      \  likely to fail the prompted baseline, which makes the effect easy to see.\
      \ A GPU\n  only speeds up generation and is never required for this chapter.\n\
      - **Hosted APIs:** most chat completion endpoints do not expose per-step logit\n\
      \  masking, so they cannot host the *constrained* side of this exact\n  implementation.\
      \ If you use a hosted model, restrict it to the `prompted`\n  baseline and run\
      \ the `constrained` condition on the local model — but keep the\n  comparison\
      \ honest by matching model and prompt wherever you compare. Vendors'\n  built-in\
      \ \"structured output\" modes are a *different* implementation of this same\n\
      \  idea, not a substitute for building the mask yourself.\n- **Cost:** effectively\
      \ **\\$0** if you run both conditions on a local model; at\n  most a few dollars\
      \ if you use a hosted model for the baseline. Comfortably\n  inside the course's\
      \ \"under \\$50 total\" target with room to spare.\n\n## Build path — Claim-Level\
      \ Citation Verification\n\n1. **Schemas + config.** Nail down `Claim`, `SourcePassage`,\
      \ `Verdict`, `Answer`\n   and load model names / thresholds / budgets from env.\
      \ Everything else imports\n   these.\n2. **Thin browsing agent.** Get `research()`\
      \ producing a synthesized answer with\n   inline citations over a couple of\
      \ fetched pages. Cache fetched pages to\n   `data/cache/` so later eval runs\
      \ are deterministic and free.\n3. **Decomposition.** Implement `decompose()`\
      \ and eyeball it on a handful of\n   answers: are the claims genuinely atomic?\
      \ Are pronouns resolved? This step\n   quietly caps your ceiling.\n4. **Entailment.**\
      \ Implement `entail()` twice — hosted LLM judge and local NLI —\n   behind the\
      \ one interface. Unit-test it on obvious entailed / neutral /\n   contradicted\
      \ triples before trusting it on real claims.\n5. **Verify pass.** Wire `locate_source`\
      \ → `entail` into `verify()`, producing a\n   per-claim verdict list. At this\
      \ point you can already *measure* an answer's\n   faithfulness.\n6. **Repair.**\
      \ Add `repair()` with one documented strategy. This is the \"after\"\n   arm\
      \ of the benchmark.\n7. **Eval harness.** Build `queries.jsonl` with ground-truth\
      \ claim labels, then\n   run the before/after comparison and produce the metrics\
      \ table.\n\n## Evaluation — the checkable artifact — Claim-Level Citation Verification\n\
      \nThe claim of the week is that a verification pass measurably lowers the\n\
      hallucination rate. Prove it by holding *everything* constant except the pass.\n\
      \n**Two arms, identical agent, identical sources:**\n\n- **Off** — the raw synthesized\
      \ answer from `research()`.\n- **On** — the same answer after `verify()` + `repair()`.\n\
      \n**Metrics, per arm, aggregated over the query set:**\n\n- **Hallucination\
      \ (unsupported-claim) rate** — the headline number:\n  $1 - \\text{faithfulness}$,\
      \ i.e. the fraction of emitted claims whose source does\n  not entail them,\
      \ judged against your gold labels.\n- **Faithfulness rate** — the complement,\
      \ for readability.\n- **Verifier quality** — because the pass is only as good\
      \ as `entail`, also report\n  the verifier's own precision/recall against gold\
      \ labels: does it correctly flag\n  the claims you *know* are unsupported, and\
      \ does it avoid flagging supported ones?\n- **Repair cost** — claims dropped/rewritten\
      \ per answer, and extra tokens/dollars\n  the pass spends, so the win is priced.\n\
      \n**Expected shape of the result** — a small table like:\n\n| arm | hallucination\
      \ rate | faithfulness | verifier precision | verifier recall | added cost /\
      \ answer |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| verification off | (higher)\
      \ | (lower) | — | — | \\$0 |\n| verification on | (lower) | (higher) | (report)\
      \ | (report) | (report) |\n\nThe direction is the point: **on** should show\
      \ a clearly lower hallucination rate\nthan **off**, and you should be able to\
      \ point at the exact claims the pass caught.\nIf the two arms are indistinguishable,\
      \ either your eval set has no unsupported\nclaims to catch (fix the trap sources)\
      \ or `entail` is rubber-stamping everything\n(check its precision/recall first).\n\
      \n**One honest sub-result worth including:** sweep the entailment `threshold`.\
      \ A high\nthreshold flags more claims (catches more hallucinations but drops\
      \ supported ones —\nlower verifier recall on the \"supported\" class); a low\
      \ threshold lets borderline\nclaims through. Plotting hallucination rate against\
      \ the drop/rewrite rate as the\nthreshold moves makes explicit that verification\
      \ trades coverage for faithfulness,\nthe same knob-tuning shape as the calibration\
      \ weeks.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment,\
      \ fixture and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command\
      \ and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."

  - content: "Version prompts, model settings, datasets, and scoring rules together.\
      \ Use paired offline comparisons or a properly assigned A/B experiment and distinguish\
      \ their conclusions. Explain repeated-run variation, judge disagreement, sample-size\
      \ planning, uncertainty, and the false-positive risk of repeatedly peeking at\
      \ a fixed-horizon test. Introduce sequential testing as an optional method when\
      \ repeated looks are required.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation\
      \ and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are\
      \ proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured\
      \ results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected\
      \ components in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nBuild\
      \ a local experiment that compares two immutable prompt versions on the same\
      \ fixed\ntask dataset. Assign each case to one version before looking at outcomes,\
      \ replay supplied\nmodel responses, and produce a report with success rates,\
      \ the difference between versions,\nan uncertainty interval, and the sample\
      \ size you planned to collect.\n\nThe exercise separates prompt experimentation\
      \ from application deployment. It needs no web\nservice, traffic router, Docker\
      \ setup, or live users. The artifact is a reproducible local\nexperiment whose\
      \ prompt text, dataset, assignment, responses, metric, and analysis can all\n\
      be inspected after the run.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n- The idea of comparing\
      \ scorers with fixed labeled data from\n  Guide 12, or equivalent experience.\n\
      - Basic Python, JSON Lines (JSONL), hashing, and binary outcomes.\n- Familiarity\
      \ with a confidence interval and a null-hypothesis test is helpful, but the\n\
      \  lesson introduces the specific quantities it uses.\n\nThe core exercise uses\
      \ recorded model responses and costs $0. Calling a hosted model is an\noptional\
      \ extension. Continuous delivery, traffic shifting, feature flags, monitoring\
      \ a\nrelease, and returning to a previous application version belong in Systems\
      \ Guide 1. This\nweek studies whether a prompt change appears to alter a defined\
      \ outcome under a controlled\nlocal comparison.\n\n## Begin with a concrete\
      \ prompt change\n\nUse a supplied set of 240 short support tickets. The task\
      \ is to return JSON containing a\n`category` and a one-sentence `summary`. The\
      \ control prompt asks for those fields. The\ntreatment adds an explicit JSON\
      \ schema, an allowed-category list, and a 30-word summary\nlimit.\n\nBefore\
      \ running the comparison, write down:\n\n- the primary outcome: `1` only when\
      \ the response parses, uses an allowed category, and\n  keeps the summary within\
      \ 30 words;\n- the minimum effect worth detecting, such as an eight-percentage-point\
      \ improvement;\n- the planned number of cases per variant;\n- the assignment\
      \ unit, which is one ticket;\n- the rule for handling missing or invalid responses;\n\
      - the analysis you will run once, after all assigned cases are scored.\n\nThis\
      \ short record is the experiment plan. Writing it first prevents you from changing\
      \ the\nmetric or stopping rule after seeing a favorable partial result.\n\n\
      ## Preserve every experimental input\n\nA prompt tag such as `v2` is convenient\
      \ but does not identify exact content. Hash the UTF-8\nprompt bytes and store\
      \ the digest with every outcome:\n\n$$\nv=\\operatorname{SHA256}(\\text{prompt\
      \ bytes}).\n$$\n\nEditing a prompt creates a new digest. Never overwrite a stored\
      \ prompt while retaining its\nold identifier. The experiment manifest also records\
      \ the dataset hash, response-fixture\nhash, metric version, assignment seed,\
      \ model label, and analysis version.\n\nUse a deterministic assignment based\
      \ on the experiment ID, seed, and case ID. Convert the\nfirst 64 bits of the\
      \ digest to a value in $[0,1)$ and assign values below $0.5$ to the\ntreatment.\
      \ Hash assignment is reproducible, but its small realized split will rarely\
      \ be\nexactly 50/50. Report the actual counts.\n\nDo not include outcome fields,\
      \ response text, or labels in the assignment key. If one user\ncould contribute\
      \ several correlated cases, the user would become the assignment unit. The\n\
      supplied fixture has one independent synthetic ticket per case, so ticket-level\
      \ assignment\nis acceptable for this exercise.\n\n## Use a fixed response fixture\n\
      \n`responses.jsonl` contains one recorded response for every `(case_id, prompt_digest)`\
      \ pair.\nAfter assignment, select only the response produced by the assigned\
      \ prompt. This lets the\nentire experiment run offline while preserving the\
      \ shape of a two-arm comparison.\n\nValidate that every assigned case has exactly\
      \ one selected response, no unknown cases or\nprompt digests exist, and all\
      \ expected cases are accounted for. A missing or malformed\nresponse receives\
      \ outcome `0` under the rule declared in the experiment plan. Keep a\nseparate\
      \ reason such as `missing`, `invalid_json`, `unknown_category`, or `too_long`\
      \ so the\naggregate score does not erase the failure mode.\n\nRecorded responses\
      \ demonstrate experiment mechanics; they are not evidence about the\ncurrent\
      \ behavior of a provider model. Label the fixture with its source and creation\
      \ date.\n\n## Project shape and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\nweek20/\n\
      ├── pyproject.toml\n├── prompts/\n│   ├── classify.v1.txt\n│   └── classify.v2.txt\n\
      ├── experiments/\n│   └── ticket-format.json\n├── prompt_experiment/\n│   ├──\
      \ schema.py\n│   ├── registry.py\n│   ├── assign.py\n│   ├── fixtures.py\n│\
      \   ├── score.py\n│   ├── analyze.py\n│   ├── report.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├──\
      \ data/\n│   ├── cases.jsonl\n│   └── responses.jsonl\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n\
      ```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom pathlib import Path\n\
      \n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass PromptVersion:\n    name: str\n    digest:\
      \ str\n    content: str\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Assignment:\n    experiment_id:\
      \ str\n    case_id: str\n    variant: str\n    prompt_digest: str\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class Outcome:\n    case_id: str\n    variant: str\n    prompt_digest: str\n\
      \    value: int\n    reason: str\n\ndef load_prompts(directory: Path) -> dict[str,\
      \ PromptVersion]: ...\n\ndef assign(\n    experiment_id: str,\n    seed: str,\n\
      \    case_id: str,\n    treatment_share: float,\n) -> str: ...\n\ndef score_response(response:\
      \ str, *, metric_version: str) -> tuple[int, str]: ...\n\ndef analyze(outcomes:\
      \ list[Outcome], *, min_effect: float) -> dict: ...\n```\n\nThe signatures leave\
      \ implementation choices open. Keep loading, assignment, selection,\nscoring,\
      \ and analysis as separate functions so a test can challenge each boundary.\n\
      \n## Analyze a binary outcome\n\nFor variant $j$, let $x_j$ be successful cases\
      \ and $n_j$ be assigned cases. Its observed\nsuccess rate is\n\n$$\n\\widehat{p}_j=\\\
      frac{x_j}{n_j}.\n$$\n\nThe primary estimate is the absolute difference\n\n$$\n\
      \\widehat{\\Delta}=\\widehat{p}_{\\mathrm{treatment}}-\n\\widehat{p}_{\\mathrm{control}}.\n\
      $$\n\nUse a maintained statistics library to calculate a 95% confidence interval\
      \ for the\ndifference and a two-sided two-proportion test. The interval describes\
      \ effect sizes\ncompatible with this experiment under the method's assumptions.\
      \ The p-value measures how\nsurprising the observed difference would be under\
      \ the test's null model; it is not the\nprobability that the treatment is better.\n\
      \nChoose the minimum effect and planned sample size before reading outcomes.\
      \ A library power\ncalculation may use the baseline rate estimated from a separate\
      \ pilot fixture. In the\nreport, distinguish these statements:\n\n- the observed\
      \ point estimate and interval;\n- whether the interval includes zero;\n- whether\
      \ the planned sample size was reached;\n- whether the interval rules out effects\
      \ smaller than the minimum worthwhile effect.\n\nDo not turn those facts into\
      \ a universal `ship` or `do not ship` decision. A local synthetic\nexperiment\
      \ cannot establish effects on production users, latency, cost, safety, or future\n\
      model versions.\n\n## Why this week exists — Sequential Testing and the Peeking\
      \ Trap\n\nEvery other week in this course ends with an A/B comparison: constrained\
      \ vs.\nprompted JSON, layout-aware vs. naive chunking, sequential vs. fixed.\
      \ Those\ncomparisons are only worth anything if the *test itself* is sound.\
      \ This chapter is\nthe meta-week: it audits the statistical procedure you've\
      \ been implicitly\ntrusting every time you said \"the new prompt won.\"\n\n\
      The specific failure is **peeking**. A classical fixed-horizon test — \"collect\n\
      $n$ samples, then compute one p-value\" — controls $\\alpha$ *only if you look\n\
      exactly once, at $n$.* Real teams don't. They watch a dashboard, and they stop\n\
      as soon as $p < 0.05$ flashes green. That single behavioral change silently\n\
      turns a 5% false-positive test into a 20–40% one. The fix is not \"peek less\"\
      \n(nobody will); it's to use a statistic that stays valid no matter how often,\
      \ or\nwhen, you look.\n\n## Concepts and theory — Sequential Testing and the\
      \ Peeking Trap\n\n### The peeking problem, precisely\n\nLet each observation\
      \ be a per-example outcome for one arm — e.g. a binary\n\"passed the eval\"\
      \ indicator, or a continuous score difference between arms on a\npaired prompt.\
      \ Under the null hypothesis $H_0$ (the two configs are equally\ngood), a fixed-horizon\
      \ test statistic $Z_n$ at the planned horizon $n$ satisfies\n\n$$\\Pr_{H_0}\\\
      !\\left(|Z_n| \\ge z_{1-\\alpha/2}\\right) = \\alpha.$$\n\nThat guarantee is\
      \ about the *single* random variable $Z_n$. Peeking asks a\ndifferent question\
      \ — the probability that the trajectory $Z_1, Z_2, \\dots, Z_n$\n*ever* crosses\
      \ the boundary:\n\n$$\\Pr_{H_0}\\!\\left(\\exists\\, t \\le n : |Z_t| \\ge z_{1-\\\
      alpha/2}\\right) \\;\\gg\\; \\alpha.$$\n\nBy the law of the iterated logarithm\
      \ the running statistic $|Z_t|$ crosses any\nfixed boundary infinitely often\
      \ as $t \\to \\infty$ under $H_0$ — so a continuously\nmonitored fixed-horizon\
      \ test rejects $H_0$ **with probability 1** eventually,\neven when nothing is\
      \ happening. That is the whole trap in one line.\n\n### Sequential probability\
      \ ratio test (SPRT)\n\nWald's SPRT is the classical escape. For a simple null\
      \ $H_0:\\theta=\\theta_0$ vs.\nalternative $H_1:\\theta=\\theta_1$, accumulate\
      \ the log-likelihood ratio after $t$\nobservations $x_{1:t}$:\n\n$$\\Lambda_t\
      \ \\;=\\; \\sum_{i=1}^{t} \\log \\frac{p_{\\theta_1}(x_i)}{p_{\\theta_0}(x_i)}.$$\n\
      \nStop and reject $H_0$ the first time $\\Lambda_t \\ge \\log(1/\\alpha)$ (roughly).\n\
      The reason this is safe under continuous monitoring is **Ville's inequality**:\n\
      for any nonnegative supermartingale $M_t$ with $M_0 = 1$,\n\n$$\\Pr\\!\\left(\\\
      sup_{t\\ge 1} M_t \\ge 1/\\alpha\\right) \\le \\alpha.$$\n\nThe likelihood ratio\
      \ $\\exp(\\Lambda_t)$ is exactly such a process under $H_0$, so\nthe *supremum\
      \ over all $t$* — i.e. peeking at every step — is controlled at\n$\\alpha$.\
      \ That's the mathematical object we want; peeking is free.\n\n### The problem\
      \ SPRT leaves open, and the mixture fix\n\nPlain SPRT needs a single point alternative\
      \ $\\theta_1$. You rarely know the true\neffect size in advance. The **mixture\
      \ SPRT (mSPRT)** removes that requirement by\nintegrating the likelihood ratio\
      \ over a prior $\\pi(\\theta)$ on the effect:\n\n$$M_t \\;=\\; \\int \\prod_{i=1}^{t}\
      \ \\frac{p_{\\theta}(x_i)}{p_{\\theta_0}(x_i)}\\; \\pi(\\theta)\\, d\\theta.$$\n\
      \n$M_t$ is still a nonnegative martingale under $H_0$ (mixtures of martingales\
      \ are\nmartingales), so Ville still applies. This yields the two artifacts you'll\
      \ ship:\n\n- an **always-valid p-value** $\\;\\; \\tilde p_t = \\min\\!\\left(1,\\\
      , \\inf_{s \\le t} 1/M_s\\right)$, which is monotone non-increasing and can\
      \ be thresholded at any time; and\n- a **confidence sequence** $\\text{CS}_t$\
      \ — a sequence of intervals with the\n  *uniform* coverage guarantee $\\Pr\\\
      !\\left(\\forall t:\\ \\theta^\\star \\in \\text{CS}_t\\right) \\ge 1-\\alpha$,\
      \ not the pointwise coverage a normal CI gives.\n\nFor a Gaussian mixture on\
      \ a mean-difference with prior variance $\\tau^2$ and\nper-observation variance\
      \ $\\sigma^2$, the mSPRT statistic has a closed form worth\nimplementing directly\
      \ rather than integrating numerically:\n\n$$M_t \\;=\\; \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sigma^2}{\\\
      sigma^2 + t\\,\\tau^2}}\\;\\exp\\!\\left(\\frac{t^2 \\tau^2\\, \\bar X_t^{\\\
      ,2}}{2\\sigma^2(\\sigma^2 + t\\,\\tau^2)}\\right),$$\n\nwhere $\\bar X_t$ is\
      \ the running mean of the paired differences. Choosing $\\tau$\nis the one real\
      \ modeling decision: it should match the smallest effect you'd\ncare to detect.\n\
      \n### The modern framing: e-values and testing by betting\n\nThe same guarantee\
      \ has an intuitive restatement. An **e-value** $E_t$ is the\npayoff of a fair\
      \ bet against $H_0$ — you start with \\$1, and Ville's inequality\nsays the\
      \ chance of ever multiplying your money by $1/\\alpha$ under $H_0$ is\n$\\le\
      \ \\alpha$. $M_t$ above *is* an e-process; $1/M_t$ is the always-valid p-value.\n\
      Implementing at least one **betting-style confidence sequence** (e.g. a Hoeffding-\n\
      or empirical-Bernstein-style one for bounded outcomes) alongside the Gaussian\n\
      mSPRT is a good stretch goal, because it needs no variance assumption and is\
      \ what\nproduction experimentation platforms increasingly use.\n\n> **Mental\
      \ model.** A fixed-horizon p-value is a photograph; an always-valid\n> p-value\
      \ is a video you can pause on any frame and still trust. You pay for that\n\
      > with a modest increase in samples-to-decision — that's the trade this chapter\n\
      > quantifies, not just asserts."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Add tests that can catch a persuasive wrong report\n\nTest\
      \ assignment stability, approximate balance over many synthetic IDs, changed\
      \ assignment\nunder a changed seed, and rejection of treatment shares outside\
      \ $[0,1]$. Test that changing\none byte of a prompt changes its digest. Test\
      \ malformed response handling and ensure that\ncase IDs are unique and aligned\
      \ across cases, assignments, and outcomes.\n\nFor the analysis, construct tiny\
      \ tables with known counts and compare the result with the\nstatistics library.\
      \ Include zero successes, all successes, an empty arm, missing outcomes,\nand\
      \ an interval that crosses zero. The program should reject an empty arm or incomplete\
      \ run\nrather than produce a polished number from invalid input.\n\nRun a negative\
      \ control by comparing two differently named variants that point to the same\n\
      prompt digest and equivalent response generation. The measured difference should\
      \ be\ncompatible with noise. A surprising difference is a reason to inspect\
      \ assignment,\nselection, or scoring.\n\n## Build sequence — 16 hours\n\n1.\
      \ **Plan and fixture validation, 3 hours.** Write the outcome and stopping rule,\
      \ inspect\n   the 240 cases, hash all inputs, and validate the recorded response\
      \ matrix.\n2. **Registry and assignment, 3 hours.** Load immutable prompts,\
      \ create deterministic\n   assignments, and test stability and balance.\n3.\
      \ **Scoring and audit rows, 3 hours.** Implement the primary metric, preserve\
      \ failure\n   reasons, and create one outcome row per assigned case.\n4. **Analysis,\
      \ 4 hours.** Compute counts, rates, difference, interval, test result, and the\n\
      \   planned-versus-observed sample-size statement.\n5. **Interpretation, 3 hours.**\
      \ Run the negative control, inspect failures by reason, and\n   write the report's\
      \ limitations.\n\n## Commands and artifact\n\nRun the complete core exercise\
      \ locally:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\nuv run python -m prompt_experiment.cli make-fixtures\
      \ --out data\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m prompt_experiment.cli\
      \ assign --experiment experiments/ticket-format.json --cases data/cases.jsonl\
      \ --out artifacts/assignments.jsonl\nuv run python -m prompt_experiment.cli\
      \ score --assignments artifacts/assignments.jsonl --responses data/responses.jsonl\
      \ --out artifacts/outcomes.jsonl\nuv run python -m prompt_experiment.cli report\
      \ --experiment experiments/ticket-format.json --outcomes artifacts/outcomes.jsonl\
      \ --out artifacts/report.md\n```\n\nThe final report contains all input hashes,\
      \ planned and actual sample counts, successes and\nfailures per arm, the absolute\
      \ difference, confidence interval, two-sided test result,\nfailure-reason counts,\
      \ the negative control, and limitations. Include counts beside rates\nand show\
      \ incomplete or invalid runs as errors rather than silently dropping rows.\n\
      \n## Hardware, cost, and optional depth\n\nThe core exercise runs on a CPU,\
      \ requires no Docker or network access, and costs $0. A live\nextension may\
      \ call one pinned model for both prompt versions on at most 40 cases with a\
      \ $3\ncap. Record the model identifier, parameters, request failures, latency,\
      \ token counts, and\nactual cost; describe that run as a smoke test because\
      \ it is too small for the planned\neffect-size claim.\n\nSequential tests, variance\
      \ reduction, multiple outcomes, user-level clustering, and online\ntraffic allocation\
      \ are optional topics. A production experiment also needs privacy review,\n\
      guardrails, monitoring, rollback, and operational ownership; those concerns\
      \ should not be\ninferred from this bounded local result.\n\n## The checkable\
      \ artifact — Peeking simulation — Sequential Testing and the Peeking Trap\n\n\
      This is the deliverable that proves the abstract's claim. Run\n`scripts/run_simulation.py`.\n\
      \n**Methodology.**\n\n- **Null study.** Generate $T$ trials (e.g. $T = 10\\\
      ,000$) of up to $n$ paired\n  observations each, all drawn under $H_0$ ($\\\
      delta = 0$). For each trial, run\n  two procedures: (a) fixed-horizon z-test\
      \ *peeked at every step*, stopping on\n  first $p < \\alpha$; (b) mSPRT with\
      \ its always-valid p-value, same peeking\n  schedule. Record whether each rejected.\n\
      - **Alternative study.** Repeat with a real effect $\\delta > 0$ (say, a 3–5pp\n\
      \  lift in pass rate) to measure **power** and the **distribution of stop times**\n\
      \  for the sequential procedure — the cost side of the trade.\n- Sweep $\\alpha\
      \ \\in \\{0.01, 0.05, 0.10\\}$ and at least two horizons $n$.\n\n**Expected\
      \ shape of the result.** A small table plus two plots:\n\n| Procedure | $\\\
      alpha$ target | Null reject rate (FPR) | Power @ $\\delta$ | Median stop time\
      \ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Fixed-horizon, peeked | 0.05 | ~0.20–0.40\
      \ (inflated) | high | early |\n| mSPRT (always-valid) | 0.05 | ≤ 0.05 (controlled)\
      \ | high, slightly lower | somewhat later |\n\n- **Plot 1:** empirical FPR vs.\
      \ number of peeks — the fixed-horizon line climbs\n  well past $\\alpha$ and\
      \ keeps climbing; the mSPRT line stays flat at or below\n  $\\alpha$. This single\
      \ figure *is* the week's thesis.\n- **Plot 2:** the price of validity — power\
      \ and expected sample size for mSPRT\n  vs. a correctly-run once-only fixed-horizon\
      \ test, so the reader sees the\n  sequential procedure trades a modest sample\
      \ increase for the freedom to peek.\n\nThe week is only done when your own numbers\
      \ show the peeked baseline's FPR\nmaterially exceeding $\\alpha$ while the sequential\
      \ FPR does not. If you can't see\nit in your output, the week isn't finished.\n\
      \n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture\
      \ and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and\
      \ one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."
