  - content: "Extend one-shot retrieval to a bounded loop that rewrites or decomposes\
      \ a question, retrieves follow-up evidence, and stops when the evidence checker\
      \ succeeds or the budget runs out. Keep source revisions and claim evidence\
      \ traceable across hops. Compare equal-budget configurations and inspect whether\
      \ additional steps retrieve missing facts or merely repeat the same evidence.\n\
      \nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces,\
      \ stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not\
      \ indicate that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone\
      \ fixture for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course\
      \ project.\n\n## Overview\n\nSingle-shot retrieve-then-generate answers a well-posed\
      \ lookup, but it fails on\nmulti-hop questions whose answer requires chaining\
      \ facts from different documents\nand on underspecified queries whose right\
      \ search terms aren't in the question as\nasked. This chapter makes retrieval\
      \ an agent-driven loop: the query is rewritten and\ndecomposed into sub-questions,\
      \ retrieval runs per hop, the model judges whether\nthe accumulated evidence\
      \ is sufficient and issues follow-up retrievals when it\nisn't, and a corrective\
      \ step re-retrieves when a drafted answer isn't grounded in\nthe retrieved text.\
      \ Answer accuracy and retrieval sufficiency are measured on a\nmulti-hop QA\
      \ set against the single-shot RAG baseline from Foundations Week 16,\nalongside\
      \ the added latency and retrieval cost per query so the improvement is\nnever\
      \ free on paper. Iterative, agentic retrieval emerges as the pattern that\n\
      earns its extra calls specifically on multi-hop and underspecified queries —\
      \ with\na measured boundary showing where one-shot RAG is still the right, cheaper\
      \ choice.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- **Week 16 (RAG With an Eval Suite)** — conceptually.\
      \ You need the single-shot\n  retrieve-then-generate pipeline and, crucially,\
      \ the *layered* eval discipline\n  (retrieval recall vs. answer faithfulness\
      \ vs. answer relevance). This chapter's\n  baseline is that pipeline; re-derive\
      \ it here rather than importing it.\n- **Week 15 (Hybrid Search + Reranking)**\
      \ — conceptually. Each hop calls a\n  retriever; assume a `retrieve(query, k)\
      \ -> list[Passage]` that fuses sparse +\n  dense and reranks. You may re-derive\
      \ a thin version or stub it behind a\n  protocol — the retriever is *not* the\
      \ object of study this chapter, the loop is.\n- **Week 8 (A ReAct Loop From\
      \ Raw API Calls)** — conceptually. The\n  decide-then-act control loop (parse\
      \ the model's chosen action, run a tool, feed\n  the observation back) is the\
      \ skeleton; here the tool is retrieval and the\n  observations are passages.\n\
      - **Practical:** comfortable calling a hosted chat-completion API, coercing\
      \ model\n  output into a schema (JSON / structured decode), and writing a small\
      \ eval\n  harness that reports per-query metrics into a table.\n\n## What you\
      \ are building\n\nA library + CLI that answers a question by *looping* over\
      \ retrieval under model\ncontrol, and a benchmark harness that pits it against\
      \ a one-shot baseline on a\nmulti-hop QA set. The core is a small state machine\
      \ — not a framework — with four\nmodel-driven decisions wrapped around a fixed\
      \ retriever.\n\n### The loop, precisely\n\nGiven a question $q$, maintain an\
      \ evidence set $E$ (deduplicated passages) and a\nsub-question queue. One *iteration*\
      \ is:\n\n1. **Decompose / rewrite.** Turn $q$ (plus what's already in $E$) into\
      \ one or more\n   search queries. On the first iteration this is query rewriting\
      \ + multi-hop\n   decomposition; on later iterations it is *gap-driven* — \"\
      what do we still not\n   know?\" — conditioned on $E$.\n2. **Retrieve.** For\
      \ each pending sub-query $s_i$, call `retrieve(s_i, k)` and\n   merge the results\
      \ into $E$ (dedup by document/chunk id).\n3. **Judge sufficiency.** Ask the\
      \ model whether $E$ now supports a complete answer\n   to $q$. If **insufficient**\
      \ and the budget allows, emit follow-up sub-queries\n   and go to step 2. If\
      \ **sufficient**, proceed.\n4. **Draft + ground-check (corrective step).** Draft\
      \ an answer from $E$, then\n   check each claim against the retrieved text.\
      \ If a claim is **ungrounded**,\n   convert it into a targeted retrieval and\
      \ loop once more; otherwise return.\n\nTermination is bounded by a hop budget\
      \ $H_{\\max}$ and a total-retrieval-call\nbudget so a confused query can't spin\
      \ forever. Formally, let $H$ be the number of\nretrieval rounds and $c_r, c_g$\
      \ the per-call retrieval and generation costs; a\nquery's cost is\n\n$$\n\\\
      text{cost}(q) = H \\cdot c_r + (2H + 2)\\, c_g\n$$\n\nroughly (one decompose\
      \ + one sufficiency judgment per round, plus one draft and\none ground-check).\
      \ The benchmark's whole job is to show this extra\n$(H{-}1)$-fold spend is *bought\
      \ back* in accuracy only on the query types that\nneed it.\n\n### File structure\n\
      \n```\nweek30-agentic-rag/\n  pyproject.toml\n  .env.example               \
      \ # API keys — never commit real .env\n  README.md\n  src/agentic_rag/\n   \
      \ __init__.py\n    types.py                  # Passage, Evidence, LoopTrace,\
      \ StepKind\n    retriever.py              # Retriever protocol + a stub/re-derived\
      \ hybrid impl\n    llm.py                    # thin chat-completion client +\
      \ structured-decode helper\n    decompose.py              # query rewrite +\
      \ sub-question generation\n    sufficiency.py            # \"is the evidence\
      \ enough?\" judge\n    ground_check.py           # claim-level grounding / corrective\
      \ trigger\n    loop.py                   # the iterative controller (the heart\
      \ of the week)\n    baseline.py               # Week-16-style single-shot RAG\
      \ (for comparison)\n    cli.py                    # `answer \"<question>\"`\
      \ entry point\n  eval/\n    dataset.py                # load/curate multi-hop\
      \ + single-hop QA items\n    metrics.py                # EM/F1, sufficiency,\
      \ latency, cost accounting\n    run_benchmark.py          # produces results/benchmark.md\
      \ + results/traces.jsonl\n  tests/\n    test_loop_termination.py\n    test_dedup.py\n\
      \    test_baseline_parity.py\n  results/                    # generated artifacts\
      \ (gitignored except the .md report)\n```\n\n*(Tree is illustrative — you build\
      \ these files. Nothing here ships as finished code.)*\n\n## Stub interfaces\n\
      \nStart from the data model and the protocols; leave the decision logic as `...`.\n\
      \n```python\n# types.py\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\nfrom enum\
      \ import Enum\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Passage:\n    doc_id: str\n\
      \    chunk_id: str\n    text: str\n    score: float\n\n@dataclass\nclass Evidence:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Deduplicated, ordered accumulator of retrieved passages.\"\"\"\n\
      \    passages: list[Passage] = field(default_factory=list)\n\n    def add(self,\
      \ new: list[Passage]) -> int:\n        \"\"\"Merge, dedup by (doc_id, chunk_id),\
      \ return count of *newly added*. # TODO\"\"\"\n        ...\n\n    def as_context(self,\
      \ budget_tokens: int) -> str:\n        \"\"\"Render evidence into a prompt context\
      \ under a token budget. # TODO\"\"\"\n        ...\n\nclass StepKind(str, Enum):\n\
      \    DECOMPOSE = \"decompose\"\n    RETRIEVE = \"retrieve\"\n    JUDGE = \"\
      judge\"\n    DRAFT = \"draft\"\n    GROUND_CHECK = \"ground_check\"\n\n@dataclass\n\
      class LoopTrace:\n    \"\"\"One row per step; the audit trail the benchmark\
      \ and tests read.\"\"\"\n    steps: list[tuple[StepKind, dict]] = field(default_factory=list)\n\
      \    retrieval_calls: int = 0\n    generation_calls: int = 0\n    def record(self,\
      \ kind: StepKind, **payload) -> None: ...\n```\n\n```python\n# retriever.py\n\
      from typing import Protocol\nfrom .types import Passage\n\nclass Retriever(Protocol):\n\
      \    def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int) -> list[Passage]:\n        \"\"\"\
      Hybrid sparse+dense + rerank (Week 15). Treated as a fixed dependency.\"\"\"\
      \n        ...\n```\n\n```python\n# decompose.py\ndef rewrite_and_decompose(question:\
      \ str, evidence, llm) -> list[str]:\n    \"\"\"\n    First round: rewrite the\
      \ question and split multi-hop asks into sub-queries.\n    Later rounds: emit\
      \ *gap-filling* sub-queries given what evidence lacks.\n    Return [] to signal\
      \ 'no further sub-queries needed'.\n    # TODO: prompt + structured decode into\
      \ a list[str]; cap the count.\n    \"\"\"\n    ...\n```\n\n```python\n# sufficiency.py\n\
      from dataclasses import dataclass\n\n@dataclass\nclass Sufficiency:\n    sufficient:\
      \ bool\n    missing: list[str]        # what facts are still needed (drives\
      \ next hop)\n    rationale: str\n\ndef judge_sufficiency(question: str, evidence,\
      \ llm) -> Sufficiency:\n    \"\"\"Ask: does E support a *complete* answer? #\
      \ TODO: structured decode.\"\"\"\n    ...\n```\n\n```python\n# ground_check.py\n\
      from dataclasses import dataclass\n\n@dataclass\nclass GroundReport:\n    grounded:\
      \ bool\n    ungrounded_claims: list[str]   # each becomes a corrective retrieval\
      \ query\n\ndef check_grounding(answer: str, evidence, llm) -> GroundReport:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Split the draft into claims; verify each against retrieved text.\
      \ # TODO.\"\"\"\n    ...\n```\n\n```python\n# loop.py\nfrom dataclasses import\
      \ dataclass\nfrom .types import Evidence, LoopTrace\n\n@dataclass\nclass LoopConfig:\n\
      \    k: int = 6\n    max_hops: int = 4\n    max_retrieval_calls: int = 12\n\
      \    context_token_budget: int = 3000\n\n@dataclass\nclass Answer:\n    text:\
      \ str\n    evidence: Evidence\n    trace: LoopTrace\n    stopped_reason: str\
      \        # \"sufficient\" | \"budget\" | \"grounded_after_correction\"\n\ndef\
      \ answer_iteratively(question: str, retriever, llm, cfg: LoopConfig) -> Answer:\n\
      \    \"\"\"\n    The heart of the week. Implement the 4-step loop with hard\
      \ budget caps.\n    # TODO:\n    #   1. decompose -> sub-queries\n    #   2.\
      \ retrieve each -> Evidence.add\n    #   3. judge_sufficiency -> loop or proceed\n\
      \    #   4. draft -> check_grounding -> corrective retrieve or return\n    #\
      \   Enforce max_hops / max_retrieval_calls; record every step in the trace.\n\
      \    \"\"\"\n    ...\n```\n\n```python\n# baseline.py\ndef answer_single_shot(question:\
      \ str, retriever, llm, k: int = 6) -> \"Answer\":\n    \"\"\"Week-16-style:\
      \ retrieve once, generate once. The thing to beat. # TODO.\"\"\"\n    ...\n\
      ```\n\n## Count the rendered context — Long-Context Management\n\nThe budget\
      \ applies to the exact rendered context, including item headers and separators.\n\
      Use the same rendering function for selection and final output, then encode\
      \ the finished\ntext again and assert its token count is within the budget.\n\
      \nAn item is indivisible in the core exercise. If the next complete item does\
      \ not fit, skip\nit and consider later items. Record an `oversized_item` reason\
      \ when a required item cannot\nfit by itself. Cutting a function halfway may\
      \ produce more text under the limit, but it\nremoves the boundary that makes\
      \ structural selection understandable.\n\nDefine utilization as\n\n$$\n\\operatorname{utilization}=\\\
      frac{\\text{selected context tokens}}{\\text{token budget}}.\n$$\n\nHigh utilization\
      \ is not automatically good. A full context of unrelated items is worse\nthan\
      \ a smaller context containing the evidence the task needs.\n\n## Measure preservation\
      \ rather than presentation — Long-Context Management\n\nFor required evidence\
      \ set $R$ and selected item IDs $S$, calculate\n\n$$\n\\operatorname{evidence\\\
      \ recall}=\\frac{|R\\cap S|}{|R|}.\n$$\n\nAlso record exact evidence coverage\
      \ (`true` only when $R$ is a subset of $S$), utilization,\nselected item count,\
      \ unrelated selected tokens, and oversized required items. Define\nunrelated\
      \ items from the fixture's gold evidence only in the evaluator; the strategies\
      \ do\nnot receive that field.\n\nCompare strategies within the same case and\
      \ budget. Report wins, ties, and losses for\nevidence recall, along with the\
      \ individual cases behind the counts. Do not conclude that a\nstrategy improves\
      \ answer quality because it improves evidence recall. An optional recorded\n\
      answer fixture can test that downstream relationship, but it is not part of\
      \ the core claim."
    lab_and_evidence: "## How to build it (milestones)\n\n1. **Types + retriever seam.**\
      \ Land `types.py` and the `Retriever` protocol.\n   Stub the retriever (even\
      \ a canned in-memory hybrid over your eval corpus) so\n   the loop can be built\
      \ against a stable interface. Get dedup right early — it's\n   where iterative\
      \ retrieval quietly wins or drowns in duplicates.\n2. **Single-shot baseline\
      \ first.** Build `baseline.py` and confirm it answers\n   simple lookups. You\
      \ cannot claim an improvement without this reference, and it\n   shakes out\
      \ your LLM client + context rendering before the loop adds moving parts.\n3.\
      \ **One hop, no judging.** Wire decompose → retrieve → draft with `max_hops=1`.\n\
      \   Confirm it equals the baseline on single-hop questions (a test asserts this).\n\
      4. **Add the sufficiency judge.** Let the loop take a *second* hop when evidence\n\
      \   is insufficient. Watch a multi-hop question that the baseline misses start\
      \ to\n   succeed — and watch a simple question correctly stop after one hop.\n\
      5. **Add the corrective ground-check.** Draft, verify claims, re-retrieve the\n\
      \   ungrounded ones. This is what fixes confidently-wrong answers built on a\n\
      \   near-miss passage.\n6. **Budgets + traces.** Enforce `max_hops` / `max_retrieval_calls`,\
      \ record every\n   step. The trace is both your debugger and the benchmark's\
      \ data source.\n\nKeep the loop a plain state machine. If you find yourself\
      \ building a plugin system\nor a general agent framework, you've overshot the\
      \ week — the point is to see the\nloop bare.\n\n## Benchmark: does the loop\
      \ earn its calls?\n\nThe deliverable that proves the abstract's claims is a\
      \ report,\n`results/benchmark.md`, generated by `eval/run_benchmark.py` from\n\
      `results/traces.jsonl`.\n\n**Dataset.** A small QA set (≈40–80 items is plenty)\
      \ partitioned by *type*:\n\n- **single-hop** — answerable from one passage (where\
      \ one-shot should win on cost);\n- **multi-hop** — answer requires chaining\
      \ ≥2 documents;\n- **underspecified** — the right search terms aren't literally\
      \ in the question.\n\nCurate from a public multi-hop set (HotpotQA / 2WikiMultiHopQA-style\
      \ items) or\nhand-write a dozen over your own corpus. Store gold answers and,\
      \ for multi-hop\nitems, the set of gold supporting documents so *retrieval sufficiency*\
      \ is checkable\nindependently of the final answer.\n\n**Systems compared.**\
      \ `answer_single_shot` (baseline) vs. `answer_iteratively`\n(this chapter),\
      \ same retriever, same generator, same $k$.\n\n**Metrics per query, then aggregated\
      \ by partition:**\n\n| Metric | What it measures | How |\n| --- | --- | ---\
      \ |\n| Answer EM / F1 | correctness | token-overlap vs. gold answer |\n| Retrieval\
      \ sufficiency | did $E$ contain all gold supporting docs? | set coverage of\
      \ gold doc ids |\n| Hops $H$ | how hard the loop worked | count of retrieval\
      \ rounds |\n| Retrieval calls | cost driver | from the trace |\n| Generation\
      \ calls / tokens | cost driver | from the trace |\n| Latency p50/p95 | wall-clock\
      \ cost | timed end-to-end |\n\n**Expected shape of the result.** A table (and\
      \ ideally a small plot) where, *by\npartition*:\n\n- on **multi-hop** and **underspecified**\
      \ items, iterative beats baseline on\n  accuracy and sufficiency by a clear\
      \ margin — at $2$–$4\\times$ the calls and\n  latency;\n- on **single-hop**\
      \ items, iterative is roughly *tied* with baseline on accuracy\n  while costing\
      \ more — the empirical **boundary** where one-shot RAG is the right,\n  cheaper\
      \ choice.\n\nReport a single crossover sentence: *\"Above ~N required hops,\
      \ iterative wins;\nat/below it, one-shot is the economical pick.\"* An improvement\
      \ stated without its\nlatency/cost column is not an accepted result this chapter\
      \ — the trade must be on the\nsame page.\n\n**Optional ablations** (each isolates\
      \ one loop component):\n- drop the corrective ground-check → measure the faithfulness/EM\
      \ regression;\n- fix `max_hops=1` → collapses to baseline, validates the harness;\n\
      - decompose off, sufficiency-judge on → shows decomposition's separate contribution.\n\
      \n## Running and testing\n\n- **CLI:** `answer \"<question>\"` prints the answer\
      \ plus a compact trace (hops,\n  calls, stop reason). A `--baseline` flag runs\
      \ the single-shot path for a quick\n  side-by-side.\n- **Benchmark:** `python\
      \ -m eval.run_benchmark` writes `results/benchmark.md` and\n  `results/traces.jsonl`.\n\
      - **Tests to write:**\n  - *termination* — a deliberately unanswerable question\
      \ stops at\n    `max_retrieval_calls` and reports `stopped_reason=\"budget\"\
      ` (no infinite loop);\n  - *dedup* — feeding overlapping retrieval results grows\
      \ `Evidence` by only the\n    genuinely new passages;\n  - *baseline parity*\
      \ — with `max_hops=1` and grounding disabled, the iterative\n    loop's answer\
      \ equals the single-shot baseline on single-hop items.\n- Make LLM calls injectable\
      \ so tests can pass a scripted fake model and assert on\n  control flow without\
      \ spending tokens or flaking on nondeterminism.\n\n## Security & hygiene\n\n\
      - **Secrets:** the API key lives in `.env`; commit only `.env.example`. Never\
      \ log\n  full keys; load via environment, not hard-coded strings.\n- **Untrusted\
      \ text is data, not instructions.** Retrieved passages and\n  model-emitted\
      \ sub-queries can carry prompt-injection (\"ignore previous\n  instructions…\"\
      ). Keep retrieved text in clearly delimited context blocks, never\n  execute\
      \ or `eval` model output, and validate every structured decode (sub-query\n\
      \  lists, sufficiency verdicts) against a schema before acting on it.\n- **Budget\
      \ as a safety control, not just cost control.** The hop and call caps\n  bound\
      \ both spend and a runaway loop triggered by adversarial input.\n\n## Hardware,\
      \ cost & subscriptions\n\n- **Hardware:** CPU-only. Retrieval runs over a local\
      \ index; no GPU required.\n- **Cost:** a few dollars total. Iterative retrieval\
      \ issues several model calls\n  per query (decompose + sufficiency + draft +\
      \ ground-check per hop), so keep the\n  eval set small, cache embeddings, and\
      \ prefer a cheap/fast hosted model or a\n  free-tier provider for the judge/decompose\
      \ calls. A small embedding budget\n  covers indexing the corpus once.\n- **Subscriptions:**\
      \ one hosted LLM API key (any of OpenAI / Anthropic / Azure AI\n  Foundry /\
      \ Bedrock / a free-tier provider such as Groq or Together). No paid GPU\n  or\
      \ managed vector-DB subscription needed — the local index from the retrieval\n\
      \  arc is sufficient.\n\n## Add failure-focused tests — Long-Context Management\n\
      \nTest exact-budget fits, header and separator accounting, an item one token\
      \ too large, a\nlarge skipped item followed by a small fitting item, duplicate\
      \ IDs, missing call targets,\nstable tie-breaking, and a changed function that\
      \ has both callers and callees. Assert that\nneither selector reads gold evidence\
      \ during selection.\n\nInclude an item containing instruction-like text and\
      \ confirm it is rendered as delimited\ndata. The selection program must never\
      \ execute fixture content. Test the final rendered\ntext with the tokenizer\
      \ again so a mismatch between estimated and actual formatting cannot\nsilently\
      \ exceed the budget.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned\
      \ environment, fixture and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction\
      \ command and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks\
      \ from actual model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost\
      \ figures and tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning\
      \ assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded\
      \ budget when implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from\
      \ the baseline report."

  - content: "Combine a small assistant's versioned corpus, retrieval, evidence policy,\
      \ generator, citations, and optional bounded tools. Select at most three interventions,\
      \ such as chunking, reranking, and citation checking. Use an ablation design\
      \ with fixed cases and record interactions. Keep deployment and enterprise operational\
      \ claims for their companion courses.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation\
      \ and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are\
      \ proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured\
      \ results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected\
      \ components in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nCombine\
      \ three retained course techniques in one supplied document-question application:\n\
      layout-aware chunking from Guide 3, semantic caching from Guide 19, and indirect\n\
      prompt-injection defense from Guide 21. Run all eight on/off combinations while\
      \ holding the\nevaluation set, model responses, prompts, and scoring rules fixed.\n\
      \nThe artifact is an ablation report showing what each technique changes, whether\
      \ two\ntechniques interact, and which conclusions remain uncertain. The capstone\
      \ depends on these\nnamed active guides and Guide 14's uncertainty concepts;\
      \ it does not use a numeric range\nthat silently includes elective guides.\n\
      \n## The project\n\nThe capstone combines three techniques in one small application\
      \ and measures what each one\ncontributes. The application is only part of the\
      \ work. A runner evaluates every on/off\ncombination while the model responses,\
      \ prompts, data, and scoring rules stay the same.\n\nA useful default is a **document\
      \ question-answering assistant** with:\n\n- layout-aware chunking from Week\
      \ 3;\n- semantic caching from Week 19; and\n- indirect prompt-injection defense\
      \ from Week 21.\n\nFor this assistant, measure faithfulness on 24–40 fixed questions.\
      \ The runner evaluates the\neight configurations from “nothing enabled” through\
      \ “all three enabled.” The resulting\ntable can answer questions that a single\
      \ before-and-after comparison cannot:\n\n- Did layout-aware chunking improve\
      \ the answer when the other two techniques were\n  enabled?\n- Did caching reduce\
      \ cost without changing answer quality?\n- Did the injection defense help on\
      \ hostile documents, and did it affect normal\n  documents?\n- Did two techniques\
      \ work better together, or did one make the other less useful?\n\nThe final\
      \ artifact is `reports/ablation.md`, a short report containing the fixed\nexperiment\
      \ settings, all eight results, uncertainty intervals, and your reading\nof the\
      \ evidence. A result showing that a technique made no measurable difference\n\
      is useful. So is a result showing that a technique hurt or that the experiment\n\
      was too small to decide.\n\n## A concrete example\n\nConsider an assistant that\
      \ answers questions about annual reports. The model,\nsystem prompt, retrieval\
      \ corpus, question set, and scorer stay the same for every\nrun. Only the three\
      \ technique switches change:\n\n| Configuration | Chunking | Cache | Injection\
      \ defense |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| Baseline | off | off | off |\n| Chunking\
      \ only | on | off | off |\n| Cache only | off | on | off |\n| Defense only |\
      \ off | off | on |\n| Chunking + cache | on | on | off |\n| Chunking + defense\
      \ | on | off | on |\n| Cache + defense | off | on | on |\n| Full system | on\
      \ | on | on |\n\nThe baseline provides the reference score. Comparing the full\
      \ system with the\nbaseline shows whether the combined application changed the\
      \ metric. Comparing the\nfull system with the same system with chunking turned\
      \ off shows what chunking adds\nin the likely shipped configuration. The other\
      \ six runs show whether that answer\nchanges when the technique's companions\
      \ change.\n\nThis comparison is called an **ablation**: one part of a system\
      \ is removed while\nthe rest stays in place. In this capstone, the “part” is\
      \ a technique switch. The\nexperiment is credible only if “off” means the exact\
      \ baseline path, rather than a\nsecond implementation with different defaults.\n\
      \n## Why the eight runs matter\n\nWith three techniques, there are $2^3 = 8$\
      \ possible on/off combinations. Running\nall eight is a **full factorial design**.\
      \ This makes it possible to study both\nindividual changes and interactions\
      \ between changes.\n\nAn **interaction** means that the effect of one technique\
      \ depends on another. For\ninstance, caching might save little with ordinary\
      \ chunking but save much more when\nlayout-aware chunking produces stable requests.\
      \ The experiment should show that\npattern instead of leaving the answer to\
      \ guesswork based on the full-system score.\n\nA one-at-a-time comparison would\
      \ need only four runs: the full system and one run\nwith each technique removed.\
      \ That is a reasonable shortcut in a larger experiment,\nbut it cannot reveal\
      \ all of the interactions. Use the full eight-run design here;\nthe evaluation\
      \ set is intentionally small enough to make it practical.\n\n## Prerequisites\
      \ and scope\n\n- **Guide 3:** layout-aware chunking and its baseline.\n- **Guide\
      \ 19:** semantic response reuse and its exact-match baseline.\n- **Guide 21:**\
      \ the bounded indirect prompt-injection defense used by the local fixture.\n\
      - **Guide 14:** uncertainty concepts for interpreting paired differences.\n\
      - **A fixed evaluation set.** This is a small collection of inputs and expected\n\
      \  answers or labels. Every configuration must use the same collection.\n\n\
      Use adapters around earlier implementations or the small conforming stubs specified\
      \ here.\nNo portfolio project or guide outside the retained active set is required.\
      \ Alternative\ntechniques are optional and must come from the retained set:\
      \ Guides 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11,\n13–16, and 19–21.\n\n## Project structure\n\
      \nThe project has two connected parts:\n\n1. an application that applies three\
      \ techniques, each controlled by an on/off\n   switch; and\n2. an evaluation\
      \ harness that runs all eight configurations and writes the report.\n\nA possible\
      \ project layout is:\n\n```\nweek22/\n├── README.md                  # this\
      \ guide\n├── pyproject.toml             # dependencies for the three fixed techniques\n\
      ├── .env.example               # key names only; never commit .env\n├── config/\n\
      │   └── ablation.yaml          # manifest and technique flags\n├── src/\n│ \
      \  ├── app.py                 # combined application pipeline\n│   ├── techniques/\n\
      │   │   ├── base.py            # shared technique interface\n│   │   ├── layout_chunking.py\n\
      │   │   ├── semantic_cache.py\n│   │   └── injection_defense.py\n│   ├── metric.py\
      \              # per-example scores and primary metric\n│   └── harness/\n│\
      \       ├── config.py          # manifest and configuration enumeration\n│ \
      \      ├── runner.py          # execute the eight configurations\n│       ├──\
      \ stats.py           # contributions, interactions, and intervals\n│       └──\
      \ report.py          # write the report and figure\n├── data/\n│   └── eval.jsonl\
      \             # frozen evaluation examples\n└── reports/\n    └── ablation.md\
      \            # generated report\n```\n\nThe layout can change, but keep the\
      \ separation between the application, the\nmetric, and the experiment runner.\
      \ It should be possible to test the statistics\nwith made-up scores without\
      \ making a model call.\n\n### The technique interface\n\nEach technique needs\
      \ a common interface so the harness can switch it on and off\nwithout knowing\
      \ how it works:\n\n```python\n# src/techniques/base.py\nfrom typing import Protocol,\
      \ runtime_checkable\n\n@runtime_checkable\nclass Technique(Protocol):\n    \"\
      \"\"One retained technique with a true on/off switch.\"\"\"\n\n    name: str\n\
      \n    def enabled(self, cfg: \"RunConfig\") -> bool:\n        \"\"\"Return whether\
      \ this technique is enabled for the run.\"\"\"\n        ...\n\n    def apply(self,\
      \ ctx: \"PipelineContext\") -> \"PipelineContext\":\n        \"\"\"Apply the\
      \ technique, or return ctx unchanged when it is off.\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO:\
      \ implement the mechanism and the exact no-op path\n```\n\nWhen a technique\
      \ is off, return the same baseline behavior that the application\nwould have\
      \ used if the technique had never been added. Test this directly. For\nexample,\
      \ disabling the cache should not leave behind a different prompt or a\ndifferent\
      \ retrieval limit.\n\n### The run configuration\n\nEach run combines the fixed\
      \ manifest with a set of enabled technique names:\n\n```python\n# src/harness/config.py\n\
      from dataclasses import dataclass\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass HeldConstant:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Settings that must be identical in every run.\"\"\"\n    model: str\n\
      \    decoding: dict          # temperature, top_p, max_tokens, ...\n    seed:\
      \ int\n    eval_set_hash: str\n    prompt_hash: str\n    scorer_version: str\n\
      \n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass RunConfig:\n    \"\"\"One point in the three-technique\
      \ on/off experiment.\"\"\"\n    flags: frozenset[str]\n    held: HeldConstant\n\
      \n    @staticmethod\n    def full_factorial(\n        technique_names: list[str],\
      \ held: HeldConstant\n    ) -> list[\"RunConfig\"]:\n        \"\"\"Return one\
      \ configuration for every subset of technique_names.\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO:\
      \ enumerate exactly 2**len(technique_names) configurations\n```\n\nThe empty\
      \ flag set is the baseline. The set containing all three names is the full\n\
      system. Store the flags as a set rather than relying on list order so each result\n\
      has an unambiguous identity.\n\n### Running and scoring configurations\n\nKeep\
      \ the per-example scores. They are needed to estimate uncertainty later, and\n\
      they make it possible to inspect which examples changed between two configurations.\n\
      \n```python\n# src/harness/runner.py\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\n\n\
      @dataclass\nclass RunResult:\n    flags: frozenset[str]\n    metric: float\n\
      \    per_example: list[float]\n\ndef run_configuration(app, eval_set, cfg) ->\
      \ RunResult:\n    \"\"\"Run every fixed evaluation example under one configuration.\"\
      \"\"\n    ...  # TODO: verify the manifest, run the app, score each example\n\
      \ndef run_ablation(app, eval_set, configs) -> list[RunResult]:\n    \"\"\"Run\
      \ all configurations and return one result for each.\"\"\"\n    ...  # TODO:\
      \ call run_configuration for each config\n```\n\nChoose one primary metric that\
      \ reflects the application's purpose. Examples\ninclude answer accuracy, faithfulness,\
      \ cost per correct answer, or end-to-end\nlatency. Keep the per-example version\
      \ of that metric whenever possible. If your\napplication has an important safety\
      \ or cost measure, record it as a secondary\nmetric, but do not replace the\
      \ primary metric with a collection of convenient\nproxies.\n\n```python\n# src/metric.py\n\
      def score_example(prediction, ground_truth) -> float:\n    \"\"\"Return one\
      \ deterministic score for one example.\"\"\"\n    ...\n\ndef aggregate(scores:\
      \ list[float]) -> float:\n    \"\"\"Reduce per-example scores to the report's\
      \ primary metric.\"\"\"\n    ...\n```\n\n### Measuring contributions\n\nLet\
      \ $M(S)$ mean the metric for the configuration whose enabled technique set is\n\
      $S$. If A is not in $S$, A's **marginal contribution** in that context is:\n\
      \n$$\n\\Delta_A(S) = M(S \\cup \\{A\\}) - M(S).\n$$\n\nThe most practical comparison\
      \ is the **ship-context contribution**:\n\n$$\n\\Delta_A(\\{B,C\\}) = M(\\{A,B,C\\\
      }) - M(\\{B,C\\}).\n$$\n\nIt asks what changes when A is added to the otherwise-complete\
      \ system. Report it\nfor all three techniques. Also report a 95% confidence\
      \ interval, which is a range\nthat describes the uncertainty in the estimated\
      \ difference. With a small fixed\nevaluation set, a paired bootstrap is a simple\
      \ choice: repeatedly resample the\nsame example indices, recompute the difference,\
      \ and use the 2.5th and 97.5th\npercentiles as the interval.\n\nThe effect of\
      \ A may differ across contexts. A **Shapley value** summarizes those\ncontexts\
      \ as a weighted average of A's marginal contribution over every subset of\n\
      the other techniques. With three techniques, all of the required scores are\n\
      already in the eight-run table.\n\n```python\n# src/harness/stats.py\ndef marginal(results,\
      \ technique: str, given: frozenset[str]) -> float:\n    \"\"\"Return M(given\
      \ + technique) - M(given).\"\"\"\n    ...\n\ndef shapley(results, technique:\
      \ str, all_techniques: list[str]) -> float:\n    \"\"\"Average marginal contribution\
      \ over all contexts.\"\"\"\n    ...  # TODO: use the standard subset-size weights\n\
      \ndef interaction(results, a: str, b: str, holding_off: frozenset[str]) -> float:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Measure whether a and b help or hinder one another.\"\"\"\n    ...\n\
      \ndef bootstrap_ci(\n    per_example_a, per_example_b, iters: int = 10_000\n\
      ) -> tuple[float, float]:\n    \"\"\"Return a 95% interval for the paired metric\
      \ difference.\"\"\"\n    ...  # TODO: resample paired example indices and take\
      \ percentiles\n```\n\nFor two techniques A and B, with C held off, the interaction\
      \ is:\n\n$$\nI_{AB} = [M(\\{A,B\\}) - M(\\{B\\})]\n       - [M(\\{A\\}) - M(\\\
      varnothing)].\n$$\n\nA positive value means the pair helps more together than\
      \ their separate changes\nwould suggest. A negative value means the techniques\
      \ overlap or interfere. Label\nthe interaction only when its uncertainty interval\
      \ supports that conclusion;\notherwise describe it as inconclusive.\n\n## Use\
      \ independent development and test cases — Capstone: Improve and Evaluate a\
      \ Small LLM Service\n\nThe 10 development cases exist for selecting the support\
      \ threshold and inspecting the\ninterfaces. The 30 test cases remain untouched\
      \ until the policy and threshold are frozen:\n\n| Test family | Cases | Expected\
      \ behavior |\n|---|---:|---|\n| Direct answer | 8 | answer with a supporting\
      \ citation |\n| Relevant chunk below rank three | 6 | use the wider candidate\
      \ set when it fits |\n| Several supporting chunks | 4 | keep required evidence\
      \ within the budget |\n| Unanswerable | 6 | abstain without citations |\n| Distracting\
      \ high-score chunk | 3 | avoid unsupported answers |\n| Invalid recorded citation\
      \ | 3 | fail closed with an explicit reason |\n\nGold labels contain answer\
      \ facts, supporting chunk IDs, and whether abstention is expected.\nThey are\
      \ loaded only by the evaluator. The selection and answer policies must not receive\n\
      gold fields.\n\nThe recorded responses include both correct and flawed outputs.\
      \ They test the service's\nhandling of an imperfect model boundary; they are\
      \ not current measurements of a provider\nmodel.\n\n## Measure the change without\
      \ hiding tradeoffs — Capstone: Improve and Evaluate a Small LLM Service\n\n\
      Report these counts and rates for the baseline and candidate:\n\n- correct answered\
      \ cases;\n- answers whose every citation belongs to the selected evidence and\
      \ gold support set;\n- correct abstentions on unanswerable cases;\n- incorrect\
      \ abstentions on answerable cases;\n- unsupported answers and invalid citations;\n\
      - median and 95th-percentile stage latency from the deterministic delay fixture;\n\
      - median selected context tokens.\n\nDefine answer coverage as the fraction\
      \ of all cases receiving a non-abstaining answer, and\nconditional answer accuracy\
      \ as\n\n$$\n\\operatorname{conditional\\ accuracy}=\n\\frac{\\text{correct non-abstaining\
      \ answers}}\n{\\text{all non-abstaining answers}}.\n$$\n\nWhen the denominator\
      \ is zero, report the value as undefined. Show coverage beside\nconditional\
      \ accuracy because a policy can appear perfectly accurate by refusing every\n\
      question.\n\nCreate a paired case table with both policies' outcomes. Count\
      \ candidate wins, baseline\nwins, and tradeoffs rather than reducing the evaluation\
      \ to a single pass/fail flag. Inspect\nevery changed outcome and connect it\
      \ to the selected evidence and policy reason.\n\n## Test component boundaries\
      \ and the whole path — Capstone: Improve and Evaluate a Small LLM Service\n\n\
      Unit tests cover exact-budget packing, a chunk one token too large, stable ranking\
      \ ties,\nthreshold equality, no supporting candidates, empty responses, citations\
      \ outside selected\nevidence, duplicate citations, and an answer that abstains\
      \ while still citing a chunk.\n\nIntegration tests use the local API test client\
      \ and verify:\n\n- one valid request crosses retrieval, selection, response,\
      \ and validation;\n- an oversized question is rejected before retrieval;\n-\
      \ an unanswerable case returns the documented abstention shape;\n- an invalid\
      \ citation cannot reach the successful response shape;\n- request IDs and stage\
      \ timings appear without raw prompt or document text;\n- baseline and candidate\
      \ use the same fixture, response rows, and evaluator.\n\nInject one controlled\
      \ regression after the candidate report, such as bypassing citation\nvalidation.\
      \ Confirm that the invalid-citation metric changes on the expected cases, then\n\
      restore the implementation. This checks that the evaluation can notice the behavior\
      \ it\nclaims to measure."
    lab_and_evidence: "## The experiment rules\n\nBefore writing the runner, make\
      \ a list of what must remain unchanged. This list is\nthe experiment manifest.\
      \ For this chapter, it includes:\n\n- the evaluation examples and their hash;\n\
      - the model and decoding settings, such as temperature and maximum tokens;\n\
      - the prompt templates and their hash;\n- the retrieval corpus;\n- the random\
      \ seed;\n- the scoring function and its version; and\n- any other setting that\
      \ could affect the result.\n\nThe only intended change between configurations\
      \ is whether technique A, B, or C\nis enabled. The runner should refuse to score\
      \ a run when a manifest value differs.\nThis turns an accidental prompt or data\
      \ change into an obvious error instead of a\nmisleading result.\n\nThe evaluation\
      \ set should contain cases that give the selected techniques a fair\nchance\
      \ to matter. For the example above, include table-heavy pages, repeated or\n\
      paraphrased questions, and documents containing clearly labeled prompt-injection\n\
      fixtures. Keep those fixtures local and defensive; do not test a disabled defense\n\
      against live third-party content.\n\n## Build sequence\n\nThe core work should\
      \ take about 15–20 hours.\n\n1. **Inspect the application and choose the metric\
      \ — about 2 hours.** Trace the supplied\n   document-question path and the three\
      \ fixed technique switches. Create\n   `config/ablation.yaml` with the model,\
      \ decoding settings, seed, prompt hash,\n   scorer version, and a placeholder\
      \ for the evaluation-set hash.\n2. **Create the evaluation set — 2–3 hours.**\
      \ Prepare 24–40 labeled examples.\n   Include examples that exercise each chosen\
      \ technique. Save the set, compute its\n   hash, and update the manifest before\
      \ running the experiment.\n3. **Make the full application work — 3–4 hours.**\
      \ Integrate all three techniques\n   and confirm that the full configuration\
      \ produces sensible output. Do this\n   before comparing scores so application\
      \ bugs are easier to separate from\n   experiment results.\n4. **Test each off\
      \ switch — about 2 hours.** For each technique, compare the\n   output with\
      \ the switch off to the baseline path. The switch must be a true\n   no-op,\
      \ not a weaker version of the technique.\n5. **Run the factorial experiment\
      \ — about 3 hours.** Enumerate the eight\n   configurations, verify the manifest\
      \ inside each run, preserve per-example\n   scores, and write the raw results\
      \ to disk.\n6. **Compute the statistics — about 2 hours.** Calculate ship-context\
      \ marginal\n   contributions, Shapley values, pairwise interactions, and confidence\
      \ intervals.\n7. **Write the report — 2–3 hours.** Render the table and one\
      \ figure, inspect cases\n   changed by each switch, and record limitations.\n\
      \n## The report\n\nWrite `reports/ablation.md` in this order:\n\n1. **Question\
      \ and setup.** Name the application, the three techniques, the primary\n   metric,\
      \ and the evaluation-set size.\n2. **Held-constant manifest.** Show the exact\
      \ model, decoding settings, seed,\n   data hash, prompt hash, and scorer version\
      \ used by every run.\n3. **Full-factorial results.** Include one row for each\
      \ of the eight configurations:\n\n   | Configuration | A | B | C | Metric |\
      \ 95% CI |\n   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n   | Baseline | off |\
      \ off | off | … | […, …] |\n   | A only | on | off | off | … | […, …] |\n  \
      \ | … | | | | | |\n   | Full system | on | on | on | … | […, …] |\n\n4. **Contribution\
      \ analysis.** For each technique, report its ship-context\n   contribution and\
      \ Shapley value, with intervals where applicable. Report the\n   three pairwise\
      \ interactions as positive, negative, or inconclusive.\n5. **One figure.** Use\
      \ a bar chart with error bars for the three ship-context\n   contributions,\
      \ or an interaction plot that makes the main comparison easy to\n   see.\n6.\
      \ **Interpretation.** Explain which changes are supported by the data, which\n\
      \   effects are uncertain, and whether the full system is worth its added cost\
      \ or\n   latency. Mention any technique that could be removed without a measurable\
      \ loss,\n   rather than treating that result as a failure.\n\nThe report should\
      \ contain enough information for another reader to understand your\nconclusion\
      \ without rerunning the application. Do not invent a positive result. A\nsmall\
      \ evaluation set may produce wide intervals or no clear winner; that is a\n\
      valid finding when the report explains the limitation.\n\n## How to run and\
      \ test\n\n```bash\n# Supply runtime configuration; retrieve secrets through\
      \ wt vault.\nuv sync                       # or use another environment manager\n\
      \n# Run all eight configurations and write the report.\nuv run python -m src.harness.runner\
      \ --config config/ablation.yaml\n\n# Inspect the generated report.\ncat reports/ablation.md\n\
      ```\n\nUseful tests include:\n\n- **Off-switch test:** turning a technique off\
      \ produces the exact baseline output\n  for the same input.\n- **Manifest test:**\
      \ changing the data hash, prompt hash, seed, model, or scorer\n  causes the\
      \ runner to stop before scoring.\n- **Repeatability test:** running a configuration\
      \ twice produces the same\n  per-example scores when the model path is deterministic\
      \ enough for the exercise.\n- **Statistics test:** synthetic scores produce\
      \ the expected marginal contributions,\n  interactions, and Shapley values.\
      \ The Shapley values should sum to the full\n  system metric minus the baseline\
      \ metric.\n- **Report test:** exactly eight configurations appear, and every\
      \ configuration\n  has the same number of per-example scores.\n\n## Security\
      \ and operating notes\n\n- Never commit `.env`; commit `.env.example` with names\
      \ but no secret values.\n- If a selected technique executes model-generated\
      \ code or reads untrusted content,\n  keep its sandbox or defensive boundary\
      \ in place for the full application.\n- A run with a disabled defense is an\
      \ intentionally unsafe baseline. Use only local,\n  clearly labeled attack fixtures\
      \ for that run; do not send it to live websites,\n  documents, or accounts.\n\
      - Validate evaluation inputs when they enter the application. Content copied\
      \ from\n  scraping or tool output is data for the experiment, not trusted instructions.\n\
      \n## Hardware, cost, and subscriptions\n\n- **Hardware:** CPU plus a hosted\
      \ language-model API is enough for the fixed application.\n- **Cost:** set a\
      \ $15 cap before the run, keep the evaluation set to a few dozen\n  examples,\
      \ and use one inexpensive hosted model for all eight configurations.\n  Embedding-based\
      \ techniques add a small embedding cost; record actual usage.\n- **Subscriptions:**\
      \ one hosted language-model key, such as OpenAI, Anthropic,\n  Azure OpenAI,\
      \ or Bedrock. Docker is needed only when a selected technique uses a\n  browser\
      \ or code-execution sandbox.\n\nA polished interface, live documents, deployment,\
      \ and additional techniques are optional\nfollow-on work. The core stops after\
      \ the fixed eight-configuration experiment and report.\n\n### Report the actual\
      \ execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration\
      \ identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation.\
      \ Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server\
      \ or cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."

planned:
  chapters:
  - content: '## What the learner will build


      Teach the software and operations needed to turn a local AI feature into an
      observable service that handles concurrent users, accepted background work,
      changing data, releases, and failures. Begin with the Python, HTTP, SQL, and
      authentication bridge from the Habit Tracker CLI. Use maintained servers and
      one cloud path while keeping algorithmic model training in the existing courses.


      A small document-processing and question-answer service with an API, Postgres,
      a background worker, and a replaceable model adapter. Independent fixture-based
      labs avoid a dependency on completing another course''s application. An optional
      cumulative service can reuse the document assistant or the text decision model.
      A fake model isolates operational failures from model quality; live inference
      is measured separately.


      The course consists of independently reproducible labs. Concepts accumulate,
      but another chapter''s source tree is not a hidden prerequisite. A supplied
      fixture or a small implementation can stand in for an earlier component. Combining
      the results into one portfolio is optional. Each lab''s command contract, interfaces
      and tests specify work to be implemented; this saved brief does not claim that
      code or benchmark results already exist.


      ## Prerequisites and execution paths


      Python programmers with basic tests and Git-diff experience. AI-Assisted Development
      supplies architecture and review habits; Build LLM Applications supplies an
      optional model-backed feature. Early chapters introduce concurrency, networking,
      relational data, and permissions rather than assuming production experience.
      A CPU, local containers, and synthetic data support the core mechanisms. One-cloud
      deployment and real open-model serving are bounded optional execution paths
      with explicit teardown and resource budgets.


      A small deterministic fixture is the first path for examining control flow and
      checking a boundary. A substantive measurement uses the actual component being
      studied: a model for model behavior, a database for locking and persistence,
      an inference server for scheduling, or a real provisioned environment for deployment.
      Reports state the path used. Recorded responses cannot establish the quality
      or resource behavior of a model that was never run. Costs in source examples
      are planning assumptions; record actual versions, hardware, usage and spending
      before making a comparison.


      ## Trace one accepted request and one background job


      The service accepts a synthetic document, authenticates the caller, stores a
      revision and enqueues indexing work. The API returns an explicit status and
      a job ID. A worker claims a time-limited lease, records an attempt, writes an
      idempotent effect and completes the job only while it still owns the lease.
      A request later reads the indexed version and may stream a bounded model response.
      Disconnecting the client must propagate cancellation to the active work, with
      measured savings and a record of any work that could not be cancelled.


      This path exposes why the database, queue, cache and model cannot be evaluated
      solely by whether one request succeeds. A concurrent debit can overwrite another
      update. A worker can commit an effect and die before acknowledgement. A cache
      fill can finish after a newer document version exists. A restored backup can
      omit accepted recent writes. Every experiment first makes one such behavior
      reproducible, then compares a bounded repair with the failing baseline.


      ## Interfaces and recorded identities


      Give requests, document revisions, jobs and attempts separate identities. Keep
      accepted, rejected, completed and cancelled counts distinct. A ReleaseManifest
      identifies code, dependency lockfile, prompt/configuration hashes, model and
      tokenizer identity, database-schema compatibility and rollback target. A request
      trace joins API, database, worker and model spans without placing credentials
      or synthetic user text into unbounded labels. A RecoveryRecord names the failure,
      detection time, restoration procedure, verification query, missing writes and
      residual limitations.


      The service fixture can use a small model adapter or a clearly labeled fake
      dependency to exercise API behavior. Inference comparisons require a pinned
      real model and request workload. A cloud exercise requires recreating and verifying
      the declared service on one selected provider; local containers validate composition
      but do not substitute for that deployment measurement.


      ## Develop operational mechanisms in dependency order


      Start with Python waiting, CPU work, concurrency and cleanup; then expose HTTP
      contracts and configuration. SQL labs connect a relational model to query plans
      and deterministic races. Authentication uses established identity mechanisms
      while application authorization remains explicit. Streaming adds disconnect
      behavior. Deployment makes the environment reproducible. Releases retain the
      previous working version and test invalid candidates. Durable work, additive
      migrations, backup restoration and cache consistency exercise their own failure
      points. Observation supplies units and correlated records for the debugging
      exercise. Serving and capacity compare admitted workload, bounded queues and
      latency. The recovery exercise and final service lab connect those components
      without requiring every earlier source tree.


      ## Compare behavior under a declared workload


      State arrival rate, request sizes, concurrency, prompt/output lengths, run duration,
      warm-up and observation interval. Open-loop load sends planned arrivals independently
      of response time so slow service does not silently reduce the offered load.
      Retain rejected, timed-out, cancelled and failed requests in their proper denominators.
      Distinguish queue wait from processing time and first-token from end-to-end
      latency. A system that returns more errors is not faster merely because its
      successful subset has lower latency.


      For recovery, record both the interval during which the service was unavailable
      and which accepted writes survive. Restore from a known snapshot, reconcile
      later changes where the plan supports it, and verify representative reads and
      authorization before serving traffic. Procedures are limited to the tested fixture
      and environment; reports identify untested dependencies rather than claiming
      a production service has been certified.'
    lab_and_evidence: '### Walkthroughs to prepare


      Trace a successful request, an unsupported question, a forbidden cross-organization
      request, and a dependency failure. For each, record the initial fixture state,
      actual inputs to each component, intended boundary decision, final response,
      and any lasting effect. A failure report needs the same identity and version
      fields as a successful run.


      ### Baselines and artifact contracts


      Each lab supplies a normal workload, a deliberately failing case, a baseline,
      and a reproducible report. Record code/configuration/schema/model versions and
      keep behavioral correctness separate from availability and speed. Capacity claims
      specify the request mix, offered rate, concurrency, hardware, duration, and
      responses meeting the latency goal. Recovery reports verify stored data and
      externally visible behavior after repair; a healthy endpoint alone is insufficient
      evidence.


      Before comparing a change, define the task set, independent expected results,
      allowed resource budget and simplest relevant baseline. Keep raw case-level
      records so the report can be recalculated. Declare which parts are fixture-based,
      which use a model, and which use actual services or provisioned resources. A
      useful artifact includes a lockfile, fixture version/hash, proposed reproduction
      command, configuration, measured units, result, observed failure and limitation.
      A negative or inconclusive comparison remains a valid completed learning artifact.


      ### Initial design exercise


      Draw the components and annotate the data passed across each boundary. Define
      one versioned fixture schema and one output record using the interfaces above.
      Write independent checks for one happy case and one failure before implementing
      the controller. Show how a result from a standalone lab can be consumed by the
      optional shared project without depending on private mutable state. Establish
      a small time and resource allowance for the first build; keep optional cloud
      or model runs separately budgeted.


      The overview deliverable is a diagram, interface/data inventory, fixture schema,
      baseline/report specification and resource plan. No benchmark value should be
      filled in until that workload has actually run. The following chapters implement
      these components and explain the results; the overview supplies their shared
      vocabulary and limits.'

  - content: "Process the same synthetic documents sequentially, using threads, using\
      \ processes, and using asynchronous tasks. Explain waiting versus computation,\
      \ shared state, event-loop blocking, bounded concurrency, and propagation of\
      \ cancellation. Use small reproducible failures such as a blocked event loop\
      \ and a raced counter. Keep AI-assisted code changes file-scoped and review\
      \ their behavior.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment\
      \ to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab\
      \ artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results already\
      \ exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nProcess 40 synthetic\
      \ documents with the same transformation using sequential code,\nthreads, processes,\
      \ and asynchronous tasks. Some documents take time to arrive; others\ntake time\
      \ to compute. You will measure the difference, deliberately block a concurrent\n\
      run, and investigate a wrong shared count. The result is a small batch processor\
      \ and\na report explaining which execution model fits each workload on your\
      \ machine.\n\nThe first action is to write a deterministic document generator\
      \ and a sequential\nprocessor. That gives every later comparison an output to\
      \ check, not just a stopwatch.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\nYou know Python\
      \ functions, exceptions, collections, files, and basic tests. No networking\n\
      or operating-systems course is assumed. Use Python 3.13 and pytest in a lesson-local\n\
      environment. This guide describes code you will implement; the directory tree\
      \ and CLI\ncommands below are target interfaces, not files already supplied\
      \ by the repository.\n\nNo earlier lesson implementation or portfolio project\
      \ is required.\n\n## One workload, two reasons for waiting\n\nGenerate 40 records\
      \ with `id`, `text`, and `delay_ms`. Repeat a short sentence to make\neach text\
      \ about 16 KB; derive delays of 20–80 milliseconds deterministically from the\
      \ ID.\nKeep input generation outside timed runs.\n\nFor the waiting experiment,\
      \ a blocking loader uses `time.sleep`, while an asynchronous\nloader uses `asyncio.sleep`.\
      \ These simulate input/output (I/O) latency without requiring\nan HTTP server\
      \ before the networking lesson. For the computing experiment, repeatedly\ncount\
      \ character categories in pure Python. Calibrate a fixed repetition count so\
      \ one\ndocument takes roughly 20–50 milliseconds, then freeze it for all variants.\n\
      \nA **process** has its own Python interpreter and memory. **Threads** execute\
      \ within\none process and can share objects. **Concurrency** means multiple\
      \ operations can be\nin progress; **parallelism** means work actually executes\
      \ simultaneously. An **event\nloop** schedules asynchronous tasks, giving another\
      \ task a turn when the current one\nawaits an operation that has not finished.\
      \ Merely adding `async def` does not make\nCPU work yield.\n\nThe usual CPython\
      \ build has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) that limits simultaneous\nexecution\
      \ of Python bytecode in threads. Native libraries may release it, and\nfree-threaded\
      \ builds change the situation. Record the interpreter build and use the\npure-Python\
      \ transform so a native numerical library does not silently change this test.\n\
      \nProcesses add startup and data-transfer costs. Put worker functions in an\
      \ importable\nmodule and guard the CLI entry point with `if __name__ == \"__main__\"\
      `; do not define\nprocess workers only inside a notebook. Executor cancellation\
      \ does not stop work that\nis already running. [Python executor documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/concurrent.futures.html)\n\
      \n## Project shape and interfaces\n\n```text\nweek32/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── execution_lab/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── fixtures.py       # deterministic\
      \ records\n│   ├── work.py           # blocking/async loaders and pure-Python\
      \ transform\n│   ├── runners.py        # sequential, thread, process, async\
      \ variants\n│   ├── faults.py         # counter race and event-loop blockage\n\
      │   ├── measure.py        # timers, memory, outcomes\n│   └── cli.py\n├── tests/\n\
      └── artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing\
      \ import Literal\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Document:\n    id: int\n\
      \    text: str\n    delay_ms: int\n\ndef transform(doc: Document, repeats: int)\
      \ -> dict[str, int]: ...\n\ndef run_batch(\n    docs: list[Document],\n    mode:\
      \ Literal[\"sequential\", \"threads\", \"processes\", \"async\"],\n    workload:\
      \ Literal[\"wait\", \"compute\"],\n    workers: int,\n) -> dict[int, dict[str,\
      \ int]]: ...\n\nasync def cancel_batch(after_s: float) -> list[dict]: ...\n\
      ```\n\nUse a bounded set of workers or tasks, not one unbounded task for every\
      \ possible input.\nReturn results by document ID so completion order does not\
      \ look like output corruption.\nRecord each task's start, finish, failure, and\
      \ cancellation acknowledgement separately."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 17 hours\n\n1. **Fixture and baseline,\
      \ 3 hours.** Generate the records, implement the transform,\n   and check sequential\
      \ output against two hand-computed short strings.\n2. **Three execution variants,\
      \ 4 hours.** Add threads, processes, and async tasks.\n   Compare each to sequential\
      \ output. Keep the async CPU variant as a demonstration\n   of blocking; do\
      \ not hide its transform in a thread for this comparison.\n3. **Measurement,\
      \ 3 hours.** Sweep 1, 2, and 4 workers for both workloads. Repeat each\n   run\
      \ three times; report the individual runs and median. Include process startup\n\
      \   in the first comparison and label a warmed comparison separately if you\
      \ add one.\n4. **Two failures, 3 hours.** Split a shared counter increment into\
      \ read and write,\n   with a barrier between them so two threads read the same\
      \ old value. Repair with\n   a lock. Separately run a 10 ms async heartbeat\
      \ alongside a blocking sleep and\n   compare heartbeat gaps after replacing\
      \ it with an asynchronous wait.\n5. **Cancellation and report, 4 hours.** Cancel\
      \ a batch with work waiting and running.\n   Stop submitting new work, request\
      \ cooperative shutdown, and drain/close resources.\n   Explain any work that\
      \ continues after the caller stops waiting.\n\nA **barrier** pauses participants\
      \ until both have arrived. Give it a timeout so a failed\ntest does not hang.\
      \ A **lock** allows only one thread at a time into the protected\nread/change/write\
      \ section. The intentionally separated counter operations expose the\nrace;\
      \ do not claim every ordinary increment will fail on every Python version.\n\
      \nAsync cancellation is delivered at opportunities where a coroutine can yield.\
      \ Cleanup\nbelongs in `finally`; after cleanup, propagate cancellation rather\
      \ than treating it as\na successful result. [Python task documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/asyncio-task.html)\n\
      \n## Commands and tests\n\nFrom this lesson directory, create its `pyproject.toml`\
      \ with Python 3.13 and pytest,\nthen implement these commands before using them\
      \ as reproduction instructions:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\nuv run pytest tests -q\n\
      uv run python -m execution_lab.cli compare --documents 40 --workers 1,2,4 --repeats\
      \ 3 --out artifacts/runs.jsonl\nuv run python -m execution_lab.cli faults --out\
      \ artifacts/faults.json\nuv run python -m execution_lab.cli cancel --after-seconds\
      \ 0.1 --out artifacts/cancellation.json\nuv run python -m cProfile -o artifacts/compute.prof\
      \ -m execution_lab.cli profile\n```\n\nTests cover equal outputs, empty input,\
      \ a worker exception, bounded active work, timeout\nof the controlled race,\
      \ counter correctness after repair, and resource cleanup. Check\noutcomes rather\
      \ than asserting a fragile machine-specific speedup.\n\n## Evidence and interpretation\n\
      \nSave wall-clock time, worker count, outcome counts, interpreter/build, CPU\
      \ count, fixture\nsettings, and one profile observation. Use `tracemalloc` for\
      \ Python allocations and state\nits limits: it is not total process memory and\
      \ does not automatically include children.\nIf reporting resident memory, measure\
      \ worker processes separately and explain aggregation.\n\nThreads or async tasks\
      \ may help waiting without helping this CPU workload. Processes\nmay lose on\
      \ small inputs. Either is a meaningful observation when results are correct\n\
      and the timing boundary is clear. Keep one unresolved question in `artifacts/report.md`.\n\
      \n## Hardware, cost, and optional depth\n\nA laptop and CPU are enough; target\
      \ cost is $0. No hosted model is used. An HTTP loader,\nnative-array workload,\
      \ or free-threaded interpreter comparison is an optional extension.\nChoose\
      \ at most one after completing the bounded core.\n\n### Report the actual execution\
      \ path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration identities,\
      \ case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation. Distinguish\
      \ offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server or\
      \ cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."
