  - content: "Send a synthetic document through a local reverse proxy into a small\
      \ HTTP API. Explain name resolution, listening addresses, ports, TLS, request/response\
      \ schemas, status codes, timeouts, and streaming at the point each appears.\
      \ Keep transport failures distinct from application errors and model failures.\
      \ Introduce bounded request sizes and explicit error contracts.\n\nThe lesson\
      \ below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs,\
      \ package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate\
      \ that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture\
      \ for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\
      \n## What you will build\n\nSend a document to a local word-count API through\
      \ a reverse proxy, then deliberately\nbreak different parts of that request.\
      \ You will distinguish an unknown hostname, a\nclosed port, an untrusted certificate,\
      \ a rejected request, and a slow server. The\nartifact is a working small service\
      \ and a request-by-request explanation of failures.\n\nBegin with `POST /count`\
      \ on localhost. It accepts `{\"text\": \"one two\"}` and returns\n`{\"words\"\
      : 2, \"request_id\": \"...\"}`. There is no model or database to obscure the\n\
      network behavior being studied.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\nUse the concurrency\
      \ concepts from Guide 32, Python functions,\nand a terminal. You need Docker\
      \ Compose, curl, and a lesson-local Python 3.13 environment\nwith FastAPI, Uvicorn,\
      \ HTTPX, and pytest. Pin the resolved Python dependencies in the\nlesson lockfile\
      \ and record the Caddy image digest used.\n\nThe code, configuration, and CLI\
      \ below describe what to create. No prior implementation\nor portfolio app is\
      \ required. Container networking is introduced here.\n\n## Follow one request\n\
      \nThe client first resolves a hostname into an address. The Domain Name System\
      \ (**DNS**)\nprovides this mapping; a local hosts-file entry is a static override.\
      \ The client opens\na Transmission Control Protocol (**TCP**) connection to\
      \ a port, which identifies a\nservice endpoint at that address. Hypertext Transfer\
      \ Protocol (**HTTP**) defines the\nrequest method, path, headers, and body sent\
      \ over the connection.\n\nFor HTTPS, Transport Layer Security (**TLS**) negotiates\
      \ encryption and checks that the\nserver certificate matches the hostname and\
      \ a trusted issuer. These steps happen before\nthe application can return an\
      \ HTTP error. The reverse proxy accepts the client connection\nand makes a separate\
      \ connection to the API.\n\n```text\ncurl / HTTPX\n    -> https://localhost:8443\
      \   Caddy (TLS ends here)\n        -> http://api:8000      FastAPI inside the\
      \ Compose network\n```\n\nInside a container, `localhost` means that container.\
      \ Compose's service name `api`\nresolves within its network; it need not resolve\
      \ from the laptop. **Publishing a port**\nmakes a container listener reachable\
      \ through a host port. For this lab, publish the\nproxy only to `127.0.0.1`;\
      \ keep the API reachable only inside the Compose network after\nthe initial\
      \ direct-request exercise.\n\n## Minimal service and configuration\n\nCreate\
      \ a bounded text body (at most 4 KB), a readiness endpoint, and one delay parameter\n\
      limited to 0–2 seconds. Validation failures should return a documented 4xx status;\n\
      exceptions represent 5xx failures. A request ID connects client observations\
      \ to server\nlogs. Log start/end times and lengths, not full document content.\n\
      \n```text\nweek33/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── compose.yaml\n├── Caddyfile\n├──\
      \ network_lab/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── api.py\n│   ├── client.py\n│  \
      \ └── exercise.py\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses\
      \ import dataclass\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Observation:\n    request_id:\
      \ str\n    elapsed_ms: float\n    status: int | None\n    failure_stage: str\
      \ | None\n\nasync def count_words(text: str, delay_ms: int) -> dict: ...\nasync\
      \ def send_request(base_url: str, text: str, timeout_s: float) -> Observation:\
      \ ...\ndef classify_failure(error: Exception) -> str: ...\n```\n\nUse this small\
      \ proxy configuration as setup scaffolding:\n\n```caddyfile\nhttps://localhost\
      \ {\n    tls internal\n    reverse_proxy api:8000\n}\n```\n\nMap host `127.0.0.1:8443`\
      \ to Caddy's container port 443. Persist Caddy's `/data` directory\nin a named\
      \ volume. After startup, copy **only** the local root certificate from\n`/data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt`\
      \ to `artifacts/local-root.crt` using\n`docker compose cp`. Use curl's `--cacert`\
      \ option so the test trusts that root without\nchanging the laptop's global\
      \ certificate store. Never copy the private key. Caddy's\ncontainer cannot be\
      \ assumed to install trust on the host automatically.\n[Caddy local TLS documentation](https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/tls)\n\
      \n## Follow one save operation — A Full-Stack App: UI, API, and Database Migrations\n\
      \nThe user enters a title and body. The **user interface (UI)** sends an HTTP\
      \ request to\nan **application programming interface (API)**. The API validates\
      \ the request, starts\nwork through a repository function, and commits the database\
      \ change before reporting\nsuccess. The UI renders the response and can later\
      \ reload the note by ID.\n\n```text\nFlet screen -> HTTP client -> FastAPI route\
      \ -> repository -> SQLModel session -> PostgreSQL\n```\n\nA **repository** here\
      \ is a small collection of data-access functions, not a second\nframework. The\
      \ UI imports its HTTP client and view models, never the database engine or\n\
      repository. The server owns persistence and validation even when the UI also\
      \ validates\nfor convenience.\n\nAn **object-relational mapping** library maps\
      \ Python objects to relational records.\nSQLModel combines table declarations\
      \ with validation models. Keep table models distinct\nfrom input and output\
      \ models: a client should not set the generated ID, creation time,\nor internal\
      \ fields. A database **session** manages an operation's database interactions;\n\
      create one per request and close it afterward instead of sharing a global session\
      \ across\nrequests. [FastAPI database tutorial](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/sql-databases/)\n\
      \nUse synchronous database functions inside normal `def` FastAPI routes for\
      \ this lab.\nFastAPI runs such route functions in its thread pool; directly\
      \ calling blocking database\ncode inside an async handler would still block\
      \ that handler's event loop. The UI can\nuse asynchronous HTTP to remain responsive.\
      \ [FastAPI concurrency guidance](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/async/)\n\n##\
      \ A bounded API contract — A Full-Stack App: UI, API, and Database Migrations\n\
      \nStart with a notes table containing `id`, `title`, `body`, and `created_at`.\
      \ Titles contain\n1–120 characters after trimming; bodies contain at most 4,000\
      \ characters. IDs and creation\ntimes are server-owned. Reject unexpected input\
      \ fields rather than accepting an attempted\nclient override. Use parameter\
      \ binding through SQLModel/SQLAlchemy for query values.\n\n| Endpoint | Behavior\
      \ |\n|---|---|\n| `POST /notes` | Accept title/body; commit and return the created\
      \ note with status 201 |\n| `GET /notes/{id}` | Return a note or 404 |\n| `PATCH\
      \ /notes/{id}` | Change supplied title/body fields; omitted fields remain unchanged;\
      \ return 404 if absent |\n| `DELETE /notes/{id}` | Delete and return 204, or\
      \ 404 if absent |\n| `GET /notes?after_id=...&limit=...` | Return notes ordered\
      \ by ID with a maximum limit of 50 |\n| `GET /ready` | Return success only when\
      \ the database can be queried |\n\nFor this small fixture, ID-based forward\
      \ pagination is sufficient; no pagination benchmark\nis required. For PATCH,\
      \ distinguish an omitted field from an explicit null. Title/body\ncannot be\
      \ null, while omitting either leaves it untouched. Missing resources, invalid\n\
      input, and temporary database failure should not all become the same generic\
      \ response.\nUse 422 for validation failures and a sanitized 503 for the controlled\
      \ database outage.\n\nThe screen needs a list, title/body inputs, save/delete\
      \ controls, and a visible status\nmessage. Disable duplicate clicks while a\
      \ save is pending, preserve typed text after a\nfailure, and show success only\
      \ after an acknowledged response. This is not exactly-once\nsubmission: if the\
      \ server commits and the response is lost, a blind POST retry can create\nanother\
      \ note. Do not automatically retry writes in this lesson; document that ambiguity.\n\
      Give the HTTP client and database connections explicit finite timeouts so the\
      \ controlled\noutage produces an observable failure instead of an indefinitely\
      \ disabled save button."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 16 hours\n\n1. **Direct API, 3 hours.**\
      \ Implement `/count` and `/ready`, test valid and malformed\n   requests, and\
      \ record a direct curl response including headers.\n2. **Proxy and TLS, 3 hours.**\
      \ Containerize the API, add Caddy, export the public local\n   root certificate,\
      \ and compare direct HTTP with verified proxy HTTPS.\n3. **Failure table, 4\
      \ hours.** Exercise each case below independently; restore the\n   working state\
      \ between cases and save both client output and matching server logs.\n4. **Timeout\
      \ and connection reuse, 3 hours.** Use a persistent HTTPX client for repeated\n\
      \   requests and compare with a new client per request. Give connection, read,\
      \ write,\n   and pool waits explicit limits; do not describe these as a guaranteed\
      \ total deadline.\n5. **Tests and explanation, 3 hours.** Add bounded integration\
      \ tests and explain where\n   the failed requests stopped. Stop the stack after\
      \ exporting results.\n\n| Case | Controlled change | What to inspect |\n|---|---|---|\n\
      | Resolution | Request an unused `.invalid` hostname | No application request\
      \ should arrive; disable environment proxy use for this test |\n| Connection\
      \ | Request a verified unused loopback port | Failure before an HTTP response\
      \ |\n| TLS trust | Omit the lab root certificate | Certificate validation failure;\
      \ do not use insecure mode as the fix |\n| Validation | Send a non-string `text`\
      \ | An HTTP error with an application response |\n| Upstream unavailable | Stop\
      \ only `api` | Proxy logs and response status distinguish this from a closed\
      \ proxy port |\n| Slow response | Delay 1500 ms with a 200 ms read timeout |\
      \ Client stops waiting; inspect whether server later finishes |\n\nClient timeout\
      \ is not automatic cancellation of application work. Check the server log\n\
      after the timed-out request; networking and application cancellation are different\
      \ steps.\n\n## Commands and tests\n\nRun from this lesson directory after implementing\
      \ the files:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\nuv run pytest tests -q\ndocker compose up\
      \ -d --build\ndocker compose cp proxy:/data/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt\
      \ artifacts/local-root.crt\ncurl --cacert artifacts/local-root.crt -i https://localhost:8443/ready\n\
      uv run python -m network_lab.exercise --base-url https://localhost:8443 --ca\
      \ artifacts/local-root.crt --out artifacts/requests.jsonl\ndocker compose logs\
      \ --no-color api proxy\ndocker compose down\n```\n\nName the proxy service `proxy`\
      \ to match these commands. Create the artifacts directory\nbefore copying the\
      \ certificate. Tests cover response shape, body limit, delay limit,\nrequest\
      \ ID propagation, and bounded client waits. Failure experiments need a running\n\
      stack and are separate from fast unit tests.\n\n## What to record\n\nSave the\
      \ URL, request ID, client exception or HTTP status, elapsed time, and server-side\n\
      evidence for each case. A 502 response and a connection-refused exception have\
      \ different\ncauses even if the user sees the same failure screen. Connection\
      \ reuse may have little\nvisible timing impact locally; report that rather than\
      \ manufacturing a speedup.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and extensions\n\nLaptop, CPU,\
      \ Docker, and about 2 GB of available memory; target cost $0. Keep the stack\n\
      on loopback. Public DNS, public certificates, cloud firewalls, and IPv6 are\
      \ extensions;\nSystems Guide 10 covers a real deployment.\n\n### Report the\
      \ actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration\
      \ identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation.\
      \ Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server\
      \ or cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."

      certificate, or timeout behavior.

  - content: "Model synthetic users, organizations, documents, jobs, and processing\
      \ credits in Postgres. Explain keys, constraints, indexes, pagination, query\
      \ plans, transaction isolation, and idempotency through application questions.\
      \ Reproduce two simultaneous seven-credit submissions against a ten-credit balance,\
      \ then enforce the rule inside the transaction. Separate a duplicate request\
      \ from a distinct concurrent request.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation\
      \ and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are\
      \ proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured\
      \ results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected\
      \ components in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nStore\
      \ synthetic users, documents, and conversations in PostgreSQL. Answer questions\n\
      such as “which documents belong to this organization?” and “what are the next\
      \ 20\nmessages in this conversation?” Then add data, inspect a slow query, and\
      \ measure what\nan index changes for both reads and writes.\n\nStart with two\
      \ organizations and a dozen hand-readable records. The larger dataset\nexists\
      \ to make behavior measurable, not to replace understanding those first rows.\n\
      \n## Prerequisites and scope\n\nYou know Python collections, files, and tests;\
      \ Guide 32 provides\nthe process concepts. SQL is taught here. Use PostgreSQL\
      \ 17 in Docker Compose, Python\n3.13, Psycopg 3, and pytest. Lock Python packages\
      \ and record the database image digest.\nThe lesson specifies code and configuration\
      \ to create, not a supplied implementation.\n\nNo web interface, language model,\
      \ earlier lesson code, or portfolio project is needed.\n\n## From Python records\
      \ to related tables\n\nA table stores records with the same columns. A **primary\
      \ key** uniquely identifies a\nrow. A **foreign key** requires a reference to\
      \ identify an existing related row. A\n**constraint** is a rule enforced by\
      \ the database, including unique values and allowed\nrelationships. These rules\
      \ still apply when a script writes data without your usual API.\n\nUse this\
      \ schema specification; choose explicit SQL types and implement its constraints:\n\
      \n| Table | Columns and rules |\n|---|---|\n| organizations | `id` primary key,\
      \ `name` required |\n| users | `id` primary key, `email` required and unique\
      \ |\n| memberships | `org_id`, `user_id`, `role`; unique organization/user pair;\
      \ role is employee or HR |\n| documents | `id`, `org_id`, `owner_id`, `title`,\
      \ `body`, `created_at`; owner must be a member of that organization |\n| conversations\
      \ | `id`, `org_id`, `owner_id`; owner must be a member of that organization\
      \ |\n| messages | `id`, `conversation_id`, `created_at`, `body`; conversation\
      \ must exist |\n\nUse a composite foreign key to memberships for each organization/owner\
      \ pair; a foreign\nkey to users alone does not enforce membership in the document's\
      \ organization. Keep\norganization deletion restricted in the core so an accidental\
      \ deletion does not cascade\nthrough every table. This schema describes ownership,\
      \ not complete read authorization;\nGuide 35 adds that decision.\n\n`SELECT`\
      \ chooses columns and `WHERE` filters rows. A `JOIN` connects rows through related\n\
      keys; it can multiply rows when a user has several documents. For one short\
      \ handwritten\ndataset, work out a join's expected rows before running it. Compare\
      \ `COUNT(*)` with\ncounting distinct users to see why the two can differ.\n\n\
      Use parameterized queries for values. SQL text and data must travel separately;\
      \ string\nformatting user input into SQL changes program structure. Psycopg's\
      \ value placeholders\ndo not substitute identifiers such as table names; use\
      \ its identifier-composition API\nif an identifier genuinely must vary. [Psycopg\
      \ parameters](https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/basic/params.html)\n\n##\
      \ Query experiment\n\nGenerate 100,000 documents distributed across 20 organizations,\
      \ with deterministic\nIDs, timestamps, and repeated titles. Include equal timestamps\
      \ deliberately. Compare:\n\n1. an organization's newest 20 documents with no\
      \ additional index;\n2. the same query with an index on `(org_id, created_at,\
      \ id)`;\n3. deep pagination using an offset versus a cursor containing the last\
      \ timestamp and ID.\n\nAn **index** stores an additional search structure. PostgreSQL\
      \ can use it to avoid\nreading/sorting every matching row, but must also maintain\
      \ it during writes. A **query\nplan** describes how the database intends to\
      \ find results. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`\nruns the query and includes observed\
      \ work; `ANALYZE` is not a harmless preview for a\nwrite statement. Use it on\
      \ reads here. [PostgreSQL EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-explain.html)\n\
      \nAn offset skips a number of rows. **Keyset pagination** asks for rows beyond\
      \ a known\nordered key. Use `(created_at, id)` in both the ordering and cursor\
      \ comparison, with\ndirections that agree. A unique tie-breaker prevents equal\
      \ timestamps from creating\nambiguous page boundaries. Neither method by itself\
      \ freezes a changing dataset.\n\n## Project shape and interfaces\n\n```text\n\
      week34/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── compose.yaml\n├── schema.sql\n├── data_lab/\n\
      │   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── seed.py\n│   ├── queries.py\n│   ├── benchmark.py\n\
      │   └── cli.py\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\nfrom datetime\
      \ import datetime\n\ndef create_document(conn, org_id: int, owner_id: int, title:\
      \ str, body: str) -> int: ...\ndef list_documents(conn, org_id: int, after:\
      \ tuple[datetime, int] | None,\n                   limit: int = 20) -> list[dict]:\
      \ ...\ndef append_message(conn, conversation_id: int, body: str) -> int: ...\n\
      def explain_query(conn, org_id: int) -> dict: ...\n```\n\nUse a transaction\
      \ when creating a conversation with its first message: both changes\ncommit\
      \ together or neither does. A **commit** makes the transaction's changes lasting;\n\
      a **rollback** discards its unfinished changes. Competing transactions are the\
      \ main\nexperiment in Systems Guide 11.\n\n## What you will build — Transactions\
      \ and Concurrent Updates\n\nGive a synthetic organization ten processing credits.\
      \ Have two clients each request a\nseven-credit job at the same time. A naive\
      \ implementation can accept both while storing\na balance of three. You will\
      \ reproduce that failure deliberately, repair the transaction,\nand check what\
      \ happens when the same submission arrives twice.\n\nThe project is a small\
      \ PostgreSQL-backed submission function with a concurrency harness.\nThere is\
      \ no real billing and no external model call. The first action is to write the\n\
      expected rule: accepted reservations plus remaining credits must equal the starting\
      \ ten,\nand the remaining balance must never be negative.\n\n## Prerequisites\
      \ and setup — Transactions and Concurrent Updates\n\nYou understand SQL, keys,\
      \ constraints, and simple transactions from\nFoundations 34, plus basic API\
      \ concepts. No earlier\nimplementation is imported. Use Python 3.13, Psycopg\
      \ 3, pytest, and PostgreSQL 17 in local\nCompose. Lock packages and record the\
      \ container digest. All files and commands below\nare the interfaces to implement\
      \ for this lesson.\n\n## Make the race reproducible — Transactions and Concurrent\
      \ Updates\n\nUse `balances(org_id, credits)` and\n`submissions(org_id, request_key,\
      \ payload_hash, cost, outcome, remaining)`.\nThe pair `(org_id, request_key)`\
      \ is unique. `cost` is a positive integer and the balance\nhas a nonnegative\
      \ check constraint. The hash represents the canonical request body;\nreusing\
      \ the same key with a different body is an error, not a repeat of the old request.\n\
      \nThe naive function reads the balance, checks it in Python, then writes the\
      \ calculated\nnew value. Coordinate two independent database connections so\
      \ both finish their read\nbefore either writes. Each reads ten, each accepts\
      \ seven, and each writes three.\nThe nonnegative constraint alone cannot catch\
      \ those two accepted reservations.\n\nA **lost update** occurs when one change\
      \ overwrites another using an outdated value.\nA transaction groups related\
      \ statements, but its **isolation level** determines what\nconcurrent work it\
      \ can observe. PostgreSQL's default Read Committed gives each statement\na committed\
      \ snapshot, not one immutable snapshot for the whole transaction. It does\n\
      not make a multi-statement Python read/compute/write sequence automatically\
      \ safe.\n[PostgreSQL isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/transaction-iso.html)\n\
      \n## Two bounded repairs — Transactions and Concurrent Updates\n\nFirst perform\
      \ the balance change as one conditional database update: subtract only if\n\
      the row still has enough credit and inspect whether a row was returned. Keep\
      \ recording\nthe accepted submission in the same transaction. A transaction\
      \ that cannot finish must\nnot leave a debit behind.\n\nThen implement one comparison\
      \ using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, a row lock that keeps\nanother transaction\
      \ from changing the selected balance until yours ends. After obtaining\nthe\
      \ lock, check the current value and perform the update. Keep the transaction\
      \ short;\ndo not wait for external work while holding the row.\n\n**Idempotency**\
      \ means repeating the same logical request has the same lasting effect.\nReserve\
      \ a request key transactionally, validate its payload hash, apply a debit at\
      \ most\nonce, and store the outcome before commit. A concurrent duplicate must\
      \ resolve to the\ncommitted original outcome or a defined retryable response.\
      \ It cannot create an extra\ndebit. Persist a rejected outcome too, so later\
      \ changes in balance do not silently turn\nthe same rejected request into a\
      \ different operation.\n\nDo not catch a uniqueness error and continue using\
      \ an aborted PostgreSQL transaction.\nUse a conflict-aware insert, or roll back\
      \ and start a clean transaction as appropriate.\nThe design needs both the request-key\
      \ constraint and the balance rule; neither substitutes\nfor the other.\n\n##\
      \ Project shape and interfaces — Transactions and Concurrent Updates\n\n```text\n\
      week11/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── compose.yaml\n├── schema.sql\n├── transaction_lab/\n\
      │   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── store.py         # baseline and two repairs\n│\
      \   ├── harness.py       # controlled two-client interleavings\n│   └── cli.py\n\
      ├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\n\
      \n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Submission:\n    accepted: bool\n    request_key:\
      \ str\n    remaining: int\n\ndef submit_once(conn, org_id: int, key: str, cost:\
      \ int,\n                payload_hash: str, mode: str) -> Submission: ...\ndef\
      \ run_interleaving(mode: str, same_key: bool) -> list[dict]: ...\ndef check_invariants(conn,\
      \ org_id: int, starting_credits: int) -> dict: ...\n```\n\nEach client uses\
      \ its own connection. Log timestamps, transaction events, request keys,\nand\
      \ outcomes; keep credentials out of traces. Use explicit events/barriers and\
      \ timeouts\ninstead of relying on sleeps. Only the naive path pauses after an\
      \ unlocked read: putting\nthat same two-party barrier after the repaired path's\
      \ row lock would manufacture a hang."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 17 hours\n\n1. **Small schema, 3 hours.**\
      \ Create tables and insert the hand-readable rows. Try a\n   missing owner,\
      \ duplicate membership, and owner from the wrong organization.\n2. **SQL queries,\
      \ 3 hours.** Implement filtered lists, a join, an aggregate, and the\n   conversation\
      \ transaction. Check them against hand-computed examples.\n3. **Large fixture\
      \ and plans, 3 hours.** Generate 100,000 documents, refresh planner\n   statistics\
      \ with `ANALYZE`, and save a plan before and after adding the index.\n4. **Pagination,\
      \ 3 hours.** Page through a fixed fixture with equal timestamps; verify\n  \
      \ no missing/duplicate IDs. Compare latency near the beginning and at a deep\
      \ page.\n5. **Write cost and report, 3 hours.** Insert the same 10,000 additional\
      \ records into\n   equivalent unindexed/indexed fixtures. Measure time and database/index\
      \ sizes.\n6. **Failure tests and cleanup, 2 hours.** Interrupt the two-write\
      \ transaction before\n   commit and verify neither row remains. Export results\
      \ and stop the database.\n\nRun timing comparisons several times, alternating\
      \ order. Record warm versus first-run\nmeasurements rather than describing a\
      \ warmed query as disk performance. The planner may\nchoose a sequential scan\
      \ on a small table; explain the plan instead of forcing an index.\n\n## Commands\
      \ and checks\n\nCreate `compose.yaml` with a service named `postgres`, a health\
      \ check, a named data\nvolume, and loopback-only database access. Keep credentials\
      \ in an ignored local file.\nImplement the following CLI and run it from this\
      \ lesson directory:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\ndocker compose up -d --wait postgres\n\
      uv run python -m data_lab.cli init\nuv run python -m data_lab.cli seed --documents\
      \ 100000 --seed 34\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m data_lab.cli benchmark\
      \ --out artifacts/query-report.json\ndocker compose down\n```\n\nTests cover\
      \ constraints, parameterized values containing quotes, join cardinality,\ntransaction\
      \ failure, empty results, and pagination ties. The seed/reset commands must\n\
      refuse a database name other than `week34_lab`; performance variants should\
      \ use separate\ntables or freshly recreated local fixtures, not delete unknown\
      \ databases.\n\n## Evidence, cost, and optional depth\n\nWrite `artifacts/report.md`\
      \ with the schema rationale, query plans, timing observations,\nwrite/storage\
      \ cost, and one remaining limitation. A database index is a tradeoff, not an\n\
      obligation for every column. CPU, Docker, and a few GB of free disk suffice;\
      \ target cost $0.\nFull-text search, multi-column statistics, and pagination\
      \ during concurrent writes are\noptional. Stop containers after use; removing\
      \ the named volume is a separate explicit\ncleanup step after the report has\
      \ been saved.\n\n## Build sequence — 17 hours — Transactions and Concurrent\
      \ Updates\n\n1. **Schema and single client, 3 hours.** Initialize ten credits,\
      \ submit one seven-credit\n   request, and hand-check the rows. Reject zero/negative\
      \ cost and invalid organization.\n2. **Controlled race, 3 hours.** Coordinate\
      \ two naive clients with different keys and\n   save the read/write sequence\
      \ that violates the accounting rule.\n3. **Atomic update repair, 3 hours.**\
      \ Add the conditional debit and transactional result.\n   Repeat the race and\
      \ a 20-client burst with fresh fixtures.\n4. **Duplicate requests, 3 hours.**\
      \ Submit the same key concurrently, repeat it after\n   commit, and reuse it\
      \ with a different cost. Test a crash after debit but before commit.\n5. **Lock\
      \ comparison, 3 hours.** Compare the row-lock version. In a separate miniature\n\
      \   test, lock two organizations in opposite orders to observe a deadlock, then\
      \ use a\n   consistent order. A deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting\
      \ for each other.\n6. **Tests and report, 2 hours.** Check committed rows and\
      \ record rejected, failed,\n   retried, and accepted submissions separately.\n\
      \nPostgreSQL can abort a deadlocked transaction. Apply a bounded retry of the\
      \ whole\ntransaction with the same request key; do not retry only its last statement.\
      \ Keep this\ncomparison separate from the core balance test. [PostgreSQL locks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/explicit-locking.html)\n\
      \n## Commands and tests — Transactions and Concurrent Updates\n\nFrom this lesson\
      \ directory after implementing the CLI:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\ndocker compose\
      \ up -d --wait postgres\nuv run python -m transaction_lab.cli init --database\
      \ week11_lab\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m transaction_lab.cli race\
      \ --modes naive,atomic,locked --out artifacts/race.jsonl\nuv run python -m transaction_lab.cli\
      \ duplicates --clients 20 --out artifacts/duplicates.jsonl\nuv run python -m\
      \ transaction_lab.cli deadlock --out artifacts/deadlock.jsonl\ndocker compose\
      \ down\n```\n\nUse an explicit fixture reset restricted to `week11_lab` between\
      \ experiments. Configure\nshort statement/lock timeouts so a bug exits with\
      \ useful evidence. Tests inspect balances\nand unique result rows, not just\
      \ HTTP status or worker return values. Verify rollback\nafter an injected exception,\
      \ concurrent duplicate identity, different-body conflict,\nand identical keys\
      \ belonging to different organizations.\n\n## Evidence, cost, and optional depth\
      \ — Transactions and Concurrent Updates\n\nRecord an event timeline for the\
      \ broken and repaired runs, the starting/ending ledger,\nisolation level, transaction\
      \ boundaries, and retry counts. If a repair still fails, the\ntrace and violated\
      \ invariant are valid learning evidence; do not label it safe.\n\nCPU and local\
      \ Docker suffice; target cost $0. External provider execution and payment\n\
      are out of scope. A database transaction cannot make an external API call execute\
      \ or\nbill exactly once. Serializable isolation and an outbox linking data to\
      \ durable jobs\nare extensions or follow-on material in Guide 2.\n\n### Report\
      \ the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration\
      \ identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation.\
      \ Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server\
      \ or cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."

  - content: "Build a minimal interface over the service using a maintained UI approach.\
      \ Integrate established authentication rather than inventing cryptography. Distinguish\
      \ authenticated identity from per-resource authorization and check every document\
      \ operation. Stream a fake model response, propagate client cancellation through\
      \ the server, and keep migrations versioned. Reuse the architecture discipline\
      \ from the Habit Tracker while adding network and user boundaries.\n\nThe lesson\
      \ below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs,\
      \ package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate\
      \ that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture\
      \ for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\
      \n## Overview\n\nBackpressure and cancellation are harder than they look once\
      \ tokens are\nstreaming, and a stop button that only halts the UI while generation\
      \ continues\nserver-side is a bug, not a minor gap. This chapter builds a chat\
      \ backend that\nstreams tokens over SSE or WebSockets and correctly cancels\
      \ the underlying\ngeneration — not just its rendering — when the user stops\
      \ it. Simulated stop\nevents at random points in generation measure the compute\
      \ saved by correct\ncancellation compared to letting generation run to completion.\
      \ Cancellation turns\nout to be a resource-cost and API-design problem, not\
      \ a frontend nicety.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- **Async Python.** You must be\
      \ comfortable with `async`/`await`, `asyncio`\n  tasks, `asyncio.CancelledError`,\
      \ `asyncio.Queue`, and task cancellation\n  semantics. This chapter *is* an\
      \ async-control-flow exercise; the LLM is almost\n  incidental.\n- **HTTP streaming\
      \ basics.** A rough mental model of chunked transfer, Server-Sent\n  Events\
      \ (SSE), and WebSockets — what each gives you and what each costs. You'll\n\
      \  pick one as the primary transport and understand why.\n- **A web framework\
      \ you can serve async endpoints with.** FastAPI/Starlette is the\n  assumed\
      \ default (ASGI, native async, `StreamingResponse` and WebSocket support),\n\
      \  but the ideas port to any ASGI stack.\n- **Conceptual only, not code:** the\
      \ idea of a serving loop that emits tokens one\n  at a time.\n  You do **not**\
      \ re-implement a model here — the token source is a hosted API's\n  streaming\
      \ endpoint. Re-derive the \"tokens arrive incrementally\" mental model\n  rather\
      \ than importing anything.\n- **HTTP client with cancellation support.** An\
      \ async client (`httpx.AsyncClient`\n  or the vendor SDK's async streaming interface)\
      \ whose request context can be torn\n  down mid-stream. This capability is the\
      \ whole ballgame — verify it before you\n  build on it.\n\n## The problem, stated\
      \ precisely\n\nStreaming a chat response is easy. The hard part is what happens\
      \ when the user\nclicks **Stop** halfway through a 2,000-token answer.\n\nThere\
      \ are three distinct places a stream can be \"stopped,\" and naive\nimplementations\
      \ only stop the first one:\n\n1. **The renderer.** The browser stops appending\
      \ tokens to the DOM. Trivial, and\n   what most tutorials mean by \"stop.\"\n\
      2. **The transport.** The client closes the SSE connection or WebSocket. Better\
      \ —\n   but on its own, a server that isn't *listening* for the disconnect will\
      \ keep\n   generating into a socket nobody is reading.\n3. **The generator.**\
      \ The server-side task driving the upstream LLM request is\n   cancelled, and\
      \ the upstream HTTP request to the provider is actually torn down,\n   so the\
      \ provider stops billing you and stops spending GPU time.\n\n**Real cancellation\
      \ means reaching level 3.** If a stop only reaches level 1, you\npay for every\
      \ token of a response the user will never see. At scale, with users\nwho bail\
      \ on long answers, that is a large fraction of your inference bill spent on\n\
      output that is discarded the instant it's produced.\n\nFormally, let a response\
      \ have $N$ total tokens if run to completion, and let the\nuser issue a stop\
      \ after observing $k$ tokens. With correct cancellation you pay\nfor $\\approx\
      \ k + \\Delta$ tokens, where $\\Delta$ is the small overshoot between the\n\
      stop signal and the generation actually halting (in-flight chunk, propagation\n\
      latency). With no real cancellation you pay for all $N$. The **wasted fraction**\n\
      is\n\n$$w = \\frac{N - (k + \\Delta)}{N} = 1 - \\frac{k + \\Delta}{N}.$$\n\n\
      The week's artifact is a direct measurement of $\\Delta$ and of the aggregate\
      \ saved\ntokens $\\sum_i \\big(N_i - (k_i + \\Delta_i)\\big)$ across many simulated\
      \ stops. Your\njob is to drive $\\Delta$ as small as the transport and provider\
      \ allow, and to\nprove you did.\n\n### Why \"just closing the socket\" isn't\
      \ enough\n\nTwo failure modes make this subtle:\n\n- **The server doesn't notice\
      \ the disconnect.** In a request-scoped streaming\n  handler, you only learn\
      \ the client left when you next try to *write* to the\n  closed connection —\
      \ which may be one full token-generation step later, or never\n  if you're blocked\
      \ awaiting the upstream provider. You must **actively poll for\n  disconnection**\
      \ (`await request.is_disconnected()` in Starlette) or structure\n  the code\
      \ so a disconnect cancels the producing task.\n- **Cancelling the task doesn't\
      \ cancel the upstream request.** `task.cancel()`\n  raises `CancelledError`\
      \ at the next `await` point *inside your code*. If your\n  code is parked inside\
      \ a context manager that owns the upstream HTTP stream, you\n  must ensure that\
      \ context manager's `__aexit__` (or `aclose()`) actually aborts\n  the socket\
      \ to the provider rather than draining it. Verify this against your\n  specific\
      \ client — some clients drain-then-close by default.\n\nThis is the core lesson\
      \ of the week: **cancellation is cooperative and it must be\nplumbed end to\
      \ end.** A break in the chain anywhere silently degrades you back to\nlevel\
      \ 1.\n\n## One concrete permission model — Authentication and Document Permissions\n\
      \nUse four users: Acme employee Alice, Acme HR user Hannah, Birch employee Ben,\
      \ and Birch\nHR user Bea. Each has exactly one membership for this exercise.\
      \ Roles are scoped to an\norganization, not globally attached to a user.\n\n\
      | Document | Organization | Minimum role | Alice | Hannah | Ben | Bea |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n\
      | A1 handbook | Acme | employee | yes | yes | no | no |\n| A2 salary policy\
      \ | Acme | HR | no | yes | no | no |\n| B1 handbook | Birch | employee | no\
      \ | no | yes | yes |\n| B2 salary policy | Birch | HR | no | no | no | yes |\n\
      \nPut the word `salary` once in each handbook and ten times in each HR document.\
      \ Rank\ndocuments by the number of case-insensitive query-token matches, breaking\
      \ ties by ID.\nApply the permission predicate before ranking and limiting the\
      \ results. This exact\nsearch makes the access decision visible without approximate-search\
      \ complications.\n\n**Authentication** establishes who is making the request.\
      \ **Authorization** decides\nwhat that identity may do. **Role-based access\
      \ control (RBAC)** grants actions through\nroles; here the action is document\
      \ reading, and organization membership constrains the\nresource scope. A successful\
      \ login alone grants no right to read an arbitrary document.\n\nUse `(issuer,\
      \ subject)` from a verified login as the stable external identity, mapped to\n\
      a local user ID. Email is display data, not the authorization key. Memberships\
      \ and role\nchanges come from the database on each request; a stale role in\
      \ a browser or token must\nnot override them. Missing membership denies access.\n\
      \n## Login through an established implementation — Authentication and Document\
      \ Permissions\n\nUse a local Keycloak realm `week35`, a confidential web client\
      \ `document-lab`, and an exact\ncallback URL `http://localhost:8000/auth/callback`.\
      \ Run its development mode on loopback\nonly, create the four users, and export\
      \ realm configuration without credentials. The\n[Keycloak Docker quickstart](https://www.keycloak.org/getting-started/getting-started-docker)\n\
      provides the provider bootstrap; do not expose this development provider publicly.\n\
      \nUse Authlib's OpenID Connect (**OIDC**) integration. OIDC supplies a verified\
      \ identity\non top of an authorization flow. Configure discovery, the `openid`\
      \ scope, a checked\nredirect URI, state, nonce, and Proof Key for Code Exchange\
      \ (**PKCE**) with S256 through\nthe library. These checks bind a response to\
      \ the login request and help prevent code\ninterception; do not implement signing\
      \ or token verification yourself.\n[Authlib client documentation](https://docs.authlib.org/en/v1.7.0/oauth2/client/web/index.html)\n\
      \nStore login state in a server-side session with a random cookie identifier.\
      \ Keep tokens\nout of URLs and readable cookie payloads. Use HttpOnly and SameSite\
      \ cookie settings;\nthe loopback HTTP lab may need Secure disabled locally,\
      \ while an HTTPS deployment needs\nit enabled. Logout clears the local session.\
      \ Normal API calls use that session rather\nthan accepting a caller-supplied\
      \ `user_id`, `org_id`, or `role` as authority.\n\n## Database enforcement and\
      \ retrieval — Authentication and Document Permissions\n\nCreate `users`, `memberships(user_id,\
      \ org_id, role)`, and\n`documents(id, org_id, min_role, title, body)`. Application\
      \ code first filters with the\nsame explicit permission predicate used in tests.\
      \ The HR role includes handbook access;\nmembership in another organization\
      \ does not.\n\nAdd PostgreSQL **row-level security (RLS)**: database policies\
      \ deciding which rows a\nquery may see. Separate a migration owner from a restricted\
      \ application role. Grant the\napplication only needed operations, enable RLS\
      \ on documents, and evaluate membership\nusing a transaction-local identity\
      \ set by trusted server code. Missing identity must\nevaluate to denial. Do\
      \ not grant the app ownership, superuser status, or `BYPASSRLS`.\nOwners normally\
      \ bypass RLS, so tests using only the migration role are insufficient.\n[PostgreSQL\
      \ row-security documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-rowsecurity.html)\n\
      \nAt each request, begin a transaction, set its local identity, perform reads,\
      \ then commit\nor roll back before returning the connection to the pool. Use\
      \ transaction-local\n`set_config(..., true)` through parameters. Test reused\
      \ connections after both normal\ncompletion and an exception. A custom identity\
      \ setting is trusted input from application\ncode, not protection against an\
      \ attacker who can execute arbitrary SQL as that role.\n\nFor this bounded lab,\
      \ each retrieval decision uses one database statement and its\nsnapshot. Define\
      \ revocation as denying requests whose authorization statement starts\nafter\
      \ the revocation commit. Do not claim that revocation recalls already returned\
      \ text\nor cancels an in-progress request that authorized before the change."
    lab_and_evidence: "## What you're building\n\nA small, real service: a chat backend\
      \ that accepts a prompt, streams tokens to the\nclient, and cancels the underlying\
      \ generation the moment the client goes away or\nsends an explicit stop — plus\
      \ a harness that proves cancellation works and\nmeasures what it saves.\n\n\
      Keep it a *backend* with a thin client. You may reuse a minimal Flet or plain-HTML\n\
      client conceptually (re-derived, not imported from Week 17), but the UI is not\
      \ the\npoint; the cancellation plumbing and the benchmark are.\n\n### Suggested\
      \ file structure\n\n```\nweek19-streaming-cancellation/\n├── README.md\n├──\
      \ pyproject.toml\n├── .env.example              # LLM_API_KEY=, LLM_BASE_URL=,\
      \ MODEL=\n├── .gitignore                # must ignore .env\n├── docker-compose.yml\
      \        # the service as a real container\n├── Dockerfile\n├── src/\n│   └──\
      \ streamchat/\n│       ├── __init__.py\n│       ├── config.py         # settings\
      \ loaded from env, validated\n│       ├── llm.py            # streaming token\
      \ source + cancellation contract\n│       ├── stream_sse.py     # SSE transport\
      \ endpoint\n│       ├── stream_ws.py      # WebSocket transport endpoint (alternative/second)\n\
      │       ├── cancellation.py   # the cancellation scope / registry\n│       ├──\
      \ metering.py       # per-request token + wall-clock accounting\n│       └──\
      \ app.py            # FastAPI app wiring transports + routes\n├── bench/\n│\
      \   ├── mock_provider.py      # deterministic fake token source for tests\n\
      │   ├── run_bench.py          # injects random stops, records saved tokens\n\
      │   └── report.py             # aggregates runs → the checkable artifact\n├──\
      \ clients/\n│   └── index.html            # trivial browser client with a Stop\
      \ button\n└── tests/\n    ├── test_cancellation.py  # proves generation stops,\
      \ not just rendering\n    └── test_metering.py\n```\n\nDo not treat this tree\
      \ as gospel — merge or split modules as your design wants.\nIt exists to show\
      \ the seams: **token source**, **transport**, **cancellation\nscope**, and **metering**\
      \ are the four things that must be separable so you can\ntest cancellation without\
      \ a real provider.\n\n### The token source and its cancellation contract\n\n\
      The single most important interface is the boundary between \"your service\"\
      \ and\n\"the thing producing tokens.\" Make it an async generator whose teardown\
      \ is\n*guaranteed* to release the upstream resource.\n\n```python\n# src/streamchat/llm.py\n\
      from __future__ import annotations\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom\
      \ typing import AsyncIterator, Protocol\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass\
      \ Token:\n    text: str\n    index: int          # 0-based position in this\
      \ response\n    finish: bool = False\n\n\nclass TokenSource(Protocol):\n   \
      \ \"\"\"Anything that can stream tokens for a prompt and stop cleanly.\n\n \
      \   Contract: if the consumer stops iterating (breaks, or the surrounding\n\
      \    task is cancelled), the underlying resource (HTTP stream to the provider)\n\
      \    MUST be released promptly. Implementations own that guarantee in their\n\
      \    `aclose()` / context-manager exit.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def stream(self,\
      \ prompt: str) -> \"AsyncIterator[Token]\":\n        ...\n\n\nclass HostedLLMSource:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Streams tokens from a hosted provider over async HTTP.\n\n    Key\
      \ requirement: entering the upstream stream must happen inside an\n    `async\
      \ with` (or try/finally) so that cancellation of the consuming\n    task aborts\
      \ the socket, not drains it.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, client, model:\
      \ str) -> None:\n        ...  # store async HTTP client + model\n\n    async\
      \ def stream(self, prompt: str) -> AsyncIterator[Token]:\n        # TODO: open\
      \ the provider's streaming completion inside `async with`.\n        # TODO:\
      \ yield Token(...) per SSE/delta chunk from the provider.\n        # TODO: in\
      \ finally/__aexit__, ensure the upstream response is aborted\n        #    \
      \   (NOT read-to-completion). This is the line that saves money.\n        ...\n\
      ```\n\n> Verification you must actually do: instrument `finally` in `stream()`\
      \ and prove,\n> in a test, that after the consumer cancels, no further upstream\
      \ chunks are\n> requested. If your client library drains on close, switch to\
      \ an explicit\n> `response.aclose()` / abort path.\n\n### The cancellation scope\n\
      \nBind each response to a cancellable unit so *any* of three triggers — explicit\n\
      stop message, transport disconnect, or a server-side budget — tears the same\
      \ task\ndown through one path.\n\n```python\n# src/streamchat/cancellation.py\n\
      import asyncio\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\n\n\n@dataclass\nclass\
      \ GenerationHandle:\n    \"\"\"One in-flight response. Cancelling it must reach\
      \ the TokenSource.\"\"\"\n    request_id: str\n    task: asyncio.Task\n    reason:\
      \ str | None = None\n\n    def cancel(self, reason: str) -> None:\n        #\
      \ TODO: record reason, then task.cancel(); idempotent.\n        ...\n\n\nclass\
      \ Registry:\n    \"\"\"Tracks live generations so an out-of-band stop can find\
      \ one by id.\"\"\"\n    _handles: dict[str, GenerationHandle] = field(default_factory=dict)\n\
      \n    def register(self, request_id: str, task: asyncio.Task) -> GenerationHandle:\n\
      \        ...  # TODO\n\n    def stop(self, request_id: str, reason: str) ->\
      \ bool:\n        ...  # TODO: look up + cancel; return whether one was found\n\
      \n    def _reap(self, request_id: str) -> None:\n        ...  # TODO: remove\
      \ on done, avoid leaks\n```\n\nThe registry matters most for the **WebSocket**\
      \ design, where a `{\"type\":\"stop\"}`\nmessage arrives on the *same* connection\
      \ while the generator task runs\nconcurrently. For **SSE**, the primary stop\
      \ signal is the transport disconnect\nplus an optional side-channel `POST /stop/{request_id}`\
      \ — which is exactly what the\nregistry serves.\n\n### Transport A — SSE\n\n\
      SSE is one-directional (server→client) and rides plain HTTP, so the client's\n\
      \"stop\" is expressed by **closing the connection** (and optionally hitting\
      \ a stop\nendpoint). Your server must watch for that disconnect.\n\n```python\n\
      # src/streamchat/stream_sse.py\nfrom fastapi import APIRouter, Request\nfrom\
      \ fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse\n\nrouter = APIRouter()\n\n@router.get(\"\
      /chat/sse\")\nasync def chat_sse(request: Request, prompt: str):\n    async\
      \ def event_stream():\n        # TODO: create the generation task from a TokenSource\n\
      \        # TODO: loop: race \"next token\" against request.is_disconnected()\n\
      \        #       - on token: yield f\"data: {json}\\n\\n\"\n        #      \
      \ - on disconnect: cancel the generation task, break\n        # TODO: in finally,\
      \ ensure the task is cancelled + awaited\n        ...\n    return StreamingResponse(event_stream(),\
      \ media_type=\"text/event-stream\")\n```\n\nThe non-negotiable detail: you cannot\
      \ just `async for token in source.stream()`\nand yield. You must **concurrently**\
      \ watch `request.is_disconnected()`, because\nwhile you're awaiting the next\
      \ token you'd otherwise be deaf to the client leaving.\nA common shape is to\
      \ pump tokens into an `asyncio.Queue` from a child task and\n`await` on both\
      \ the queue and a disconnect poll with `asyncio.wait(...,\nreturn_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`.\n\
      \n### Transport B — WebSocket\n\nBidirectional, so an explicit `{\"type\":\"\
      stop\"}` can arrive mid-stream on the same\nsocket — more precise than SSE (you\
      \ can stop without dropping the connection).\n\n```python\n# src/streamchat/stream_ws.py\n\
      from fastapi import APIRouter, WebSocket\n\nrouter = APIRouter()\n\n@router.websocket(\"\
      /chat/ws\")\nasync def chat_ws(ws: WebSocket):\n    await ws.accept()\n    #\
      \ TODO: read the initial prompt frame\n    # TODO: spawn a generation task that\
      \ sends tokens as frames\n    # TODO: concurrently read inbound frames; on {\"\
      type\":\"stop\"} -> cancel\n    # TODO: also cancel on WebSocketDisconnect\n\
      \    # TODO: send a terminal {\"type\":\"done\"|\"cancelled\", \"usage\": {...}}\
      \ frame\n    ...\n```\n\nBuild **one** transport fully and the other at least\
      \ to a working stop; the\nbenchmark should be runnable on whichever you make\
      \ primary. SSE is the simpler,\nmore instructive default for *this* week's lesson\
      \ (disconnect detection); do that\none first.\n\n### Metering\n\nTo measure\
      \ savings you must count tokens and time per request, and record *why*\neach\
      \ request ended.\n\n```python\n# src/streamchat/metering.py\nfrom dataclasses\
      \ import dataclass\nfrom enum import Enum\nimport time\n\n\nclass EndReason(str,\
      \ Enum):\n    COMPLETED = \"completed\"\n    CANCELLED = \"cancelled\"\n   \
      \ DISCONNECTED = \"disconnected\"\n    ERROR = \"error\"\n\n\n@dataclass\nclass\
      \ Meter:\n    request_id: str\n    started: float = 0.0\n    tokens_emitted:\
      \ int = 0          # tokens actually produced upstream\n    tokens_delivered:\
      \ int = 0        # tokens the client received before stop\n    end_reason: EndReason\
      \ | None = None\n\n    def on_token(self) -> None:\n        ...  # TODO increment\
      \ emitted; delivered tracked at transport edge\n\n    def finish(self, reason:\
      \ EndReason) -> None:\n        ...  # TODO stamp wall-clock, reason\n\n    @property\n\
      \    def overshoot(self) -> int:\n        \"\"\"tokens_emitted - tokens_delivered\
      \ = Δ (post-stop overshoot).\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO\n```\n\nThe `overshoot`\
      \ (the $\\Delta$ above) is the headline number: with correct\ncancellation it\
      \ should be tiny and roughly constant; with fake cancellation it\ngrows to \"\
      the rest of the whole response.\"\n\n## How to build it (milestones)\n\n1. **Mock\
      \ provider first.** Write `bench/mock_provider.py`: a `TokenSource` that\n \
      \  emits deterministic tokens at a configurable delay and records exactly how\
      \ many\n   tokens it was asked to produce. This lets you test cancellation with\
      \ zero API\n   cost and no flakiness. *Everything* about the lesson is provable\
      \ against the\n   mock.\n2. **Naive streaming.** SSE endpoint that streams the\
      \ mock to a browser. No\n   cancellation yet. Confirm tokens render.\n3. **Wire\
      \ real cancellation.** Add disconnect detection + task cancellation.\n   Prove,\
      \ against the mock, that after the client disconnects the mock stops being\n\
      \   asked for tokens (assert on the mock's internal counter).\n4. **Add the\
      \ WebSocket transport + explicit stop message.** Prove an in-band stop\n   cancels\
      \ without needing a disconnect.\n5. **Swap in the hosted LLM source.** Confirm\
      \ the upstream request is genuinely\n   torn down on cancel (watch provider-side\
      \ usage or network teardown). Keep runs\n   short/cheap.\n6. **Build the benchmark\
      \ + report.** Inject random stops, aggregate, produce the\n   artifact below.\n\
      \nDeliberately keep the LLM swap for step 5: if cancellation is correct against\
      \ the\nmock, the only new risk with a real provider is whether *its* client\
      \ aborts the\nsocket — which is precisely the one thing left to verify.\n\n\
      ## Checkable artifact — the Cancellation Savings benchmark\n\n**Claim to demonstrate\
      \ (from the abstract):** correct cancellation saves real\ncompute versus letting\
      \ generation run to completion, and the saving is measured,\nnot asserted.\n\
      \n**Methodology.**\n\n- Configure the mock provider (and optionally a small\
      \ hosted model) to produce\n  responses of a known length $N$ (or draw $N$ from\
      \ a fixed distribution).\n- For each of many trials, pick a stop point $k \\\
      sim \\mathcal{U}(0, N)$ tokens.\n  Start a stream, let it deliver $k$ tokens,\
      \ then trigger a stop (disconnect for\n  SSE; stop message for WS).\n- Record,\
      \ per trial: $N$, $k$, `tokens_emitted` (how many the source was actually\n\
      \  driven to produce), and $\\Delta = \\texttt{tokens\\_emitted} - k$.\n- Run\
      \ the **same** trials in two modes:\n  - **Real cancellation ON** (your correct\
      \ path).\n  - **Real cancellation OFF** (a deliberately broken mode that only\
      \ stops\n    delivery/rendering and lets the source run to $N$) — the strawman\
      \ you're\n    beating.\n\n**Expected shape of the result.** A table plus one\
      \ plot:\n\n| mode                | mean $\\Delta$ (tokens) | mean tokens paid\
      \ | wasted fraction $w$ |\n| ------------------- | ---------------------- |\
      \ ---------------- | ------------------- |\n| cancellation ON     | small, ~constant\
      \       | $\\approx k+\\Delta$ | low, $\\to 0$ as $N$ grows |\n| cancellation\
      \ OFF    | $\\approx N-k$          | $\\approx N$      | high              \
      \  |\n\n- A scatter/line plot of **tokens paid vs. stop point $k$**: the ON\
      \ line hugs\n  $y=x$ (plus a flat offset $\\Delta$); the OFF line is flat at\
      \ $y=N$ regardless of\n  $k$. The vertical gap between them at each $k$ is the\
      \ compute saved.\n- A single **aggregate saved-tokens** figure across all trials:\n\
      \  $\\sum_i (N_i - (k_i + \\Delta_i))$, and the same as a percentage of total\
      \ tokens\n  that *would* have been generated. This one number is what you report.\n\
      \n**Pass criteria.** With cancellation ON, $\\Delta$ is bounded and independent\
      \ of\n$N$ (it does not grow as responses get longer); the OFF/ON gap widens\
      \ linearly\nwith $N-k$. If $\\Delta$ grows with $N$ in your \"ON\" mode, cancellation\
      \ is not\nactually reaching the source — go back to the `finally`/`aclose` path.\n\
      \n## How to run and test it\n\n- **Run the service:** `docker compose up` starts\
      \ the backend as a real container\n  (the point of running it as a service,\
      \ per the course's Docker-from-Week-4\n  requirement). Open `clients/index.html`\
      \ against it and click **Stop** mid-answer.\n- **Unit tests (no API cost):**\n\
      \  - `test_cancellation.py` asserts that after a simulated disconnect/stop,\
      \ the\n    mock provider's \"tokens requested\" counter stops advancing within\
      \ a small\n    bound — i.e. generation halted, not just rendering.\n  - `test_metering.py`\
      \ asserts `overshoot` ($\\Delta$) is small in the ON path and\n    large in\
      \ the OFF path, locking in the benchmark's core distinction as a\n    regression\
      \ test.\n- **Benchmark:** `python bench/run_bench.py` runs the trials against\
      \ the mock;\n  `python bench/report.py` emits the table + plot described above.\n\
      - **Smoke test against the real provider:** a handful of short prompts with\
      \ a mid\n  stream stop, confirming the upstream request tears down (short and\
      \ cheap by\n  design).\n\n## Security & operational notes\n\nThis chapter exposes\
      \ a **network service that spends money per request**, so treat it\nlike one:\n\
      \n- **Secrets:** the LLM API key comes from the environment only. Commit\n \
      \ `.env.example`, never `.env`; ensure `.gitignore` excludes `.env`. No key\
      \ in\n  code, logs, or error responses.\n- **Input validation at the boundary:**\
      \ cap prompt length and reject oversized or\n  malformed frames before starting\
      \ a generation — an unbounded prompt is both a\n  cost and a DoS vector.\n-\
      \ **Per-connection limits:** enforce a max concurrent generations per client\
      \ and a\n  server-side token/time budget on each generation (a `GenerationHandle`\
      \ your\n  registry can cancel), so a client that opens streams and walks away\
      \ can't pin\n  resources. This budget-cancel path reuses the exact same cancellation\
      \ plumbing —\n  a nice proof that the abstraction is right.\n- **Don't trust\
      \ the client to stop for you.** The whole week's thesis is that the\n  server\
      \ must own cancellation. Disconnect detection and budgets are the\n  server-side\
      \ backstops for clients that never send a clean stop.\n- You are streaming model\
      \ output to a browser but **not executing it**, so no code\n  sandboxing is\
      \ needed here — just standard output-escaping in the client so token\n  text\
      \ can't inject markup.\n\n## Hardware, cost & subscriptions\n\n- **Hardware:**\
      \ CPU-only. No local model runs; the token source is a hosted API\n  (or, for\
      \ all tests and the benchmark, the zero-cost mock provider).\n- **Cost:** a\
      \ few dollars at most. Nearly all development and the entire benchmark\n  run\
      \ against the mock provider for **\\$0**; only the step-5 swap and the final\n\
      \  smoke test spend on real short, small-model streaming calls.\n- **Subscriptions:**\
      \ one hosted LLM API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure AI Foundry,\n  Bedrock, or\
      \ a free-tier provider such as Groq/Together — any that offers a\n  **streaming**\
      \ completion endpoint whose async client can abort mid-stream).\n- **Docker:**\
      \ required — the backend runs as a real containerized service via\n  `docker\
      \ compose up`, consistent with the course's from-Week-4 service\n  convention.\n\
      \n## Commands and tests — Authentication and Document Permissions\n\nImplement\
      \ the CLI below. Fast permission tests may inject an already verified identity;\n\
      label them as authorization tests. They do not substitute for a real login smoke\
      \ test.\n\n```bash\nuv sync\ndocker compose up -d --wait\nuv run python -m permissions_lab.cli\
      \ init-db\nuv run python -m permissions_lab.cli seed\nuv run pytest tests -q\n\
      uv run uvicorn permissions_lab.api:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000\n```\n\n\
      In a second terminal, complete the four-user browser demonstration and record\
      \ results\nwith `uv run python -m permissions_lab.cli report --out artifacts/access-report.json`.\n\
      The report reads saved experiment results; it must not invent a login success\
      \ from\nunit-test identity injection. Run `docker compose down` after finishing.\n\
      \nAssertions must inspect the exact generator input, snippets, and citation\
      \ lookups, not\njust the final answer. Include a request with forged identity\
      \ fields and verify those\nfields cannot elevate access. Check all allowed cases\
      \ too: blocking everyone is not\ncorrect authorization. Authorization should\
      \ be checked on each request.\n[OWASP authorization guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html)\n\
      \n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture\
      \ and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and\
      \ one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."
    summary: Connect a small UI, identity, resource permissions, migrations, and streaming
      cancellation.

  - content: "Package the API, database, and worker for a local container path. Develop\
      \ one optional cloud-VM deployment behind HTTPS, with health checks, least necessary\
      \ host access, and persistent storage. Separate code, configuration, secrets,\
      \ and data. Record dependencies and deployment inputs without copying secret\
      \ values into reports. Include teardown and spending limits for the cloud path.\n\
      \nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces,\
      \ stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not\
      \ indicate that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone\
      \ fixture for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course\
      \ project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nDeploy a tiny document-processing service\
      \ to one Linux virtual machine. Submit a\nsynthetic document over HTTPS, observe\
      \ a worker save its word count, restart the\nservices, and verify the result\
      \ remains. Then recreate the deployment on a clean host\nfrom recorded configuration.\
      \ You will see which parts are code, configuration, secrets,\nand persistent\
      \ data.\n\nThe default provider is DigitalOcean. One host is enough for the\
      \ experiment. The result\ndemonstrates repeatable deployment, not uninterrupted\
      \ service when that host fails.\n\n## Prerequisites and starting fixture\n\n\
      You understand networking, a basic API, streaming, and identity concepts from\
      \ Foundations\n33, 18,\n19, and 35.\nNo earlier source code or portfolio repository\
      \ is required.\n\nAssemble this small lesson fixture during the first three\
      \ hours. An AI coding assistant\nmay generate routine API/container boilerplate\
      \ from this contract; review it and keep\nthe deployment decisions as the work\
      \ you investigate. This guide does not ship a hidden\nstarter repository or\
      \ ask you to build a complete AI application.\n\n| Component | Fixture contract\
      \ |\n|---|---|\n| API | `POST /jobs` accepts up to 4 KB of text; `GET /jobs/{id}`\
      \ returns state and result; `/live` and `/ready` report process/dependency health\
      \ |\n| Worker | One process polls queued jobs, counts words, and saves a result\
      \ in PostgreSQL; no real model call |\n| Database | `jobs(id, text, state, word_count)`\
      \ in database `week10_lab`; named persistent volume |\n| Identity | One synthetic\
      \ service account using a random bearer token read from a secret file; no public\
      \ registration |\n| Proxy | Caddy terminates HTTPS and forwards to the private\
      \ API port |\n\nUse separate database credentials for schema ownership, API\
      \ access, and worker access.\nThe API inserts/reads jobs; the worker claims/updates\
      \ them. This is a deployment fixture,\nnot the durable-job implementation taught\
      \ in Guide 2; record its crash limitations.\n\n## Concepts through the deployment\n\
      \nA **virtual machine (VM)** is a rented computer with its own operating system.\
      \ A\ncontainer packages a process and its dependencies while using the host's\
      \ kernel. An\nimage is its packaged starting filesystem; a running container's\
      \ writable layer should\nnot be the only place important database data lives.\
      \ A **volume** preserves selected\ndata independently of a container's replacement.\n\
      \nSecure Shell (**SSH**) provides authenticated remote access. A public key\
      \ can be placed\non the host; the private key stays on your laptop. Linux file\
      \ permissions determine which\naccount can read a secret or change deployment\
      \ files. Docker access grants substantial\nhost control, so treat the deployment\
      \ account as privileged and keep application\ncontainers separate from that\
      \ account's credentials.\n\n**Liveness** answers whether a process is running.\
      \ **Readiness** answers whether it can\naccept useful work now. Database startup\
      \ can lag behind its container starting. Compose\nhealth conditions help with\
      \ startup ordering, while application connections still need\nbounded retry\
      \ behavior after a later dependency failure.\n[Compose startup documentation](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/startup-order/)\n\
      \n## Network and deployment shape\n\n```text\nclient -- HTTPS:443 --> Caddy\
      \ -- private HTTP:8000 --> API\n                                           \
      \       |\n                              worker --------> PostgreSQL:5432\n\
      SSH:22 is reachable only from the learner's address\n```\n\nOnly Caddy publishes\
      \ application ports. The provider firewall allows SSH from your\ncurrent address\
      \ and ports 80/443 as needed for HTTPS. PostgreSQL and the API have no\npublicly\
      \ published host ports. Inspect actual listeners and test externally; a host\n\
      firewall rule alone does not establish how Docker-published traffic is handled.\n\
      [Docker Ubuntu installation notes](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/)\n\
      \nUse a subdomain you control and point its address record at the host. Caddy\
      \ can manage\nthe public certificate when the hostname and reachable challenge\
      \ ports are configured.\nIf you have no domain, use Caddy's internal certificate\
      \ authority and explicitly trust\nits public root for the lab; label that as\
      \ private trust, not public certificate issuance.\n[Caddy HTTPS documentation](https://caddyserver.com/docs/automatic-https)\n\
      \n```text\nweek10/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── app/                  # small fixture\
      \ API and worker\n├── Dockerfile\n├── compose.yaml\n├── deploy/\n│   ├── cloud-init.yaml\
      \   # host setup, no credentials\n│   ├── Caddyfile\n│   ├── schema.sql\n│ \
      \  ├── provision.sh     # create host from recorded settings\n│   ├── install.sh\
      \       # transfer image/config, initialize, start\n│   └── destroy.sh     \
      \  # exact recorded lab resource IDs only\n├── deployment_lab/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n\
      │   └── cli.py           # smoke, persistence, manifest\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n\
      ```\n\n```python\ndef check_readiness(base_url: str, deadline_s: float) -> dict:\
      \ ...\ndef submit_and_observe(base_url: str, token_file: str, text: str) ->\
      \ dict: ...\ndef record_manifest(resource_id: str, image_id: str, config_paths:\
      \ list[str]) -> dict: ...\n```\n\nPin the base OS image and record the resolved\
      \ application and dependency image digests.\nCreate an image locally and transfer\
      \ an archive, or use one private registry; either\npath must identify the exact\
      \ deployed image. Do not require two registries. Store\nsecrets outside the\
      \ checkout with restrictive permissions and mount them only into the\nservices\
      \ that need them. Do not put secrets in cloud-init, image layers, or the manifest."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 18 hours\n\n1. **Fixture locally, 3 hours.**\
      \ Assemble the small service, complete one job, reject\n   missing/bad tokens,\
      \ and restart containers without deleting the database volume.\n2. **Host configuration,\
      \ 3 hours.** Configure a small supported Ubuntu host, an SSH\n   key, Docker\
      \ from its official packages, and startup after reboot. Record the exact\n \
      \  setup in cloud-init. Use read-only inspection commands such as `ps`, `ss`,\
      \ `df`,\n   and `journalctl` to connect running processes, ports, disk, and\
      \ service logs.\n3. **Hosted deployment, 4 hours.** Provision one VM, transfer\
      \ the image/config, create\n   secrets on the host, initialize the database,\
      \ and make a verified HTTPS request.\n4. **Persistence and networking, 3 hours.**\
      \ Restart the stack and reboot once. Verify\n   the saved job; stop the API\
      \ and identify the proxy symptom; restore it. Confirm\n   database and API ports\
      \ are unreachable from outside the host.\n5. **Recreation, 3 hours.** Export\
      \ your evidence, remove the disposable first host,\n   provision a fresh one,\
      \ and repeat the scripted deployment and smoke test. Fresh\n   fixture data\
      \ is expected: host recreation does not restore destroyed database data.\n6.\
      \ **Report and teardown, 2 hours.** Record limitations and charges, delete only\
      \ the\n   tracked lab resources, and confirm no separately billed disk or snapshot\
      \ remains.\n\n## Provisioning and verification commands\n\nOn the laptop, use\
      \ `doctl auth init` without recording its secret in a script. Discover\ncurrent\
      \ regions, Ubuntu image slugs, and sizes with `doctl compute region list`,\n\
      `doctl compute image list --public`, and `doctl compute size list`. Choose about\
      \ 2–4 GB\nof memory after checking the fixture locally. Save the choice, expected\
      \ duration, and\ncost cap in your own config. `provision.sh` wraps `doctl compute\
      \ droplet create` with\nexplicit size, image, region, SSH key, and `--user-data-file`;\
      \ capture the returned ID.\n[doctl create reference](https://docs.digitalocean.com/reference/doctl/reference/compute/droplet/create/)\n\
      \nImplement these lesson commands before running them:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\n\
      uv run pytest tests -q\nbash deploy/provision.sh\nbash deploy/install.sh\nuv\
      \ run python -m deployment_lab.cli smoke --config artifacts/host.json\nuv run\
      \ python -m deployment_lab.cli persistence --config artifacts/host.json\nbash\
      \ deploy/destroy.sh\n```\n\n`host.json` contains public metadata and file paths,\
      \ not secret values. Destruction must\ncheck the exact ID and the lab name/tag;\
      \ never delete by a broad account-wide filter.\nTests cover fixture behavior,\
      \ readiness failure, token rejection, config validation,\nand refusal to destroy\
      \ an unrecognized resource. Manual checks cover external port\nreachability\
      \ and HTTPS trust. Save their commands and observations.\n\n## Evidence, cost,\
      \ and limits\n\nRecord OS, image/config revisions, resource IDs, network diagram,\
      \ recreation steps,\nrequest results, and persistence observations. State that\
      \ the worker and database are\non one host and what would be lost with its disk.\n\
      \nCap the exercise at $10 of hosted spend; it is a budget, not a price quotation.\
      \ Check\n[current provider pricing](https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/details/pricing/)\n\
      before creation, including any separately billed resources. Delete the VM when\
      \ finished;\nshutting down software is not a reliable way to end infrastructure\
      \ charges. A domain\npurchase is optional and outside this cap. Local-only execution\
      \ costs $0 but cannot\ndemonstrate cloud routing. Managed databases, rolling\
      \ releases, and multiple hosts are\nextensions; release behavior is the subject\
      \ of Guide 1.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment,\
      \ fixture and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command\
      \ and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."
    summary: Recreate a service from recorded configuration while separating secrets
      and persistent data.
