    section: state-and-releases
  - content: "Version code, dependencies, configuration, database schema, prompts,\
      \ model labels, adapters, and thresholds as a release manifest. Automate the\
      \ relevant checks and compare a candidate with the current service. Use a local\
      \ proxy to switch traffic after validation. Explain compatibility constraints\
      \ and why returning application code cannot blindly reverse a destructive data\
      \ migration.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment\
      \ to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab\
      \ artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results already\
      \ exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nRelease three\
      \ versions of a supplied small API: one healthy candidate, one that changes\
      \ its\nresponse shape, and one that returns a behaviorally wrong answer. Start\
      \ each candidate next\nto the current version, run the same supplied behavior\
      \ checks, and either direct the local\nproxy to it or return the proxy to the\
      \ previous working version.\n\nThe artifact is a release transcript showing\
      \ the exact code, configuration, prompt, model\nlabel, and schema associated\
      \ with every decision. The exercise runs locally and does not\nrequire an application\
      \ built in an earlier lesson.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n- Deploying a\
      \ containerized API and checking readiness from\n  Guide 10, or equivalent local\
      \ Docker Compose experience.\n- Git revisions, HTTP requests, tests, and basic\
      \ continuous-integration workflow syntax.\n\nThe fixture supplies one API, a\
      \ local reverse proxy, three candidate configurations, and a\nfrozen behavior\
      \ test. You implement the release manifest, checks, switching state machine,\n\
      and report. A hosted registry, Kubernetes, multi-region traffic, artifact signing,\
      \ and\norganizational approval system are optional.\n\n## Begin with the previous\
      \ version available\n\nRun version `v1` behind the proxy and save its image\
      \ digest and successful behavior-test\nresult. Then start candidate `v2` on\
      \ a different local port without changing proxy traffic.\nWait for readiness,\
      \ send the fixed requests directly to `v2`, and switch the proxy only\nafter\
      \ every required check has a result.\n\nRunning old and new versions side by\
      \ side is a **blue/green release**. The brief check of a\ncandidate before full\
      \ promotion is a **canary check**. Returning traffic to the recorded\nworking\
      \ version is a **rollback**. In this lesson rollback changes application code\
      \ and\nconfiguration; it does not reverse an unsafe database migration.\n\n\
      Measure the time from the rollback decision until the fixed behavior test passes\
      \ through\nthe proxy again. Keep the old version running until that verification\
      \ completes.\n\n## Record an immutable release manifest\n\nEach candidate manifest\
      \ contains:\n\n- Git revision and container-image digest;\n- dependency-lock\
      \ hash;\n- configuration and prompt hashes;\n- API schema version;\n- model\
      \ and tokenizer labels;\n- database migration revision, even though the fixture\
      \ does not migrate data;\n- behavior-test revision and build timestamp.\n\n\
      Reject a floating image tag such as `latest`, a missing field, and an unknown\
      \ manifest\nschema. Canonically serialize the manifest before hashing it. A\
      \ human-readable name may\npoint to a digest, but it cannot replace the digest\
      \ in the release record.\n\n## Use four visible check layers\n\n1. **Fast checks:**\
      \ unit tests, types, dependency lock, and fixture secret scan.\n2. **Compatibility\
      \ checks:** API response schema and declared migration compatibility.\n3. **Behavior\
      \ checks:** the supplied normal, abstention, and denied-access requests.\n4.\
      \ **Candidate check:** readiness, bounded latency, error count, and one complete\
      \ request\n   through the candidate port.\n\nEach layer emits a machine-readable\
      \ result with status, duration, and reason. Missing or\ntimed-out evidence is\
      \ a failed check, not an implied pass. The promotion decision names\nevery failed\
      \ layer.\n\nThe frozen behavior test is intentionally small. It makes the lesson\
      \ runnable early and\nchecks the fixture's important contract; it does not prove\
      \ general model quality.\n\n## Project shape and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\n\
      week01/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── fixture/\n│   ├── api.py\n│   ├── versions/\n\
      │   └── behavior_cases.jsonl\n├── release_lab/\n│   ├── schema.py\n│   ├── manifest.py\n\
      │   ├── checks.py\n│   ├── switch.py\n│   ├── report.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├──\
      \ deploy/\n│   ├── compose.yml\n│   └── proxy/\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n\
      ```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import Literal,\
      \ Protocol\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass CheckResult:\n    name: str\n \
      \   passed: bool\n    duration_ms: float\n    reason: str\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class ReleaseDecision:\n    action: Literal[\"promote\", \"hold\", \"rollback\"\
      ]\n    reasons: tuple[str, ...]\n\nclass DeploymentPort(Protocol):\n    def\
      \ start_candidate(self, manifest_digest: str) -> str: ...\n    def switch_proxy(self,\
      \ deployment_id: str) -> None: ...\n    def current_deployment(self) -> str:\
      \ ...\n\ndef decide_release(results: list[CheckResult], *, candidate_received_traffic:\
      \ bool) -> ReleaseDecision: ...\n```\n\nKeep the decision function independent\
      \ of Docker and the proxy. State changes occur only\nthrough the deployment\
      \ adapter, which makes transition tests fast and deterministic.\n\n## Exercise\
      \ three candidates\n\nThe healthy candidate preserves the response schema and\
      \ passes the behavior cases. The\nincompatible candidate renames a required\
      \ response field. The behavioral regression keeps\nthe schema but answers one\
      \ frozen case incorrectly.\n\nFor each candidate, record:\n\n- manifest digest\
      \ and candidate deployment ID;\n- result of every check layer;\n- whether proxy\
      \ traffic changed;\n- final active deployment;\n- time to verified recovery\
      \ when rollback was needed.\n\nThe healthy candidate should promote. The schema\
      \ change should stop before traffic moves.\nThe behavioral regression may stop\
      \ before promotion or trigger rollback during the bounded\ncandidate check,\
      \ depending on the state-machine path you implement. Do not tune checks after\n\
      seeing the intended failure."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Failure-focused tests\n\nTest canonical manifest hashing,\
      \ missing and floating identifiers, unknown schema versions,\ncheck timeout,\
      \ missing result, readiness failure, promotion, hold before traffic, rollback\n\
      after traffic, repeated rollback, and loss of the previous-version reference.\
      \ A repeated\nrollback must leave the same version active.\n\nOne local integration\
      \ test starts `v1` and the healthy candidate, switches the proxy, and\nthen\
      \ returns to `v1`. Assert the behavior test passes before and after. Keep unit\
      \ tests on\nfake deployment adapters.\n\n## Build sequence — 15 hours\n\n1.\
      \ **Run the fixture, 2 hours.** Start `v1`, exercise the proxy, and inspect\
      \ all three\n   candidates and the frozen behavior cases.\n2. **Manifest and\
      \ checks, 4 hours.** Implement canonical records and the four result layers.\n\
      3. **Release state machine, 3 hours.** Add candidate start, promotion, hold,\
      \ rollback, and\n   idempotent recovery.\n4. **Candidate exercise, 3 hours.**\
      \ Run all three versions and save complete transcripts.\n5. **CI wrapper and\
      \ report, 3 hours.** Make one workflow call the same local CLI and explain\n\
      \   the observed decisions and limitations.\n\n## Commands and artifact\n\n\
      ```bash\nuv sync\nuv run pytest tests -q\ndocker compose -f deploy/compose.yml\
      \ up -d current proxy\nuv run python -m release_lab.cli baseline --out artifacts/baseline.json\n\
      uv run python -m release_lab.cli exercise --candidates healthy incompatible\
      \ regressed --out artifacts/report.md\nuv run python -m release_lab.cli rollback\
      \ --to artifacts/baseline.json\n```\n\nThe report contains immutable manifests,\
      \ check results, transition transcripts, final proxy\ntarget, rollback timing,\
      \ and one limitation. A strict check that blocks a healthy candidate\nor a slow\
      \ rollback is useful evidence when reported rather than hidden.\n\n## Safety,\
      \ hardware, and cost\n\nUse only the local disposable Compose project. Candidate\
      \ containers run without root,\nprivileged mode, or a mounted Docker socket.\
      \ Keep secrets in local environment or CI secret\nstorage and out of manifests\
      \ and logs.\n\nThe exercise runs on a laptop and costs $0. A hosted deployment\
      \ and manual approval flow\nare optional after the local state machine and evidence\
      \ are complete.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned\
      \ environment, fixture and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction\
      \ command and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks\
      \ from actual model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost\
      \ figures and tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning\
      \ assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded\
      \ budget when implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from\
      \ the baseline report."

      return decisions.

  - content: "Store accepted jobs durably and define queued, running, completed, retryable,\
      \ and final-failure states. Explain leases or claims, retry policy, idempotent\
      \ effects, and the boundary between job completion and an external side effect.\
      \ Use database transactions where they can provide an atomic guarantee, and\
      \ document where external calls need an explicit duplicate-handling strategy.\n\
      \nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces,\
      \ stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not\
      \ indicate that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone\
      \ fixture for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course\
      \ project.\n\n## Overview\n\nThis chapter you build a small background-job service\
      \ backed by Postgres. Submit 50 jobs,\nkill workers at three carefully chosen\
      \ moments, restart them, and see which jobs finish,\nrun twice, or disappear.\
      \ Then compare that behavior with a list held only in Python\nmemory. The database\
      \ version should keep every accepted job and prevent a repeated\nattempt from\
      \ repeating the job's lasting effect.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- Guide 1's versioned\
      \ service and release discipline.\n- Python concurrency, transactions, and basic\
      \ message-queue vocabulary.\n- Docker Compose, SQL, and Postgres.\n\n## The\
      \ experiment in plain language\n\nA client submits work, such as indexing one\
      \ document. A worker claims the job, performs\nthe work, and marks it complete.\
      \ Your test script kills the worker:\n\n1. before it changes anything;\n2. after\
      \ it changes the database but before it says “finished”; and\n3. after it stops\
      \ renewing its claim on the job.\n\nAfter each kill, start another worker and\
      \ inspect the database. This makes the failure\nbehavior visible instead of\
      \ leaving it as queueing theory.\n\n## The rules the database needs to enforce\n\
      \nUse Postgres as both authoritative job store and lease queue. A transactional\
      \ claim\nwith `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` exposes the important semantics without\
      \ adding another\nbroker. Redis, NATS, RabbitMQ, workflow DAGs, priorities,\
      \ and a dashboard are optional.\n\n- **At-least-once delivery:** a job may be\
      \ attempted again after a crash.\n- **Idempotent effect:** repeating the same\
      \ job does not repeat its lasting change. A\n  unique key can make “insert this\
      \ indexed document” happen only once.\n- **Lease:** a time-limited claim on\
      \ a job. The worker periodically renews it with a\n  small “still alive” update\
      \ called a heartbeat. A late completion from an expired\n  worker cannot overwrite\
      \ a newer attempt.\n- **Retry:** try temporary failures again, with a limit\
      \ and a delay. Invalid input goes\n  directly to a final failed state, sometimes\
      \ called a dead-letter state.\n- **Backpressure:** reject or delay new work\
      \ when the queue is already too large.\n- **Cancellation:** store it durably\
      \ and check it at named safe points.\n\n## What to build\n\n```text\njobs/\n\
      ├── schema.sql             # jobs, attempts, outbox, and constraints\n├── models.py\
      \              # states and command/result types\n├── store.py             \
      \  # submit, lease, heartbeat, complete, cancel\n├── worker.py             \
      \ # bounded loop and cancellation checkpoints\n├── retry.py               #\
      \ classification, jitter, and dead-letter policy\n├── api.py               \
      \  # submit, inspect, and cancel endpoints\n├── fault_injector.py      # named\
      \ crash points for the experiment\n├── cli.py                 # init, serve,\
      \ worker, submit, exercise\n└── tests/\n```\n\n```python\n@dataclass\nclass\
      \ Job:\n    id: str\n    idempotency_key: str\n    state: Literal[\"queued\"\
      , \"leased\", \"succeeded\", \"failed\", \"cancelled\", \"dead\"]\n    attempt:\
      \ int\n    lease_until: datetime | None\n\nclass JobStore(Protocol):\n    def\
      \ submit(self, payload: bytes, idempotency_key: str) -> Job: ...\n    def lease(self,\
      \ worker_id: str, ttl_s: float) -> Job | None: ...\n    def heartbeat(self,\
      \ job_id: str, worker_id: str, ttl_s: float) -> bool: ...\n    def complete(self,\
      \ job_id: str, worker_id: str, result: bytes) -> bool: ...\n    def request_cancel(self,\
      \ job_id: str) -> bool: ...\n```\n\nModel attempts separately from jobs so duplicate\
      \ attempts remain observable without\nbeing confused with duplicate committed\
      \ effects. Enforce state transitions in the\nstore, not only in worker code.\
      \ Use a transactional outbox when one request changes\ndomain state and enqueues\
      \ work.\n\n## Security and operational boundaries\n\n- Validate payload size\
      \ and type; never deserialize arbitrary Python objects.\n- Use a least-privilege\
      \ database role and keep credentials outside the repository.\n- Do not place\
      \ secrets or raw sensitive prompts in payloads or logs.\n- Bound accepted jobs,\
      \ attempts, result size, and execution time."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build path — about 15–18 hours\n\n1. **Schema and state\
      \ machine, 3 hours.** Draw legal transitions; encode idempotency,\n   lease\
      \ ownership, attempts, and terminal-state constraints.\n2. **Submit and lease,\
      \ 3 hours.** Duplicate submission returns the original job;\n   concurrent workers\
      \ claim jobs transactionally.\n3. **Heartbeat, completion, cancellation, 3 hours.**\
      \ Reject stale owners and check\n   cancellation at explicit safe points.\n\
      4. **Retries and dead letters, 2 hours.** Implement one transient and one terminal\n\
      \   failure. Keep the policy small and deterministic under test.\n5. **Outbox\
      \ boundary, 2 hours.** Demonstrate one domain update plus job publication\n\
      \   without a dual-write gap.\n6. **Fault experiment and report, 2–3 hours.**\
      \ Run three kill points against the\n   durable system and an in-memory baseline.\n\
      \nStop there. Exactly-once execution and arbitrary workflow graphs are not this\
      \ chapter.\n\n## How to run and test\n\n```bash\ndocker compose up -d postgres\n\
      uv sync\nuv run python -m jobs.cli init-db\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python\
      \ -m jobs.cli exercise --jobs 50 \\\n  --crash-points before-effect after-effect-before-ack\
      \ heartbeat-loss \\\n  --report artifacts/durability-report.md\n```\n\nTests\
      \ should cover transition legality, duplicate submission, lease expiry, stale\n\
      completion, retry exhaustion, direct dead-lettering, cancellation, and outbox\n\
      publication. One integration test runs two workers and proves that only the\
      \ current\nlease owner can commit an effect.\n\n## Failure experiment\n\nKill\
      \ workers before a side effect, after the side effect but before acknowledgement,\n\
      and after heartbeat loss. Compare with an in-memory queue on accepted, completed,\
      \ lost,\nduplicate attempts, duplicate committed effects, cancelled, dead-lettered,\
      \ completion\ntime, and p95 queue age.\n\nThe measured target is zero lost accepted\
      \ jobs and zero duplicate committed effects—not\nzero duplicate attempts. Record\
      \ Postgres version, schema revision, worker count, lease\nTTL, retry policy,\
      \ payload size, fault seed, and hardware. A failed invariant is useful\nevidence\
      \ when the trace identifies the boundary that failed.\n\n## Hardware, cost &\
      \ subscriptions\n\n- Laptop and Docker Compose; CPU only.\n- Cost target: $0.\
      \ Postgres is the only required service.\n- Time budget: 15–18 hours for the\
      \ Postgres-only core.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the\
      \ pinned environment, fixture and configuration identities, case-level outcomes,\
      \ reproduction command and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism\
      \ checks from actual model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements.\
      \ Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are\
      \ planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set\
      \ a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate\
      \ from the baseline report."
    summary: Preserve accepted work and prevent repeated attempts from duplicating
      lasting effects.

  - content: "Change a populated document schema while an older client still reads\
      \ it. Design a compatible migration, resumable backfill, and explicit retirement\
      \ of old fields. Take a backup and restore into a clean database. Define recovery\
      \ duration and the data-loss window implied by backup timing; inspect credentials,\
      \ indexes, permissions, and jobs as well as table rows.\n\nThe lesson below\
      \ specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package\
      \ layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that\
      \ executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture\
      \ for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\
      \n## What you will build\n\nChange a populated document database while an older\
      \ client still reads it. Then take\na backup, add more data, damage the disposable\
      \ source, and restore into a clean database.\nYou will measure which data returns\
      \ and how long it takes to become usable.\n\nThe first exercise renames a field\
      \ without immediately removing the old field. The\nsecond distinguishes a backup\
      \ file that exists from a backup you have successfully\nrestored. Neither exercise\
      \ needs a live application or a cloud account.\n\n## Prerequisites and setup\n\
      \nYou understand schema design and migrations from Foundations\n34 and 18,\n\
      deployment from Guide 10, release versions from\nGuide 1, and transactions from\
      \ Guide 11.\nOnly these concepts carry over; this lab creates its own small\
      \ fixture.\n\nUse Python 3.13, Psycopg, Alembic with SQLAlchemy for migration\
      \ bookkeeping, pytest,\nand PostgreSQL 17 with matching-major client tools.\
      \ Lock dependencies and record image\ndigests. Create the files described below;\
      \ commands are target interfaces after that work.\n\n## A compatible data change\n\
      \nStart with `documents(id, title, body, created_at)` containing 1,000 deterministic\
      \ rows.\nThe old client reads and writes `title`; the new client uses `display_title`.\
      \ A direct\nrename immediately breaks the old query, even when returning to\
      \ the old application\nimage would otherwise be possible.\n\nA **migration**\
      \ is a versioned database change. An **additive change** introduces new\nstructure\
      \ while preserving what existing callers need. A **backfill** populates the\
      \ new\nstructure for old records. Use three stages:\n\n1. Add nullable `display_title`\
      \ while preserving `title`.\n2. Populate it in small batches and keep writes\
      \ through either client synchronized.\n3. After the compatibility experiment,\
      \ remove the old interface in a separately named\n   migration. Explain why\
      \ the old client cannot be restored after that step unchanged.\n\nFor this lab,\
      \ implement a small database trigger as compatibility scaffolding: an\nold-client\
      \ title update copies into `display_title`; a new-client update copies back\n\
      into `title`; conflicting simultaneous values in one statement are rejected.\
      \ On inserts,\nfill either missing counterpart before constraints run. Test\
      \ this rule explicitly so\nthe migration cannot silently overwrite a recent\
      \ edit with a stale backfill value.\n\nUse `WHERE display_title IS NULL` for\
      \ the backfill's eligible set, commit batches, and\nmake rerunning a completed\
      \ batch harmless. Keep durable checkpoints only if they add\ninformation beyond\
      \ what the rows already say. An exception before commit rolls back\nthat batch;\
      \ prior committed batches remain.\n\n## Backup and restoration experiment\n\n\
      Use a logical backup produced by `pg_dump` in custom format. It captures a consistent\n\
      database snapshot and can be restored with `pg_restore`. Cluster-wide roles\
      \ are separate\nfrom a single-database dump; provision the lab roles from versioned\
      \ SQL on the new\ninstance. [PostgreSQL pg_dump](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/app-pgdump.html)\n\
      \nFor a clear expected result, pause fixture writes while creating the core\
      \ backup and\nits verification manifest. Save the manifest of IDs, content hashes,\
      \ schema revision,\nand relevant constraints beside the backup, outside the\
      \ source database volume. Then\nresume writes and add exactly 25 new records\
      \ before damaging the source.\n\nRestore into a second fresh PostgreSQL instance\
      \ with its own volume. Database restoration\ncan succeed while the application\
      \ still cannot connect or lacks needed privileges, so\nalso run the client checks\
      \ using the ordinary application role. Configure restored roles\nand grants\
      \ explicitly if using `--no-owner` or omitting access privileges.\n[PostgreSQL\
      \ pg_restore](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/app-pgrestore.html)\n\nThe\
      \ missing 25 later records represent this backup's observed data-loss window.\
      \ Do not\nclaim that all accepted writes can be recovered from a snapshot that\
      \ predates them.\nContinuous log archiving and point-in-time restoration are\
      \ optional follow-on work.\n\n## Project and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\n\
      week12/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── compose.yaml          # source and restore\
      \ database instances\n├── roles.sql\n├── migrations/           # additive, backfill,\
      \ removal stages\n├── recovery_lab/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── clients.py\
      \        # old and new request shapes\n│   ├── fixtures.py\n│   ├── verify.py\n\
      │   └── cli.py\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/            # dump, manifest, timeline,\
      \ report\n```\n\n```python\ndef backfill_batch(conn, batch_size: int) -> int:\
      \ ...\ndef verify_clients(conn) -> dict: ...\ndef snapshot_manifest(conn) ->\
      \ dict: ...\ndef compare_restore(expected: dict, actual: dict) -> dict: ...\n\
      def require_disposable_target(database_name: str, lab_marker: str) -> None:\
      \ ...\n```"
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 18 hours\n\n1. **Fixture and two clients,\
      \ 3 hours.** Seed the initial schema. Give the old/new\n   client helpers a\
      \ few read/write operations, and make the direct-rename failure visible.\n2.\
      \ **Compatible migration, 4 hours.** Add the new column and compatibility trigger;\n\
      \   backfill while alternating old/new writes. Verify equal logical values afterward.\n\
      3. **Interrupted backfill, 3 hours.** Stop after a committed batch and again\
      \ inside an\n   uncommitted batch. Resume and check all expected rows without\
      \ losing concurrent edits.\n4. **Backup, 2 hours.** Pause fixture writers, produce\
      \ the dump and manifest, then add\n   the 25 late records and record their IDs\
      \ separately.\n5. **Restoration, 4 hours.** Damage only the marked source fixture,\
      \ provision the fresh\n   destination, restore, and run schema/data/client/grant\
      \ checks. Time from the start\n   of recovery through the first successful client\
      \ read, including setup time.\n6. **Report, 2 hours.** Explain rollback limits\
      \ before/after the removal migration,\n   recovered and missing data, measured\
      \ duration, and one unresolved edge.\n\n## Commands and verification\n\nImplement\
      \ the CLI from this directory; it may invoke native database tools using a\n\
      subprocess argument list. Credentials come from a restricted password file or\
      \ local\nsecret mount, not arguments printed to the report.\n\n```bash\nuv sync\n\
      docker compose up -d --wait source restore\nuv run python -m recovery_lab.cli\
      \ init --target week12_source\nuv run python -m recovery_lab.cli migration-experiment\
      \ --out artifacts/migration.json\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m recovery_lab.cli\
      \ backup --out artifacts/baseline.dump\nuv run python -m recovery_lab.cli add-late-records\
      \ --count 25\nuv run python -m recovery_lab.cli damage --target week12_source\
      \ --lab-marker week12-disposable\nuv run python -m recovery_lab.cli restore\
      \ --from artifacts/baseline.dump --target week12_restore\nuv run python -m recovery_lab.cli\
      \ verify --out artifacts/recovery-report.json\ndocker compose down\n```\n\n\
      `backup` also writes the matching manifest while writers remain paused. `damage`\
      \ deletes\nfixture document rows only after checking both the exact target name\
      \ and a marker table;\nit must refuse an arbitrary connection URL or an unmarked\
      \ database. `restore` refuses a\nnonempty destination and runs the appropriate\
      \ migrations only after checking the dump's\nschema revision. Never apply a\
      \ destructive cleanup option against an unknown destination.\n\nTests cover\
      \ old/new writes, conflict rejection, backfill resumption, foreign keys,\nconstraints,\
      \ deterministic content hashes, application grants, and target refusal.\nRestoration\
      \ checks compare individual IDs/content, not only row counts. Save failure\n\
      messages as well as successes; an unusable backup is important evidence.\n\n\
      ## Results, hardware, and extensions\n\nRecord dump/tool versions, schema revisions,\
      \ manifest hashes, recovery timings, late-write\nIDs, and the exact verification\
      \ boundary. A laptop with a few GB of disk and two small\ndatabase containers\
      \ suffices; target cost $0. Copy evidence outside the Compose volumes\nbefore\
      \ removing them. Using the same disk for source and backup demonstrates logical\n\
      restoration only, not survival of disk loss.\n\nOff-host encrypted backups,\
      \ point-in-time recovery, and measuring lock time during a\nlarger schema change\
      \ are optional. Returning to old code and recovering old data remain\ndifferent\
      \ operations even when both are called rollback in casual conversation.\n\n\
      ### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture\
      \ and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and\
      \ one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."
    summary: Measure migration compatibility, interrupted backfills, restored data,
      and the possible loss window.

  - content: "Start with an exact response cache and define keys from document revisions,\
      \ model and prompt versions, and authorization scope. Explain expiration, invalidation,\
      \ simultaneous fills, and failure behavior. Treat semantic similarity as a separate\
      \ quality decision and compare it only after exact-cache correctness is understood.\
      \ Prevent a previously authorized result from being reused after access changes.\n\
      \nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces,\
      \ stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not\
      \ indicate that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone\
      \ fixture for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course\
      \ project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nCache a synthetic document answer, edit\
      \ the source, and revoke a user's permission.\nObserve what an answer-only cache\
      \ gets wrong, then design a cache that checks access\nand document revisions\
      \ before returning a value. Finally, request the same uncached\nanswer from\
      \ several clients at once and measure duplicate computation.\n\nThe first action\
      \ is a single-document example: Alice can read revision 1, an editor\ncommits\
      \ revision 2, and then Alice's membership is removed. Each change asks a different\n\
      question: is the answer current, and is Alice still allowed to receive it?\n\
      \n## Prerequisites and scope\n\nUse permissions from Foundations 35, transactions\n\
      from Guide 11, and retry concepts from Guide 2.\nCreate a fresh small fixture;\
      \ no previous source code or portfolio app is used.\n\nUse Python 3.13, Psycopg,\
      \ redis-py, pytest, PostgreSQL 17, and Redis in Compose. Pin and\nrecord resolved\
      \ dependencies. Commands and interfaces below describe the lab to implement.\n\
      The response function is deterministic and sleeps 100 ms before formatting the\
      \ document\ntitle/body; there is no model provider and no semantic similarity\
      \ search.\n\n## Define what can be cached\n\nPostgreSQL is the **source of truth**,\
      \ the store whose records decide current content\nand permissions. Redis holds\
      \ disposable copies. A **cache hit** finds a reusable copy;\na miss computes\
      \ or fetches a value. **Invalidation** makes a previous copy unusable.\nTime-to-live\
      \ (**TTL**) is an expiry duration, not an authorization decision.\n\nUse these\
      \ database records:\n\n- `documents(id, org_id, revision, title, body)`;\n-\
      \ `memberships(user_id, org_id, can_read)`;\n- a deterministic fixture with\
      \ two organizations and three users.\n\nThe initial unsafe cache keys only on\
      \ `(document_id, question)` and checks permission\nonly on a miss. Demonstrate\
      \ both stale text after an edit and a cached answer returned\nafter revocation.\
      \ Keep this baseline on synthetic local data and visibly label its mode.\n\n\
      The repaired request follows a precise rule: authorize and read document revision\
      \ in\none current database statement, then look up a key containing organization,\
      \ document ID,\nrevision, question, and formatter version. In this lab every\
      \ permitted user sees the\nsame full document; personalized answers would additionally\
      \ need their personalization\nscope in the key. Unauthorized requests never\
      \ return cached text.\n\nOn a miss, fetch the body at that same revision. If\
      \ it changed between the revision read\nand the fetch, retry the bounded lookup\
      \ with the new revision. After computation, check\naccess and current revision\
      \ again before returning/publishing the value; discard obsolete\nresults. Define\
      \ the final database authorization snapshot as the decision point. A\nrevocation\
      \ committed afterward cannot recall content already in flight to the client.\n\
      \nOld revision keys can expire later without being selected for current requests.\
      \ Deleting\nold keys saves space but is not the correctness mechanism. An edit\
      \ that commits while\nan old fill is computing must not publish stale bytes\
      \ under the new revision's key.\n\n## Concurrent fills and cache failure\n\n\
      A **cache stampede** is many clients recomputing the same missing value at once.\
      \ For\none Redis instance, use a short lease stored with `SET NX PX`: create\
      \ a key only if\nabsent and give it an expiry. Include a random owner token.\
      \ Release it with an atomic\ncheck-and-delete operation that compares that token;\
      \ a plain delete could release a\nnew owner's lease after yours expired. [Redis\
      \ SET](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/set/)\n\nThe lease reduces repeated\
      \ work, not the need for correct revision keys and access\nchecks. It can expire\
      \ while work is running. Count duplicate fills and keep publication\nsafe even\
      \ then. This is one-instance coordination, not a claim of a general distributed\n\
      lock. [Redis locking guidance](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/clients/patterns/distributed-locks/)\n\
      \nWhen Redis is unavailable, use a bounded direct computation path or return\
      \ a documented\ntemporary failure. When the authorization database is unavailable,\
      \ do not fall back to\nunchecked cached content. Those two failures have different\
      \ consequences.\n\n## Project and interfaces\n\n```text\nweek13/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── compose.yaml\n├── schema.sql\n├── cache_lab/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├──\
      \ store.py\n│   ├── cache.py\n│   ├── formatter.py\n│   ├── harness.py\n│  \
      \ └── cli.py\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\ndef get_visible_response(user_id:\
      \ int, document_id: str, question: str) -> dict: ...\ndef cache_key(org_id:\
      \ int, document_id: str, revision: int,\n              question: str, formatter_version:\
      \ str) -> str: ...\ndef publish_if_current(user_id: int, document_id: str, revision:\
      \ int,\n                       response: str) -> bool: ...\ndef release_owned_lease(key:\
      \ str, owner_token: str) -> bool: ...\n```\n\nThese functions receive test identities\
      \ directly because login is not the experiment.\nThey are not an invitation\
      \ for a public API to trust a caller-supplied user ID. Test\nfixtures assign\
      \ identities through the harness; a deployed service needs authentication.\n\
      \n## Fix the eligibility boundary first — Semantic Caching\n\nEvery request\
      \ and cache entry has an eligibility key:\n\n```text\n(synthetic_tenant_id,\
      \ permission_scope, knowledge_revision, response_schema_version)\n```\n\nSearch\
      \ only entries with the identical key, then apply semantic similarity. A high\
      \ score\nmust never cross a tenant, permission scope, knowledge revision, or\
      \ response schema. The\nquery text cannot override any part of this key.\n\n\
      This key prevents the exercise from teaching unsafe global reuse, but it does\
      \ not implement\npermission revocation or invalidation. Systems Guide 13 changes\
      \ data and permissions while\ncached responses exist, tests concurrent fills,\
      \ and handles cache failure. Here those fields\nremain fixed during a replay\
      \ so the measured error is specifically semantic mismatch.\n\n## Account for\
      \ value and harm — Semantic Caching\n\nReport these counts for each configuration:\n\
      \n- exact or semantic hits and misses;\n- true and false hits;\n- backend calls;\n\
      - malformed backend responses;\n- mean cost units and mean/95th-percentile latency.\n\
      \nDefine hit precision as\n\n$$\n\\operatorname{hit\\ precision}=\n\\frac{\\\
      text{true hits}}{\\text{true hits}+\\text{false hits}}.\n$$\n\nDefine reusable-query\
      \ recall as the fraction of events that had a valid earlier answer in\ntheir\
      \ eligibility group and were served that answer from cache. Preserve the counts\
      \ and\nreport an undefined value when a denominator is zero.\n\nEvery lookup\
      \ pays its embedding and search latency. A miss also pays backend latency and\n\
      cost; a hit does not. Use the fixture's `cost_units` rather than current provider\
      \ prices.\nCompare exact cache, semantic cache, and no cache using the same\
      \ ordered events."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 17 hours\n\n1. **Fixture and uncached path,\
      \ 3 hours.** Check permissions and deterministic output\n   before adding Redis.\
      \ Record the computation counter separately from client requests.\n2. **Unsafe\
      \ baseline, 2 hours.** Cache a response, edit its document, and revoke access.\n\
      \   Save the observed mistakes in explicit regression cases.\n3. **Repaired\
      \ read/fill, 4 hours.** Add revision keys and per-request authorization.\n \
      \  Coordinate an edit during a fill with events, then check publication and\
      \ response.\n4. **Concurrent misses, 3 hours.** Start 20 clients on the same\
      \ empty key; compare\n   computation counts with and without the lease. Force\
      \ a fill past lease expiry.\n5. **Dependency failures, 3 hours.** Stop Redis,\
      \ then stop PostgreSQL in a separate\n   experiment. Check fallback limits,\
      \ authorization behavior, and recovery on restart.\n6. **Report, 2 hours.**\
      \ Summarize freshness, access behavior, hit rate, duplicate fills,\n   and latency.\
      \ State the exact decision point and any remaining race limitation.\n\n## Commands\
      \ and tests\n\nRun from this lesson directory after implementing the CLI:\n\n\
      ```bash\nuv sync\ndocker compose up -d --wait postgres redis\nuv run python\
      \ -m cache_lab.cli init --fixture two-orgs\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python\
      \ -m cache_lab.cli mutations --out artifacts/mutations.jsonl\nuv run python\
      \ -m cache_lab.cli burst --clients 20 --out artifacts/fills.jsonl\nuv run python\
      \ -m cache_lab.cli failures --out artifacts/dependencies.jsonl\ndocker compose\
      \ down\n```\n\nTests include allowed reads, cross-organization denial, edit\
      \ and deletion, revocation\nwith a populated cache, stale fill completion, expired\
      \ lease ownership, Redis outage,\ndatabase outage, and formatter-version changes.\
      \ Use unique per-run prefixes rather than\n`FLUSHALL`. Controlled schedules\
      \ should expose races without relying on timing luck.\n\n## Evidence, cost,\
      \ and extensions\n\nRecord each request's identity, decision, document revision,\
      \ hit/miss, output hash,\nelapsed time, and fill ownership in a synthetic trace.\
      \ The core result includes both\nvalid responses and clean denials; hit rate\
      \ alone is not a success measure. An unresolved\npermission leak is a failed\
      \ protection with useful diagnostic evidence, not a safe cache.\n\nCPU and local\
      \ containers suffice; target cost $0. Keep database and Redis access private\n\
      to the lab. Semantic caching, multi-document answers, external permission synchronization,\n\
      and distributed lease algorithms are optional; each introduces a new consistency\
      \ question.\n\n## Failure-focused tests — Semantic Caching\n\nTest an empty\
      \ cache, exact repeat, safe paraphrase, close near miss, similarity exactly\
      \ at\nthe threshold, equal-score tie, non-unit vector, unknown response, malformed\
      \ response, and\nevery differing eligibility-key field. Confirm that the same\
      \ vector cannot hit across two\ntenants or revisions.\n\nTest replay isolation\
      \ by running configurations in different orders and comparing outputs.\nTest\
      \ metric denominators, cost arithmetic, and event alignment by ID. Verify that\
      \ lookup\nnever reads the gold answer-equivalence group.\n\n### Report the actual\
      \ execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration\
      \ identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation.\
      \ Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server\
      \ or cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."

      concurrent fills, and outages.

  - content: "Instrument validation, permission checks, retrieval, job processing,\
      \ and model invocation. Define request and job identifiers, durations, errors,\
      \ token accounting, and cost estimates without retaining unnecessary user text.\
      \ First inspect disclosed healthy and failing workloads; then diagnose one undisclosed\
      \ fault using competing explanations and evidence. Preserve enough version identity\
      \ to connect failures to a release.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation\
      \ and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are\
      \ proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured\
      \ results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected\
      \ components in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nRun\
      \ a small service with one selected fault: blocking its asynchronous request\
      \ handler,\nleaking database connections, or retaining document objects after\
      \ requests finish.\nUse logs, traces, and resource measurements to decide which\
      \ explanation fits. Make one\nrepair and repeat the same requests to see whether\
      \ the evidence changes.\n\nStart with a healthy `/process` request and record\
      \ its path. A later slow request is\nmuch easier to explain when you know which\
      \ stages normally take time.\n\n## Prerequisites and bounded setup\n\nYou know\
      \ Python execution from Foundations 32,\ninstrumentation concepts from Foundations\
      \ 22,\nand jobs, deployment, and transactions from Guides 2,\n10, and 11. Prior\
      \ implementations and\nportfolio apps are not required.\n\nUse Python 3.13,\
      \ FastAPI/Uvicorn, Psycopg with a connection pool, HTTPX, pytest,\nOpenTelemetry's\
      \ Python instrumentation, and PostgreSQL 17. Record versions and lock\ndependencies.\
      \ The guide supplies a fixture contract, not prewritten executable code.\nAllow\
      \ three hours for routine scaffolding, using an AI coding assistant if useful.\n\
      Do not spend the week building a dashboard platform.\n\n## Fixture contract\n\
      \nCreate one API process with these routes:\n\n| Route | Normal behavior |\n\
      |---|---|\n| `GET /live` | Respond immediately without querying the database\
      \ |\n| `POST /process` | Accept at most 64 KB text, acquire a connection, query\
      \ a tiny lookup table, asynchronously wait 50 ms, return a word count |\n| `GET\
      \ /lab-stats` | Return active requests, connections checked out, pool wait count,\
      \ and retained-object count; local lab only |\n\nUse a pool of four database\
      \ connections and an explicit acquisition timeout. Add an\nevent-loop heartbeat\
      \ every 20 ms and record the actual gaps. Export OpenTelemetry\nspans to the\
      \ console initially; a collector/viewer is optional. Automatic instrumentation\n\
      can capture library boundaries, while manual spans name your own application\
      \ stages.\n[OpenTelemetry Python instrumentation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/python/)\n\
      \nA **log** records an event. A **metric** summarizes a quantity over time.\
      \ A **trace**\nconnects operations belonging to one request; each timed operation\
      \ is a **span**. Use\nrequest and trace IDs to connect evidence. Log stage names,\
      \ sizes, and outcomes, not raw\ndocument text or credentials. A slow request\
      \ trace alone cannot explain CPU use or\nmemory growth; collect those observations\
      \ too.\n\n## Three fault switches\n\nImplement three small fault functions behind\
      \ a local-only `LAB_FAULT` setting. Keep a\nhealthy mode and include a hard\
      \ limit on experiment duration and retained bytes.\n\n1. **Blocking handler:**\
      \ replace the 50 ms asynchronous wait with a 250 ms synchronous\n   sleep inside\
      \ the async handler. Observe heartbeat and `/live` responsiveness.\n2. **Connection\
      \ leak:** check out a connection and omit returning it on one injected\n   exception\
      \ path. After enough requests, new database work waits for an available slot.\n\
      3. **Retained objects:** append each input buffer to a process-global list after\
      \ the\n   response. Cap retention at 32 MB so the experiment does not exhaust\
      \ the laptop.\n\nSelect one fault at launch and store its identity in a local\
      \ answer file. Do not inspect\nthat file until after recording a hypothesis.\
      \ You may know the possible implementations;\nthe exercise is selecting among\
      \ explanations from evidence, not proving a blind study.\nThe fault implementation\
      \ must not print its name into ordinary request logs.\n\n## Project and incomplete\
      \ interfaces\n\n```text\nweek14/\n├── pyproject.toml\n├── compose.yaml\n├──\
      \ debugging_lab/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── api.py\n│   ├── faults.py\n│\
      \   ├── instrumentation.py\n│   ├── load.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├── tests/\n└──\
      \ artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\ndef configure_observation(service_name: str)\
      \ -> None: ...\nasync def process_document(text: str) -> dict: ...\nasync def\
      \ probe_service(base_url: str, seconds: int, clients: int) -> list[dict]: ...\n\
      def capture_memory_snapshot(label: str) -> str: ...\ndef compare_runs(before_path:\
      \ str, after_path: str) -> dict: ...\n```\n\nThe test load uses fixed-size text\
      \ with reproducible content. Configure one worker\nprocess so a second process\
      \ cannot hide a blocked event loop or split the memory evidence.\nIf you later\
      \ add workers, report that as a separate experiment.\n\n## Use a stable telemetry\
      \ contract — Instrumenting an LLM Request Path\n\nDefine names and attributes\
      \ before adding instrumentation. This lesson uses:\n\n| Span | Required attributes\
      \ |\n|---|---|\n| `app.request` | route, outcome, synthetic principal ID |\n\
      | `auth.filter` | candidate count, readable count, permission snapshot |\n|\
      \ `retrieval.search` | requested $k$, returned count, index revision |\n| `prompt.assemble`\
      \ | selected chunk count, estimated input tokens |\n| `model.generate` | model\
      \ label, input/output tokens, response status |\n\nDo not store query text,\
      \ document text, prompt text, access tokens, or group memberships in\ntelemetry\
      \ by default. Counts, stable synthetic identifiers, revisions, and bounded error\n\
      categories answer this exercise's questions without copying sensitive content.\n\
      \nAttribute names form a data contract. Keep them in one module, test their\
      \ presence, and\nversion deliberate changes. Avoid placing high-cardinality\
      \ values such as full request IDs\nor arbitrary error messages in metric labels\
      \ because each distinct value creates another\ntime series. Request and trace\
      \ IDs belong in traces and logs.\n\n## Preserve context across the call path\
      \ — Instrumenting an LLM Request Path\n\nThe active trace and span identifiers\
      \ are **context** that instrumentation carries through\nnested calls. A child\
      \ span receives its parent from that active context rather than from a\nglobal\
      \ variable shared by all requests. Run two requests concurrently and assert\
      \ that each\nchild attaches to the correct root.\n\nRecord exceptions on the\
      \ span where they occur, set an error status, and close every span\nin `finally`\
      \ behavior. Instrumentation must not swallow the application's exception or\n\
      change its return value. Turning telemetry off should leave application behavior\
      \ unchanged.\n\nCreate one structured log when the fixture model raises its\
      \ known error. Include the trace\nID, span ID, component, and bounded error\
      \ category. Use those identifiers to join the log\nto the failed trace in the\
      \ report.\n\n## Add measurements with explicit units — Instrumenting an LLM\
      \ Request Path\n\nRecord durations in milliseconds, token counts as integers,\
      \ and estimated cost in US\ndollars. For request $r$ using model label $m$,\
      \ calculate the estimate from a checked-in,\nsynthetic price table:\n\n$$\n\\\
      operatorname{cost}(r)=\n\\frac{p^{\\mathrm{in}}_m t^{\\mathrm{in}}_r +\np^{\\\
      mathrm{out}}_m t^{\\mathrm{out}}_r}{10^6}.\n$$\n\nHere $t^{\\mathrm{in}}_r$\
      \ and $t^{\\mathrm{out}}_r$ are recorded token counts, while\n$p^{\\mathrm{in}}_m$\
      \ and $p^{\\mathrm{out}}_m$ are the fixture's prices per million tokens.\nCall\
      \ the result an estimate, record the price-table version, and reject unknown\
      \ model\nlabels. Provider invoices may include cached tokens, batches, rounding,\
      \ or other rules not\nrepresented by this exercise.\n\nCreate these aggregates\
      \ from completed requests:\n\n- request count by outcome;\n- request and stage\
      \ latency distributions with count, median, and 95th percentile;\n- input and\
      \ output token totals;\n- estimated cost by model label;\n- error count by bounded\
      \ component and category.\n\nPercentiles describe the observed fixture only.\
      \ With a small sample, do not present the\n95th percentile as a stable production\
      \ service objective.\n\n## Run four disclosed scenarios — Instrumenting an LLM\
      \ Request Path\n\nThe fixture contains 80 requests divided evenly among four\
      \ labeled scenarios:\n\n| Scenario | Supplied behavior | Trace evidence to find\
      \ |\n|---|---|---|\n| Healthy | all stages return normally | complete tree and\
      \ bounded stage times |\n| Slow retrieval | retrieval waits for a fixed delay\
      \ | longer `retrieval.search` and root spans |\n| Oversized context | retriever\
      \ returns long readable chunks | higher input tokens and estimated cost |\n\
      | Model error | model raises a known fixture exception | errored model/root\
      \ spans and correlated log |\n\nThe labels are available before inspection.\
      \ This makes the task an instrumentation check:\ncan the emitted data reveal\
      \ a condition whose cause is already known? Do not tune the\nreport until every\
      \ scenario looks dramatic. A weak or missing signal is a result that may\nexpose\
      \ incomplete instrumentation.\n\nFor each scenario, select one trace and reconstruct\
      \ its path. Then aggregate all 80\nrequests and compare stage latency, token\
      \ use, cost, and errors. Explain which recorded\nfields support each statement\
      \ and which conclusions the telemetry cannot support.\n\n## Check instrumentation\
      \ quality — Instrumenting an LLM Request Path\n\nUnit tests cover nested parent/child\
      \ relationships, independent concurrent contexts,\nmonotonic nonnegative durations,\
      \ span closure after exceptions, bounded attributes,\nunknown price entries,\
      \ and unchanged application outputs with telemetry enabled or\ndisabled.\n\n\
      Integration tests run one case per scenario and verify:\n\n- every request has\
      \ one root span and the expected children;\n- every completed span shares the\
      \ request's trace ID;\n- model usage appears only on the model span and request\
      \ rollup;\n- the known error is visible in the span status and correlated log;\n\
      - no forbidden content keys or fixture canaries appear in exported telemetry;\n\
      - metric counts equal the number of completed requests.\n\nAlso measure instrumentation\
      \ overhead. Run the deterministic healthy fixture with a no-op\nadapter and\
      \ with local export, alternating their order across repetitions. Report both\n\
      distributions and the limitations of such a small local comparison. The lesson\
      \ does not\nrequire a particular percentage improvement or overhead ceiling."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Investigation sequence — 17 hours\n\n1. **Scaffolding and\
      \ healthy run, 3 hours.** Assemble the fixture, confirm connections\n   return\
      \ to the pool, and save a 30-second baseline with four concurrent clients.\n\
      2. **Known guided case, 2 hours.** Enable the blocking-handler fault. Compare\
      \ heartbeat\n   gaps with `/live` response time, then return to healthy mode.\n\
      3. **Select and observe, 3 hours.** Randomly select one fault and collect request\
      \ outcomes,\n   stage durations, pool statistics, heartbeat gaps, and memory\
      \ snapshots. List at\n   least two plausible explanations before inspecting\
      \ the answer file.\n4. **Distinguishing experiment, 3 hours.** Change one diagnostic\
      \ condition. For example,\n   compare a database-free probe with `/process`,\
      \ or stop traffic and check whether\n   retained Python allocations remain.\
      \ Record the predicted observation first.\n5. **Repair and repeat, 4 hours.**\
      \ Reveal the selected fault and compare it with your\n   diagnosis. Repair its\
      \ cause, restart into equivalent initial state, and rerun the\n   same traffic.\
      \ Keep an unchanged healthy control run.\n6. **Report and cleanup, 2 hours.**\
      \ Explain why the evidence supports or rejects the\n   diagnosis, document remaining\
      \ ambiguity, and stop the service and containers.\n\nUse `cProfile` when CPU\
      \ execution is a plausible cause; it cannot account for every\nexternal wait.\
      \ Use `tracemalloc` snapshots to identify retained Python allocations.\nResident\
      \ process memory can remain elevated after objects are freed because allocators\n\
      retain memory; distinguish those measurements before declaring a leak.\n\n##\
      \ Commands and tests\n\nImplement the CLI and run from this lesson directory.\
      \ `start` launches one recorded\nlocal API process, writes its PID and bound\
      \ address, and returns; `stop` terminates only\nthat recorded lab process. Avoid\
      \ broad process-name kill commands.\n\n```bash\nuv sync\ndocker compose up -d\
      \ --wait postgres\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m debugging_lab.cli\
      \ start --fault healthy\nuv run python -m debugging_lab.cli probe --seconds\
      \ 30 --clients 4 --out artifacts/healthy.jsonl\nuv run python -m debugging_lab.cli\
      \ stop\nuv run python -m debugging_lab.cli start --fault random --answer-file\
      \ artifacts/answer.json\nuv run python -m debugging_lab.cli probe --seconds\
      \ 30 --clients 4 --out artifacts/unknown.jsonl\nuv run python -m debugging_lab.cli\
      \ snapshot --label unknown\nuv run python -m debugging_lab.cli stop\ndocker\
      \ compose down\n```\n\nRepeat the probe after repair and save it as `repaired.jsonl`.\
      \ Tests cover pool return\nafter exceptions, bounded input and retention, response\
      \ correctness, distinct request IDs,\nfault setting validation, and process\
      \ cleanup. Performance claims come from measured\nruns, not tight latency assertions\
      \ in unit tests. Include failures and timeouts in the\ndenominator instead of\
      \ reporting only successful requests.\n\n## What to record and how to interpret\
      \ it\n\nKeep a short investigation note: symptoms, hypotheses, predicted discriminator,\
      \ observed\nresult, revealed cause, repair, and before/after evidence. A **percentile**\
      \ describes a\nposition in the sorted latency observations; the 95th percentile\
      \ exposes slow requests\nthat a mean can hide. Always report the sample size\
      \ and error count alongside it.\n\nHigher latency with normal heartbeat and\
      \ exhausted connections suggests a different\ninvestigation from heartbeat stalls\
      \ on a database-free route. Rising retained allocations\nafter repeated identical\
      \ requests suggests something different again. These patterns\nguide a test;\
      \ they are not universal proofs of a cause.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and optional\
      \ depth\n\nCPU, Docker, and about 2–4 GB of free memory suffice; target cost\
      \ $0. Keep the fault\nroutes on loopback and the retention cap enabled. Distributed\
      \ traces across an actual\nworker, a collector UI, or a CPU-heavy rather than\
      \ sleep-based fault are optional.\nAn inconclusive diagnosis with useful evidence\
      \ is an acceptable learning result.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\
      \nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration identities, case-level\
      \ outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline\
      \ mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements.\
      \ Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are\
      \ planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set\
      \ a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate\
      \ from the baseline report."

      and verify the repair.

  - content: "Separate model-file loading, tokenization, prefill, decoding, scheduling,\
      \ and queueing. Use a fake token generator for CPU mechanism checks and one\
      \ small open model with a maintained inference server for optional live measurement.\
      \ Explain batching, KV-cache memory, quantization, admission limits, and client\
      \ cancellation. Library and server internals supply production kernels and schedulers.\n\
      \nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces,\
      \ stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not\
      \ indicate that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone\
      \ fixture for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course\
      \ project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nRun one small open model with an established\
      \ inference server and compare its request\nhandling with a supplied bounded\
      \ baseline scheduler. Send the same seeded requests through\nboth, first one\
      \ at a time and then concurrently. Measure queueing, time to first token,\n\
      output rate, rejection when full, and what happens to generation after a client\
      \ cancels.\n\nYou will adapt and measure servers rather than implement a production\
      \ scheduler. The\nhandmade baseline is deliberately small and supplied as a\
      \ fixture; continuous batching,\nmemory paging, and device kernels remain the\
      \ established server's responsibility.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n- Autoregressive\
      \ decoding and key/value caching from Foundations Guide 4.\n- Quantization concepts\
      \ from Foundations Guide 6.\n- Request-stage instrumentation from Foundations\
      \ Guide 22.\n- HTTP streaming, asynchronous clients, and basic accelerator-memory\
      \ vocabulary.\n\nThe continuous-batching and speculative-decoding electives\
      \ are not prerequisites. Use one\npinned runtime and model. A CUDA/Linux path\
      \ may use an established continuous-batching\nserver; the CPU path may use an\
      \ established server for a small GGUF model. Comparing\nseveral runtimes, quantization\
      \ modes, or speculative-decoding methods is optional.\n\n## Start with one request\n\
      \nSend a short prompt with a 32-token output limit. Record when the request\
      \ enters the proxy,\nenters the runtime, produces its first token, produces\
      \ later tokens, and finishes. Repeat\nthe same request through the baseline\
      \ adapter.\n\n**Time to first token** is the duration from accepted request\
      \ to first output token.\n**Inter-token latency** is the time between later\
      \ output tokens. **Throughput** is total\noutput tokens divided by elapsed experiment\
      \ time. **Goodput** counts only requests that\nfinish within the stated latency\
      \ and correctness requirements.\n\nRecord the model revision, tokenizer revision,\
      \ runtime and container versions, launch\nflags, driver, accelerator or CPU\
      \ description, and request limits. Results apply only to\nthat combination.\n\
      \n## Use a bounded baseline\n\nThe supplied baseline accepts at most four running\
      \ requests and queues at most eight. It\nprocesses each running request with\
      \ a simple round-robin decode loop. Complete these\ninterfaces rather than adding\
      \ paging, speculative decoding, or a distributed controller:\n\n```python\n\
      from dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import AsyncIterator, Protocol\n\
      \n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass GenerationRequest:\n    request_id: str\n \
      \   prompt: str\n    max_output_tokens: int\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass\
      \ RequestMetrics:\n    queue_ms: float\n    first_token_ms: float | None\n \
      \   inter_token_ms: tuple[float, ...]\n    output_tokens: int\n    finish_reason:\
      \ str\n\nclass ModelServer(Protocol):\n    async def generate(self, request:\
      \ GenerationRequest) -> AsyncIterator[str]: ...\n    async def cancel(self,\
      \ request_id: str) -> None: ...\n\ndef admit(running: int, queued: int, *, max_running:\
      \ int, max_queued: int) -> bool: ...\n```\n\nThe baseline exists to expose queue\
      \ and cancellation behavior. Do not treat its performance\nas a realistic competitor\
      \ to an optimized server.\n\n## Put both servers behind one adapter\n\nThe adapter\
      \ validates prompt and output limits, maps server-specific streaming events\
      \ into\none token stream, propagates cancellation, and records the same metrics.\
      \ Readiness becomes\ntrue only after weights load and a tiny warm-up request\
      \ succeeds.\n\nReject work before it enters an unbounded queue. A rejection\
      \ has a structured reason and\ndoes not count as zero-latency success. Timeouts,\
      \ client disconnects, runtime errors, and\nadmission rejections remain distinct\
      \ terminal states.\n\nDo not log raw prompts by default. Use fixture IDs, lengths,\
      \ hashes, and synthetic text in\nthe experiment.\n\n## Run a fixed workload\n\
      \nCreate 48 requests across four prompt/output-size buckets. Use the same order,\
      \ limits, and\nrandom seed for both servers. Sweep concurrency through 1, 2,\
      \ 4, 8, and 16, stopping early\nif the safety cap rejects most requests or memory\
      \ approaches the configured limit.\n\nAt concurrency 4, cancel one quarter of\
      \ requests after their first token. Check whether:\n\n- the client stream closes;\n\
      - queued or running work is removed;\n- token generation stops within a bounded\
      \ delay;\n- capacity becomes available to later requests.\n\nMeasure generated\
      \ tokens after cancellation. A server that stops rendering but continues\ngeneration\
      \ has not propagated cancellation.\n\n## Project shape\n\n```text\nweek04/\n\
      ├── pyproject.toml\n├── serving_lab/\n│   ├── schema.py\n│   ├── baseline.py\n\
      │   ├── runtime_adapter.py\n│   ├── proxy.py\n│   ├── workload.py\n│   ├── benchmark.py\n\
      │   ├── report.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├── deploy/\n│   └── compose.yml\n├── data/\n\
      │   └── requests.jsonl\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\nKeep workload generation,\
      \ admission, server adapters, and metric calculation separate. The\nreport consumes\
      \ saved request rows and never scrapes a running dashboard for its numbers.\n\
      \n## Compare observable behavior\n\nFor every concurrency and server, report\
      \ offered, accepted, rejected, completed, errored,\nand cancelled request counts.\
      \ For completed requests, report median and 95th-percentile time\nto first token,\
      \ 95th-percentile inter-token latency, output tokens per second, peak memory,\n\
      and goodput under a written target.\n\nPlot queue time and goodput against concurrency.\
      \ The point where added concurrency mostly\nincreases waiting is the observed\
      \ saturation region. The established runtime may move that\nregion or may not\
      \ on the chosen CPU/model combination. Either result is valid when the\nenvironment\
      \ and counts are complete.\n\nCompare cancellation with a control run in which\
      \ the same clients disconnect but the\nadapter intentionally does not cancel\
      \ server work. Report the extra generated tokens and\ntime until capacity returns."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Failure-focused tests\n\nTest input and output limits, queue\
      \ boundary equality, readiness before and after loading,\nstream order, disconnect\
      \ propagation, repeated cancellation, unknown request IDs, admission\nrejection,\
      \ timeout, and complete terminal metrics. A cancelled request cannot later be\n\
      reported as successfully completed.\n\nUse fake token streams for unit tests\
      \ and one real-server smoke test for the artifact. Cap\nevery workload's duration,\
      \ output tokens, concurrency, and memory use.\n\n## Build sequence — 16 hours\n\
      \n1. **Environment and one request, 3 hours.** Pin one model/runtime and capture\
      \ a complete\n   streamed trace through each adapter.\n2. **Bounds and readiness,\
      \ 3 hours.** Add validation, warm-up, admission, and structured\n   terminal\
      \ states.\n3. **Cancellation, 3 hours.** Propagate client disconnects and measure\
      \ server work after\n   cancellation.\n4. **Concurrency sweep, 4 hours.** Run\
      \ the seeded workload on both servers and save every\n   request row.\n5. **Report,\
      \ 3 hours.** Reconcile counts, plot queue/goodput behavior, and state the tested\n\
      \   environment's limits.\n\n## Commands and artifact\n\n```bash\nuv sync\n\
      docker compose -f deploy/compose.yml up -d runtime\nuv run pytest tests -q\n\
      uv run python -m serving_lab.cli benchmark --target baseline --concurrency 1,2,4,8,16\
      \ --out artifacts/baseline.jsonl\nuv run python -m serving_lab.cli benchmark\
      \ --target runtime --concurrency 1,2,4,8,16 --out artifacts/runtime.jsonl\n\
      uv run python -m serving_lab.cli report --runs artifacts --out artifacts/report.md\n\
      ```\n\nThe report contains environment metadata, workload hash, request accounting,\
      \ latency and\ngoodput plots, cancellation comparison, peak memory, and at least\
      \ one limitation.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and safety\n\nA CPU-only path demonstrates\
      \ adapters, queues, cancellation, and measurement but does not\nestablish GPU-serving\
      \ capacity. The preferred measured path uses one 8–16 GB accelerator\nwith a\
      \ small model. Cap rented compute at $10 and stop it immediately after the sweep.\n\
      \nLoad weights from a pinned revision and safe serialization format. Run containers\
      \ without\nroot, restrict outbound access after download, and never aim the\
      \ load generator at a public\nor production endpoint.\n\n## Benchmarks (the\
      \ checkable artifact) — On-Device Inference (GGUF/ONNX)\n\nThe deliverable is\
      \ a reproducible **benchmark report** that would substantiate the\nabstract's\
      \ claim. It must contain:\n\n- **A sweep table**, one row per (quant, threads):\n\
      \n  | quant  | threads | TTFT p50 (s) | tok/s | peak RSS (MB) | quality |\n\
      \  | ------ | ------- | ------------ | ----- | ------------- | ------- |\n \
      \ | Q8_0   | 4       | …            | …     | …             | …       |\n  |\
      \ Q4_K_M | 4       | …            | …     | …             | …       |\n  | …\
      \      | …       | …            | …     | …             | …       |\n\n- **A\
      \ thread-scaling readout** showing TTFT (prefill) improving with threads\n \
      \ while decode tokens/sec saturates and possibly regresses past the physical-core\n\
      \  count — connecting back to the compute-bound vs. bandwidth-bound distinction.\n\
      \n- **The latency-versus-quality curve.** Plot quality (y) against tokens/sec\
      \ or\n  TTFT (x) for each quant level, with the **hosted-API baseline drawn\
      \ as a\n  reference point/line** (its latency and, at quality = 1.0 by construction,\
      \ its\n  answer). The shape you expect: higher-precision exports sit up-and-left\
      \ (better\n  quality, slower/heavier), aggressive quantization sits down-and-right\
      \ (faster,\n  lighter, slightly worse).\n\n- **A named operating point.** One\
      \ paragraph identifying the (quant, threads)\n  cell you would ship: the fastest/smallest\
      \ configuration whose `quality` stays\n  above a threshold you set in advance\
      \ (e.g. ≥ 0.95 retention vs. baseline).\n  State the threshold *before* looking\
      \ at results.\n\n**Expected shape of the result** (not a target to hardcode\
      \ — what \"done\" looks\nlike): a monotone-ish quality drop as precision falls,\
      \ a several-fold\ntokens/sec gain and a large peak-memory reduction from the\
      \ most aggressive\nquant, thread scaling that helps TTFT more than steady-state\
      \ decode, and a clearly\nidentifiable knee where further quantization buys little\
      \ speed but starts costing\nreal quality. That knee is your operating point.\n\
      \n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture\
      \ and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and\
      \ one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."

      latency, throughput, and cancellation.
