  - content: "Generate scheduled requests through the API, database, worker, and model\
      \ adapter. Distinguish offered requests, accepted work, and completed responses\
      \ meeting a latency goal. Specify arrival rate, request mix, duration, concurrency,\
      \ warm-up, hardware, and backlogs. Test one bottleneck repair and one added\
      \ API process separately so scaling claims can be attributed to observed changes.\n\
      \nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces,\
      \ stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not\
      \ indicate that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone\
      \ fixture for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course\
      \ project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nSend scheduled traffic through a supplied\
      \ API, PostgreSQL database, job worker, and fake\nmodel service. Increase offered\
      \ work until one component limits completed requests. Make\none repair aimed\
      \ at the measured bottleneck, then separately add a second API process and\n\
      see which change actually improves responses completed within the stated time\
      \ goal.\n\nThe artifact answers a bounded question such as “Can this exact deployment\
      \ support 300\nactive sessions following this workload?” It does not convert\
      \ an account count into a\ncapacity claim without defining request frequency,\
      \ duration, concurrency, and user behavior.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n\
      - Release configuration and rollback from Guide 1.\n- Durable jobs from Guide\
      \ 2.\n- Inference-server admission and measurements from Guide 4.\n- Concurrent\
      \ database behavior from Guide 11.\n- Reading request traces and resource evidence\
      \ from Guide 14.\n\nThe fixture supplies synthetic data, a fake model with delay\
      \ and rate-limit controls, and\na deterministic workload generator. A real model-provider\
      \ run is optional. Autoscaling\ncontrollers, Kubernetes, multi-region traffic,\
      \ and a production capacity guarantee are\noutside the core.\n\n## Define “100–1,000\
      \ users” as a workload\n\nKeep these quantities distinct:\n\n- **accounts:**\
      \ identities stored in the database;\n- **active sessions:** users represented\
      \ during the test window;\n- **simultaneous requests:** work in progress at\
      \ one instant;\n- **request rate:** requests offered per second;\n- **request\
      \ duration:** how long each request occupies resources;\n- **background work:**\
      \ jobs created per foreground request.\n\nThe default profile models 300 active\
      \ sessions over ten minutes. Each session follows a\nseeded schedule containing\
      \ document reads, one model-backed question, and occasional\nbackground indexing.\
      \ The profile determines the offered request rate; the number 300 alone\ndoes\
      \ not.\n\nRun additional profiles representing 100, 600, and 1,000 active sessions\
      \ while keeping the\nper-session behavior fixed. These are workload labels,\
      \ not claims about all possible users.\n\n## Use an open-loop generator\n\n\
      Schedule arrivals against a monotonic clock independently of response completion.\
      \ This is\nan **open-loop load test**: overload remains visible because slow\
      \ responses do not reduce\nthe planned arrival rate.\n\nFor every scheduled\
      \ request, record one terminal row:\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\n\
      from typing import Literal\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass RequestResult:\n\
      \    request_id: str\n    kind: str\n    scheduled_ms: float\n    started_ms:\
      \ float | None\n    finished_ms: float | None\n    outcome: Literal[\"completed\"\
      , \"rejected\", \"failed\", \"cancelled\"]\n    status_code: int | None\n  \
      \  queue_ms: float | None\n    trace_id: str | None\n\ndef schedule(profile:\
      \ dict, *, seed: int) -> list[dict]: ...\n\ndef run_open_loop(events: list[dict],\
      \ target: str, limits: dict) -> list[RequestResult]: ...\n```\n\nAccount for\
      \ offered, accepted, rejected, failed, cancelled, and completed requests. Do\
      \ not\ncalculate latency only from fast successes while dropping rejected or\
      \ unfinished work.\n\n## State the response goal\n\nUse a concrete service-level\
      \ objective (SLO), a measured target for this experiment:\n\n> During a ten-minute\
      \ run, at least 95% of offered interactive requests complete within\n> three\
      \ seconds, and no accepted background job waits more than 30 seconds to start.\n\
      \n**Goodput** is offered work completed within its applicable goal. Raw throughput\
      \ may rise\nwhile goodput falls if a queue grows and responses finish too late.\n\
      \nLittle's Law relates average number in the system $L$, completed arrival rate\
      \ $\\lambda$,\nand average time in the system $W$ under a stable period:\n\n\
      $$\nL\\approx\\lambda W.\n$$\n\nUse it as a consistency check over a steady\
      \ interval, not as proof that a changing or\noverloaded run is stable.\n\n##\
      \ Observe each component\n\nCollect the smallest evidence set that can distinguish\
      \ likely limits:\n\n| Component | Evidence |\n|---|---|\n| API | running requests,\
      \ event-loop delay, CPU, memory |\n| Database | active connections, query latency,\
      \ lock waits |\n| Worker | queued jobs, oldest-job age, completions, retries\
      \ |\n| Fake model | running calls, imposed delay, rate-limit rejections |\n\n\
      Correlate requests with the stage traces introduced earlier. A slow end-to-end\
      \ request does\nnot identify the bottleneck by itself. Form at least two hypotheses\
      \ and name the observation\nthat distinguishes them before changing configuration.\n\
      \n## Bound queues and running work\n\nSet explicit limits for API in-flight\
      \ requests, database connections, queued jobs, worker\nconcurrency, and model\
      \ calls. Reject or defer excess work with a structured reason before an\nunbounded\
      \ queue consumes memory and makes every accepted request late.\n\nThe baseline\
      \ intentionally includes one constrained component selected by fixture\nconfiguration.\
      \ Diagnose it from telemetry before reading the setting. After recording the\n\
      evidence, reveal the configuration and implement one matching repair, such as\
      \ increasing a\ntoo-small database pool, adding a worker, or lowering model\
      \ concurrency to avoid rate-limit\nthrashing.\n\nAdding a second API process\
      \ is a separate comparison. It may not help when the database,\nworker, or model\
      \ is limiting the system.\n\n## Project shape\n\n```text\nweek05/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── fixture/\n│   ├── api.py\n│   ├── worker.py\n│   ├── fake_model.py\n│  \
      \ └── fault_config.py\n├── capacity_lab/\n│   ├── profiles.py\n│   ├── loadgen.py\n\
      │   ├── limits.py\n│   ├── collect.py\n│   ├── analyze.py\n│   ├── report.py\n\
      │   └── cli.py\n├── deploy/\n│   └── compose.yml\n├── configs/\n├── tests/\n\
      └── artifacts/\n```\n\nKeep workload profiles, safety limits, deployment variants,\
      \ collection, and analysis in\nversioned files. Record image digests and host\
      \ resources with every run.\n\n## Compare three configurations\n\nRun the same\
      \ profiles against:\n\n1. the bounded baseline;\n2. the baseline plus one repair\
      \ aimed at the diagnosed component;\n3. the original bounded baseline plus a\
      \ second API process.\n\nUse identical seeds, synthetic data, fake-model behavior,\
      \ run duration, and response goals.\nRun each configuration at least twice when\
      \ timings vary and show both observations rather\nthan selecting the more favorable\
      \ one.\n\nFor every profile and configuration, report:\n\n- offered, accepted,\
      \ rejected, failed, cancelled, completed, and timely-completed counts;\n- median,\
      \ 95th-, and 99th-percentile end-to-end latency;\n- oldest request and job queue\
      \ age;\n- component utilization and resource limits;\n- estimated cost per timely\
      \ completed request.\n\nState the largest tested profile meeting the goal. Do\
      \ not interpolate an untested claim for\n1,000 users from a successful 300-session\
      \ run."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Failure-focused tests\n\nTest schedule independence from\
      \ response time, missed arrival deadlines, bounded queues,\nadmission boundary\
      \ equality, request timeout, complete terminal accounting, percentile\ncalculation,\
      \ profile reproducibility, and cancellation cleanup. The sum of terminal outcomes\n\
      must equal offered requests after the drain deadline.\n\nTest the fake model's\
      \ delay, failure, and rate-limit controls without network access. Add one\n\
      small integration test that exercises API, database, worker, and fake model\
      \ in the same\nrequest/job flow.\n\n## Build sequence — 18 hours\n\n1. **Fixture\
      \ and workload, 3 hours.** Run one request/job path and define the four seeded\n\
      \   session profiles and response goals.\n2. **Open-loop generator, 3 hours.**\
      \ Schedule independently, impose drain deadlines, and\n   preserve every terminal\
      \ outcome.\n3. **Boundaries and telemetry, 3 hours.** Configure finite work\
      \ limits and collect the four\n   component evidence sets.\n4. **Baseline diagnosis,\
      \ 3 hours.** Run increasing profiles, record hypotheses, and identify\n   the\
      \ limiting component.\n5. **Two comparisons, 3 hours.** Test one targeted repair\
      \ and, separately, a second API\n   process under the unchanged workload.\n\
      6. **Report, 3 hours.** Reconcile counts, state the largest passing tested profile,\
      \ and\n   document what the fake model cannot establish.\n\n## Commands and\
      \ artifact\n\n```bash\nuv sync\ndocker compose -f deploy/compose.yml up -d\n\
      uv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m capacity_lab.cli run --config configs/baseline.toml\
      \ --profiles 100,300,600,1000 --out artifacts/baseline\nuv run python -m capacity_lab.cli\
      \ run --config configs/repaired.toml --profiles 100,300,600,1000 --out artifacts/repaired\n\
      uv run python -m capacity_lab.cli run --config configs/two-api.toml --profiles\
      \ 100,300,600,1000 --out artifacts/two-api\nuv run python -m capacity_lab.cli\
      \ report --runs artifacts --out artifacts/capacity-report.md\n```\n\nThe report\
      \ contains workload definitions, environment metadata, response goals, terminal\n\
      accounting, stage/resource evidence, competing hypotheses, comparisons, cost\
      \ assumptions,\nand at least one limitation.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and safety\n\
      \nThe default fixture runs locally with a fake model and costs $0. Limit offered\
      \ rate, test\nduration, queues, concurrent work, database size, and Compose\
      \ resources. Never point the\ngenerator at a production or billable endpoint.\n\
      \nAn optional real-provider smoke run must use a separate configuration with\
      \ a $5 cap. It can\nmeasure that provider path for the small sample but cannot\
      \ replace the controlled fake-model\ncapacity experiment.\n\n### Report the\
      \ actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration\
      \ identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation.\
      \ Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server\
      \ or cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."
    summary: Find the limiting component under a defined workload and test whether
      a targeted repair improves completed work.

  - content: "Use a disposable synthetic-data service to stop a worker during a job,\
      \ slow a dependency, and release an incompatible API response. Write recovery\
      \ instructions before injecting each failure. Observe degradation, execute the\
      \ repair, and verify completed work and stored state. Improve one weak instruction\
      \ or control and repeat its failure.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation\
      \ and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are\
      \ proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured\
      \ results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected\
      \ components in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nRun\
      \ a supplied disposable application and deliberately cause three known failures:\
      \ stop a\nworker during a job, make a dependency too slow, and release an incompatible\
      \ API response.\nUse short recovery instructions written before the exercise,\
      \ verify application behavior\nand stored data after each repair, then improve\
      \ one weak instruction or control and repeat\none failure.\n\nThe fixture contains\
      \ an API, PostgreSQL database, job worker, and fake model service. It\nuses\
      \ synthetic data and local Docker Compose, so the exercise does not depend on\
      \ a portfolio\napplication or a system assembled across previous labs.\n\n##\
      \ Prerequisites and scope\n\n- Returning to a previous version from Guide 1.\n\
      - Worker recovery and repeated-delivery concepts from Guide 2.\n- Backup and\
      \ restoration checks from Guide 12.\n- Reading traces, metrics, and logs from\
      \ Guide 14.\n\nThe three failure mechanisms and healthy checks are supplied.\
      \ You write recovery pages,\nrun the exercise, improve one thing, and record\
      \ evidence. Random undisclosed faults,\nproduction incident command, disaster\
      \ recovery across regions, and a broad chaos-engineering\nplatform are outside\
      \ the core.\n\n## Establish healthy behavior first\n\nStart the fixture and\
      \ run one command that checks:\n\n- a normal API question returns the expected\
      \ response shape;\n- one accepted background job produces exactly one lasting\
      \ database effect;\n- seeded rows and their content hashes remain present;\n\
      - the fake model's healthy response begins within the stated two-second target.\n\
      \nRecord the image digests, database fixture hash, API schema version, and check\
      \ output. Do\nnot inject a failure until this baseline passes and the cleanup\
      \ command has been tested.\n\nA **game day** is a planned practice session that\
      \ causes bounded failures in a disposable\nenvironment. A **runbook** is the\
      \ short recovery instruction used during that session. The\ngoal is to find\
      \ unclear system behavior and unclear instructions, not to perform a flawless\n\
      drill.\n\n## Use three bounded failures\n\n### Worker stopped during lasting\
      \ work\n\nPause the worker after it accepts a job but before or just after the\
      \ database effect. The\nfixture exposes a synchronization point so timing is\
      \ repeatable. Restart the worker and\ncheck whether the job disappears, repeats\
      \ its lasting effect, completes once, or reaches a\ndocumented final failure\
      \ state.\n\n### Slow model dependency\n\nConfigure the fake model to respond\
      \ after three seconds. Observe the API timeout, whether\nthe dependency call\
      \ is cancelled, whether a queue grows, and how a normal request behaves\nafter\
      \ the delay is removed. A client timeout alone does not prove server work stopped.\n\
      \n### Incompatible API release\n\nRelease a candidate that renames the required\
      \ `answer` field to `text`. Use the supplied\nbehavior test to detect the mismatch\
      \ and return the proxy to the recorded previous version.\nVerify both the response\
      \ shape and stored data afterward.\n\nEvery failure switch has `enable`, `status`,\
      \ and `undo` operations, a maximum duration, and\na check that refuses any target\
      \ except `local-staging`.\n\n## Write one-screen recovery pages\n\nBefore the\
      \ exercise, write one page per failure answering:\n\n1. What symptom should\
      \ be visible?\n2. Which two observations should be checked first?\n3. What action\
      \ repairs or contains the problem?\n4. How are the user path and stored data\
      \ verified afterward?\n5. How is the injected condition removed?\n\nUse ordinary\
      \ commands and expected outputs. “Check the logs” is incomplete; name the\n\
      service, event, and request or job identifier to look for. Test each page once\
      \ while setup\nis visible, then freeze it for the game-day run.\n\n## Project\
      \ shape and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\nweek09/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── fixture/\n│   ├── api.py\n│   ├── worker.py\n│   ├── fake_model.py\n│  \
      \ └── schema.py\n├── game_day/\n│   ├── config.py\n│   ├── failures.py\n│  \
      \ ├── health.py\n│   ├── exercise.py\n│   ├── timeline.py\n│   └── cli.py\n\
      ├── runbooks/\n├── deploy/\n│   └── compose.yml\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n\
      ```\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import Protocol\n\
      \n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass HealthResult:\n    passed: bool\n    checks:\
      \ dict[str, bool]\n    details: dict[str, str]\n\nclass Failure(Protocol):\n\
      \    name: str\n    def enable(self, target: str) -> None: ...\n    def status(self,\
      \ target: str) -> dict: ...\n    def undo(self, target: str) -> None: ...\n\n\
      def check_health(base_url: str, expected_fixture_hash: str) -> HealthResult:\
      \ ...\n```\n\nFailure code changes only fixture controls. Recovery code follows\
      \ normal service, release,\nand data interfaces. This separation prevents the\
      \ repair from silently deleting evidence\nor bypassing the behavior being tested.\n\
      \n## Run the exercise\n\nUse a fixed seed to shuffle the three failure names\
      \ and reveal them one at a time. The cause\nis known after reveal; this lesson\
      \ practises recovery rather than unknown-fault diagnosis.\n\nFor each failure:\n\
      \n1. record its start time and identifier;\n2. enable it and use the application\
      \ until the symptom appears;\n3. record the first useful observation;\n4. follow\
      \ the frozen recovery page without editing it;\n5. run the complete health and\
      \ data check;\n6. undo the injected condition and verify cleanup;\n7. save the\
      \ trace, relevant bounded logs, and timeline row.\n\nStop the exercise if a\
      \ control targets anything outside `local-staging`, the verified backup\nis\
      \ unavailable, fixture hashes differ unexpectedly, or cleanup fails."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Record recovery evidence\n\nThe report includes this table:\n\
      \n| Failure | First useful signal | Time to notice | Time to verified recovery\
      \ | User impact | Data check |\n|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|\n| Worker stopped\
      \ | … | … | … | … | pass/fail |\n| Dependency slow | … | … | … | … | pass/fail\
      \ |\n| Incompatible release | … | … | … | … | pass/fail |\n\nTimes are observations\
      \ rather than pass thresholds. Also record jobs lost or repeated,\nrequests\
      \ left running after timeout, the final active release digest, and any data\
      \ written\nafter the backup that would not appear in a restore.\n\nChoose one\
      \ weakness supported by the evidence: for example, a missing job-state check,\
      \ an\nunclear log field, a dependency cancellation gap, or a hard-to-find previous\
      \ image digest.\nMake one bounded change and repeat only the related failure.\
      \ Compare the two attempts without\nclaiming the change generally improves all\
      \ incidents.\n\n## Failure-focused tests\n\nTest refusal of non-staging targets,\
      \ maximum failure duration, idempotent `undo`, cleanup\nafter an interrupted\
      \ exercise, detection of each failure by the health command, job-effect\ncounting,\
      \ response-schema validation, data hashes, and restoration into a separate database.\n\
      \nOne integration test enables and undoes each failure in turn. It must leave\
      \ the fixture\nhealthy and all seeded rows intact. Keep failure controls unavailable\
      \ from the application\nAPI.\n\n## Build sequence — 16 hours\n\n1. **Fixture\
      \ and baseline, 3 hours.** Start the supplied services, verify behavior and\
      \ data,\n   and test cleanup and restoration.\n2. **Recovery pages, 3 hours.**\
      \ Write and dry-run the three one-screen instructions.\n3. **Game day, 3 hours.**\
      \ Run the shuffled failures, preserve timelines, and verify recovery.\n4. **Evidence\
      \ review, 2 hours.** Reconcile jobs, requests, releases, and stored data.\n\
      5. **One improvement and repeat, 3 hours.** Repair one observed weakness and\
      \ rerun its\n   related failure.\n6. **Report, 2 hours.** Compare attempts and\
      \ record remaining limits.\n\n## Commands and artifact\n\n```bash\nuv sync\n\
      docker compose -f deploy/compose.yml up -d\nuv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python\
      \ -m game_day.cli baseline --target local-staging --out artifacts/baseline.json\n\
      uv run python -m game_day.cli exercise --target local-staging --seed 100 --out\
      \ artifacts/first-run\nuv run python -m game_day.cli repeat --target local-staging\
      \ --failure selected --out artifacts/repeat-run\nuv run python -m game_day.cli\
      \ report --runs artifacts --out artifacts/report.md\ndocker compose -f deploy/compose.yml\
      \ down\n```\n\nThe report contains the baseline identity, frozen recovery pages,\
      \ timeline, health/data\nchecks, bounded logs and traces, first/repeat comparison,\
      \ cleanup result, and at least one\nlimitation.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and safety\n\
      \nA laptop running Docker Compose is sufficient, and the fake model keeps cost\
      \ at $0. Use\nonly synthetic data in the disposable fixture. Keep backups outside\
      \ disrupted volumes,\ngive every failure a maximum duration and explicit undo,\
      \ and verify no fixture containers\nremain after cleanup.\n\nHosted incident\
      \ tooling, Kubernetes fault injection, and additional failures are optional.\n\
      The core stops after the three local failures and one measured repeat.\n\n###\
      \ Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture\
      \ and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and\
      \ one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."
    summary: Rehearse recovery instructions and verify behavior and data after each
      failure.

  - content: "Operate the supplied service or an optional application from the companion\
      \ courses. Freeze release and workload identities. Identify one capacity limitation\
      \ and one recovery weakness, then make at most two targeted improvements. Recheck\
      \ authentication, permitted documents, jobs, caches, and restored state so operational\
      \ repairs do not silently change application behavior.\n\nThe lesson below specifies\
      \ an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts\
      \ and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable\
      \ code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each\
      \ lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\n## What\
      \ you will do\n\nRun a disposable document service, identify one capacity bottleneck,\
      \ and practise recovery\nfrom one failure. Make at most two targeted repairs\
      \ and compare their effects under the\nsame workload. Your final artifact explains\
      \ what improved, what data survived, and which\nclaims the experiment does not\
      \ support.\n\nThis is a bounded course capstone. It is independent of every\
      \ portfolio project and\ndoes not require collecting earlier lessons' source\
      \ code. The service below is a small\nlab fixture, not a new product to build\
      \ and polish.\n\n## Prerequisites and fixture setup\n\nYou understand release/recovery\
      \ work from Guides 1 and\n9, durable jobs from 2, capacity from\n5, and data\
      \ recovery, caching, and debugging from\n12, 13, and 14.\nPermissions come from\
      \ Foundations 35 and\nEnterprise 3. No training or RL implementation\nis a code\
      \ dependency.\n\nUse Python 3.13, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis, HTTPX, and pytest\
      \ with locked versions and\nrecorded container digests. The fixture contract\
      \ below replaces a dependency on an\nexisting application. Assemble its routine\
      \ scaffolding in the first three hours, with\nan AI coding assistant if useful,\
      \ and inspect it before testing. The CLI and interfaces\nare implementation\
      \ targets, not preinstalled tools. A command-line client is enough.\n\nIf setup\
      \ consumes the allocation, reduce fixture size or report partial progress instead\n\
      of adding a frontend or rebuilding all prior mechanisms. Advanced policy and\
      \ scheduling\nvariants are outside the capstone's scope.\n\n## Minimal service\
      \ contract\n\n```text\ntest client -> API -> PostgreSQL (documents, memberships,\
      \ jobs)\n                |       ^\n                |       |\n            \
      \    |     worker -> deterministic fake model\n                |\n         \
      \       +-> Redis (disposable document-response cache)\n```\n\n| Component |\
      \ Small required behavior |\n|---|---|\n| Identity | Two organizations with\
      \ employee and HR users; random per-user test tokens mapped in trusted server\
      \ configuration |\n| Documents | 40 short synthetic documents with organization,\
      \ minimum role, and revision; exact keyword retrieval only |\n| API | Submit\
      \ document ingestion, inspect job state, search/read visible documents, and\
      \ report readiness |\n| Jobs | PostgreSQL queue; one worker; expiring ownership;\
      \ unique result per job; at most three attempts |\n| Fake model | Deterministic\
      \ response using supplied document IDs/text; configurable 50–500 ms delay and\
      \ temporary failures |\n| Cache | Exact request/revision keys and current authorization\
      \ checks; bounded direct fallback when Redis is unavailable |\n| Observation\
      \ | Request/job IDs, outcomes, queue age, dependency wait times, and counters\
      \ |\n\nThe test-token identity shortcut is restricted to this local lab. It\
      \ is not a deployed\nlogin implementation. The fake model records its context\
      \ so tests can inspect forbidden\ndocuments before generation. It does not send\
      \ content to a provider.\n\nKeep two selectable baseline problems: a database\
      \ pool restricted to one connection and\na worker that may crash after computing\
      \ a result but before committing it. The fixture\nstill needs clear authorization\
      \ and data constraints before performance comparisons.\nAn unsafe access rule\
      \ is a finding to record, not a performance tradeoff to accept.\n\n## Questions\
      \ to answer before changing code\n\nWrite a one-page experiment note with:\n\
      \n- **Workload:** 80% searches, 20% job submissions, fixed document sizes, and\
      \ a fixed\n  fake-model delay. Use synthetic identities with a documented distribution.\n\
      - **Response goal:** for example, successful searches within 500 ms and accepted\
      \ jobs\n  completed within five seconds during a short run. These are lab goals,\
      \ not promises\n  to customers.\n- **Data rules:** no result from another organization\
      \ or forbidden role enters model\n  context; accepted jobs remain accounted\
      \ for; each completed job has at most one\n  published result.\n- **Recovery\
      \ question:** which jobs finish after worker restart, or which records return\n\
      \  after restoring a named backup? Choose one, not both.\n\nA **bottleneck**\
      \ is the resource currently limiting useful completed work. More API\nprocesses\
      \ will not necessarily help if each waits for the same constrained database.\n\
      Use evidence to choose a change rather than assuming that adding replicas is\
      \ the repair.\n\n## Project shape and interfaces\n\n```text\nweek15/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── compose.yaml\n├── schema.sql\n├── operations_lab/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n\
      │   ├── fixture.py\n│   ├── api.py\n│   ├── worker.py\n│   ├── fake_model.py\n\
      │   ├── load.py\n│   ├── checks.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├── configs/\n│   └── workload.toml\n\
      ├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\ndef check_data_rules(database_url:\
      \ str, captured_contexts: list[dict]) -> dict: ...\nasync def run_workload(config_path:\
      \ str, output_path: str) -> dict: ...\ndef activate_failure(name: str, target_marker:\
      \ str) -> None: ...\ndef restore_normal_operation(name: str) -> None: ...\n\
      def compare_evidence(baseline_path: str, changed_path: str) -> dict: ...\n```"
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build and investigation sequence — 19 hours\n\n1. **Fixture\
      \ and access checks, 3 hours.** Assemble the minimal components, seed data,\n\
      \   and perform one search/job as each identity. Test restricted direct reads\
      \ and model\n   context before the load experiment.\n2. **Baseline workload,\
      \ 3 hours.** Schedule requests at 1, 2, and 4 per second for\n   60 seconds\
      \ each, independently of response speed. Repeat with the same fixture,\n   timing\
      \ seed, and fake-model configuration. Drain accepted jobs for a bounded period.\n\
      3. **Diagnosis, 3 hours.** Inspect waits and resource counts. Form a hypothesis,\
      \ then\n   compare the constrained pool with one chosen larger size. If the\
      \ original hypothesis\n   is wrong, report why; do not keep changing knobs until\
      \ a graph improves.\n4. **One recovery experiment, 3 hours.** Use explicit fault\
      \ timing: by default kill the\n   worker after computation/before commit, restart\
      \ it, and account for jobs. Alternatively,\n   restore one backup and account\
      \ for writes after its snapshot. Record the boundary.\n5. **At most two repairs,\
      \ 4 hours.** Keep the performance change and, if needed, one\n   recovery repair.\
      \ Repeat identical workload/failure conditions and rerun access checks.\n6.\
      \ **Explanation and cleanup, 3 hours.** Save the reproducible evidence, describe\
      \ one\n   alternative considered, record limits, and stop the disposable stack.\n\
      \nSchedule requests independently of responses so a slow service cannot quietly\
      \ reduce\nthe offered load. If the load generator itself falls behind, record\
      \ scheduling lag;\nthat run does not establish the service's capacity. Report\
      \ unfinished jobs after the\ndrain window as unfinished, not successful or silently\
      \ lost.\n\n## Commands and meaningful checks\n\nFrom this lesson directory after\
      \ implementing the CLI:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\ndocker compose up -d --wait\nuv\
      \ run python -m operations_lab.cli seed --fixture two-orgs --documents 40\n\
      uv run pytest tests -q\nuv run python -m operations_lab.cli baseline --config\
      \ configs/workload.toml --out artifacts/baseline\nuv run python -m operations_lab.cli\
      \ failure --name worker-before-commit --target local-week15\nuv run python -m\
      \ operations_lab.cli recover --name worker-before-commit --target local-week15\n\
      uv run python -m operations_lab.cli check-data --out artifacts/recovery.json\n\
      uv run python -m operations_lab.cli compare --baseline artifacts/baseline --changed\
      \ artifacts/changed\ndocker compose down\n```\n\nThe `baseline` command also\
      \ supports `--out artifacts/changed` for the post-repair run;\nit uses the same\
      \ workload configuration. Failure commands must check a local fixture\nmarker\
      \ and exact container/process identity, and offer a matching undo/recovery command.\n\
      They never target a portfolio deployment or another running project.\n\nTests\
      \ cover allowed and denied contexts, guessed resource IDs, duplicate job submission,\n\
      stale worker ownership, revision-aware cache reads, and cleanup. Use a deterministic\n\
      barrier for the worker crash so the same boundary can be tested after a repair.\
      \ Keep\nthe access and data checks the same across performance variants.\n\n\
      ## Final evidence\n\nCreate `artifacts/report.md` with a small architecture\
      \ diagram, the frozen workload,\nbaseline and changed results, recovery timeline,\
      \ and limitations. Include offered,\naccepted, rejected, failed, completed,\
      \ cancelled, and unfinished requests/jobs; record\nlatency percentiles and sample\
      \ counts. Distinguish request outcomes from job outcomes.\n\nReport whether\
      \ each data rule held and link the test or trace that supports it. A negative\n\
      or inconclusive performance result is valid. A rule violation means the protection\
      \ needs\nmore work; documenting it is more useful than claiming success from\
      \ a happy-path demo.\n\nThe fake model establishes neither real-provider capacity\
      \ nor model quality or pricing.\nForty documents and synthetic traffic do not\
      \ prove capacity for an unspecified number\nof real users. Explain the supported\
      \ workload instead.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and optional depth\n\nLaptop, CPU,\
      \ Docker, and about 4 GB of available memory; core target cost $0. Stop all\n\
      lab processes and export evidence before removing volumes. A short hosted run\
      \ with an\nexplicit spending cap, a real-provider comparison, or a second worker\
      \ is optional.\nThere is no required portfolio polish, presentation, external\
      \ review, or ongoing product\nmaintenance attached to this capstone.\n\n###\
      \ Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture\
      \ and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and\
      \ one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."

planned:
  chapters:
  - content: '## What the learner will build


      Teach the application and decision-making controls needed when an AI service
      handles organizational documents and actions: resource authorization, permission-aware
      retrieval, synchronization and revocation, sensitive-data handling, audit records,
      deletion, adversarial testing, cost attribution, and vendor evaluation. Express
      each control as ordinary code, an observable test, or a reviewable decision
      document. Technical exercises do not certify legal compliance or complete security.


      An internal support/document assistant for two fictional organizations with
      different users and roles. Independent fixtures cover tickets, document permissions,
      revisioned search indexes, logs, caches, and simulated tools. A cumulative optional
      implementation can extend the application course''s assistant. Use synthetic
      canaries to detect forbidden data and simulated actions to inspect authorization
      without contacting real users or systems.


      The course consists of independently reproducible labs. Concepts accumulate,
      but another chapter''s source tree is not a hidden prerequisite. A supplied
      fixture or a small implementation can stand in for an earlier component. Combining
      the results into one portfolio is optional. Each lab''s command contract, interfaces
      and tests specify work to be implemented; this saved brief does not claim that
      code or benchmark results already exist.


      ## Prerequisites and execution paths


      Python programmers familiar with tool calling, retrieval-augmented generation,
      a web API, relational data, and identity versus authorization. Build LLM Applications
      and the first four chapters of Deploy and Operate AI Systems provide this background.
      Core labs use two fictional organizations, supplied identities, local fixtures,
      and synthetic data. Real workplace connectors, production identity providers,
      and private cloud networking are optional extensions with recorded versions
      and bounded costs.


      A small deterministic fixture is the first path for examining control flow and
      checking a boundary. A substantive measurement uses the actual component being
      studied: a model for model behavior, a database for locking and persistence,
      an inference server for scheduling, or a real provisioned environment for deployment.
      Reports state the path used. Recorded responses cannot establish the quality
      or resource behavior of a model that was never run. Costs in source examples
      are planning assumptions; record actual versions, hardware, usage and spending
      before making a comparison.


      ## Follow one user across four trust boundaries


      Two fictional organizations have different document collections and support
      tickets. An analyst can read assigned tickets; a support lead can add an internal
      note within the same organization. The authenticated user identity comes from
      a trusted application boundary. A model may propose a tool and resource identifier,
      but it cannot supply a trusted role or organization. The dispatcher checks the
      requested action and the downstream handler checks the protected resource again
      before a lasting change occurs.


      Retrieval is another resource request. A search stage filters candidate membership
      before forbidden text reaches the generator. Source permissions and document
      revisions change over time, so synchronization must update content and access
      metadata together and expose cursor/freshness state. The application defines
      what happens when the source authority cannot be reached or a revocation has
      not yet been applied; a stale cache is an observable condition rather than permission
      to ignore the rule.


      ## Data copies, event records and proposed interfaces


      Maintain a UserContext, ResourceRef and PermissionDecision independent of model
      text; a SourceEvent with cursor, object revision and permission revision; and
      a RetrievalRun retaining candidate IDs, permitted context and cited sources.
      An AuditEvent records identity references, evidence versions, observed tool
      outcomes and control decisions with minimized data. A DeletionPlan enumerates
      primary rows, chunks, vectors, caches, logs, keys, derived artifacts and backups,
      plus the verification operation for each. A CostRecord names measured units,
      owner and the pricing assumptions used for allocation.


      The fixture uses synthetic names and canaries. A canary is a known marker placed
      in a forbidden document so tests can detect whether it appears in retrieval
      results, model context, citations or a simulated external action. Expected access
      labels come from an independent permission matrix and source snapshot. Tests
      must not ask the same permission function under test to manufacture their oracle.


      ## Develop controls and inspect their consequences


      Authorization and synchronization establish resource access first. Redaction
      and audit then make data handling and past events inspectable; a detector''s
      performance and a log''s tamper properties are separate measurements. Decision
      traces reconstruct evidence and application effects without claiming that a
      generated rationale reveals a model''s internal causes. Lifecycle work verifies
      expiry and deletion against the declared inventory and replays deletion history
      on restore. Injection tests place hostile instructions in documents and tool
      output while ordinary code still checks capabilities. Artifact provenance verifies
      identity and compatibility before loading a release. Network tests measure the
      allowed and denied paths of a declared environment. Regression cases retain
      both successful attacks and legitimate tasks.


      A hash confirms file identity relative to a trusted reference; it does not establish
      that an unknown source is safe. A hash chain detects changes relative to a trusted
      head, with separate limits if the attacker controls the whole file. Encryption-based
      deletion depends on complete key handling, including cached and backed-up keys.
      An observed packet trace covers the instrumented workload and interval. These
      limits help the learner choose the right test rather than turn a fixture result
      into a general security or compliance claim.


      ## Translate evidence into a decision a reviewer can use


      Attribute requests, tokens, storage and background work to the fictional team
      that generated them. Keep actual usage separate from prices or rates assumed
      in a simulation. A vendor comparison begins with a fixed use case and requirements,
      uses the same task set where possible, and marks missing evidence explicitly.
      A weighted score is a model of the decision; sensitivity analysis exposes when
      a modest change of assumptions reverses the recommendation.


      The final design memo links each important claim to a trace, test, workload
      or explicit assumption. Its stakeholder page explains the user problem, proposed
      scope, costs, alternatives, surviving failures and ownership of remaining decisions.
      The technical appendix retains the permission matrix, source/freshness policy,
      copy inventory, regression results and recovery evidence. It supports a bounded
      rollout decision rather than promising that the assistant is universally safe.'
    lab_and_evidence: '### Walkthroughs to prepare


      Trace a successful request, an unsupported question, a forbidden cross-organization
      request, and a dependency failure. For each, record the initial fixture state,
      actual inputs to each component, intended boundary decision, final response,
      and any lasting effect. A failure report needs the same identity and version
      fields as a successful run.


      ### Baselines and artifact contracts


      Produce permission matrices, allowed/denied traces, synchronization and deletion
      reports, labeled benign/adversarial cases, cost reports, and a decision memo.
      Measure both harmful actions allowed and legitimate tasks blocked. Freeze test
      cases before comparing defenses and report surviving attacks and untested conditions.
      Audit records describe actual input identities, evidence IDs, tool outcomes,
      and versions; generated explanations are not proof of a model''s internal causal
      reasoning.


      Before comparing a change, define the task set, independent expected results,
      allowed resource budget and simplest relevant baseline. Keep raw case-level
      records so the report can be recalculated. Declare which parts are fixture-based,
      which use a model, and which use actual services or provisioned resources. A
      useful artifact includes a lockfile, fixture version/hash, proposed reproduction
      command, configuration, measured units, result, observed failure and limitation.
      A negative or inconclusive comparison remains a valid completed learning artifact.


      ### Initial design exercise


      Draw the components and annotate the data passed across each boundary. Define
      one versioned fixture schema and one output record using the interfaces above.
      Write independent checks for one happy case and one failure before implementing
      the controller. Show how a result from a standalone lab can be consumed by the
      optional shared project without depending on private mutable state. Establish
      a small time and resource allowance for the first build; keep optional cloud
      or model runs separately budgeted.


      The overview deliverable is a diagram, interface/data inventory, fixture schema,
      baseline/report specification and resource plan. No benchmark value should be
      filled in until that workload has actually run. The following chapters implement
      these components and explain the results; the overview supplies their shared
      vocabulary and limits.'

    section: main
  - content: "Give a simulated support agent read-ticket and add-note tools. Define\
      \ analyst and support-lead roles within two organizations. Check permissions\
      \ inside the application dispatcher and downstream resource handler for every\
      \ invocation. Reject unknown tools and invalid arguments before use; keep identity\
      \ trusted and independent of user text. Explain capability discovery, identity,\
      \ role, and authorization as separate objects.\n\nThe lesson below specifies\
      \ an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts\
      \ and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable\
      \ code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each\
      \ lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\n## What\
      \ you will build\n\nBuild a small support agent that can read tickets and add\
      \ internal notes. An analyst\ncan read tickets assigned to them; a support lead\
      \ can read and annotate tickets in their\norganization. Neither can access another\
      \ organization's tickets. You will deliberately\nmake the agent request forbidden\
      \ operations, then inspect the tool results and stored\nnotes to see where authorization\
      \ was enforced.\n\nThe artifact is a permission matrix, an enforced tool dispatcher,\
      \ and a reproducible\nreport of allowed and denied calls. Login concepts come\
      \ from Foundations; this chapter\nfocuses on checking the user, action, and\
      \ particular resource at every tool call.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n\
      - Tool-calling and bounded agent loops from Foundations 8\n  and 9, or equivalent\
      \ experience.\n- Authentication and document permissions from Foundations 35.\n\
      \  Equivalent understanding of verified identity, scoped roles, and server-side\
      \ access\n  checks suffices.\n- Python functions, exceptions, simple SQL, and\
      \ tests. No other Enterprise guide or\n  portfolio project is required, and\
      \ no earlier implementation is imported.\n\nUse Python 3.13, SQLite from the\
      \ standard library, and pytest in a lesson-local project.\nA deterministic model\
      \ double supplies tool calls for the core experiment. A hosted model\nand real\
      \ login integration are optional extensions, not prerequisites for running the\n\
      permission tests. The tree, interfaces, and commands below describe code you\
      \ will build.\n\n## Begin with specific users and records\n\nCreate these synthetic\
      \ users and memberships:\n\n| User | Organization | Role |\n|---|---|---|\n\
      | Alice | Acme | analyst |\n| Liam | Acme | lead |\n| Ben | Birch | analyst\
      \ |\n| Bea | Birch | lead |\n\nCreate ticket `A1` assigned to Alice, ticket\
      \ `A2` assigned to Liam, and ticket `B1`\nassigned to Ben. Each ticket has its\
      \ own organization's ID and a short body. Store notes\nin a separate table referencing\
      \ the ticket. There is no global administrator in this lab.\n\n| Operation |\
      \ Acme analyst Alice | Acme lead Liam | Birch lead Bea |\n|---|---|---|---|\n\
      | Read A1 | allow | allow | deny |\n| Read A2 | deny | allow | deny |\n| Read\
      \ B1 | deny | deny | allow |\n| Add note to A1 | deny | allow | deny |\n| Add\
      \ note to B1 | deny | deny | allow |\n\nAdd Ben's cases when writing the full\
      \ matrix. Check allowed actions as carefully as denied\nones: a dispatcher that\
      \ refuses everything has not implemented this policy correctly.\n\n**Authentication**\
      \ establishes identity. **Authorization** decides whether that identity\nmay\
      \ perform an action on a resource. **Role-based access control (RBAC)** grants\
      \ actions\nthrough roles, but a role such as lead still needs a resource scope:\
      \ Liam is a lead in\nAcme, not Birch. A **principal** is the identity on whose\
      \ behalf the operation runs.\n\nStart with an intentionally incomplete baseline\
      \ that checks only role-to-action\nmembership. Show that Liam can read B1 through\
      \ this baseline. Then add organization and\nassignment checks and rerun the\
      \ identical call. Keep the baseline in the test harness,\nnot as an alternate\
      \ route exposed by the repaired service.\n\n## Keep identity separate from model\
      \ arguments\n\nThe core runner selects a synthetic authenticated user from trusted\
      \ fixture configuration\nand passes an immutable principal to the agent loop.\
      \ This is an authorization test\nadapter, not a real authentication mechanism.\
      \ The model can supply a ticket ID and note\ntext; it cannot supply its principal,\
      \ roles, organization, or a policy decision.\n\nAn optional web adapter obtains\
      \ the principal from a verified session using an established\nlogin library.\
      \ Neither a request-body `user_id` nor a model-generated `role=lead` establishes\n\
      identity. Membership and assignment data are read from the store when each tool\
      \ executes,\nnot copied into an agent's initial prompt and treated as permanent\
      \ authority.\n\nExpose exactly two tools:\n\n- `read_ticket(ticket_id)` returns\
      \ a visible ticket and its notes.\n- `add_note(ticket_id, text)` appends one\
      \ bounded note to a permitted ticket.\n\nUse a fixed registry mapping tool names\
      \ to argument schemas, action names, and protected\nhandlers. Unknown tools\
      \ and unexpected fields are rejected. Limit IDs to the fixture's\nID format\
      \ and note text to 500 characters. Validate structure before resource lookup;\n\
      resolve the ticket's organization and owner from the database, never from supplied\
      \ metadata.\n\nThe dispatcher checks permission before returning content or\
      \ changing data. Handlers are\ninternal functions; the agent loop and any future\
      \ HTTP adapter must use the dispatcher.\nNo `eval`, dynamic imports, generic\
      \ SQL tool, or direct unprotected tool route belongs in\nthis lab. Tool schemas\
      \ guide model output but do not enforce permissions by themselves.\n\n```text\n\
      trusted identity adapter -> principal ---------------------+\n             \
      \                                            |\nmodel -> tool name + validated\
      \ arguments -> dispatcher -> permission decision\n                         \
      \                                |\n                                     allow\
      \ -> read/write -> filtered result\n                                     deny\
      \  -> generic denial, no ticket content\n```\n\nThe dispatcher is the **policy\
      \ enforcement point**: the code that applies the decision.\nThe policy function\
      \ makes that decision from the principal, action, membership, and\nresource.\
      \ Its name is less important than keeping every invocation on the checked path.\n\
      Default denial and checks on every request follow\n[OWASP authorization guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html).\n\
      \n## Decision timing and failure behavior\n\nFor a small SQLite fixture, begin\
      \ a short transaction before resolving membership and\nresource state, deciding,\
      \ and applying a note. Use `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` for mutations and\nfor membership/assignment\
      \ changes so another writer cannot change those facts between\npermission evaluation\
      \ and the write. Do not hold a transaction while waiting for a model.\nThis\
      \ simple serialization is a lab choice, not a high-throughput database design.\n\
      [SQLite transaction documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html)\n\
      \nSet a bounded database busy timeout. If a transaction cannot acquire its lock,\
      \ return a\ntemporary failure without executing the tool; roll back unfinished\
      \ work on errors.\n\nRead decisions use the snapshot in their read transaction.\
      \ A membership revocation\ncommitted before the next tool transaction begins\
      \ must affect that call, even within the\nsame conversation. The exercise does\
      \ not promise to recall text already returned or\ncancel a call that authorized\
      \ before revocation committed.\n\nMissing identity, missing membership, unknown\
      \ role/action, absent resource, and failed\npolicy lookup all prevent execution.\
      \ Distinguish a temporary store error from a policy\ndenial in internal logs,\
      \ but return no restricted record details. Log a request/call ID,\nuser ID,\
      \ action, resource ID, decision/reason code, and whether a mutation committed.\n\
      Do not log credentials, ticket bodies, or note text. This is diagnostic logging,\
      \ not an\nimmutable audit system; Guide 2 studies audit records.\n\n## Project\
      \ shape and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\nweek01/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── schema.sql\n├── gated_agent/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n│   ├── principal.py\n\
      │   ├── fixtures.py\n│   ├── store.py\n│   ├── policy.py\n│   ├── enforcement.py\n\
      │   ├── tools.py\n│   ├── agent.py\n│   └── cli.py\n├── tests/\n│   ├── test_policy.py\n\
      │   ├── test_enforcement.py\n│   └── test_agent.py\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\n\
      ```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import Any\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class Principal:\n    user_id: str\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Resource:\n\
      \    ticket_id: str\n    org_id: str\n    assigned_user_id: str\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class Decision:\n    allowed: bool\n    reason_code: str\n\ndef is_allowed(principal:\
      \ Principal, action: str, resource: Resource,\n               membership_role:\
      \ str | None) -> Decision:\n    \"\"\"Role is resolved for this principal in\
      \ resource.org_id by trusted store code.\"\"\"\n    ...\n\ndef enforce(conn,\
      \ principal: Principal, tool_name: str,\n            arguments: dict[str, Any])\
      \ -> dict:\n    \"\"\"Validate, resolve facts, decide, and execute within the\
      \ defined transaction.\"\"\"\n    ...\n\ndef run_agent_turn(principal: Principal,\
      \ message: str, model, store) -> dict:\n    \"\"\"Route every proposed call\
      \ through enforce; stop after four calls or a final answer.\"\"\"\n    ...\n\
      ```\n\nKeep policy expectations in a handwritten test matrix, not generated\
      \ by calling\n`is_allowed` itself. Test data for membership lookups must include\
      \ two users with the\nsame role in different organizations."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 17 hours\n\n1. **Fixture and matrix, 3\
      \ hours.** Seed users, memberships, tickets, and notes. Write\n   expected decisions\
      \ and run the role-only baseline showing the cross-organization bug.\n2. **Scoped\
      \ policy, 3 hours.** Implement organization, assignment, and action checks.\n\
      \   Compare every matrix entry, including missing identities and memberships.\n\
      3. **Enforced handlers, 4 hours.** Validate arguments, resolve authoritative\
      \ metadata,\n   add transaction boundaries, and route reads/writes through the\
      \ dispatcher. Inspect\n   both returned content and database changes after denied\
      \ attempts.\n4. **Agent integration, 3 hours.** Use a model double that emits\
      \ exact tool-call JSON.\n   Exercise authority spoofing, guessed resource IDs,\
      \ and a repeated call after denial.\n   Keep a four-call limit so an agent cannot\
      \ loop on the same refusal forever.\n5. **Changing permissions, 2 hours.** Remove\
      \ Liam's membership between two tool calls\n   in the same conversation. Commit\
      \ that change, then verify the next call is denied.\n6. **Evidence and review,\
      \ 2 hours.** Generate the report, inspect all tool entry paths,\n   and document\
      \ one limitation. Do not add a login tutorial or broad policy framework.\n\n\
      ## Tests and interpreting model behavior\n\nFor each forbidden operation, the\
      \ deterministic suite forces the tool request to occur.\nThis tests enforcement\
      \ even when a real model would refuse the prompt. Include:\n\n- allowed reads\
      \ and writes for the expected users;\n- an analyst requesting a lead-only write;\n\
      - a lead naming another organization's ticket;\n- forged `role`, `org_id`, or\
      \ `user_id` arguments;\n- malformed IDs, oversized notes, and unknown tool names;\n\
      - a revoked membership between calls;\n- a store exception before a write, with\
      \ no committed note;\n- an agent repeating a denied call until its call budget\
      \ is exhausted.\n\nUse a handler spy and inspect the database to verify a denied\
      \ request never invokes the\nprotected operation. For denied reads, also inspect\
      \ the tool result and subsequent model\ncontext for restricted content. A valid\
      \ in-scope call must still succeed.\n\nAn optional real-model run can place\
      \ an instruction in a synthetic ticket asking the\nagent to read another organization's\
      \ ticket. Record whether the model attempted the\ncall. If it did not, enforcement\
      \ was **not exercised** for that sample; do not count the\nmodel's refusal as\
      \ a dispatcher denial. Keep this exploratory result separate from the\ndeterministic\
      \ regression suite.\n\n## Commands and evidence\n\nFrom this lesson directory,\
      \ create a local project with pytest and implement these CLI\ncommands before\
      \ using them as reproduction instructions:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\nuv run python\
      \ -m gated_agent.cli seed --database artifacts/tickets.sqlite\nuv run pytest\
      \ tests -q\nuv run python -m gated_agent.cli compare --cases matrix --out artifacts/policy-comparison.json\n\
      uv run python -m gated_agent.cli exercise --model scripted --out artifacts/enforcement-report.md\n\
      ```\n\nThe seed command creates a dedicated fixture; replacing existing data\
      \ requires an explicit\nreset flag and a check that the database is the marked\
      \ lab database. Tests use isolated\ntemporary databases. Pin dependencies in\
      \ the local lockfile and record Python/SQLite versions.\n\nThe report includes\
      \ principal, action, resource, expected decision, observed decision,\nwhether\
      \ a tool was requested, whether it executed, and whether data changed. Add a\n\
      comparison of the role-only and repaired versions and a revocation timeline.\
      \ Missing\nor failed checks are reported as such, not turned into claims that\
      \ the entire system is\nsecure. Finite tests support the tested rules and invocation\
      \ paths only.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and optional depth\n\nCPU and a local filesystem\
      \ suffice; the core target cost is $0. No Docker, identity\nprovider, or hosted\
      \ model subscription is required for the deterministic experiment.\n\nOptional\
      \ extensions are an established login adapter, a small hosted-model run capped\n\
      at $2, or a list tool with permission-constrained queries. Login belongs in\
      \ Foundations\n35; external document permission synchronization belongs in Guide\
      \ 3.\nSystems security lessons later add narrower execution capabilities and\
      \ larger attack\nexperiments. No portfolio work or outside reviewer is required\
      \ here.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment,\
      \ fixture and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command\
      \ and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."
