  - content: "Copy documents, revisions, and access metadata from a simulated workplace\
      \ source. Filter authorized candidates before final ranking and before text\
      \ reaches the generator. Handle incremental updates, deletions, permission revocation,\
      \ stale indexes, and failed synchronization. Define an explicit freshness and\
      \ failure policy. Inspect citations and result identifiers as possible leaks,\
      \ not only generated text.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and\
      \ experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed\
      \ lab artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results\
      \ already exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## What you will build\n\nBuild a small\
      \ document assistant that copies documents and permissions from a simulated\n\
      workplace source. Ask the same question as an employee and as a human-resources\
      \ (HR)\nuser, then remove the HR user's access while the search index is out\
      \ of date. Inspect\nwhich documents reach retrieval results, citations, and\
      \ the answer generator.\n\nYou will implement incremental synchronization, permission-constrained\
      \ retrieval, and\nchecks for deletion, revocation, and failed synchronization.\
      \ The result is a local\nexperiment showing both what a user can retrieve and\
      \ how quickly source changes become\nusable. No real workplace account or hosted\
      \ model is required.\n\n## Prerequisites and scope\n\n- Retrieval and generation\
      \ concepts from Foundations 16,\n  or equivalent experience. Retrieval-augmented\
      \ generation (**RAG**) supplies retrieved\n  source text to a model when generating\
      \ an answer.\n- Identity, action, and resource permissions from Guide 1.\n \
      \ Login concepts are covered by Foundations 35,\n  and no login flow is implemented\
      \ again here.\n- Basic Python, SQL, transactions, and tests. No previous lesson\
      \ code or portfolio\n  repository is required.\n\nUse Python 3.13, SQLite, and\
      \ pytest. The core source is an in-process adapter backed by\nits own database;\
      \ the local index uses a separate database. This keeps the source/index\nfailure\
      \ boundary explicit without requiring a cloud connector. All files and commands\n\
      below describe what to implement, not a supplied executable service.\n\n## A\
      \ small source with changing permissions\n\nCreate two organizations, Acme and\
      \ Birch, each with an employee and an HR user. Source\nuser and group IDs are\
      \ qualified by organization so a group named `hr` in one organization\ncannot\
      \ grant access in the other. The harness supplies a trusted synthetic user identity;\n\
      query text and model output cannot select or override that identity.\n\nAn **access\
      \ control list (ACL)** specifies who may read a document. For this fixture,\n\
      allow direct user grants or group membership, require the same organization,\
      \ and let an\nexplicit user denial override either grant. Empty or malformed\
      \ permissions deny access.\nThis is the mock source's policy, not a universal\
      \ interpretation of every provider's ACL.\n\n| Source record | Initial access\
      \ | Controlled change |\n|---|---|---|\n| Acme handbook | Acme employee group,\
      \ including HR | Edit body without changing access |\n| Acme salary memo | Acme\
      \ HR group | Remove the HR grant without changing body |\n| Acme private appendix\
      \ | Direct grant to Acme HR user | Add an explicit denial for that user |\n\
      | Birch salary memo | Birch HR group | No change; cross-organization control\
      \ |\n| Acme draft policy | Acme employee group | Delete the document |\n\nAdd\
      \ filler records to reach 30 documents and a query set of ten questions. Include\
      \ an\nHR-membership removal as a separate event: it changes access without modifying\
      \ any\nof the documents that grant that group access.\n\nSplit each document\
      \ into chunks of at most 80 whitespace-separated words. Use exact\nquery-token\
      \ match counts for ranking, breaking ties by document ID and chunk number.\n\
      Make the restricted salary memo rank above a visible handbook passage for a\
      \ salary\nquery. A deterministic scorer makes permission errors reproducible;\
      \ embeddings are optional.\n\nThe answer generator records its input chunks\
      \ and returns a fixed answer with their\nIDs as citations. Testing that captured\
      \ input is stronger evidence of filtering than\nhoping the final answer does\
      \ not mention a forbidden document.\n\n## Synchronize state without skipping\
      \ changes\n\nA **connector** adapts source data to your local representation.\
      \ **Incremental sync**\nprocesses changes since a saved position, called a **cursor**,\
      \ instead of rereading every\nrecord. A **tombstone** records a deletion even\
      \ after the source body is gone.\n\nImplement the mock source with a monotonically\
      \ increasing event number and a durable\nchange log. Each event carries its\
      \ organization, kind, entity ID, and the full state\nat that event's revision;\
      \ deletions carry a tombstone. Include document-body changes,\nACL-only changes,\
      \ and group-membership changes. Event numbers, rather than wall-clock\nmodification\
      \ times, avoid ambiguous ties in this exercise.\n\nThe connector returns pages\
      \ of at most five events and a next cursor. In one local\nindex transaction,\
      \ apply the entire page and save its cursor. If the process fails\nbefore commit,\
      \ neither page nor cursor advances; replay is expected. Applying the same\n\
      event again must not create duplicate chunks or roll an entity back to an older\
      \ revision.\n\nOn a body change, atomically replace the document's complete\
      \ chunk set. Upserting only\nexisting chunk positions leaves orphan chunks when\
      \ the new document is shorter. An\nACL-only change updates its permission record\
      \ without rebuilding chunks. A deletion\nremoves its chunks and retains the\
      \ deletion revision so older events cannot resurrect it.\nKeep the local membership\
      \ mirror for comparison, but do not treat it as current authority.\n\nReal providers\
      \ have their own change-tracking rules. For example, Microsoft Graph uses\n\
      opaque continuation/delta links and warns that items may appear repeatedly;\
      \ a connector\nmust follow the provider contract rather than inventing a timestamp\
      \ cursor.\n[Microsoft Graph delta guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/delta-query-overview)\n\
      \n## Decide what stale permissions mean\n\nFirst implement an intentionally\
      \ incomplete path that filters only on the local permission\nmirror. After a\
      \ source revocation and before sync, show whether this path still returns\n\
      restricted content. This baseline runs only on synthetic fixtures.\n\nThe repaired\
      \ core uses the source as the authority for each request:\n\n1. Ask the source\
      \ for a snapshot of the user's currently permitted document IDs and\n   content\
      \ revisions, resolving current group memberships in the same snapshot.\n2. Restrict\
      \ the local candidate set to those IDs and matching content revisions before\n\
      \   ranking or returning text. A missing or stale local revision is unavailable\
      \ until synced.\n3. Before constructing generator context, batch-check the selected\
      \ ID/revision pairs\n   against current source permissions and content revisions\
      \ again. Use one snapshot\n   for the whole batch. Drop any candidate that is\
      \ no longer valid.\n4. Send only the approved chunks to generation. If candidates\
      \ were dropped, returning\n   fewer results is acceptable; replenishing them\
      \ is an optional bounded retry.\n\nThe initial eligibility snapshot is a small-corpus\
      \ teaching interface, not a claim that\nreal directories offer a cheap list\
      \ of every permitted document. In a larger deployment,\nsource APIs and indexed\
      \ permission predicates require their own design and measurement.\n\n**Revocation\
      \ boundary:** the final source validation snapshot is the authorization decision\n\
      point for generation. A revocation committed before that check must exclude\
      \ the document.\nA change committed afterward cannot recall content already\
      \ authorized and in flight.\nUse an event barrier in tests to place a revocation\
      \ between candidate selection and this\ncheck. Avoid an unqualified claim of\
      \ instantaneous revocation.\n\nIf authoritative validation is unavailable, generation\
      \ does not proceed. Return a temporary\nfailure, not an old permissive result\
      \ or an empty result labeled successful. A stalled sync\nwith a working authority\
      \ can still serve current indexed revisions; stale content is\nwithheld. This\
      \ trades availability and completeness for current access decisions.\n\nSearch\
      \ snippets and direct document/citation reads also validate identity, permission,\n\
      and content revision before returning text. The source connector's broad ingestion\n\
      credential, if added later, does not grant that same access to the end user.\
      \ Request-level\nchecks follow [OWASP authorization guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html).\n\
      \n## Separate retrieval quality from access correctness\n\nOn a frozen source/index\
      \ snapshot, compare three paths with the same scoring function:\n\n- **Relevance\
      \ only:** rank everything; an unsafe local baseline.\n- **Rank then filter:**\
      \ take the top five globally ranked candidates, filter by current\n  access,\
      \ then return at most three. Filtering happens before any user/model output.\n\
      - **Filter then rank:** rank the exact authorized, current candidate set and\
      \ return at\n  most three. This is the repaired core's selection strategy.\n\
      \nThe rank-then-filter path can return fewer useful results when restricted\
      \ candidates fill\nits initial five slots. Neither protected path should return\
      \ unauthorized content. They\nneed not return identical sets: that difference\
      \ is part of the experiment.\n\nUse exhaustive scoring over the authorized snapshot\
      \ as the retrieval reference. Measure\nagreement with its top three separately\
      \ from human-labeled question relevance. Also report\nhow often a path returns\
      \ fewer than three when at least three eligible chunks exist;\nthat count alone\
      \ is not a recall metric. Do not treat queries with no eligible chunks\nas retrieval\
      \ failures or divide their overlap by zero.\n\nExact filtering here does not\
      \ establish perfect recall for approximate vector search.\nSome engines apply\
      \ metadata filters after scanning an approximate index, and scan limits\ncan\
      \ affect the returned set. A vector extension needs its own comparison against\
      \ exact\nsearch. [pgvector filtering documentation](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#filtering)\n\
      \n## Project shape and incomplete interfaces\n\n```text\nweek03/\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── source_schema.sql\n├── index_schema.sql\n├── permission_rag/\n│   ├── __init__.py\n\
      │   ├── source.py        # authoritative fixtures, events, access snapshots\n\
      │   ├── connector.py     # paginated event interface\n│   ├── sync.py      \
      \    # atomic page application and cursor\n│   ├── retrieval.py     # baseline\
      \ and protected candidate selection\n│   ├── context.py       # final validation\
      \ and generator spy\n│   └── cli.py\n├── tests/\n└── artifacts/\n```\n\n```python\n\
      from dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom typing import Protocol\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class Principal:\n    user_id: str\n    org_id: str\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class Candidate:\n    org_id: str\n    document_id: str\n    content_revision:\
      \ int\n    chunk_number: int\n    text: str\n\nclass Source(Protocol):\n   \
      \ def changes(self, cursor: int, limit: int) -> tuple[list[dict], int]: ...\n\
      \    def visible_revisions(self, principal: Principal) -> dict[str, int]: ...\n\
      \    def validate_batch(self, principal: Principal,\n                      \
      \ candidates: list[Candidate]) -> list[bool]: ...\n\ndef apply_page(index_conn,\
      \ events: list[dict], next_cursor: int) -> None: ...\n\ndef retrieve(query:\
      \ str, principal: Principal, source: Source,\n             index_conn, strategy:\
      \ str, limit: int = 3) -> list[Candidate]: ...\n\ndef build_checked_context(principal:\
      \ Principal, candidates: list[Candidate],\n                          source:\
      \ Source) -> str: ...\n```\n\nStore documents/chunks, ACL records, memberships,\
      \ entity revisions, and the cursor in the\nindex database. Preserve content\
      \ revision independently of permission revision. The source\nand index use separate\
      \ transactions; the code does not pretend their state changes atomically.\n\
      Do not log source text or unfiltered candidate bodies in ordinary request logs."
    lab_and_evidence: "## Build sequence — 19 hours\n\n1. **Fixture and policy oracle,\
      \ 3 hours.** Write the expected user/document matrix and\n   query labels by\
      \ hand. Implement the source policy and exact scoring on small examples.\n2.\
      \ **Paged sync, 4 hours.** Add event pages, revision guards, complete chunk\
      \ replacement,\n   and cursor commits. Crash before commit and replay; compare\
      \ the final index to a clean sync.\n3. **Retrieval comparison, 3 hours.** Implement\
      \ the three frozen-snapshot strategies,\n   capture context, and measure access\
      \ outcomes and retrieval completeness separately.\n4. **Current authority, 4\
      \ hours.** Add initial eligibility and final batch validation.\n   Revoke a\
      \ document grant and a group membership while sync is paused; verify the result.\n\
      5. **Failures and changing content, 3 hours.** Delete a document, shorten another,\
      \ break\n   authoritative validation, and revoke between selection and context\
      \ assembly. Repeat\n   after recovery and verify legitimate results remain available.\n\
      6. **Report and scope review, 2 hours.** Save timelines, cursor evidence, query\
      \ results,\n   and limitations. Keep real connectors and embedding experiments\
      \ optional.\n\n## Commands, checks, and evidence\n\nImplement these commands\
      \ and run from the lesson directory:\n\n```bash\nuv sync\nuv run python -m permission_rag.cli\
      \ seed --source artifacts/source.sqlite --index artifacts/index.sqlite\nuv run\
      \ python -m permission_rag.cli sync --page-size 5\nuv run pytest tests -q\n\
      uv run python -m permission_rag.cli compare --out artifacts/retrieval.json\n\
      uv run python -m permission_rag.cli lifecycle --out artifacts/access-timeline.jsonl\n\
      uv run python -m permission_rag.cli report --out artifacts/report.md\n```\n\n\
      Seed creates only marked lesson databases; destructive reset requires an explicit\
      \ flag.\nThe sync command uses those same default fixture paths. Tests use isolated\
      \ temporary\nfiles, deterministic event barriers, and a controllable source-outage\
      \ switch.\n\nTest direct/group grants, organization separation, explicit denial,\
      \ unknown identities,\nACL-only updates, membership-only updates, repeated pages,\
      \ crash-before-commit, shorter\ncontent, tombstones, stale-event replay, and\
      \ source failure. Check current metadata against\nan independent handwritten\
      \ oracle rather than generating expectations with the same policy\nfunction\
      \ being tested. Inspect generator input, snippets, and citation reads, including\n\
      allowed controls. Denying every request is not a correct implementation.\n\n\
      In the report, record source event/permission revisions, index cursor, content\
      \ revisions,\nquery identity, selected IDs, final validation outcome, and whether\
      \ generation occurred.\nMeasure the lag until changed content is usable separately\
      \ from access revocation behavior.\nA blocked request during a source outage\
      \ is an availability cost to report. Any leaked\nfixture content is a failed\
      \ access check to investigate, not a safe result.\n\n## Hardware, cost, and\
      \ optional depth\n\nA laptop and CPU suffice; core target cost is $0 with no\
      \ Docker, cloud, provider account,\nor real organization data required. Pin\
      \ local dependencies and record Python/SQLite versions.\nA real connector, nested\
      \ groups, inherited permissions, approximate vector search, or an\nanswer cache\
      \ is an extension, not another required build. Inherited and explicit-deny\n\
      semantics must match the chosen source rather than this simplified mock.\n\n\
      The live-source validation path demonstrates this source contract only. If a\
      \ provider\ncannot support current validation, a different design must state\
      \ its freshness limit\nand outage behavior explicitly. The exercise does not\
      \ establish a universal permission\nmodel, complete security, or capacity for\
      \ a production document collection.\n\n### Report the actual execution path\n\
      \nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration identities, case-level\
      \ outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation. Distinguish offline\
      \ mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements.\
      \ Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are\
      \ planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set\
      \ a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate\
      \ from the baseline report."

  - content: "Process synthetic names, account identifiers, and contact details through\
      \ independent input/output redaction and validation stages. Preserve only the\
      \ audit fields needed to reconstruct identity references, evidence versions,\
      \ model/tool outcomes, and control decisions. Explain access restrictions, append-only\
      \ behavior, tamper detection, retention, and the limits of immutability claims.\
      \ Use ephemeral controlled mappings if a fixture needs reversible substitution.\n\
      \nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces,\
      \ stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not\
      \ indicate that executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone\
      \ fixture for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course\
      \ project.\n\n## Scope of the experiment\n\nThe evaluation uses labeled synthetic\
      \ names, emails and identifiers. Measure detector misses and unnecessary redactions;\
      \ the absence of the known fixture strings is a bounded check, not a guarantee\
      \ for arbitrary personal data. Hash chaining detects edits relative to a retained\
      \ trusted head; an attacker able to rewrite the file and head can produce a\
      \ consistent new chain. Separate append-only permissions, detection, external\
      \ anchoring, and retention. Pseudonymized identifiers remain sensitive.\n\n\
      ## Overview\n\nCompliance isn't \"did we do the right thing,\" it's \"can we\
      \ prove we did,\" after\nthe fact, without re-running anything. This chapter\
      \ builds a pipeline that redacts\nPII before it reaches the LLM and reversibly\
      \ reconstructs it in the response,\nalongside an append-only audit log recording\
      \ every request, redaction, and\ndecision. What happened and why for a past\
      \ request is reconstructed from the\naudit log alone, with no access to the\
      \ original live request. Compliance\nbecomes a provable, after-the-fact-checkable\
      \ property rather than a policy\nstatement.\n\nThe shift in mindset this chapter\
      \ is from *doing* to *proving*. A pipeline that\nredacts PII correctly but keeps\
      \ no durable, tamper-evident record is worthless\nto an auditor six months later:\
      \ they can't re-run last quarter's traffic, and\nyour word that \"it worked\"\
      \ is not evidence. So you build two things that must\nhold each other honest\
      \ — a redaction layer that never lets raw PII reach the\nmodel or the logs,\
      \ and an append-only ledger that lets a third party\nreconstruct any past request's\
      \ handling and *detect* if anyone edited the\nrecord. The deliverable is the\
      \ reconstruction itself: given only the log, prove\nwhat happened.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\
      \n- **Service basics:** you can build a small HTTP service, wire up a hosted\
      \ LLM API\n  key, and run a container.\n- **No prior week required.** Week 1's\
      \ RBAC-gated agent is the natural host to\n  drop this pipeline into (redact\
      \ at the same boundary you authorize at), but\n  this chapter stands alone.\n\
      - **Conceptual comfort with:** cryptographic hashes as one-way, collision-\n\
      \  resistant fingerprints (SHA-256 level — you *use* a hash, you don't implement\n\
      \  one); symmetric encryption at the \"I can call `encrypt`/`decrypt` with a\
      \ key\n  from an env var\" level; and regular expressions for the deterministic\
      \ slice of\n  detection.\n- **Tooling:** Python 3.11+, `git`, a package manager\
      \ (`uv` recommended), and\n  Docker. One hosted LLM API key (OpenAI/Anthropic/Azure\
      \ OpenAI/Bedrock — any).\n\n## What you'll be able to do by the end\n\n- Detect\
      \ PII in free text with a **layered detector** (deterministic patterns +\n \
      \ an optional NER model) and reason about its precision/recall tradeoffs.\n\
      - **Reversibly pseudonymize** PII: replace each entity with a stable token,\n\
      \  store the mapping in an encrypted vault, and reconstruct the original in\
      \ the\n  model's response — without the original ever touching the LLM or the\
      \ log.\n- Distinguish **reversible** from **irreversible** redaction and pick\
      \ correctly\n  per field.\n- Build an **append-only, hash-chained audit log**\
      \ and *prove* tamper-evidence:\n  any edit, reorder, or deletion of a past record\
      \ is detectable.\n- Reconstruct \"**what happened and why**\" for an arbitrary\
      \ past request from the\n  log alone — the week's headline check.\n\n## Mental\
      \ model: two ledgers that distrust each other\n\nHold two objects in mind. The\
      \ **vault** is the only place raw PII lives; it is\nencrypted at rest and never\
      \ leaves your trust boundary. The **audit log** is a\nrecord auditors can read;\
      \ it must contain *enough to explain every decision*\nwhile containing *no raw\
      \ PII at all*. The tension between them is the whole week:\nthe log must be\
      \ rich enough to reconstruct what happened, yet it can only ever\nreference\
      \ PII by token, never by value. If you ever find yourself about to write\na\
      \ real email address into the log, you've made a mistake the audit is\nspecifically\
      \ designed to catch.\n\nA useful test for every field you're about to log: *\"\
      If this file leaked\ntomorrow, is anyone's personal data exposed?\"* If yes,\
      \ it belongs in the\nencrypted vault as ciphertext or a token — never in the\
      \ log as plaintext.\n\n## Key concepts & definitions\n\n- **PII (personally\
      \ identifiable information).** Data that identifies a person:\n  names, emails,\
      \ phone numbers, national IDs, addresses, account numbers. Some\n  is structured\
      \ (matches a pattern), some is contextual (a name only\n  identifiable as a\
      \ name from surrounding words).\n- **Redaction vs. pseudonymization.** *Redaction*\
      \ removes information\n  (`[REDACTED]`) — irreversible. *Pseudonymization* replaces\
      \ it with a token\n  (`<PERSON_1>`) whose mapping is stored separately — reversible\
      \ if and only if\n  you hold the mapping.\n- **Reversible pseudonymization.**\
      \ Each detected entity → a stable token; the\n  `token → ciphertext(original)`\
      \ mapping lives in the vault. The LLM sees only\n  tokens; on the way back,\
      \ tokens in the response are swapped for decrypted\n  originals. This lets the\
      \ model do useful work (\"email the customer\") without\n  ever seeing the customer's\
      \ real address.\n- **Irreversible redaction.** For fields you must *never* be\
      \ able to recover\n  (e.g. a raw password accidentally pasted in), replace with\
      \ a fixed sentinel\n  and store *nothing* recoverable — not even a token.\n\
      - **Token vault.** An encrypted store mapping tokens to originals. Protected\
      \ by a\n  symmetric key held outside the code (env var / secrets manager). Losing\
      \ the key\n  means the mapping is unrecoverable — which is the point for deleted\
      \ data.\n- **Audit log / append-only.** A sequence of records where the only\
      \ permitted\n  operation is *append*. No update, no delete. Enforced structurally\
      \ (see hash\n  chaining), not just by policy.\n- **Tamper-evidence.** You cannot\
      \ make edits *impossible* on a normal disk, but\n  you can make any edit *detectable*.\
      \ A verifier that walks the log will fail at\n  the exact record where history\
      \ was altered.\n- **Hash chaining.** Each record embeds the hash of the previous\
      \ record, so the\n  records form a linked chain (a minimal blockchain-without-consensus).\
      \ Change\n  one record and every hash after it no longer matches.\n- **After-the-fact\
      \ reconstruction.** The property that a disinterested third\n  party, given\
      \ only the log, can both *reconstruct* handling and *verify* the\n  log wasn't\
      \ altered — with no access to the original live request or your code.\n\n##\
      \ The integrity math you'll implement\n\nThe audit log is a chain of records\
      \ $r_0, r_1, \\dots, r_n$. Let $H$ be a\ncryptographic hash (SHA-256). Each\
      \ record carries the hash of its predecessor:\n\n$$\nh_i = H\\big(\\,\\text{payload}_i\
      \ \\,\\Vert\\, h_{i-1}\\,\\big), \\qquad h_{-1} = h_{\\text{genesis}}\n$$\n\n\
      where $\\Vert$ is a canonical, unambiguous concatenation (serialize the payload\n\
      deterministically — sorted keys, fixed encoding — so the same record always\n\
      hashes identically) and $h_{\\text{genesis}}$ is a fixed public constant that\n\
      anchors the chain.\n\n**Why this gives tamper-evidence.** Suppose an adversary\
      \ edits record $r_k$ into\n$r_k'$ with $r_k' \\neq r_k$. By collision resistance\
      \ of $H$,\n$H(\\text{payload}_k' \\Vert h_{k-1}) \\neq h_k$ with overwhelming\
      \ probability. To\nkeep the stored chain internally consistent they must recompute\
      \ $h_k'$, which\nchanges the input to $h_{k+1}$, and so on — they must rewrite\
      \ *every* record from\n$k$ to $n$. A **verifier** recomputes each $h_i$ from\
      \ scratch and compares:\n\n$$\n\\textsf{verify}(r_0,\\dots,r_n) = \\bigwedge_{i=0}^{n}\
      \ \\Big[\\, h_i \\stackrel{?}{=} H(\\text{payload}_i \\Vert h_{i-1}) \\,\\Big]\n\
      $$\n\nThe first index where this fails localizes the tampering. This does not\
      \ stop an\nattacker who controls the whole file from rebuilding a fresh consistent\
      \ chain —\nfor that you'd anchor $h_n$ externally (periodically publish the\
      \ latest hash to a\nplace you don't control, or sign each head with a key the\
      \ writer doesn't hold).\nNote that dependency as a stretch goal; the in-repo\
      \ chain gives you *detection of\nedits*, which is the week's claim.\n\n**Determinism\
      \ is load-bearing.** If serialization isn't canonical, an honest\nre-verification\
      \ can fail (two encodings of the \"same\" record hash differently).\nPin a canonical\
      \ form and test that `serialize` is stable across runs.\n\n## What you're building\
      \ & how it's organized\n\nA small service: text goes in, redacted text goes\
      \ to the LLM, the response is\nreconstructed, and every step is logged to an\
      \ append-only chain. Everything below\nis yours to build from the stubs — nothing\
      \ here is a finished implementation.\n\n```\nweek02/\n├── README.md\n├── pyproject.toml\n\
      ├── docker-compose.yml          # the redaction service + a persistent log volume\n\
      ├── Dockerfile\n├── .env.example                # LLM_API_KEY=, VAULT_KEY= \
      \ (never commit .env)\n├── src/\n│   └── pii_week02/\n│       ├── __init__.py\n\
      │       ├── detect.py           # PiiDetector: regex layer + optional NER layer\n\
      │       ├── redact.py           # tokenize/detokenize against the vault\n│ \
      \      ├── vault.py            # encrypted token <-> original store\n│     \
      \  ├── audit.py            # append-only hash-chained log + verifier\n│    \
      \   ├── pipeline.py         # orchestration: detect -> redact -> LLM -> reconstruct\
      \ -> log\n│       ├── llm.py              # thin hosted-API client (sees redacted\
      \ text only)\n│       └── service.py          # HTTP endpoint wrapping the pipeline\n\
      ├── tools/\n│   ├── reconstruct.py          # rebuild \"what happened & why\"\
      \ from the log ALONE\n│   └── verify_chain.py         # walk the chain, report\
      \ first broken link (if any)\n├── data/                       # log file + vault\
      \ (git-ignored)\n└── tests/\n    ├── test_detect.py\n    ├── test_redact_roundtrip.py\n\
      \    ├── test_audit_chain.py\n    └── test_no_pii_in_log.py\n```\n\n### Stub\
      \ interfaces\n\nSignatures and docstrings only — bodies are `...`/`# TODO`.\
      \ Fill them in.\n\n```python\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nfrom enum import\
      \ Enum\n\nclass PiiType(str, Enum):\n    EMAIL = \"EMAIL\"\n    PHONE = \"PHONE\"\
      \n    PERSON = \"PERSON\"\n    NATIONAL_ID = \"NATIONAL_ID\"\n    # TODO: extend\
      \ as your detector grows\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass PiiSpan:\n    \"\"\
      \"One detected entity: its type and its [start, end) char offsets.\"\"\"\n \
      \   type: PiiType\n    start: int\n    end: int\n    reversible: bool  # True\
      \ -> vault + token; False -> irreversible sentinel\n\nclass PiiDetector:\n \
      \   def detect(self, text: str) -> list[PiiSpan]:\n        \"\"\"Return non-overlapping\
      \ spans. Layer detectors: deterministic regex\n        for structured PII (email/phone/ID),\
      \ then an optional NER pass for\n        contextual PII (PERSON). Resolve overlaps\
      \ deterministically.\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO: regex layer -> NER layer ->\
      \ merge/dedupe spans\n```\n\n```python\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass RedactionResult:\n\
      \    redacted_text: str            # tokens in place of PII; safe to send to\
      \ the LLM\n    token_map_id: str             # handle into the vault for this\
      \ request\n    spans: list[PiiSpan]          # what was found (types + offsets,\
      \ NOT values)\n\nclass Redactor:\n    def __init__(self, detector: PiiDetector,\
      \ vault: \"Vault\") -> None: ...\n\n    def redact(self, text: str) -> RedactionResult:\n\
      \        \"\"\"Detect PII; for each reversible span mint a stable token (e.g.\n\
      \        <EMAIL_1>) and store token->ciphertext(original) in the vault; for\
      \ each\n        irreversible span substitute a fixed sentinel and store nothing\n\
      \        recoverable. Return text safe to log/send.\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO\n\
      \n    def reconstruct(self, text_with_tokens: str, token_map_id: str) -> str:\n\
      \        \"\"\"Swap every reversible token in an LLM response back to its original\n\
      \        by decrypting the vault entry. Unknown tokens are left as-is.\"\"\"\
      \n        ...  # TODO\n```\n\n```python\nclass Vault:\n    \"\"\"Encrypted token\
      \ <-> original store. Symmetric key comes from VAULT_KEY;\n    it is never written\
      \ to disk in plaintext and never enters the audit log.\"\"\"\n\n    def put(self,\
      \ token_map_id: str, token: str, original: str) -> None:\n        \"\"\"Encrypt\
      \ `original` and store under (token_map_id, token).\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO:\
      \ encrypt-then-store\n\n    def get(self, token_map_id: str, token: str) ->\
      \ str | None:\n        \"\"\"Decrypt and return the original, or None if absent\
      \ (e.g. deleted).\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO\n```\n\n```python\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\n\
      class AuditRecord:\n    seq: int\n    ts: str                       # ISO-8601\
      \ UTC\n    event: str                    # \"request\" | \"redaction\" | \"\
      llm_call\" | \"decision\"\n    payload: dict                 # PII-FREE: token\
      \ ids, span types/offsets, model id...\n    prev_hash: str\n    hash: str\n\n\
      class AuditLog:\n    \"\"\"Append-only, hash-chained. The only mutating method\
      \ is `append`.\"\"\"\n\n    GENESIS = \"0\" * 64\n\n    def append(self, event:\
      \ str, payload: dict) -> AuditRecord:\n        \"\"\"Serialize (payload, prev_hash)\
      \ canonically; hash to get this record's\n        hash; append. MUST reject\
      \ any payload that fails the no-PII check.\"\"\"\n        ...  # TODO: canonical\
      \ serialize -> H(payload || prev_hash) -> append\n\n    def verify(self) ->\
      \ tuple[bool, int | None]:\n        \"\"\"Recompute the whole chain. Return\
      \ (ok, first_bad_seq). first_bad_seq\n        is None when ok is True.\"\"\"\
      \n        ...  # TODO\n```\n\nNote what the `AuditRecord.payload` may and may\
      \ not contain: token ids, span\n*types* and *offsets*, model name, latency,\
      \ a decision label — never a raw email,\nname, or the pre-redaction text."
    lab_and_evidence: "## How to build it — milestones\n\n1. **Detector.** Start with\
      \ regex for email/phone/national-ID (high precision).\n   Add an optional NER\
      \ pass (a small local model such as a spaCy pipeline, or a\n   hosted call)\
      \ for `PERSON`. Merge layers; resolve overlaps deterministically.\n   Do **not**\
      \ send raw text to a hosted detector if that would itself leak PII —\n   prefer\
      \ local NER, or accept that hosted detection is a trust decision to note.\n\
      2. **Vault.** Wrap symmetric encryption with a key from `VAULT_KEY`. `put`\n\
      \   encrypts, `get` decrypts. Never log the key or plaintext. Missing key →\
      \ hard\n   fail at startup, not a silent fallback.\n3. **Redactor.** Tokenize\
      \ reversible spans (`<EMAIL_1>`, stable within a\n   request), sentinel the\
      \ irreversible ones, and stash mappings in the vault.\n   Implement `reconstruct`\
      \ as the inverse over LLM output.\n4. **Audit log.** Canonical serialization\
      \ first (sorted keys, fixed encoding),\n   then the hash chain, then `append`\
      \ (append-only — no update/delete method\n   exists), then `verify`. Add a **no-PII\
      \ guard** in `append` that rejects\n   payloads containing anything that looks\
      \ like raw PII.\n5. **Pipeline.** Orchestrate: log `request` (redacted) → `redaction`\
      \ (spans, token\n   ids) → `llm_call` (model id, redacted-prompt hash) → reconstruct\
      \ → `decision`.\n   The LLM client only ever receives redacted text.\n6. **Service\
      \ + Docker.** Expose one endpoint; `docker compose up` runs the\n   service\
      \ with a persistent volume for `data/` (log + vault). Confirm the log\n   survives\
      \ a container restart.\n7. **Tools.** `tools/reconstruct.py` and `tools/verify_chain.py`\
      \ — the artifact.\n\n## Checkable artifact — Event reconstruction and tamper\
      \ checks\n\nThree checks together demonstrate the abstract's claim. Each runs\
      \ from the\ncommand line against a log/vault produced by real traffic through\
      \ the pipeline.\n\n**A. Reconstruct \"what happened and why\" from the log alone**\n\
      (`tools/reconstruct.py`). Given a request id or sequence range, and *only* the\n\
      audit log file (the script must not touch `service.py`, replay the request,\
      \ or\nread live state), emit a human-readable narrative: request received →\
      \ these PII\ntypes were detected at these offsets → redacted to these tokens\
      \ → this model was\ncalled → this decision was returned. It may resolve tokens\
      \ to originals *only* if\nexplicitly given vault access, and must clearly mark\
      \ when it does.\n\n- *Methodology:* parse records by `seq`; join `redaction`/`llm_call`/`decision`\n\
      \  events for the same request; render as ordered prose.\n- *Expected shape\
      \ of result:* a short report per request, e.g.\n\n  ```text\n  req 42 @ 2026-08-31T10:04:11Z\n\
      \    detected: EMAIL @[18,37], PERSON @[0,11]   (values not in log)\n    redacted\
      \ -> \"<PERSON_1> ... <EMAIL_1>\"; tokens minted: 2\n    llm: gpt-x; redacted-prompt-hash\
      \ 9f3c...; latency 812ms\n    decision: answered; response reconstructed (2\
      \ tokens re-expanded)\n  ```\n\n  Crucially: this reads coherently with **no\
      \ raw PII present** in the log, and a\n  reviewer who never saw the original\
      \ request understands exactly what happened.\n\n**B. Reversible round-trip**\
      \ (`test_redact_roundtrip.py` + a CLI demo). For a\nbatch of inputs containing\
      \ known PII: `redact` then `reconstruct` must return the\noriginal text exactly,\
      \ while the intermediate `redacted_text` contains **zero**\noriginal PII substrings.\n\
      \n- *Expected shape of result:* 100% exact round-trip on reversible spans; a\
      \ report\n  line per case confirming `original_pii not in redacted_text`. Irreversible\n\
      \  spans must **not** round-trip (recovery returns the sentinel, proving the\
      \ vault\n  holds nothing for them).\n\n**C. Tamper-evidence** (`tools/verify_chain.py`\
      \ + `test_audit_chain.py`).\n`verify` on an untouched log returns `(True, None)`.\
      \ Then mutate one historical\nrecord's payload on disk and re-run: it must return\
      \ `(False, k)` pointing at the\nfirst broken link.\n\n| log state | `verify()`\
      \ result |\n| --- | --- |\n| untouched | `(True, None)` |\n| record $k$ edited\
      \ | `(False, k)` |\n| record deleted / reordered | `(False, ·)` at the first\
      \ inconsistency |\n\n- *Expected shape of result:* a table like the above in\
      \ your run output, plus the\n  `test_no_pii_in_log.py` assertion that scanning\
      \ the entire log for known PII\n  patterns finds nothing. That \"no PII anywhere\
      \ in the log, yet full\n  reconstruction is possible\" pairing is the week's\
      \ headline result.\n\n## How to run & test\n\nCPU-only. One hosted LLM key;\
      \ Docker for the service + persistent log.\n\n```bash\n# from within courses/enterprise-ai/week02/\n\
      # Supply runtime configuration; retrieve secrets through wt vault.\nuv sync\
      \                              # or: pip install -e .\n\ndocker compose up --build\
      \            # runs the redaction service + persistent data/ volume\n\n# drive\
      \ some traffic through the endpoint (curl / a small client), then:\nuv run python\
      \ tools/verify_chain.py           # -> (True, None) on an honest log\nuv run\
      \ python tools/reconstruct.py --req 42   # narrative from the LOG ALONE\nuv\
      \ run pytest\n```\n\nWhat the tests assert (mechanism, not just \"it ran\"):\n\
      \n- `test_detect.py`: known emails/phones/IDs are found at the right offsets;\n\
      \  non-PII is left alone; overlap resolution is deterministic.\n- `test_redact_roundtrip.py`:\
      \ reversible spans round-trip exactly; original PII\n  never appears in `redacted_text`;\
      \ irreversible spans do not recover.\n- `test_audit_chain.py`: `append` is the\
      \ only mutator; `verify` passes on an\n  honest chain and localizes a single-record\
      \ edit; deletion/reorder is caught.\n- `test_no_pii_in_log.py`: scanning the\
      \ full serialized log with the detector's\n  own patterns yields zero matches.\n\
      \n## Security practice (non-negotiable this chapter)\n\n- **PII never in the\
      \ clear anywhere durable.** Only the vault holds originals, as\n  ciphertext.\
      \ The log holds tokens, types, and offsets — never values.\n- **Key hygiene.**\
      \ `VAULT_KEY` and `LLM_API_KEY` come from the environment, never\n  hard-coded,\
      \ never logged, never committed. Ship `.env.example` with empty\n  placeholders;\
      \ keep real `.env` git-ignored. Missing key = startup failure.\n- **Redact before\
      \ the boundary.** The LLM client must be structurally incapable\n  of seeing\
      \ pre-redaction text — pass it `RedactionResult.redacted_text` only.\n- **Append-only\
      \ in the type system, not just in spirit.** `AuditLog` exposes no\n  update/delete\
      \ method; deletion of user data (a later week) happens by dropping\n  the *vault*\
      \ entry, which leaves the log's tokens dangling but intact — the\n  record that\
      \ something happened survives, the PII does not.\n- **Detector trust boundary.**\
      \ If you use a *hosted* NER model, note that you're\n  sending raw text to a\
      \ third party to find PII — a real tradeoff to document, or\n  avoid by keeping\
      \ detection local.\n\n## Exercises (optional)\n\n- **External anchoring.** Periodically\
      \ write the chain head $h_n$ to somewhere the\n  service can't rewrite (append\
      \ to a separate signed file, or print it to an\n  operator log) and have `verify`\
      \ cross-check it — closing the \"attacker rewrote\n  the whole file\" gap.\n\
      - **Signed records.** Sign each record's hash with a key the writer process\n\
      \  doesn't hold, so even a full-file rewrite is detectable.\n- **Consistent\
      \ tokens across requests.** Make `<EMAIL_1>` for the same address\n  stable\
      \ across requests (deterministic keyed hash → token) so analytics can join\n\
      \  on identity without ever seeing it.\n- **Right-to-delete dry run.** Given\
      \ a subject, delete their vault entries and\n  show reconstruction now yields\
      \ tokens with `value unavailable (deleted)` while\n  the chain still verifies\
      \ — previewing Week 8.\n\n## References\n\n- NIST SP 800-122 — guidance on protecting\
      \ the confidentiality of PII (read for\n  the definitions and the redaction/de-identification\
      \ framing).\n- Any SHA-256 / hash-chain explainer — for the chaining intuition;\
      \ you only need\n  `hashlib`, not a from-scratch hash.\n- Your chosen crypto\
      \ library's docs (e.g. `cryptography`'s Fernet) — for\n  authenticated symmetric\
      \ encryption in the vault.\n\n## Hardware, cost & subscriptions\n\n- **Hardware:**\
      \ CPU-only. Regex detection is free; a small local NER model (e.g.\n  a spaCy\
      \ pipeline) runs comfortably on a laptop CPU. No GPU helps here.\n- **Cost:**\
      \ a few dollars — one hosted LLM API key for the pipeline's model call,\n  well\
      \ within the course's under-\\$50 budget. Detection can be \\$0 if kept local.\n\
      - **Subscriptions / secrets:** one hosted LLM key (OpenAI/Anthropic/Azure\n\
      \  OpenAI/Bedrock — any). Docker required for the service and its persistent\
      \ log\n  volume. Keep secrets in the OS keyring through `wt vault`; commit configuration\
      \ placeholders only;\n  never commit a real key or the vault key.\n\n### Report\
      \ the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture and configuration\
      \ identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and one observed limitation.\
      \ Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual model, database, inference-server\
      \ or cloud measurements. Cost figures and tool choices in these source-derived\
      \ lab specifications are planning assumptions; verify maintained APIs, record\
      \ actual usage and set a bounded budget when implementing the experiment. Keep\
      \ optional work separate from the baseline report."

  - content: "Trace a ticket routing or document-answer decision through input references,\
      \ retrieved passages, classifier or model version, thresholds, tool outcomes,\
      \ permission checks, and final response. Separate an application event record\
      \ from a model-generated rationale. Avoid treating a reasoning trace as proof\
      \ of internal causation. Explain how the existing text classifier's calibration\
      \ and structured outputs support a reviewable interface.\n\nThe lesson below\
      \ specifies an implementation and experiment to build. Interfaces, stubs, package\
      \ layouts and commands are proposed lab artifacts; they do not indicate that\
      \ executable code or measured results already exist. Use a standalone fixture\
      \ for each lab or combine selected components in the optional course project.\n\
      \n## Scope of the experiment\n\nCapture actual inputs, evidence versions, tool\
      \ requests/results and executed rules. A generated explanation is a model claim,\
      \ not proof of its internal causes. Neither this lab nor its blind reviewer\
      \ requires hidden chain-of-thought. A reviewer should reconstruct what information\
      \ was available and what the application actually did; test claims about influencing\
      \ factors against observable records.\n\n## Overview\n\nExplainability, in practice,\
      \ is a logging and UI design problem at least as much as\na model-choice problem.\
      \ This chapter builds a system that produces a human-readable\ntrace for a consequential\
      \ decision — ticket routing, an approval or denial —\ncovering inputs considered,\
      \ retrieved evidence, reasoning steps, and the final\ndecision, sufficient for\
      \ someone who didn't build the system to review it\nafterward. A reviewer with\
      \ no access to the builder or the code correctly\nreconstructs why a specific\
      \ decision was made using only the trace. Explainability\nbecomes a concrete\
      \ deliverable a non-builder can actually use, not an abstract\nproperty claimed\
      \ of the model.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- **Application basics:** you can already\
      \ build a small agent or retrieval-augmented\n  generation (RAG) pipeline and\
      \ stand up a service in Docker; this chapter wraps a\n  decision-making pipeline\
      \ in a trace layer rather than teaching the pipeline itself.\n- **Conceptually\
      \ useful, not required:** Week 2's append-only audit log (a trace is\n  a richer,\
      \ decision-scoped cousin of that log) and Week 3's permission-aware RAG (a\n\
      \  natural source of the \"retrieved evidence\" a trace surfaces). You do not\
      \ need\n  their code — re-derive what you need.\n- **Comfort with:** dataclasses/`TypedDict`-style\
      \ schemas, JSON serialization, and a\n  minimal web view (Flask/FastAPI + a\
      \ template, or Streamlit). No frontend framework\n  required; the review UI\
      \ is deliberately plain.\n- **A mental split you must already believe:** the\
      \ thing that *makes* a decision and\n  the thing that *explains* it are two\
      \ different concerns. This chapter keeps them\n  separate on purpose.\n\n##\
      \ The core idea: explainability is a capture-and-render problem\n\nA model \"\
      being explainable\" is not a property you can point at. What a reviewer can\n\
      actually use is an **artifact**: a record, produced at decision time, complete\n\
      enough that a stranger reconstructs the *why* without re-running anything and\n\
      without asking you. That reframes the whole week away from model choice and\
      \ toward\ntwo engineering questions:\n\n1. **Capture** — what must be written\
      \ down, at the moment of decision, so the\n   decision is reconstructable later?\
      \ (A logging-schema problem.)\n2. **Render** — how is that record presented\
      \ so a non-builder can follow it in a few\n   minutes, not an afternoon? (A\
      \ UI/information-design problem.)\n\nThe trap is to conflate the two. A raw\
      \ JSON dump is fully faithful and nearly\nuseless to a human; a pretty summary\
      \ is readable and quietly lossy. You will build\n**both representations from\
      \ one source of truth** and keep them in sync: a\nmachine-readable trace (complete,\
      \ replayable, the record of authority) and a\nhuman-readable view rendered *from*\
      \ it (curated, ordered, redacted).\n\n### What a consequential-decision trace\
      \ must capture\n\nThink of a trace as the answer to \"if this decision is challenged\
      \ in three months,\nwhat do we need to have written down?\" At minimum, four\
      \ families of fact:\n\n- **Inputs considered** — the request as received, plus\
      \ any derived features or\n  normalized fields the system actually used. Distinguish\
      \ *what was provided* from\n  *what was used*; a field that arrived but was\
      \ ignored is itself informative.\n- **Retrieved evidence** — every document,\
      \ record, policy, or lookup the system\n  pulled in, with enough identity (source,\
      \ id, version/timestamp, a snippet) that a\n  reviewer could go find the original.\
      \ Evidence that was retrieved but *not* used\n  still belongs in the trace,\
      \ marked as such.\n- **Reasoning steps** — the ordered sequence of intermediate\
      \ steps between input and\n  output: tool calls and their results, an optional\
      \ model-generated explanation, labeled as a claim, rule evaluations,\n  scores,\
      \ and any branch taken. This is the spine of the \"why.\"\n- **Final decision**\
      \ — the outcome, the confidence or score if any, and an explicit\n  link back\
      \ to *which* evidence and *which* steps drove it. A decision that doesn't\n\
      \  cite its own trace is not auditable.\n\nA useful discipline: every claim\
      \ in the final decision should be traceable to a\nnode earlier in the trace.\
      \ If the outcome says \"routed to Tier-2 billing because the\naccount is enterprise-tier\
      \ and the issue mentions an invoice,\" both of those\npremises must appear as\
      \ captured facts, not as prose invented at the end.\n\n### Human-readable vs.\
      \ machine logs\n\n| | Machine trace (log of authority) | Human-readable view\
      \ (rendered) |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Audience | replay, audit tooling, diffing\
      \ | a reviewer who didn't build it |\n| Form | complete structured JSON, append-only\
      \ | ordered narrative + evidence cards |\n| Fidelity | lossless | curated, may\
      \ omit noise, **redacted** |\n| Failure mode | unreadable at a glance | quietly\
      \ loses a detail that mattered |\n| Rule | never edited after write | always\
      \ derived, never authored |\n\nThe machine trace is the source of truth. The\
      \ human view is a **pure function** of\nit. If a reviewer needs a fact that\
      \ isn't derivable from the machine trace, the bug\nis in *capture*, not in rendering\
      \ — and that distinction is exactly what this chapter\ntrains you to see.\n\n\
      ## What you're building & how it's organized\n\nA small decision service that\
      \ (a) makes a consequential decision through a traced\npipeline, (b) writes\
      \ a complete machine trace per decision, and (c) serves a\nhuman-readable, access-controlled\
      \ review UI over those traces. Pick **one** concrete\ndecision and commit to\
      \ it — ticket routing is the recommended default (rich inputs,\nobvious evidence,\
      \ a discrete outcome), with approve/deny (e.g. a refund or access\nrequest)\
      \ as an equally good alternative.\n\nToy-scale everything: a handful of synthetic\
      \ tickets, a small local evidence store,\none hosted LLM call per decision.\
      \ It all runs on a laptop under Docker.\n\n```\nweek05/\n├── README.md\n├──\
      \ pyproject.toml\n├── docker-compose.yml          # decision service + trace\
      \ viewer (2 small services or 1)\n├── Dockerfile\n├── .env.example         \
      \       # LLM_API_KEY=, VIEWER_TOKEN=, REDACTION_SALT= (never commit .env)\n\
      ├── src/\n│   └── trace_week05/\n│       ├── __init__.py\n│       ├── schema.py\
      \            # TraceEvent / DecisionTrace dataclasses + the DecisionRecord protocol\n\
      │       ├── recorder.py          # TraceRecorder: opens a trace, appends events,\
      \ seals it\n│       ├── store.py             # append-only trace persistence\
      \ (JSONL/SQLite) + read-by-id\n│       ├── evidence.py          # tiny retriever\
      \ over a local evidence corpus (stub)\n│       ├── pipeline.py          # the\
      \ traced decision: input -> retrieve -> reason -> decide\n│       ├── redaction.py\
      \         # redact sensitive fields for the human view\n│       └── viewer/\n\
      │           ├── app.py           # access-controlled web UI: list + single-trace\
      \ render\n│           └── render.py        # DecisionTrace -> human-readable\
      \ view model (pure function)\n├── data/\n│   ├── tickets.jsonl            #\
      \ synthetic input decisions\n│   └── evidence/                # synthetic policies\
      \ / KB docs to retrieve\n├── traces/                      # written machine\
      \ traces (git-ignored)\n├── eval/\n│   └── blind_review.md          # the reviewer\
      \ protocol + scoring sheet (you write this)\n└── tests/\n    ├── test_schema.py\n\
      \    ├── test_recorder.py\n    └── test_render.py\n```\n\n### Stub interfaces\n\
      \nSignatures and docstrings only — bodies left as `...`/`# TODO`. Build these;\
      \ do not\nhand yourself a finished implementation.\n\n```python\n# schema.py\n\
      from __future__ import annotations\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass, field\n\
      from datetime import datetime\nfrom enum import Enum\nfrom typing import Any,\
      \ Protocol\n\nclass EventKind(str, Enum):\n    INPUT = \"input\"           \
      \ # a field/feature the decision considered\n    RETRIEVAL = \"retrieval\" \
      \   # an evidence item pulled in\n    REASONING = \"reasoning\"    # a step,\
      \ tool result, or model rationale\n    DECISION = \"decision\"      # the final\
      \ outcome (exactly one per trace)\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass TraceEvent:\n\
      \    \"\"\"One captured fact. Ordered by `seq`. `used` marks whether this fact\
      \ actually\n    influenced the outcome (retrieved-but-unused evidence still\
      \ gets recorded).\"\"\"\n    seq: int\n    kind: EventKind\n    summary: str\
      \                       # one human-readable line\n    payload: dict[str, Any]\
      \            # structured detail (source id, snippet, score, ...)\n    used:\
      \ bool = True\n    sensitive: bool = False            # if True, redact in the\
      \ human view\n    ts: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.utcnow)\n\n\
      @dataclass\nclass DecisionTrace:\n    \"\"\"The machine log of authority for\
      \ one decision. Append-only until sealed.\"\"\"\n    trace_id: str\n    subject:\
      \ str                       # what is being decided (e.g. ticket id)\n    events:\
      \ list[TraceEvent]\n    outcome: str | None = None         # set at seal time\n\
      \    sealed: bool = False\n    # TODO: helper to assert every outcome premise\
      \ references an earlier event\n\nclass DecisionRecord(Protocol):\n    \"\"\"\
      Anything that can explain itself produces a DecisionTrace.\"\"\"\n    def to_trace(self)\
      \ -> DecisionTrace: ...\n```\n\n```python\n# recorder.py\nfrom .schema import\
      \ DecisionTrace, EventKind\nfrom typing import Any\n\nclass TraceRecorder:\n\
      \    \"\"\"Threads through the pipeline; every step logs through it so nothing\
      \ is\n    reconstructed after the fact.\"\"\"\n    def __init__(self, trace_id:\
      \ str, subject: str) -> None: ...\n\n    def record(self, kind: EventKind, summary:\
      \ str, *,\n               payload: dict[str, Any], used: bool = True,\n    \
      \           sensitive: bool = False) -> None:\n        \"\"\"Append one TraceEvent\
      \ with the next seq number. Raise if already sealed.\"\"\"\n        ...\n\n\
      \    def seal(self, outcome: str) -> DecisionTrace:\n        \"\"\"Freeze the\
      \ trace, set the outcome, and return it. No writes after this.\"\"\"\n     \
      \   ...  # TODO: enforce exactly one DECISION event; validate premise linkage\n\
      ```\n\n```python\n# pipeline.py\nfrom .recorder import TraceRecorder\nfrom .schema\
      \ import DecisionTrace\n\ndef decide(ticket: dict, recorder: TraceRecorder)\
      \ -> DecisionTrace:\n    \"\"\"The traced decision. Each stage records as it\
      \ goes — do NOT build the trace\n    at the end from memory.\n\n    1. record\
      \ INPUT events for fields actually considered\n    2. retrieve evidence; record\
      \ a RETRIEVAL event per item (used or not)\n    3. call the LLM / rules; record\
      \ events for observable steps and any separately labeled generated explanation\n\
      \    4. seal with the final outcome, citing the events that drove it\n    \"\
      \"\"\n    ...  # TODO\n```\n\n```python\n# viewer/render.py\nfrom ..schema import\
      \ DecisionTrace\n\ndef to_view_model(trace: DecisionTrace, *, reveal_sensitive:\
      \ bool) -> dict:\n    \"\"\"Pure function: machine trace -> ordered, human-readable\
      \ view model.\n    Groups events, orders reasoning steps, links the decision\
      \ back to its premises,\n    and applies redaction unless the caller is authorized\
      \ to reveal. Must add NO\n    fact not already present in `trace`.\"\"\"\n \
      \   ...  # TODO\n```\n\n```python\n# redaction.py\ndef redact(value: str, *,\
      \ salt: str) -> str:\n    \"\"\"Deterministically mask a sensitive value so\
      \ the same input reads consistently\n    across a trace (e.g. a stable token)\
      \ without exposing the raw value.\"\"\"\n    ...  # TODO: keyed one-way transform;\
      \ never store the reverse mapping in the view\n```"
    lab_and_evidence: "## How to build it — milestones\n\n1. **Schema first.** Nail\
      \ down `TraceEvent`, `DecisionTrace`, and the\n   `DecisionRecord` protocol.\
      \ Decide your invariants now: exactly one `DECISION`\n   event, monotonically\
      \ increasing `seq`, and every outcome premise pointing at an\n   earlier event.\
      \ Write `test_schema.py` against these before any pipeline code.\n2. **Recorder\
      \ + store.** Implement `TraceRecorder` and append-only persistence\n   (JSONL\
      \ is enough; SQLite if you want indexed reads). The store is **write-once**:\n\
      \   sealing writes the trace and nothing edits it afterward — the same append-only\n\
      \   discipline as an audit log.\n3. **Traced pipeline.** Wire the recorder through\
      \ a real (small) decision. Retrieve\n   from `data/evidence/`, call the hosted\
      \ LLM for the routing/approval rationale, and\n   record as you go. Resist the\
      \ urge to summarize after the fact — capture happens\n   *inline* or it's fiction.\n\
      4. **Human-readable render.** Implement `to_view_model` as a pure function of\
      \ the\n   trace: ordered narrative, evidence cards (with source + snippet +\
      \ used/unused),\n   and a decision block that visibly cites its premises. If\
      \ you can't render a \"why\"\n   from the trace, fix capture, not rendering.\n\
      5. **Review UI + access control.** Serve a list view and a single-trace view.\
      \ Put it\n   behind a token/login check (`VIEWER_TOKEN` or a real login if you\
      \ did Week 1), and\n   apply redaction by default — sensitive fields reveal\
      \ only for an authorized role.\n6. **Blind-review dry run.** Hand a trace to\
      \ someone (or a fresh AI session with no\n   code access) and see if they can\
      \ reconstruct the decision. Their confusion is your\n   backlog for capture\
      \ and rendering.\n\n## Checkable artifact — Blind Reviewer Protocol\n\nThe abstract's\
      \ claim is behavioral: *a reviewer with no access to the builder or the\ncode\
      \ correctly reconstructs why a decision was made using only the trace.* So the\n\
      artifact is a **protocol and its scored result**, not a metric your own code\
      \ emits.\nWrite it up in `eval/blind_review.md`.\n\n**Setup.**\n\n- Freeze a\
      \ set of decisions — at least **5**, chosen to span the interesting cases:\n\
      \  a clear approve, a clear deny/route, at least one where the *retrieved-but-unused*\n\
      \  evidence matters, and at least one near-miss the model could plausibly get\
      \ wrong.\n- For each, you (the builder) privately write the **ground-truth \"\
      why\"** in 2–3\n  sentences: the outcome and the specific inputs + evidence\
      \ that drove it. Seal these\n  away from the reviewer.\n\n**Blind review.**\n\
      \n- The reviewer receives **only the rendered human-readable traces** — no code,\
      \ no\n  access to you, no ability to re-run the pipeline. Anyone unfamiliar\
      \ works: a\n  colleague, or a fresh AI chat session given the trace text and\
      \ nothing else.\n- For each decision the reviewer writes, in their own words:\
      \ (a) what the outcome\n  was, (b) the top 1–3 factors that produced it, and\
      \ (c) their confidence.\n\n**Scoring.** For each decision, mark reconstruction\
      \ as one of:\n\n| grade | meaning |\n| --- | --- |\n| ✅ correct | outcome right\
      \ **and** the driving factors match your sealed ground truth |\n| ⚠️ partial\
      \ | outcome right but a key factor missed or a wrong factor invented |\n| ❌\
      \ wrong | outcome misread, or \"why\" unrecoverable from the trace |\n\n**Expected\
      \ shape of the result.** A small table — one row per decision — of\nreviewer\
      \ reconstruction vs. sealed ground truth, plus a one-paragraph reading. A\n\
      passing week is **all decisions ✅**, including the retrieved-but-unused and\
      \ near-miss\ncases; each ⚠️/❌ is a concrete capture or rendering gap you name\
      \ and, ideally, fix.\nThe deliverable that proves the week is this filled-in\
      \ table together with the\nrendered traces it was scored from — evidence a *non-builder*\
      \ could use the traces,\nnot a claim that they could.\n\n> Guard against a false\
      \ pass: if the reviewer reconstructs the \"why\" from their own\n> domain knowledge\
      \ rather than from the trace, it doesn't count. Include at least one\n> decision\
      \ whose correct rationale is *counterintuitive* (the obvious answer is\n> wrong),\
      \ so a right reconstruction can only have come from reading the trace.\n\n##\
      \ How to run & test\n\n```bash\n# from within courses/enterprise-ai/week05/\n\
      # Supply runtime configuration; retrieve secrets through wt vault.\ndocker compose\
      \ up --build            # decision service + trace viewer\n\n# generate traces\
      \ for the frozen decision set\ndocker compose run --rm app python -m trace_week05.pipeline\
      \ --input data/tickets.jsonl\n\n# open the review UI (token-gated) and read\
      \ a trace end to end\n#   http://localhost:8000/traces        (list)\n#   http://localhost:8000/traces/<id>\
      \   (single, redacted unless authorized)\n\nuv run pytest                  \
      \      # or: docker compose run --rm app pytest\n```\n\nWhat the tests assert\
      \ (behavior, not just \"it ran\"):\n\n- `test_schema.py`: a trace enforces exactly\
      \ one `DECISION` event, `seq` is strictly\n  increasing, and sealing rejects\
      \ a decision whose stated premises don't reference\n  earlier events.\n- `test_recorder.py`:\
      \ appends land in order; recording after `seal()` raises; a\n  round-trip through\
      \ the store returns an identical trace (append-only, no mutation).\n- `test_render.py`:\
      \ `to_view_model` is a **pure function** — it introduces no fact\n  absent from\
      \ the trace, preserves reasoning order, links the decision to its\n  premises,\
      \ and redacts every `sensitive=True` event unless `reveal_sensitive` is\n  set.\n\
      \n## Security & privacy notes\n\nTraces are a privacy hazard precisely because\
      \ they're thorough: a good trace records\nthe exact inputs and evidence behind\
      \ a decision, which for real enterprise decisions\nmeans names, account data,\
      \ ticket contents, and internal policy text.\n\n- **Gate the viewer.** The review\
      \ UI reads consequential records — put it behind\n  access control (a `VIEWER_TOKEN`\
      \ at minimum, real SSO/RBAC if you carry Week 1's\n  work forward). Never expose\
      \ an ungated trace endpoint.\n- **Redact by default.** Sensitive fields render\
      \ masked (`redaction.py`) and reveal\n  only for an explicitly authorized role\
      \ — the human *view* is redacted even though\n  the machine trace stays complete\
      \ for authorized audit.\n- **Secrets stay out of the repo and out of traces.**\
      \ Ship `.env.example`, never a\n  real `.env`; the LLM key lives in the environment.\
      \ Scrub the API key and any\n  auth headers from anything the recorder writes\
      \ — a trace must never capture the\n  credential used to make the call.\n- **Treat\
      \ the trace store as append-only.** Sealed traces are evidence; mutating one\n\
      \  after the fact destroys the property the week exists to demonstrate.\n\n\
      ## Hardware, cost & subscriptions\n\n- **Hardware:** CPU-only. The work is trace\
      \ schema, storage, and a small review UI;\n  there is no model training and\
      \ nothing a GPU would help.\n- **Cost:** a few dollars at most — one hosted\
      \ LLM API key (OpenAI / Anthropic /\n  Azure OpenAI / Bedrock) for the decision\
      \ the pipeline traces, well under the\n  course's \\$50 ceiling. The frozen\
      \ decision set is small, so total token spend is\n  negligible.\n- **Subscriptions\
      \ / secrets:** the one LLM API key, plus a viewer token (or a reused\n  SSO\
      \ login) for the review UI. **Docker** required — the decision service and trace\n\
      \  viewer run as containers. Keep the key in `.env` (git-ignored), commit only\n\
      \  `.env.example`, and never let a real secret reach the repo or a trace.\n\n\
      ### Report the actual execution path\n\nRetain the pinned environment, fixture\
      \ and configuration identities, case-level outcomes, reproduction command and\
      \ one observed limitation. Distinguish offline mechanism checks from actual\
      \ model, database, inference-server or cloud measurements. Cost figures and\
      \ tool choices in these source-derived lab specifications are planning assumptions;\
      \ verify maintained APIs, record actual usage and set a bounded budget when\
      \ implementing the experiment. Keep optional work separate from the baseline\
      \ report."
