  - content: "Use the supplied fixture or an optional assistant integrating current-user\
      \ authorization, restricted retrieval, audit records, lifecycle controls, and\
      \ a tested injection defense. Explain alternatives, data flows, measured operating\
      \ limits, failure and recovery behavior, and ownership of remaining decisions.\
      \ Reuse the production course's release and recovery evidence instead of repeating\
      \ its exercises.\n\nThe lesson below specifies an implementation and experiment\
      \ to build. Interfaces, stubs, package layouts and commands are proposed lab\
      \ artifacts; they do not indicate that executable code or measured results already\
      \ exist. Use a standalone fixture for each lab or combine selected components\
      \ in the optional course project.\n\n## Overview\n\nThis document, not the code,\
      \ is usually the actual gate a project has to pass\nbefore it ships in an enterprise.\
      \ This capstone takes one earlier week's system and\nwrites a full design doc\
      \ — problem statement, alternatives considered, chosen\napproach and why, rollout\
      \ plan, risks — as if it needs sign-off from a VP who isn't\nan engineer, paired\
      \ with a one-page ROI summary for a non-technical stakeholder. The\nproof is\
      \ a blind review: a non-engineer reviewer is able to approve or reject the\n\
      doc with specific, addressable feedback rather than confusion. The result is\
      \ the\nartifact that actually gates enterprise AI projects, produced and rehearsed\
      \ once,\nend to end.\n\nThis is the synthesis week for the whole course. Weeks\
      \ 1–8 taught you to build the\nenforcement, compliance, isolation, reliability,\
      \ cost, and lifecycle layers that\nenterprise buyers gate on; Week 9 taught\
      \ you to compare options against a written\nrubric and defend a recommendation.\
      \ Here you do the thing all of that was in service\nof: **get a real project\
      \ approved by someone who will never read your code.** You\nwrite nothing new\
      \ in Python. You write the document that decides whether the code\never ships\
      \ — and then you rehearse saying it out loud in five minutes to a skeptic\n\
      who controls the budget.\n\n## Prerequisites\n\n- **Course-level:** the Enterprise\
      \ AI Engineering prerequisites\n  — you can already build agents/RAG/serving,\
      \ and you're comfortable writing\n  structured prose (a memo, a rubric, a design\
      \ doc). That last one is the actual\n  skill this chapter exercises.\n- **One\
      \ earlier week's system, conceptually, as your subject.** Pick exactly one and\n\
      \  reuse it as the thing being proposed. Good candidates (referenced by title\
      \ only —\n  you do not rebuild them):\n  - **Week 1 — SSO/RBAC-Gated Agent:**\
      \ a clean \"why authorization lives outside the\n    model\" story a VP already\
      \ half-believes.\n  - **Week 3 — Permission-Aware RAG:** a leak-prevention story\
      \ with an obvious\n    business-risk framing.\n  - **Week 6 — SLA-Driven Reliability\
      \ and Rollback:** reliability/uptime maps\n    directly onto revenue and trust.\n\
      \  - **Week 8 — Data Lifecycle and Right-to-Delete:** a recorded retention and\
      \ deletion policy with a declared completion window.\n- **Week 7 — Cost Attribution\
      \ and Chargeback** and **Week 9 — Build-vs-Buy Vendor\n  Evaluation**, conceptually,\
      \ feed this chapter directly. Week 7's dollar-framing is the\n  spine of your\
      \ ROI one-pager; Week 9's rubric scores are the raw material for your\n  \"\
      alternatives considered\" section. If you did them, mine them.\n- **A non-engineer\
      \ reviewer, ideally.** Ask a PM, manager, finance/ops friend, or\n  non-technical\
      \ relative for an asynchronous one-hour review before you start. If no\n  one\
      \ is available within 48 hours, use the fallback below, record that limitation,\n\
      \  and continue rather than blocking the course.\n\n## Core scope, fallback,\
      \ and timebox\n\nBudget 15–20 hours. Slides are optional. One design doc,\n\
      one ROI page, one review round, one revision pass, and one five-minute rehearsal\
      \ are\nthe core.\n\nThe preferred evidence is a blind human review. The momentum\
      \ fallback is to put the\ndraft away for 24 hours, review it cold using the\
      \ same rubric while role-playing the\nnamed stakeholder, and mark the result\
      \ `self-review`. This is weaker evidence, not a\nfailed week. Choose “obtain\
      \ an external review” as the next step and move on.\n\n## Why the document is\
      \ the real gate\n\nEvery other week in this course ended in something a machine\
      \ can check: a denied\ntool call, an audit-log replay, a zero-egress trace,\
      \ a rollback run. This chapter ends\nin something only a *person* can check,\
      \ and that's the point. In an enterprise, the\nsequence that actually ships\
      \ a project is almost never \"the demo worked.\" It's:\n\n1. An engineer proposes\
      \ a thing.\n2. A **design doc** circulates to people who won't read the code\
      \ — a VP, a security\n   lead, a finance partner, a legal reviewer.\n3. Those\
      \ people either approve, reject, or (most often) send it back with questions.\n\
      4. Only after sign-off does the thing get budget, headcount, and a production\
      \ slot.\n\nThe failure mode this chapter inoculates you against is the strong\
      \ engineer whose great\nsystem dies at step 2 because the doc assumed the reader\
      \ already agreed it was worth\ndoing. The doc is where you lose — or win — the\
      \ argument. Treat writing it as\nengineering, not paperwork: it has a spec (the\
      \ reader can decide), an interface (the\ntemplate), and a test (the blind review).\n\
      \nA blunt reframe worth internalizing: **the reader is not evaluating your system.\n\
      They are evaluating whether to spend money and reputation on it, using only\
      \ your\ndocument.** Every section below exists to answer a question that reader\
      \ is actually\nasking.\n\n## Anatomy of a design doc\n\nA design doc is not\
      \ a spec, a README, or a research paper. It is a **decision\nrecord aimed at\
      \ an approver.** Its job is to make one specific person comfortable\nsaying\
      \ yes. The canonical enterprise shape — and the one this chapter requires —\
      \ has\nfive load-bearing sections, each answering a question the VP is really\
      \ asking:\n\n| Section | The question it answers | Failure if you skip it |\n\
      | --- | --- | --- |\n| **Problem statement** | \"Why are we spending anything\
      \ on this?\" | Reader can't tell if the problem is real or worth money. |\n\
      | **Alternatives considered** | \"Did you actually think, or just build your\
      \ favorite?\" | Reader suspects you're an unexamined advocate, not an engineer.\
      \ |\n| **Chosen approach & why** | \"What exactly am I approving, and why this?\"\
      \ | Reader approves a vague thing and feels tricked later. |\n| **Rollout plan**\
      \ | \"How does this reach production without breaking prod?\" | Reader assumes\
      \ the risk lands on them, and says no. |\n| **Risks & mitigations** | \"What\
      \ goes wrong, and have you thought about it?\" | Reader's own risk radar fires;\
      \ unaddressed, it's a veto. |\n\nThe order matters. **Problem first, solution\
      \ last.** A doc that opens with the\narchitecture diagram has already lost the\
      \ reader who hasn't yet agreed there's a\nproblem. Earn the \"yes, that's a\
      \ real problem\" before you spend a word on your clever\nanswer.\n\n### Writing\
      \ for a non-technical VP\n\nThe single hardest muscle this chapter trains: **explaining\
      \ a technical decision to\nsomeone who is smart, busy, skeptical, and non-technical.**\
      \ Concrete rules:\n\n- **Lead with the business consequence, not the mechanism.**\
      \ Not \"we filter\n  retrieval by ACL\"; instead \"an employee can never surface\
      \ a document they aren't\n  cleared to see — even if it's the best answer to\
      \ their question.\" The mechanism is\n  a supporting detail, not the headline.\n\
      - **Every acronym is a tax on the reader.** Define RBAC, RAG, SLA, PII, TTL,\
      \ egress\n  on first use in one plain clause, or don't use them. A VP who has\
      \ to Google your\n  jargon is a VP who stops reading.\n- **Quantify the problem\
      \ in their units.** Dollars, hours, headcount, regulatory\n  fines, customer\
      \ churn, audit findings. \"Slow\" is an engineering word; \"each\n  support\
      \ ticket takes 12 extra minutes across 40 agents\" is a business fact.\n- **Say\
      \ what you're NOT doing.** A scoped \"out of scope: X, Y\" paragraph signals\n\
      \  judgment and prevents the reader from imagining you're boiling the ocean.\n\
      - **One diagram, maximum, and it must be legible to a non-engineer.** A boxes-and-\n\
      \  arrows flow of *who touches what* beats a class diagram every time.\n- **Cut\
      \ every sentence that only an engineer would enjoy.** If it's there to show\
      \ you\n  know a thing rather than to help the reader decide, delete it.\n\n\
      A useful test while drafting: read each paragraph and ask *\"would my reviewer\
      \ act\ndifferently after reading this?\"* If not, it's decoration.\n\n## ROI\
      \ framing: turning a system into a dollar argument\n\nThe one-page ROI summary\
      \ is a *separate* deliverable from the design doc, aimed at\nan even more impatient\
      \ reader (finance, a budget owner). It answers one question:\n**does the money\
      \ make sense?** You did the mechanics of this in spirit in Week 7\n(cost attribution)\
      \ — here you point it forward at a proposed investment instead of\nbackward\
      \ at usage.\n\nKeep the math honest and simple. Two numbers a budget owner actually\
      \ recognizes:\n\n**Net benefit** over a period is the value delivered minus\
      \ the cost to deliver it:\n\n$$\n\\text{Net benefit} = \\underbrace{B}_{\\text{annual\
      \ benefit}} - \\underbrace{C_{\\text{run}}}_{\\text{annual run cost}}\n$$\n\n\
      **Return on investment**, as a percentage, against the one-time build cost:\n\
      \n$$\n\\text{ROI} = \\frac{B - C_{\\text{run}}}{C_{\\text{build}}} \\times 100\\\
      %\n$$\n\n**Payback period** — the single number budget owners fixate on — is\
      \ how long until\ncumulative benefit repays the one-time build cost:\n\n$$\n\
      T_{\\text{payback}} = \\frac{C_{\\text{build}}}{\\,B - C_{\\text{run}}\\,}\n\
      \\quad\\text{(only meaningful when } B > C_{\\text{run}}\\text{)}\n$$\n\nA worked,\
      \ deliberately small example you can adapt (all numbers are illustrative —\n\
      yours must be defensible, not precise):\n\n- Benefit $B$: 40 support agents\
      \ each save ~10 min/day; at a loaded rate of \\$40/hr\n  over ~220 working days,\
      \ that's $40 \\times \\tfrac{10}{60} \\times 40 \\times 220 \\approx \\$58{,}600/\\\
      text{yr}$.\n- Run cost $C_{\\text{run}}$: hosted LLM tokens + a small always-on\
      \ service ≈\n  \\$6,000/yr.\n- Build cost $C_{\\text{build}}$: ~6 engineer-weeks\
      \ ≈ \\$30,000 one-time.\n\nThen $B - C_{\\text{run}} \\approx \\$52{,}600/\\\
      text{yr}$, so\n$T_{\\text{payback}} \\approx 30{,}000 / 52{,}600 \\approx 0.57\\\
      text{ yr}$ (about 7\nmonths), and first-year $\\text{ROI} \\approx 75\\%$. Whether\
      \ those numbers survive\nscrutiny is exactly what your reviewer is there to\
      \ pressure-test.\n\n**Honesty rules that keep the ROI credible:**\n\n- State\
      \ your assumptions *on the page*, not in your head. A reviewer can accept a\n\
      \  stated assumption; they can only reject a hidden one.\n- Give a **range or\
      \ a conservative case**, not a single hero number. \"Payback in\n  7–14 months\
      \ depending on adoption\" reads as honest; a suspiciously precise number\n \
      \ reads as invented.\n- Separate **hard** savings (a license you cancel, a vendor\
      \ you drop) from **soft**\n  savings (time saved that may or may not become\
      \ fewer hires). Label them.\n- Never let the benefit depend on a claim you can't\
      \ defend when the VP asks \"how do\n  you know?\"\n\n## Risk and rollout: the\
      \ two sections engineers skip and VPs read first\n\nAn experienced approver\
      \ reads **risks** and **rollout** before the architecture,\nbecause those two\
      \ sections tell them whether *their* neck is on the line.\n\n**Rollout plan**\
      \ answers \"how does this get to production without a bad day?\" A\ncredible\
      \ one is phased and reversible:\n\n- **Shadow / dry-run** — the system runs\
      \ but its output isn't trusted; you compare\n  it to the current process.\n\
      - **Limited pilot** — one team, one region, or a small % of traffic, with a\
      \ defined\n  success metric and an exit criterion.\n- **General availability**\
      \ — full rollout, only after the pilot's metric is met.\n- **A rollback trigger\
      \ and owner** — the one sentence that most reassures a VP:\n  *\"if metric X\
      \ crosses threshold Y, we revert to the current process within Z, and\n  here's\
      \ who has the button.\"* (If you built Week 6, you already have a playbook to\n\
      \  point at.)\n\n**Risks & mitigations** answers \"what goes wrong, and have\
      \ you thought about it?\"\nList them as a small table — a risk with no mitigation\
      \ is a veto; a risk you named\n*first*, before the reviewer did, is trust earned:\n\
      \n| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\n|\
      \ Model surfaces data a user shouldn't see | Med | High | ACL-filter at retrieval;\
      \ audit log; pilot on non-sensitive corpus first |\n| Cost overruns as usage\
      \ grows | Med | Med | Per-team token budget + alert (Week 7 pattern); monthly\
      \ review |\n| Adoption stalls; benefit never lands | Med | High | Pilot success\
      \ metric gates GA; exit criterion defined up front |\n\nThe move that separates\
      \ a senior doc from a junior one: **name the risk the reviewer\nis about to\
      \ raise, before they raise it.** It converts their objection into your\nforesight.\n\
      \n## The non-technical pitch\n\nThe final artifact is spoken, not written: a\
      \ **five-minute pitch** you can deliver to\na non-engineer, and a set of slides\
      \ (optional) to support it. The pitch is the ROI\none-pager and design doc compressed\
      \ to what a busy executive retains from a hallway\nconversation. A workable\
      \ shape:\n\n1. **The problem, in one sentence, in their units.** (30 sec)\n\
      2. **What we'll do, in one sentence, no jargon.** (30 sec)\n3. **Why this over\
      \ the alternatives — the one comparison that matters.** (60 sec)\n4. **The money\
      \ — payback period and the single number that anchors it.** (60 sec)\n5. **How\
      \ we ship it safely — phased rollout + the rollback sentence.** (60 sec)\n6.\
      \ **The ask — exactly what you want them to approve.** (30 sec)\n\nThe pitch\
      \ is done when you can give it once through, out loud, in under five minutes,\n\
      without reading, and answer three skeptical follow-ups without flinching. \"\
      Rehearse\"\nbelow is the run step for this.\n\n## What you're producing & how\
      \ it's organized\n\nNo `src/`. The deliverables are documents. Keep them in\
      \ one small, self-contained\nfolder so the whole capstone travels as a portfolio\
      \ artifact:\n\n```\nweek10/\n├── README.md                     # this guide\n\
      ├── design-doc.md                 # the full design doc (five load-bearing sections)\n\
      ├── roi-one-pager.md              # the one-page ROI / pitch summary\n├── pitch-notes.md\
      \                # 5-minute spoken outline + likely Q&A\n├── review/\n│   ├──\
      \ rubric.md                 # the blank rubric you hand the reviewer\n│   ├──\
      \ review-round-1.md         # reviewer's filled-in rubric + freeform feedback\n\
      │   └── revision-log.md           # what each piece of feedback changed (or\
      \ why not)\n├── slides/                       # optional; export or a simple\
      \ markdown deck\n│   └── pitch.md\n└── assets/\n    └── flow.png           \
      \       # the single non-engineer-legible diagram\n```\n\nNothing here is generated\
      \ for you — you write each document. The stubs below are\n*templates to fill*,\
      \ the writing equivalent of function signatures with `# TODO`\nbodies.\n\n###\
      \ Template — `design-doc.md`\n\n```markdown\n# Design Doc: <system name> — <one-line\
      \ what it does>\n\n**Author:** <you>   **Reviewers:** <VP, security, finance>\
      \   **Status:** Draft\n**One-line summary:** <plain-language sentence a VP could\
      \ repeat in a meeting>\n\n## 1. Problem statement\n<!-- What's broken/costly\
      \ TODAY, quantified in business units. No solution yet.\n     Who feels the\
      \ pain, how often, what it costs. Earn \"yes, that's real.\" -->\n\n## 2. Alternatives\
      \ considered\n<!-- 2-3 real options incl. \"do nothing\" and \"buy it.\" One\
      \ paragraph each:\n     what it is, why it's plausible, why it loses here. Pull\
      \ from a Wk9-style\n     rubric if you have one. Fairness here is what makes\
      \ your pick credible. -->\n\n## 3. Chosen approach & why\n<!-- Exactly what\
      \ you're proposing, at a level the VP can approve. ONE legible\n     diagram.\
      \ State the key decision and the one reason it beats the runner-up.\n     Explicit\
      \ \"out of scope\" list. -->\n\n## 4. Rollout plan\n<!-- Phased + reversible:\
      \ shadow -> pilot (metric + exit criterion) -> GA.\n     Name the rollback trigger,\
      \ threshold, time-to-revert, and owner. -->\n\n## 5. Risks & mitigations\n<!--\
      \ Table: risk | likelihood | impact | mitigation. Name the reviewer's\n    \
      \ objection before they do. No unmitigated high-impact risks. -->\n\n## Appendix\
      \ (optional)\n<!-- Links to the earlier week's system, deeper technical detail\
      \ the VP can skip. -->\n```\n\n### Template — `roi-one-pager.md`\n\nHard constraint:\
      \ it fits on **one page**. If it doesn't, cut until it does.\n\n```markdown\n\
      # <system name> — Investment Summary (1 page)\n\n**The ask:** <one sentence:\
      \ approve $X / N weeks to do Y>\n\n**Problem (business terms):** <1-2 sentences,\
      \ quantified>\n\n**What we'll do:** <1-2 sentences, no jargon>\n\n**The numbers**\
      \ (state assumptions inline; ranges over false precision):\n| | Value | Assumption\
      \ |\n|---|---|---|\n| Annual benefit (B)        | $<...> | <who saves what,\
      \ how measured> |\n| Annual run cost (C_run)   | $<...> | <tokens + infra> |\n\
      | One-time build (C_build)  | $<...> | <eng-weeks × rate> |\n| **Payback period**\
      \        | <~N months> | B − C_run vs C_build |\n| **First-year ROI**      \
      \  | <~N%>  | (B − C_run) / C_build |\n\n**Why now / why this option:** <one\
      \ sentence>\n\n**How we de-risk it:** <phased rollout + rollback in one sentence>\n\
      ```\n\n### Template — `review/rubric.md`\n\nThis is what you hand the reviewer.\
      \ Keep it in *their* language, not yours.\n\n```markdown\n# Reviewer rubric\
      \ — score each 1 (no) / 2 (unsure) / 3 (yes)\n\nYou do NOT need to be technical.\
      \ Score only whether the DOCUMENT let you decide.\n\n1. Could you tell what\
      \ problem this solves and why it's worth money?      [ ]\n2. Were you convinced\
      \ the chosen approach beats the alternatives?         [ ]\n3. Did the ROI numbers\
      \ make sense, with assumptions you could accept?     [ ]\n4. Did the rollout/rollback\
      \ plan make you comfortable it won't break prod?[ ]\n5. Were the risks the ones\
      \ YOU worried about — and were they addressed?   [ ]\n6. Was there jargon you\
      \ had to skip or Google?  (list it)                  [ ]\n\n**Overall: APPROVE\
      \ / APPROVE-WITH-CHANGES / REJECT**\n**The single thing that most made you hesitate:**\
      \ ____________________\n**One change that would move you toward approve:** ___________________\n\
      ```\n\n## Why this is the capstone\n\nEverything upstream in this course produced\
      \ a machine-checkable proof — a denied\ncall, a replayed audit trail, a zero-egress\
      \ trace, a rollback, a chargeback report.\nThis chapter produces the only proof\
      \ that a *person* signs: a document and a pitch that\nmove a non-engineer from\
      \ \"I don't get it\" to \"approved.\" That is the actual gate an\nenterprise\
      \ AI project passes, and it's the artifact almost no engineer's portfolio\n\
      has. Build one system across ten weeks if you like — but the thing you'll be\
      \ asked to\ndo on the job, over and over, is the thing you did here: **make\
      \ the case, in writing\nand out loud, to someone who will decide with your words\
      \ and never your code.**"

      \ and it's a *useful* fail, the whole point of doing it\nbefore an interview:\
      \ the reviewer gives up, hedges everything to \"unsure,\" or their\nfeedback\
      \ is *\"I don't really understand what this is.\"* That's confusion, not a\n\
